#1
Just a fun idea that popped into mind.

As always, this isn't a full story yet - just a snippet until we see how it goes.

It's also fun for me because it's my first time writing first person in quite some time.

The monsters were nearly on us when the truth finally came out.

"Daniel." My uncle took both of my shoulders in a vice grip and pulled me in closer, a manic frenzy in voice - probably from sheer mortal terror - and looked me dead in the eyes. "Your father is the Greek God Apollo."

I didn't miss a beat.

"Well, I'm screwed."

I could tell that wasn't the reaction he was expecting, but it was either that, or me screaming 'I know, and I'm still screwed!' right in his face loud enough to wake the dead, and at this point that just seemed counter productive.

To be fair, I didn't know about the Apollo bit specifically.

The fact that I was a demigod?

Sure.

A small part of me had figured that out ages ago while the rest of me ignored the possibility with such force of denial that the river in Egypt was probably seething with jealousy.

But that I was a demigod of Apollo, specifically?

Nah.

I'd been too afraid to ask.

See, there's this pretty widespread misconception from my first go-around at life - the idea, nay, the trope, that the average Joe off the street could die, probably instantly and/or traumatically, wake up in a new, fantastical world with equally fantastical dangers and stakes around every corner, and still come out alright.

Sure, there'd be a mandatory period of adjustment. Things wouldn't be too easy - They'd hit a few walls, they'd stumble and they'd fall, probably more than once even, but they wouldn't let that keep them down.

Eventually, in the end, they'd take life by the reigns and rise to the occasion.

That's what you'd do, isn't it?

You'd go in swinging and aiming for the top, overcoming all the challenges in between, even fate itself, right?

Right?

...

The absolute hell you would, you delusional hack.

Life isn't an isekai adventure. If you find yourself in a world where the average supernatural element you're likely to encounter would either want to eat you or could flatten you like a bug on a windshield with contemptuous ease, you don't start messing around and entertaining delusions of grandeur - you keep your head down and you play possum like your life depends on it, because odds are?

It probably does.

That's what I did.

Daniel Winchester.

Thirteen, nearly fourteen.

Lived and has lived with his uncle's family in the little town of Maple, Upstate New York ever since his mom died in a car crash when he was little.

If you look a little closer, the uncle is distant and more than a little cold at times, and the aunt isn't all that much better even if she does try, but their kids are pretty cool, and that's good enough to even out.

All in all, Daniel's pretty normal.

That's me.

That was who and all I was happy being.

And it worked.

I don't know if my sheer desire had something to do with it, or maybe it was just the Mist playing ball, but I made it that long through life unscathed, even as the oddities continued to pile up.

Familiar oddities.

The Dyslexia, the ADHD, the blatantly impossible understanding of written Greek I'd tested out on a suspicious whim, and the occasional things I'd see when I was out and about - people that weren't quite people. Pets with too many teeth - and promptly convince myself were tricks of the light I shouldn't be giving any second thoughts to.

False alarm, nothing to see here, move along please.

Despite it all, I was still ordinary.

Still safe.

But the crappy thing about inordinately good luck?

It always runs out.

I'd had a good run, almost a decade and a half, and it had been good.

Great, even. I wasn't picky.

Until today.

I had been running late after school. I'd signed up for the basketball club this year - and wow, did that make a lot of sense in hindsight - and by the time we were done with practice, it was already getting dark out.

I took a shower, changed into something fresh, horsed around with a few friends for a while before I decided to head home.

Then, I took five steps out of the front gate when I saw them and froze.

Three guys, standing under a street lamp across the street, dressed in dark winter coats and scarves that wrapped around half their lower faces, the upper halves distinct and hazy. Each of them was huge, six foot-something, and with shoulders almost too broad to be physically possible.

Worse, each of them held a leash with a spike-collared dog on the end. They looked like black labrador retrievers at first glance, but when they scented the air and their heads abruptly snapped to me, growls slipping through their muzzles, their forms seemed to flicker and glitch into something distinctly sharper before reimposing themselves.

And their eyes?

Deep, deep crimson - and no way in hell that shade was natural.

I swallowed roughly as the lead scarf-face turned and stared me down, before raising a gloved hand to pull his scarf down, revealing a too-wide mouth pulled into a sinister grin and filled with sharp, crooked yellowing teeth.

The shimmer to his face burst, then, and I saw his eyes-

No.

Cold, existential fear lanced down my spine.

His Eye.

Singular. Just the one.

Too large, inhuman, placed right smack dab in the center of his - its - face.

Cyclops.

Three of them.

No, no, no.

My denial died a violent death right then and there because there was proof.

Vicious, bloodthirsty proof.

The lead cyclops's smile grew that much more unhinged as I trembled.

They had me.

I knew it, they knew it, and their goddamned dogs probably knew it before either of us did.

In the face of that imminent threat, I did the only thing I could.

Namely, I turned tail and took off at a dead sprint faster than anything I'd moved in my entire soon-to-be-over life.

Behind me, I could have sworn I heard a laugh, loud and cruel, but it almost immediately faded, replaced by the whistle of cold air in my ear as I ran so hard my feet went numb.

I didn't stop until I got home, running up the driveway to our two-story house and vaulting clear over the picket fence in one bound the way I'd ordinarily skip a step going up the stairs, before tearing across the garden, not even noticing the trampled flower beds over the thrumming of my heartbeat in my head as I reached the door and threw it open hard enough for it to crack against the back wall.

"What the- Urgh!"

"Monsters!" I gasped as I slammed right into my uncle David, and he went still in my grip as I grabbed onto his shirt with both fists and tried my hardest to freaking breathe. "Monsters!"

"...What?"

He didn't sound confused, or doubtful.

Instead, he sounded deathly afraid, and that was somehow worse.

His eyes had gone glassy and distant behind the rim of his square glasses - Like he was seeing something that wasn't there, or maybe even remembering it instead.

"Cyclopes." I managed to say, and swallowing to wet my sand-paper dry throat felt like I was trying to force a brick down an already clogged pipe. "There are cyclopes coming after me."

I wasn't worried about him not believing me - his voice alone was proof enough that he'd known something like this was possible, which would have raised so many more questions about how's and why's if I wasn't so damn scared right then.

Sure enough, as soon as the last word was out of my mouth, he staggered back like I'd socked him in the gut.

"Oh god... Sarah." He whispered before he abruptly spun around and roared down the hallway. "Sarah!"

"What!?" My Aunt yelped and came running our way "David, what-?"

He pointed at me.

"Monsters. They've come for him."

She blanched in horror.

"Oh god." Her breathing went from lukewarm to hysterical gasping in no time flat. "Oh god, oh god, oh god-"

My uncle took two steps and grabbed her by the arm, giving her a good sharp jolt that had her mouth clamping shut despite the wild look in her eyes.

"Grab the girls, and get our go-bags." He gave her another jerk for good measure. "Now!"

"Go-bags?" I stared at him incredulously as she took off, the saxophone of fight-or-flight instincts finally smothered long enough for me to think properly. "You have go-bags?"

I know, my priorities are shit, but something about the way he said that just about forced me to do a spit-take - the way my straight-laced, no-nonsense uncle just spat out a line that sounded like something out of a cheesy action flick with a straight face didn't quite compute.

Or it might just been my own hysteria setting in.

Dealer's choice.

Either way, he didn't answer me.

Instead, he took off down the same hallway and took a sharp left, disappearing out of my sight. I didn't pay attention, too busy staring out of the window and expecting the Cyclops from before to leer in at me from the dark at any moment, but I could hear his frantic footsteps going up the stairs, and then the sharp sound of hinges and a descending ladder from the attic.

When something up above crashed against the floorboards it felt like my heart was about to claw its way out of my ribcage, and I could hear aunt Susan screaming in fright in the other room, but the thump of my uncle going down the stairs kicked right back up again, and not a blink later he was coming back around the corner and running right at me, something held in each arm.

"These are for you."

The longbow didn't look like anything special, at first glance.

Well crafted, sure, and the golden brown was a pleasant shade, but it wasn't anything you'd stop to gawk at.

Somehow, though, the moment my uncle pressed it into my hand and my fingers closed around the leather grip, the feel of it still hit like a religious experience.

Which, again, made a lot of sense in hindsight.

My eyes widened and I exhaled as warmth seemed to radiate from it, leeching up my arm and all the way up my spine, pushing away the terrible fear from before and replacing it with utter wonder. I twitched and raised it, and it felt perfect, its weight both feather-light and perfectly proportioned even though it shouldn't have possibly been quite so easy to move.

I almost didn't notice it when my uncle moved my free arm to sling the accompanying quiver loaded with arrows over my right shoulder before he grabbed both and finally jolted me out of my trance with real, harried force.

"Daniel, your father is the Greek God Apollo."

"Well, I'm screwed."

"..."

There. He said his thing, I said mine - All caught up.

And not a moment too soon.

I didn't have time to react to the way the name seemed to thrum in the air, a weight to it that shouldn't have come from a mere word, because some lizard-brained instinct screamed bloody murder at me out of nowhere and I was suddenly throwing myself at my uncle and tackling him down right as the wall behind us exploded.

I mean that - it sounds pretty straightforward when you put it like that, but I don't think any number of words could actually give you a good picture of what it was like when the solid wall was forcibly retired from being a wall and instead became a wave of spraying wood, plaster, glass and all kinds of pulverised projectile debris that shot off everywhere with a roar like an avalanche as something massive was driven through it.

For about a solid five seconds, I thought we were goners.

Then the sound of stuff breaking and the instant of stunned silence that followed it took a back burner as my aunt' renewed screaming won out over it, this time with both my little cousins adding to the chorus, and I realized that we were still alive and still very much in deep shit.

I shot up to my feet, debris and bits of just about everything pouring off me as I staggered back and pulled my uncle to his feet.

Credit where credit was due, he immediately took off again and nearly left me in his sawdust as he clambered across the ruined hallway.

"Sarah!"

The good news was that my aunt was alive and unhurt. My cousin's room was fine, garish pink wallpaper and all - they hadn't been hit.

The bad news was that she looked like she was a step away from going into catatonic shock, four bags slung over one shoulder, little Alex shivering in her grip with her head tucked into the crook of her neck.

Katie, on the other hand, was standing right beside her when we came into the room, and she took one look at her dad and me and burst into big, ugly sobs before she took off like a missile and leaped into his shaking grip.

"David?"

The three of them trembled in terror as they stared at my uncle, who looked like his entire life was both metaphorically and very literally falling apart, and...

The pieces of some puzzle I hadn't even known I was playing at clicked into place with awful clarity.

We were all going to end up dead if we didn't-

No.

I'm the demigod here.

We were all going to die if I didn't do anything.

But I could do something.

Better yet, I knew what to do.

"You guys need to run."

The bow in my hand seemed to pulse with another burst of warmth as they rounded on me in disbelief, almost like it was encouraging me to keep talking.

I decided to oblige it.

"You need to run now," I repeated, feeling strangely, absurdly calm despite the stares and the insanity of the situation. "They only want me. I can keep them busy, but you guys need to leave right now."

I didn't even understand where the words and the sheer resolve were coming from, but it was another thing I couldn't afford to question right this second.

My uncle looked like he was losing his mind.

"Daniel-"

"It's not up for debate!" I snapped, and then hissed sharply as I heard it - a series of low, sharp growls and heavy thudding - footfalls - echoing out there in the dark.

From the way they paled, everybody else heard them just fine.

"Time to move. Now."

I didn't wait for them to answer before I turned around and slipped back out of the room, reaching over my shoulder to draw an arrow before nocking it into my bow in a single fluid movement.

I'd never so much as held either a bow or an arrow in my life, but the act was still somehow easy, as natural as breathing.

Son of Apollo, huh?

It made me feel strong and capable in a way I almost certainly wasn't.

Not in this - but the feeling was all I had, so I clung to it like a lifeline as we crept back the way we came.

Behind me, Aunt Sarah choked.

"Is that our car?"

I blinked in realization and stared, because... yeah.

It totally was.

The family's Dodge Caravan was stuck halfway into our destroyed living room, trunk first, with its windows and tail lights shattered and its tires flattened into an unrecoverable mess. Parts of the roof had collapsed and pinned it in place, and the rest of the ceiling was creaking and tilting dangerously.

I'm no real-estate prospector or anything, but I'd bet you pennies on the dollar that everything from the car to a good chunk of the house was a total right-off.

"Well, look on the bright side." I managed to crack a grin with confidence I didn't feel and a voice that was the fakest thing I'd ever managed in my life. "You guys always wanted to rework the living room, and now...well..."

I kicked a little pile of dust away.

"You kinda have to. And hey, a new minivan wouldn't hurt."

Uncle David's eyes were going all glassy again.

"You're not funny, you little sh- punk."

Almost swearing in front of the girls?

Yep, forget maybe - that hysteria thing was definitely in the bag now.

"I'm hilarious."

Another set of growls killed the next words on the tip of my tongue like they had a personal grudge against them, and my grip on the bow tightened until it hurt. Out of the corner of my vision, through a gap in the ruined wall, I thought I saw something flicker past, and the adrenaline in my veins shot right back up through the stratosphere.

The cold breeze sweeping into the room was suddenly arctic, even if the warmth of the bow in my had seemed to offset it.

"Go." I took a deep breath and another step forwards. "Through the back door and out into the woods."

Aunt Sarah looked sick.

"We can't leave you."

Oh, for the love of-!

"You're not leaving me." It was a struggle to keep my breathing even, my attention caught between them and the sounds outside the house. Why hadn't they attacked yet? "You're protecting Katie and Alex."

That got her, I could tell from her eyes. In her grip, Alex shifted, finally raising her head and giving me a confused look, like she didn't understand what was happening.

Katie didn't understand everything either, but she understood enough - kids had sharper instincts than people gave them credit for - that I could see her tearing up again and reaching for me with both hands.

The relief I felt when my uncle held her back was indescribable.

I did not need a hug from my cute baby cousin right now, because then I'd probably start crying too, and going off to certain death with tears in my eyes like some kind of crybaby would just be embarrassing for everybody involved.

If I was dying, I could at least pretend to be a badass about it.

"Daniel-"

"I'll be right behind you, Uncle Dave." I gave the quietly distraught man another smile with just about all the strength and composure I had left to offer. "I just have to take care of this first."

Liar, he probably wanted to say, but in the end he could only nod.

"Be safe." He hesitated. "Your mother would be proud of you."

The last I saw of my family was my uncle herding them off through the back in a run, leaving me gaping after them - and him - like an absolute idiot.

"That was..." I swallowed and strangled the feelings welling up inside me with ease of practice. "You absolute dick."

My eyes didn't sting as I turned around - they didn't.

"What kind of stereotypical cliché bullshit was that? Gross."

I turned around and was out into the night in less than ten steps.

The cyclopes were waiting for me in the driveway.

"Finally!"

The leader of the stood at the helm, the one who'd flashed his teeth at me - only, he was worse now.

A lot worse.

Eight tall instead of six, just like his friends, and his upper clothes had melted away leaving only rusty bronze bracers on either arm and orange-tinted skin that stretched over an enormously muscled frame that would have had professional bodybuilders either weeping with envy or recoiling in horror. His biceps alone were probably the size of my head, and his head was bald and a little too long to look quite human, that one single eye glaring horrible over the crooked maw beneath it.

The other two had stripped down as well, so I suppose the autumn chill didn't mean all that much to them, and one of them had an enormous, misshapen wooden club that was stained with something I desperately tried not to think about.

The dogs the group had brought with them weren't leashed anymore either - instead, two of them had almost tripled in size, their features growing sharper and more savage, their muzzles barred and slobbering as their own red eyes zeroed in on me just the same as their masters.

Hellhounds, or something. I didn't know enough to tell.

The third one, though...

It didn't change size. It didn't shift - it just stood there, a little labrador with its hackles lowered, ears drooping, looking vaguely miserable even as the lead cyclops took a step forward and forced me to turn my attention away from it to him.

"Demigod!" His voice boomed, joyous and nasty all at once. "There you are!"

Another thrum of warmth from the bow had me raising an eyebrow, trying to look indifferent.

"Do I know you?"

He actually frowned

"No-"

"STRANGER DANGER!" I roared and loosed the arrow I'd been pulling back on with all my strength, and it sailed through the air with perfect, supernatural accuracy, a bronze-tipped shot fuelled by the ghost of a chance and sheer audacity.

The cyclops's eye barely had time to widen before the arrow struck it and went right through, the arrowhead piercing out the back of his skull with a sound I'd never forget ever.

For a moment, even the air seemed to hold its breath. The cyclops's mouth twitched and opened, almost in disbelief, and then he swayed, once, twice, before promptly exploding into a cloud of raining golden dust that was quickly cast into the night breeze and dissipated into nothingness.

Only my arrow was left, falling down into the asphalt with a faint, almost anticlimactic clatter.

".."

"..."

"..."

The other two cyclopes looked at the spot where their boss had just been standing, before exchanging a look and turning over to me. Even the dogs seemed to have their jaws hanging wide open.

You could almost hear disbelieving crickets chirping in the background.

"...Holy shit, that actually worked?" I muttered, just as stunned as them even as I drew another arrow and quickly nocked it "Like, seriously, how the hell did that even work?"

Then I quickly readjusted my aim and prepared to fire again-

"!"

-before cursing viciously and leaping over the porch and to my left as the first of the hellhounds went from standing to attention to murder mode in the blink of an eye, a rabid growl tearing out of its throat as it charged up the path between us and leaped for mine. It slammed into the debris behind me with another thunderous crash that signaled the start of the carnage in earnest.

It felt like the neurons in my brain were firing off a mile a minute as I landed on the balls of my feet, eyes and ears screaming warnings as I tried to keep every threat in sight.

The cyclopes were slow-moving, but bad doggie the second was already closing in on me even as the first poked its snout out of the house and let out a baleful noise like a chainsaw cleaving through rock.

Seems that it was pissed.

Joy

Two hellhounds coming at me, one arrow, and not a chance in hell of nocking a second after taking the first shot without ending up with a face full of teeth.

No time to think, no missteps.

Only non-stop movement.

So I pulled what was, at first glance, the most insanely suicidal stunt I could have under the present circumstances, following instincts I'd never exercised a day in my life.

Instead of running away from the charging hellhound, I charged towards it.

The hellhound obviously didn't see that one coming, because its jaws snapped halfway shut and it almost seemed like it was about to try backing up out of its run to figure out what kind of stupid it was dealing with here - or maybe that was just me - but I didn't give it the chance to do a thing.

I made it five feet away from it before I leaped, planting my foot straight down on its forehead before shooting off of it and launching myself even higher up into the air.

For the second time that night, it was as if everything paused - and there I was.

Flying through the air, upper body twisting to one side in the same motion, locking my sights on the second hellhound just now clawing its way out of the house and almost enjoying the absolute sentient incredulity in the way it balked as I took aim and fired.

One second my arrow was shooting through the intervening space between us, and the next it was buried right up to the fletching in the wanna-be Cujo's skull.

It didn't even get to whimper before it, too, was bursting into golden dust.

Watching that happen in what felt like slow motion was... an indescribable sensation. The victory was almost heady, and coupled with the instant relief and the idea that, hey, I might actually not die here...

For a second, I felt like a hero - invincible.

And then the cyclops with the club swung it and caught me right in the chest, and that feeling, plus all the air in my lungs and what felt like a good number of my ribs all collectively called it quits.

The blow knocked me right out of the air and I the ground hard, gasping and nearly swallowing a mouthful of displaced dirt, but I didn't have the luxury of a moment to get my breath.

Move or die.

I managed to scramble onto my feet and take off into the beginning of a run just as the hellhound whose skull I'd used as a springboard darted past, its growl filled with hate.

Before, I was just a convenient chew toy, but now?

Now it was personal.

I tried to move off to the side again, nocking another arrow, but the other cyclops was right there and nearly took my head off with a backhanded swing of his fist that I dodged by the skin of my teeth. My ribs cried foul at all the rapid movement, but the pain seemed so distant I barely felt it.

"Hold still!"

I took several steps back, but both cyclopes were closing in on my right and left respectively, while the hellhound remained directly in my line of sight, prowling forward with a promise filled with deadly malice.

I couldn't even turn back and take off into a run across the woods behind - I knew with almost iron-clad certainty that the hellhound would run me down in a straight race if I tried, and then I'd be toast.

I exhaled, fingers white against the fletching of my third arrow, frame wired with enough tension to grind diamonds into dust and ready to bolt anyway at a split-second's notice.

"I don't suppose we could talk about this, fellas?"

I tried for a smile, but it fell flat. Sweat ran down my brow and stung my eyes, and my heartbeat was back to ringing in my ears again.

The cyclops with the club grunted at me.

"You killed my brother."

... That was...

"Sorry?"

"I hated him." The cyclops actually shrugged, which made me blink before his one eye narrowed pointedly. "But I'm still going to eat you."

Worth a shot.

"You shouldn't do that. I taste awful."

The other cyclops seemed to pause.

"Really?"

"Downright terrible," I said with a completely straight face while cursing out to every god and goddess and everything in between that I could think of at the moment for this utter crap. "Have you seen me? I'm only thirteen. A shrimp. Not even ripe by demigod standards."

"Oh."

He seemed disappointed, and I blinked again.

Was this seriously-?

The other cyclops scowled at his friend.

"He's lying."

Damn it.

"Oh!" The gullible cyclops perked up, taking another step toward me, before he suddenly reared back. "Eh?"

He'd nearly stepped over the third hellhound - the one that still hadn't made a move and instead seemed to have hunched down and focused on making itself as small as possible.

"Oi. Why aren't you helping?" The little dog whimpered, eyes flickering all over the place, and the cyclops's frown twisted into something ugly. "Stupid mutt."

He gave it a sharp kick that sent it tumbling away and had me backing up several paces in case it got too close.

"You really shouldn't be calling anyone stupid, buddy." I couldn't help but blurt it out - I blame my terrible survival instincts going haywire for it. "That dog probably has more braincells than you do eyes."

The cyclops stared at me funny.

"I only have one eye."

"...Exactly."

Honestly, I doubt he actually understood the insult, but he must have eventually figured out that it was one because his face screwed up in rage and he took a heavy step froward.

The other hellhound growled at me and picked up the pace of its prowling in return, and I felt real fear closing in again as they did, and I barely noticed the runt of the pair taking it's chance and bolting off away from all of us, to busy trying and failing to find a way to do anything to save myself.

But I had nothing.

There was no way I was coming out of this alive, not at this range.

I'd need a damned miracle to even-

...

...

There's an idea.

Hope was a killer, but it was better than death by hellhound, so I desperately tried to clear my mind and play the only card I might have left to play.

Apollo?

Greek Gods in this world paid attention to their kids entirely depending on their whims, but maybe, just maybe-

Dad?

Nothing.

Look, I know you're probably really busy doing all kinds of super important sun god stuff, but if you could help me out here, that'd be awesome.

Still nothing.

I swallowed again, trying very hard not to let my fear consume me as the monsters got even close.

Dad, I'm only thirteen. I don't want to die yet.

I closed my eyes, just for a second.

Please.

"Alright." The cyclops with the club grunted again. "Time for dinner."

The hellhound snarled its agreement, and all of them made to move-

Suddenly it hit me - a flash of inspiration, somewhere in between a gut instinct and a literal premonition that slipped into my head out of nowhere, along with a feeling of reassurance that had me nearly going weak at the knees - And I knew what to do.

"WAIT!" I yelled, and they paused. Then they stared as I let the arrow I'd nocked slip from my fingers and hit the ground at my feet. "I give up!"

"..."

The cyclops with the club slowly lowered it, eye twitching for some unknowable reason.

"...Really?

"Well-"

My hand shot up, far faster than it had before, and pulled an arrow from my quiver that hadn't been there before.

It glinted a shade of brilliant gold that seemed to light up the night as I nocked and aimed with a furious glare of my own this time around.

"-no."

I let it rip just as the hellhound leaped, and threw myself off to the side - but I wasn't fast enough.

The golden arrow flew-

Fire lanced across my chest as a clawed paw tore across it, the pain instant and blinding, and instead of my feet, I hit the ground on my side, blood quickly spreading through the shredded remains of my shirt.

But I still grinned savagely, because I'd already won.

- before hitting home and sinking into just the right spot in the asphalt between the cyclopes

The unholy, cataclysmic eruption of noise that followed seemed to split the world in half. Impossibly loud and off-pitch and wrong in all the worst ways, and attack that shook and wrecked the ground around us as echoed right down to my bones - but it didn't actually hurt me.

Not even a little.

The cyclopes, on the other, suffered and wailed silently as the noise quite literally ripped them apart, their forms buckling and twisting this way and that before they were reduced to golden dust and banished away, not with a bang, and not even with a whimper that anyone would have cared to hear.

Good freaking riddance.

The murderous hellhound lasted just a second longer - Long enough for me to get my head off the ground and stare it dead in the eyes as it staggered in pained terror before I gave it another grin, this one as nasty as it was victorious, and flipped it off.

"Bad doggie."

And just as soon as I'd finished mouthing the last word, it popped like a balloon full of dust, and the world abruptly went silent.

...

"...Huh. Is it really over?"

At least, that's what I tried to say.

Instead, it came out as a garbled, wordless mess around the same time as I registered the taste of iron in my mouth.

Blood. Lots of it.

That's when the pain hit, and my head was on the ground again as everything seemed to go cold and hot all at once, and I lost nearly all strength in my limbs.

Wow.

I'd felt it when it happened, but that hellhound really messed me up, didn't it?

The realization only made the pain get worse, and my lungs rattled in my chest in a way that was all wrong even as I tried to swallow down the blood in my mouth uselessly.

I couldn't move to see the wound, but I knew that it was horrific

I'm actually dying, aren't I?

Then things started going numb, and a part of me began to really panic.

Uh, dad?

Wasn't Apollo the god of healing?

It might be ungrateful to ask for more, since you just saved my bacon and all, but...

I couldn't even finish the prayer.

My vision was starting to go black around the edges. The contrast made the stars up above in the sky seemed that much brighter.

Help

Everything was growing distant. I couldn't move at all anymore

Somebody.

I was drifting away, feeling as heavy as an anvil.

Please.

Abruptly, the agony in my gut changed.

It didn't grow any less horrible, but the quality of it shifted. It went from a burning to a tugging, like something inside of me was bieng torn out by an inexorable force.

I would have screamed, but I didn't have the strength and that would have just ended up with me gargling my own blood like a total loser.

The parts of the world I could see seemed to glitch, the way the monsters had earlier before it unraveled, and...

L̵͚͑͆i̶̗͒̊g̵̠͖͆h̸̡̖̀̆t̷͚̗̓͑s̵̜̰͠​


For a beat, space itself seemed to melt into some kind of collapsing vortex of multi-fractal lights, filled with things I didn't have the presence of mind to even register.

Pretty, I thought, utterly delirious.

And then those lights went supernova, scorching and all-consuming, and I was suddenly weightless and tumbling into nothingness like a feather in the wind, and the last thing I heard was something that sounded strangely like a canine whimper of fear.

What was that about?

And then-

...

The lights went out.​

...

#61
Going as far back as I can remember, I was always an early riser - and by early riser, I mean that sometimes it took effort for me not to be up at the crack of dawn every morning.

Unless I'd had a hell of day or night before, the moment the first rays of sunlight streaked through my bedroom window, my eyes would be blinking open, no alarm clock or wake-up call needed.

Knowing what I do now, I honestly couldn't tell you if it was a general demigod thing, a son of Apollo thing, or just a me thing, but it was usually pretty convenient - and ordinarily gradual.

It still took a little time -maybe a minute or two- for my brain to properly kick itself into gear, and during said time I tended to enjoy that slow, fuzzy feeling everybody gets in the morning when they're still half-asleep and stretching in bed like spoiled cats.

The warm sunlight tickling my face just made it better.

When I woke up this time, though, there was no such feeling.

One second, I was totally dead to the world.

The next, I was suddenly wide awake and gasping, eyes flying open as the phantom images of fracturing lights and stuff so weird I could barely understand or even remember it for the life of me slipped away like grains of sand between my fingers, replaced by another frantic, incredulous thought going off in my head like an old-school air-raid siren at full volume.

Jesus christ, did I just die!?

... Even thinking that was probably technically blasphemous on multiple levels given all the context surrounding my life, but right then I wasn't so much thinking as I was moving on survival-driven auto-pilot and disorientation as I leaped to my feet and quickly pressed both hands against my chest, the memory of the fiery pain and the numbness that followed still fresh in my mind.

I could almost still taste the overpowering tang of iron in my mouth.

But I felt nothing.

My zip-up hoodie and the shirt beneath it weren't the shredded, bloody messes I was expecting - both were untorn, practically spotless.

Confused and panicking, I lifted my shirt right then and there, uncaring of who might see - I wasn't even registering my surroundings yet - and abruptly found myself tracing smooth, unblemished skin.

Not so much as a scratch on it - on me.

What?

Slowly, the instinctive panic began to subside, but the confusion seemed to readily bubble up to take its place.

So...

Observation - I wasn't dead.

Conclusion - Nice. No complaints there - I happened to be very fond of living.

Question - How in the hell though?

I'd felt a good chunk of my insides get turned into minced meat - and wow had that sucked - but now...

"..."

It was at that point that I'd finally straightened myself out enough to finally look up and realize something important.

I have no idea where I am.

Standing in front of a bench I must've been passed out on, in the middle of a park or some other generic outdoorsy garden I didn't recognize at all, a few rows of trees and stretches of flower beds and artistically maintained bushes growing out in front past a winding walkway of paved white stone that swept out in either direction before curving around the greenery to lead who knows where with no one around and the only light coming from the sunrise peaking over the treetops in the distance.

There was even a nice, cool breeze brushing against my skin and ruffling my hair.

"Where...?"

I turned right around and blinked.

My bow and quiver were propped up against the bench behind me, looking as pristine and untouched as I did, somehow.

Besides them was a small, black backpack that wasn't mine, but there wasn't anyone around it could have belonged to.

I even turned about to look, just to make sure.

And then I heard the bark.

The familiar bark.

And I moved.

Clearly, I was already getting better at this demigod thing fast, because my mind cleared. My bow was in my hand with an arrow nocked in less time than it took me to breathe, the tip aimed dead center at the patch of shadows beneath the nearest tree some twelve feet away from me and ready to go at a twitch.

I'd have done it too, but the next thing I knew, the shadows began to ripple and sway before suddenly ballooning up and spitting out the same little Labrador-looking hellhound from before, inky black fur and red eyes sticking out sharply against the muted colors of the bark and the grass beneath it.

It rose out of it's crouch after a second of shaking it's head in disorientation, before it padded out from under the tree cover, spotted me and my primed arrow, and froze.

"Seriously?" I snapped with real heat in my voice. It whimpered and dropped its head so low its snout was practically buried in the dirt, which made me hesitate a second. "How- No, why are you still here?"

I wasn't scared of it.

The thing was the least threatening of its friends, downright wimpy even, but that didn't mean I wasn't angry.

Hadn't I already hit the mandatory quota for my first demigod monster encounter?

Sure, I'd only made it out near the end because of literal divine intervention, but it still counted! Three cyclopes and two hellhounds was at least equal to a minotaur, and I'd fight anyone who said otherwise.

The hellhound seemed to quail even more under my glare.

I didn't have time for this - I had to figure out where I was and how to get back home, and I needed to make sure the others were fine and that things hadn't been too rough on their end.

I may have dealt with all the monsters except for this one, but running through the woods at night in the middle of December the way they'd been forced to wasn't exactly safe to begin with.

I should have just shot it and gotten it all over with already. How it survived the sonic arrow Apollo had blessed me with was anyone's guess, but it didn't seem particularly menacing as it tried to make itself look smaller and smaller, and it couldn't get away when I had it pinned at point-blank range.

...

But...

As the seconds ticked by and neither of us moved, I found myself wavering.

I wasn't having a good day, but I wasn't blind.

The little hellhound hadn't hurt me at all - Even when its buddies tried to have me for dinner, and one of them nearly succeeded, it looked like it was having about as much fun as I was.

It hadn't even attacked when I was out cold and easy pickings for it with how close it probably had been, and the longer I stared at it, the harder it was to see it as some mythical monster out to get me when I wasn't looking.

It just looked like a scared dog.

I hesitated.

What kind of evil jerk shoots a dog?

It gave another little whimper as my aim wavered, just a little, and I grit my teeth in uncertainty.

What now?

...

Damn it.

Ever so slowly, and ignoring the part of me that was cursing out my bleeding heart like a professional sailor, I lowered my bow and removed the arrow.

The dog perked up, obviously astonished, and I was almost tempted to smile at how dopey it looked.

"Go."

It stared.

I could almost hear it going 'Dude, for real?'

"Go. Shoo, shoo." I even gestured slowly to put it at ease, and it seemed to work. "Beat it, and don't come back."

I had bigger things to worry about.

But the dog didn't leave.

Instead, it began to trot up to me.

My bow hand twitched when it did, and it slowed down a little, but when I didn't do more than stare at it warily, it picked up the pace and came right up to me.

Then it barked and began to wag its tail happily.

"You..." I blinked. "Sit."

It sat, though its wagging didn't slow down a bit.

"...huh."

I'm not going to lie and pretend I held out longer than I did - I folded like wet tissue paper and loaded my arrow back in my quiver, got down on one knee, and started petting it - him, I guess - like I would any other dog.

What?

I like dogs, sue me.

A close call at death-by-hellhound wasn't going to change that.

Granted this one was far from ordinary himself, but he lapped the affection right up, wiggling in place and panting excitedly as I ran my free hand through his soft fur.

You'd think he'd be a little more reserved with me after everything, but I guess his previous owners really sucked all around on his end too, so I must have ended up doing him a favor after all.

"...You're not half bad, I guess." I begrudgingly admitted, before I tried to give him another hard look even though my heart wasn't in it anymore. "But if you have a change of heart and try to eat me after this, I'm going to be so damn mad."

All I got for my attempt at a warning was an unexpected attack of slobber as he started enthusiastically trying to lick me and almost bowled me over.

"Oh, dude, gross! Quit it!"

I didn't even realize I was laughing until I stood up after giving him another ruffle and remembering my priorities, and that quickly sobered me up.

Still, I felt lighter than before.

More focused too.

"I need to go now." His tail stopped wagging and his excitement turned into mournful despair so quickly it had me wincing from the whiplash. The sad sigh just made it worse. "Don't give me that. I need to start figuring things out and you need to..."

I had no idea, actually.

"... go home, or something?"

I swear he was questioning my intelligence with the look he gave me.

"Well, good luck."

I even gave him a little nod, before turning around and walking back to the bench. The backpack was still there, and I wasn't a thief or anything, but extraordinary circumstances and all that, and I needed a clue to get started.

I frowned when I picked it up - Empty, or close to it.

I unzipped it and rummaged through the pockets, but the only thing I managed to come up with was a wad of bills folded inside the mesh pocket - and if that was the kind of thing I was looking for, I might've considered the find a score.

Only, they weren't dollars.

"Are these euros?"

They were.

Crisp, clean, six-hundred all in all. A hefty sum in a currency that was useless to me.

Okay, fine.

It might've been a coincidence or something - the bag probably belonged to a tourist or something, and they'd just forgotten it here.

Wherever here was.

Not a big deal.

I tried to dismiss the bad feeling beginning to build up in my gut as I shoved the money back into the bag and zipped it back up.

"Alright." I glanced to the right and eyed the pathway stretching out in front of me, before nodding to myself. I'd just have to put in a little effort, that's all. "The hard way then."

A bark interrupted me before I could take the first step, though, and I found the dog staring up at me resolutely.

"What?"

A pointed bark.

My eyes narrowed as I understood what he was getting at.

"You are not coming with me."

More insistent barking was my answer even as I shook my head.

"Are you kidding me? No."

I could just tell that was what he wanted, and the answer was laughingly obviously.

A little petting was one thing, but anything more than that was a whole other bucket of nope.

"Absolutely not."

There was no way.

None at all.

And that was final.

...​

Ten minutes later and he was still keeping pace with me happily even as I shot him the occasional dirty glare.

...​

Five minutes after that, I figured out where we were.

Athens.

As in Athens, Greece.

...

Oh, I'm sorry, was that too abrupt?

I'd have eased you into it better, except there's really no way to describe the sheer lunacy I felt as we walked until we passed through a conveniently open metal gate with no one in sight, turned a corner out into a street that was only now beginning to fill with people passing us by, and caught a perfect view of the Acropolis of Athens rising in the distance, framed by the sunrise in a way that almost made it glint to the eyes.

You couldn't have more thoroughly stunned me if you'd whacked me in the face with a celestial bronze warhammer.

I might have preferred that, actually.

See, I knew what it was and recognized it just fine - fifth and sixth-grade history class loved to talk about ancient Greece, complete with modern-day pictures and everything - and frankly?

I deserve a reward for not having a nervous breakdown right then and there, street full of people be damned.

The Acropolis, Athens, Greece.

Also recognized as part of the ancient lands by those in the know - the original dominion and stomping grounds of the Greek and Roman gods before they'd packed their bags and hightailed it after the flame of Western Civilisation when it moved on to greener pastures.

But just because they'd dipped out half a bajillion years ago out didn't mean that everyone and everything that used to live in their old estate had also vacated the premises - oh no.

That would be too easy.

Instead, the older, stronger, and nastier monsters and borderline forces of nature that didn't get with the times' way back when stuck behind and refused to budge to this day, like a malevolent pest infestation thousands of years in the making, and I was right smack dab in the middle of it.

Sounds fun, right?

I'd say I jumped out of the frying pan and into the fire, but honestly?

This was more like jumping out of the frying pan and into a nuclear reactor mid-meltdown.

The only places a living demigod could have ended up that were worse were Alaska, the Underworld and Tartarus itself - in exactly that order.

So... yeah.

A delayed freakout was definitely in the books somewhere down the line.

In the meantime, the Acropolis continued to loom out there in my field of vision like a giant monolithic testament to how utterly dead I was, and all the while I stared at it, my eyes twitching uncontrollably and my mouth opening and closing soundlessly.

Eventually, after what felt like a million years, something nudged the back my knee with enough gentle pressure to make me stumble half a step forward and bring me back to reality.

The labrador gave me a funny look as I craned my neck down towards him.

So what now, he seemed to ask.

"Isn't it obvious?"

I smiled down with a upturn of my lips so fake you'd think it was made in China.

"We try not to die."

...​

To my credit, I didn't immediately pray to Apollo.

I'm not going to pretend that was because of any pride on my part - No, this was just caution.

From what I knew, Apollo was much more... mild and easy going that most gods, but that bar was buried so deep in the ground you'd need an oil drill to dig it back out again.

The Olympians as I knew them to be in this world took an approach with their kids that alternated on a sliding scale between hands-off and completely divorced from reality.

I didn't need the only one of them I could nominally count on to be in my corner writing me off as the ungrateful kid who kept asking for handouts... but I wasn't exactly swimming in options.

Also, I didn't know if he had any part of me landing here, and if he did and I got some kind of answer proving as much, I had no idea if I'd be able to keep my mouth shut or my prayers mild.

Though it didn't make sense that he would.

Spiriting me away to one of the most dangerous places I could possibly be netted him a grand total of jack... unless this was some kind of applied karma for saving my life, or something different.

Didn't gods like sending their kids on stupidly absurd quests?

Was that what this was?

Hey son! You know how I saved your life? Well, I hope you didn't think that was a freebie, buddy. I'm going to need you to do this, this, and that within the next three to five business days at the latest, so get your game face on! Try not to die horribly!

Just the thought of it had me wanting to punch something, but I managed to hold off on the impulse and stop myself from calling out to Apollo for the first few hours.

Instead, I walked through the streets of Athens for a while, flinching at every particularly loud noise and staying far away from any corners or narrow alleyways as I tried to figure something out.

I kept expecting something enormous and half-made of teeth to jump out at me at any second, and when it didn't I only got more tense.

By the time the first hour was up, I was wired up like a bomb ready to blow.

And then, by some stroke of stupid luck, I found an internet café, and for the first time in my life my being hardwired to read and understand Greek fluently came in handy.

It had a sign out front in bold lettering that read: Inspot, for all your internet needs! , and you could see through the double window front outside that it was a neat little place, all warm brown woods and carpeted floors, with two rows of pay-to-use monitors, a little library near the back, and a couple of couches and reading tables propped against the farthest wall inside.

There was a counter and seating area for people looking for coffee and snacks off to the left as well, but I didn't care about that - it was the other half that was exactly what I needed.

The glass door jingled as I quickly stepped into the place. It was mostly empty, but the attendant at the counter was still startled as I speed-walked over and pressed my hands against it - whether that was because there was something on my face or because I was a teenager with a geniune bow and quiver strapped to my back was anyone's guess at that point.

"I'd like to use your phone and a monitor, please."

The Greek flowed off my tongue easily enough, and I think I almost managed a polite smile.

She still gave me an uncertain look over the rim of her glasses.

"It'll cost-"

I slapped down a wad of bills from the backpack before she'd even finished talking.

She paused.

"Is that enough?"

"Yes." But then she shook her head. Why-?" Your dog will have to stay outside. No pets allowed."

Ah. Right.

"That's fine. He can wait by the door."

He jolted by my feet and gave me a look of complete betrayal, but I rounded on him with a stony glare before he could start barking.

"This won't take long." I hissed to him under my breath. "Wait by the freaking door and I'll be out in a minute!"

The attendant cleared her throat as I looked up.

"Will he be alright?"

I waved her off.

"Totally fine." Wimp or not, he was still a hellhound. If he was determined to stick around then a few minutes by a door wouldn't kill him. "Now about that phone..."

She shrugged, and in short order I was holding a bog-standard cellphone in my hand and punching in my uncle's personal number like my life depended on it.

And the thing that sucked, though?

As I dialled in the last digit of his number, I honestly fooled myself into thinking that it would ring a couple of times, he'd pick up, I'd make sure everyone was fine and that they knew I was alive and rolling with the punches - probably while putting in the effort not to do something mortally embarrassing like tearing up - and we'd go from there.

I really thought that was it.

But that wasn't how it played out - Instead, I filled out the number, brought the phone to my ear with bated breath, and then I heard a loud, irritating beep and the automatic message that followed.

The number you have dialled is not in service.

I froze.

Not in service? What?

Confused, I tried to redial.

The number you have dialled is not in service.

I checked the number over and did it again.

The number you have dialled is not in service.

I tried a fourth time.

The number you have dialled-

I cleared over the slot and punched in the number all over again, making sure to get every last digit right. I triple-checked it three times before hitting the button.

Same difference.

The number you have dialled is not in service.

A little freaked now, I tried my Aunt Sarah's number instead.

The number you have dialled-

Then our landline.

The number-

I even tried the neighbour's landline which I knew only for emergencies.

The number-

"What the hell?"

I stared at the phone in my hand like it was the root of all evil, thoroughly spooked now. Even my breathing was starting to dip into an uneven pattern.

In a sudden panic I could barely describe, I half-stumbled, half-bolted over to the nearest monitor and tried to log onto my MySpace account. Maybe if I could leave a message to some of my friends-

I couldn't even finish forming the thought before my username and password were rejected.

"!"

I bit the inside of my mouth to stop from yelling out and nearly put my fist through the monitor screen before I managed to get a hold of myself.

Then I tried again.

And again.

And again.

I got a blaring rejection every time - it was as if my account had been deleted in the three days since I'd used it last.

"What. The. Hell?"

Was this some kind of divine bullshit? It had to be, right?

Right?

As a last-ditch resort, I looked up the Maple's Gazette - our town's community newspaper. It wasn't anything impressive, but the owner had a webpage built for it that he liked to update, and

I mean, our car had ended up through our house, and even if the Mist was working overtime to hide the truth behind what happened, there's no way some version of a story like that wouldn't be noticed and spread like wildfire-

Then the results loaded up, and I stopped breathing.

There was nothing.

Nothing.

Not just about the story, but also the town.

My home.

The closest I got to the Maple's Gazette was the name of some random other newspaper based out of Maple Town in Douglas County, Wisconsin.

Maple, Upstate New York, the town I'd liven in for years, wasn't up there on the list of results.

It didn't show up - not even when I reworded my search three different times, each more frantic than the last.

It was as if the whole place had vanished - or never even existed at all.

Just gone.

By the time I stopped typing and pulled back my trembling hands from the keyboard, I'd nearly ripped out half a dozen letters. There was an odd ringing in my ears that may or may not have been real.

In the end, I guess it didn't matter.

Gone.

Something was terribly, terribly wrong.

...​

An hour or so of failing attempts and confused denial later, I was all out of options. When everything was said and done, I ended my morning the same way I started it.

Slumped on a bench out on the edge of this open tourist square I'd manage to stumble on in a daze, feeling desperately unmoored as my head filled with questions and questions and questions I couldn't even begin to sort out, let alone answer.

At some point, my new dog had scrambled up onto the bench beside me and tucked his head onto my lap with a huff.

Maybe it was his way of trying to make me feel better.

Or maybe he just wanted attention.

I ended up scratching under his jaw numbly, and he rumbled in delight - not that I could enjoy it. Instead, I took a deep breath after a while, and closed my eyes as I bit the bullet and began to pray.

Literally.

Dad, what gives?

It was about as politely worded as I could put it.

Maybe I should have been more formal, and called him 'father' or 'Lord Apollo' or something, but I'd already started.

In for a penny, in for a pound.

If this is some kind of test, I thought, and swallowed in an effort to keep down against the sick feeling welling up in my stomach, I'd really appreciate a clue. A hint. Anything at all.

I didn't get an answer - not that I truly expected onw.

I didn't even know if he was listening.

I was trying just for the sake of it at this point.

At least tell me if my family made it out okay.

...

Nothing.

I almost started cursing his name, consequences be damned.

Then a shadow fell over me.

I looked up just as the centaur raised a hand in a calm greeting.

"Hello there."

...

Did that sound surreal and ridiculous to you too?

Because it was.

It really, really was.

I couldn't even make a face as the - again - literal centaur stared down at me, his human half towering above on account of his horse-like lower body, a relatively enormous trunk of muscle and sinew under course white fur, hoofs gleaming with reflected light.

His upper half was more ordinary, dressed in a muted but oddly comfortable-looking brown suit that matched with the hair falling past his ears and his beard, and as I met his eyes, I saw that they were vibrant but... old.

I couldn't tell you why that was the first word that popped into my head, but it fit.

His eyes were old - The kind of you could look into and immediately makes you realize that the person in front of you was positively ancient.

Nearly a solid minute passed without either of us saying anything.

For my part, I was still stuck on the half-horse thing as I took him in.

After all, knowing centaurs exist was one thing. Actually seeing it with my own eyes was another - and I had a hellhound that had gone utterly still lying in my lap, so that's saying something.

"Good morning, young man." His smile was politely warm. "You seem to be having a rough day."

...Oh my god, this is my life now, isn't it?

"...Who the heck are you?"

I probably sounded as completely done to him as I did to my own ears, but his smile didn't waver.

You might find it strange that I wasn't... I don't know, freaking out and going for my bow or something - not all centaurs were benevolent or good, after all - but I held off on that.

Maybe it was my demigod instincts or something else, but I could tell that wouldn't have been a good idea.

His presence wasn't threatening or intimidating as the other monsters had been. He didn't set me on edge, and even though I was wary, I didn't feel in danger from him.

... Also, he felt strong.

That's the best way I could put it - just standing in his general vicinity had me feeling this muted but nearly overwhelming impression of quiet power that clashed with the harmless look on his face - like he was someone or something several orders of magnitude above me even if he was playing nice for now.

It was... something to behold and probably why the dog was as still and stiff as a marble statue, not quite daring to breathe.

...

That, or it might have just been shock.

The man was literally half horse.

"Who are you?" I repeated after a beat, a little more firm this time.

"Ah, introductions of course." He raised a hand and pressed it against his chest. "I am Chiron."

"..."

"..."

"..."

"..."

"...No you're not."

...Yeah, I know. I'm an idiot, but come on.

After everything I've been through in the last twelve to twenty-four hours, I've earned a little slack.

"I assure you I am."

I almost flushed as he raised an eyebrow and gave me a bemused look.

And he sounded completely serious about it too.

I couldn't even even call him out on the lie because I didn't think he was lying.

"Why aren't you at Camp Half-Blood?

He frowned

"Where?"

... I could tell this conversation was going to go somewhere screwy and I already hated it.

"The place where you train heroes? Demigods? Isn't that..." I hesitated. "Isn't that your whole thing?"

"I have not heard of it" His frown deepened as my jaw dropped. "And I have not properly trained a hero in centuries, young man. Demigod or otherwise."

What?

No, really, what?

"Are you alright?"

"I-"

I wish that the conversation had ended there.

A break, even a five-minute time out, would have given me the time I needed to wipe the bug-eyed look off my face and get my feet back under me.

I wasn't even questioning how a literal centaur could stand in a crowd full of ordinary people and not draw attention, Mist or no, still stuck on the fact that I was in Athens, Chiron was in Athens, and he'd never heard of Camp Half-Blood.

That should have been enough for one day, right?

But of course, the world wouldn't even let me have that.

"There you are!"

I jumped as someone yelled out from across the square and began to sprint towards us - a guy in a jogging suit who couldn't have been more than a year older than me with dark hair and an intensely determined look in his eyes as he caught sight of Chiron - apparently - and came charging right over.

This time, I did twitch for my bow, but the stranger didn't even seem to register the threat as he skidded to a halt in front of Chiron and pointed at him with a victorious smile.

"Got you!"

"I'll admit, you are remarkably persistent." Chiron sighed, sounding noticeably tired as he raised a hand to pinch the bridge of his nose. "How did you manage to find me this time?"

"You kept tricking my bats into flying the wrong way whenever they spotted you." The guy's grin only got wider. "So when they told me where you were going, I just ran in the opposite direction!"

"... dogged hard-headedness and luck, then." Chiron mused. "And arguably a dash of creativity."

"Thanks!"

"Your request is still denied, young devil."

Young devil?

Was that some kind of insult?

A nickname?

"I will not be taking you on as a student." Chiron continued, in a tone of long-suffering patience. "As I've told you before, I have too many conflicting priorities."

"Then I'll just keep trying until you change your mind!" His smile didn't waver as his voice boomed - and then he finally seemed to register my existence, because his eyes snapped over to me.

They were almost bright violet.

"Hello!" He stuck a hand out at me so fast I nearly leaped back out of my seat on reflex before forcing myself to hold still. "Are you here to train with Chiron too?"

"...Not right now?"

It was an automatic response - I didn't even know what was happening anymore.

Which was an achievement, considering I'd already been lost before whatever this was had started.

"So you might, then?"

The other guy was undeterred, and I turned back to Chiron - for help, maybe.

The centaur just gave me another bemused smile.

Real helpful, dude.

"Possibly?"

"That's good!" He nodded as I finally took his hand, shaking vigorously with a strong grip. "It's nice to meet you! Call me Sairaorg!"

"Daniel." I offered, before blinking. "Wait, what was that?"

"My name. It's Sairaorg" He gave me another bright smile. "Sairaorg Bael."

That was...

Sairaorg Bael

Why was that name familiar?

I don't remember ever hearing-

...

...

...


Wait.

Sairaorg Bael

...

...

...

...

...

...

No

no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no-

NO

I was just out of it and letting my thoughts spiral into the realm of insanity.

This is not a thing.

...

...

....

Sairoarg Bael.

Chiron had called him a young devil.

...

...

...

HOW IS THIS A THING!?

I tried to cut it off at the roots, but denying the idea that was rapidly crystallising in my head was about as useful as trying to push back the tide with my hands.

I woke up in another country, all of my numbers and accounts not registering, my hometown seemingly not even existing at all.

A Chiron who wasn't where he was supposed to be, and a devil who shouldn't exist.

Not in this world.

This one, at least - but there others, weren't there?

I grabbed my head with a low keening noise as the memory of fractal, overlapping shards of light slipped back into it with all the grace of a knife being stabbed into my frontal lobe, along with the accompanying burst of instinctual, almost reflexive realisation, and all the pieces began to click in place.

Sairaorg- frigging -Bael!

At that point, I felt that I could be completely forgiven for leaping to my feet in sudden fury before the surprised centaur and the devil next to him and beginning to swear at the top of my voice.

"Motherf-!"

And things just sort of kicked off from there.

...​

When you realize that Daniel is not just a teenager again, but a teenager cursed to live in the era before YouTube and the internet culture that followed:
