That night, I had a vivid dream.

I was in a motel room—a small but warmly lit place with red carpeting, a pair of single beds against one wall, a double window to another end, and a TV against the opposite wall beside a small coffee table and a couple of chairs.

Nothing to write home about, but it looked decent enough.

That wasn't what had the part of me that wasn't distantly aware I was dreaming seizing in shock - it was my family.

Katie and Alex were sharing one of the beds, curled up together like they were huddling for warmth.

My aunt, though, was sitting over at the table and crying her eyes out into her palms, while my uncle wrapped a hand around her and tried to comfort her.

"We left him." She was sobbing as her shoulders heaved, and my breath hitched. "We just left him there!"

They were talking about me.

"He'll be alright." The words were supposed to be confident and soothing, but my uncle sounded haggard, and far too quiet, like he was desperately trying to believe them himself. "He's a demigod, and he's a good, strong kid. He'll pull through."

I did, I wanted to say, I'm fine!

It might have been by the very skin of my teeth, but I'd survived.

But neither of them heard me.

I tried to call to both of them again and again, but each word that fell out of my mouth was utterly silent - not even the ghost of a whisper.

So I tried to reach out for them instead, even though a part of me knew it was useless.

I couldn't - My feet refused to move, like they were buried in cement. I gritted my teeth and tried to push forward anyway, but with each step I took, it felt like I was being forced down by the weight of the entire world.

Even the space between us seemed to stretch the closer I got, like a rubber band being pulled on each end to keep us apart.

But I still almost made it.

I was only a few feet away from them when I threw my hands out, desperately trying to grab onto one of them.

Look at me! I'm right here!

Neither of them noticed. My fingertips only just managed to brush against the back of my uncle's chair, and suddenly they, my cousins, and everything else in the room exploded into mist and melted away.

At the same time, the pressure on me vanished, and I stumbled forward and nearly face-planted as my surroundings reformed into something different.

"My lord?"

I looked up, and my eyes went wide.

There was a man standing there who couldn't have been any older than his early twenties, dressed in jeans, a shirt and a white jacket with gold accents. He was tall, with skin that sported a mild, healthy tan from spending time in the sun, and his sandy-blonde hair fell just past his ears.

He looked so much like me I almost couldn't believe it.

"Where is he?"

Then he turned to stare at something over my shoulder, a pulsing golden glow wafting off of him and thrumming deep in his eyes, and suddenly the resemblance wasn't nearly as uncanny.

"My lord?"

Somebody behind me spoke again - a servant, or an attendant or something, I didn't know which - but I didn't turn around to see.

I couldn't look away from the god in front of me as his expression screwed up in frustration and real, dangerous anger, the light from him reflecting back off the golden walls of the room he was standing in until all of his surroundings seemed to shimmer and beat like they were alive.

"He was right there. I was reaching out to put him back together, and then something happened. He slipped out of my grasp, and now I cannot see him." His voice echoed, like a dozen people were speaking at once, and all of them were absolutely furious. "Where is he?"

His eyes ignited with power and radiance, and the room trembled.

"̴̗͆Ẃ̷͖h̵̫̿ẹ̸̆r̷̢͘e̸̠̎ ̶͙͗i̸̹͛s̴̗̀ ̷̙̃m̴̢̈́y̷͈͊ ̴̲͐ṡ̴̗ǫ̷̏n̵̗̎!?̵̬̍"̵͔́

The next wave of power slammed into me like a freight train and knocked me back as everything was blown to pieces around me-

...​

-And then I was shooting up in bed with a sharp inhale, back in the land of the living.

Holy crap.

My heart hammered in my chest.

That was...

...

I swallowed.

Look, I'd had bad dreams before.

Me and a couple of friends once ran a horror movie marathon all night at a sleepover two summers ago, and I spent a week and a half afterwards seeing corny demons and goofy killer clowns jumping out at me every time I closed my eyes at night - and then my aunt found out, so I got grounded on top of that.

Talk about insult to injury, right?

But what I just saw wasn't anything like that - it had been different, and real.

And I knew why.

Demigod dreams.

I knew what those were, in theory - Random flashes of insight, bits and pieces of context and ominous warnings that could be vaguely helpful, arguably useful and were just about always messy and complicated.

Almost a monkey's paw in their own right or close to it if they got bad.

That was the first one I'd ever had - or at least the only one I could ever remember having myself.

Naturally, it sucked.

With a sigh, I started rubbing my face tiredly.

On second thought, it wasn't as terrible as it could have been.

At least I knew now that the others had made it out ok, right?

Sure, they looked about as miserable as I felt, but they were safe.

That should count for something, and in my mind, it did - Maybe not what I'd hoped for, but I'd take what I could get.

And then there was... Apollo.

Dear old dad, the god who looked so much like me until he didn't.

That was who that had been, at the end. I knew that with the same certainty that I knew the sky was blue or that water was wet.

I mulled it over for a second before shaking my head.

Nope.

Not diving into that anytime soon.

Not when I still didn't even know how I'd dreamt and saw any of it at all, given that I wasn't even sharing a world with any of them presently.

And yeah, I was past my denial phase on that one.

It would have taken some real Olympic-tier mental gymnastics not to be at this point, given where I was right now.

See, after I admittedly lost it and went off like a lunatic in the middle of a public area, Chiron had stepped in.

The centaur had been nice enough to patiently wait out the good ten to fifteen minutes it had taken for me to finally run out of steam and stagger back onto the nearest bench, red-faced and out of breath and absolutely losing my mind, and then he offered me a hand.

"I'm not one to turn away a lost traveler, even in this day and age." His smile was kind as he spoke, and genuine in a way that was hard to describe. "You are welcome beneath my roof if you need it, young man."

"..."

I took that in slowly, staring at his outstretched hand blankly.

Now, kids, this is important - if an older stranger you've only known for all of fifteen minutes tops suddenly asks you to come home with them, that would usually be a good sign that you need to run away very far, very quickly.

Possibly after kicking them somewhere they'd really feel it, if you can get away with it.

If things had been even a little different, I'd have never taken him up on that offer.

Only, in this case:

a) I didn't have anywhere else to go.

B) Again, there was this air of trustworthiness to him that I couldn't quite put into words. I could tell he meant no harm - and he absolutely could harm me if he wanted to, I had zero doubts on that end after spending the little time in his presence I did.

C) Going by the looks I was getting, I was pretty sure that somebody would call the cops on me If I wandered off alone.

Whatever magic or power that Chiron had been using to walk around the city without drawing attention to himself didn't do anything to hide me from the square full of people we'd been standing in, and I'd been going off the rails and spitting out words that would have probably given my eight-grade English teacher a stroke if she'd been around to hear them.

Seriously, I'm pretty sure I invented at least twelve new curses in English and Greek by the time I was done ranting, and everyone around was staring at me funny.

One little kid had actually started crying, and his mom shot me a nasty glare before hurrying off to shush him.

Honestly, I felt a little bad about that one, but right then I could barely register it, still staring at nothing at all and trying to filter through the white noise drowning out the sound of my own thoughts right at the source.

Turns out that compounding existential crises isn't good for your processing capacity - who knew? - and the fact that Sairoarg Bael was still just standing there to Chiron's left looking awkward and increasingly uncomfortable was just making it harder to screw my head back on properly.

You get the idea.

Eventually I managed to reach out and take Chiron's hand and let him help pull me to my feet, and I even offered something that might've generously been called a thankful nod, despite the fact that it was so slow and mechanical you could have almost heard the imaginary hinges in my neck creaking from the careful force of it.

"Wonderful."

The rest was pretty straightforward.

We wasted no time and ended up spending the better part of half an hour trekking our way back through the city in the direction of the Acropolis, before slipping out off the crowded streets and into an area that felt distinctly more... exclusive than the rest.

Chiron's home ended up being this sprawling, private estate dominated by a massive mansion built around an open courtyard, with engraved marble pillars and supports everywhere and all kinds of murals and artistic touches I couldn't properly appreciate if I tried.

The place looked like half of it had been pulled straight from ancient Greece and polished up until every other part glinted in the sun, and the sprawling greenery and curated gardens surrounding it just made it seem even more than it already was.

There was also something in the air that I could vaguely... sense? Feel?

Something like that.

Magic.

I wasn't sure how, but I could tell that it was there. Not uncomfortable or anything - just present.

I didn't ask, even though a part of me really wanted to. I didn't even take the tour that was offered.

Chiron directed me to a room up the nearest flight of stairs - sparse but spacious, with just a bed and a desk near a window that opened up to a view of the other face of the Acropolis far in the distance - and I didn't hesitate before I was marching into it and locking the door behind me.

I couldn't put up with any more eyes on me, even if it was the person who was helping me out, and I slumped against the door and staggered onto the floor the second I shut it, suddenly exhausted like no one would believe.

This is really happening.

I couldn't tell you how long I stayed like that, but at some point I decided to flop down onto the bed, and before I knew it I was out like a light.

The stress had done me in - And now here I was.

Waking up in a different world for the second time in as many days.

A place where the supernatural was even more dangerous than it was back home, and one of the few things I knew for sure was that everything was set to go to hell in a handbasket - somewhat literally - at some point down the line after some other random kid halfway around the world whose goals, dreams, and general IQ score were probably all just the word 'boobs' in big bold letters gets killed, resurrected, and gets a magic dragon gauntlet of obscene power out of it for his troubles.

And that was just for starters - the opening act, even.

I almost snorted, but it wasn't because it sounded funny.

Actually, it sounded stupid - the kind of stupid so hardcore it'd make you wish it had a face so you could smack it - but it was reality for me now.

A reality I couldn't get away from, because I didn't know how I'd gotten into it in the first place and I didn't have a clue how I was possibly getting home-

"Arf!"

A low, familiar bark distracted me from that spiral before I could decide whether I wanted to laugh incredulously or get up and start smacking my head against the wall until things made sense again - or at least pretended to - and I turned to find the source of it.

It was dark out, with the moonlight shining over the Acropolis and the fields I could see from my angle on the bed and spilling into the room through the open window, but it didn't reach the shadows pooling against the farthest corner to my right.

I stared into them, and a pair of glowing red eyes stared back.

I'll admit, I made an embarrassing sound and nearly jumped out of my skin for about half a second before I remembered who they belonged to.

"Dude." I tried to glare, but it was halfhearted at best. "Don't do that."

Another bark, and those eyes seemed to blink innocently.

Who, me?

"You know what you did."

Instead of arguing against that heinous accusation, my new hellhound came padding out of the darkness before leaping up onto the bed and dropping his head into my lap, huffing pointedly.

"I can't believe I almost forgot you were here," I muttered, scooting back up a little to make room before I started running my hands through his fur. "Guess you're in it for the long haul too, huh?"

It's not like he could go home anymore than I could, wherever that was for him, and from the satisfied rumble I got, he didn't much mind that - And honestly?

I didn't either.

"Well, if you're going to be sticking around, you're going to need a name."

He perked up in surprise.

"Yeah, I can't keep calling you dog or hellhound in my head. You need something better." I stared at him for a second before cracking a grin. "How about..."

His tail started wagging in excitement.

"...Wimp?"

I swear, the betrayed look on his face was priceless. I had to duck down to muffle my snorts into the blanket or I'd have woken up the entire house.

"Relax, I'm just kidding." I had to raise my hands in self defense when he started bumping his snout against my chest like he was trying to knock some sense into me. "Besides, it does fit. Your friends were much more impressive when they were trying to eat me."

At that, he actually growled in irritation -he'd liked those two about as much as I had- and redoubled his little attacks.

"I'm serious! The two of them were fearsome beasts of the Underworld that had me fearing for my life, and then there was you - the cute little puppy shaking in the wind." I could barely keep a straight face as he tried to push me over - this dog was going to be fun, I could just tell. "I won't judge, but you gotta admit that was some real cowardly-"

I froze as a lightbulb abruptly went off in my head.

There was this Saturday morning cartoon I was into a couple of years ago - this whacky Tom and Jerry-esque show about this total scaredy cat of a dog who probably flinched at his own shadow and kept getting into crazy slap-stick shenanigans when his owners weren't looking.

It was a fun pastime - then I made the mistake of letting Katie watch one of the scarier episodes with me this one time, and she wouldn't stop bawling for an hour. I got an earful and a half for that one and I was banned from watching it when the girls were in the room, and then I forgot about all about it after a while.

But I still remembered the little dog's name just fine.

"Courage," I said, and my dog finally quit trying to thump me in favor of blinking up in surprise. "Courage the cowardly dog - or maybe Courage the terrifying hellhound for you instead."

He seemed to think about that for a second, head-titled to the side and tail wagging slowly.

I smiled.

"Sounds good, doesn't it?

"Arf!"

The next thing I knew, I was getting an armful of over-enthusiastic dog, complete with slobber and everything, so I guess that was a yes.

After tossing and turning a little more, I got out of bed.

It was still dark out, but I couldn't get back to sleep.

It was too quiet, and my head was too loud.

"Let's get some air," I told the newly minted Courage as I unlocked the door and crept down the flight of stairs.

The house was eerily unfamiliar as we made our way across it, and
I noticed that Chiron must have had something against internal decoration, because everything along the hallways we took was about as lowkey as you could get, with the walls bare and the furniture surprisingly simple and understated for a place that seemed so... stately from the outside.

Still, not my problem.

Neither of us knew our way around the place, but we managed to follow the whistle of the wind and the cool breeze that carried hints of grass and soil from the gardens toward the open courtyard I'd seen before just fine.

It was only a change of pact that I was after, but I'd barely stepped out under the moonlight before I was getting more than what I'd bargained for.

"Having trouble sleeping?

Now, I did not scream, and anyone who tells you otherwise is a lying liar who lies, but I did leap aside and almost hissed out something inordinately nasty before I got a hold of myself and realized who was talking.

Chiron

"I just wanted some air," I repeated, and he smiled agreeably. His suit looked exactly the same - like he hadn't changed it since the morning.

"It is a pleasant night." He titled his head to the stone bench beside him, a clear invitation. "And fortuitous. I think we're both well aware that a conversation is due."

...

Right.

I guess we were doing this now.

"Alright." I nodded and stepped up towards the bench, taking the offered spot. Courage trailed behind me and parked himself at my feet loyally, even though I could tell he was just as wary of Chiron as he'd been before.

"Would you like some tea? I have a mountain blend that is simply delightful, and some sweet pastries I've been saving for the right time."

"Not... right now. But thanks."

I hope that came across firmer than it sounded to me. As soon as he pointed it out, I realized that I was starving - I hadn't eaten anything since yesterday afternoon before basketball practice, but I was too nervous for food now.

"It's not a problem." He said, before giving me a careful look. "I think it would be for the best if we speak plainly, yes?"

"Sure?"

That was the entire point of this.

"Good. So tell me, then: How does a young demigod such as yourself end up on the streets of Athens, wounded and half-dead with only an insensate hellhound pup for company?"

I tried to keep a straight face, really I did, but I was still flinching before he'd even finished speaking - and then I actually registered what he said, and my jaw dropped.

"You know about that?

"Surely you didn't think you healed yourself of the state you were in?"

What?

No, seriously, what?

"We woke up alone."

The backpack with the money - one mystery solved and cashed in for about seven thousand more.

The whole time, when I was stumbling around the city and expecting monsters to leap out at me any second?

I wasn't even angry - just stunned.

Why do any of this?

"I did not know who you were, young man - merely what you were, and not what kind of person you might turn out to be - and believe it or not, this is far from the first time I've stumbled upon some manner of an injured child or the like, only to later discover that some other party attempted to manipulate, extort or in some shape or way inconvenience me through whatever scheme it is they've concocted.."

That... made sense?

I still wasn't sure what to feel about this, still stuck in some kind of consistent whiplash between incredulous and angry that ended up keeping me right in between the two.

Confused as all hell.

I went ramrod straight in half a second flat.

Apollon. Apollo.

Same difference, except not even close.

"-would have been happy to hear that I let a child of his so young wander the streets when he very clearly had nowhere else to go."

"Daniel." I cut him off stiffly. "Daniel Winchester. I'm sleeping in your house, you can use my name."

He sounded warmly pleased.

I wasn't, because he was right, but also hilariously wrong... only I didn't feel like laughing, and I sure as anything couldn't and wouldn't be correcting him anytime soon.

So I just need to figure out how to-

"Does your father know where you are?"

"..."

...someone up there hates me, don't they?

"Perhaps I should reach out-"

"No," I said, thinking so fast my tongue was moving before I was even aware of the words. "Don't do that."

Drawing my alternate dad's attention sounded like such a terrible idea on so many levels I could spend a day going through them all and still have plenty left over for the next week.

Chiron was already looking at me expectantly, so I kept going.

"I've never even met him - he's a stranger to me."

His eyes narrowed, not quite in suspicion, but too heavy to just be thought.

"That's unusual."

He didn't believe me - or he doubted, at least.

"It's true." I insisted, praying to no one in particular that he would listen to me. "I've never met him before - Heck, I didn't know he was my dad until yesterday."

Chiron's brows rose to his hairline, but I was on a roll now.

"And I've never been to Athens, either. I lived with my family in the States my whole life - and then a few monsters attacked last night." I didn't say which, though. "I managed to kill them, but I got hurt really bad and blacked out, and the next thing I knew I was waking up on that bench."

The best part was that none of it was a lie.

Oh, it was so vague it practically bordered on one, and it definitely was by omission, but no one was counting right now.

And it was everything Chiron was getting out me anyway.

"I... see."

He didn't, I could tell that much even as he raised a hand to stroke his chin in consideration. "And your family?"

I...

Right in the gut, huh?

I swallowed.

"They're gone."

I didn't have to fake the emotion in that one, and Chiron's face softened a little.

"I'm sorry."

I just shook off the apology, because it made me feel like a lying scumbag.

"Just don't bring up my... father again, please." Wincing at the word probably didn't help my case any, but I couldn't stop myself. "I want nothing to do with him."

The last thing I needed now was for some other god I knew virtually nothing about to take offense at me for 'pretending' to be his son or something along those lines and blasting me into smithereens for the insult.

"Very well."

...

"... What?"

"I agree." Chiron shrugged, like the blasé attitude wasn't all kinds of ridiculous coming from him. "I won't make Lord Apollon aware of your presence, and you may stay here for as long as you need."

"J-" My tongue nearly tied itself into knots as I went to speak, because how exactly had that worked? "Just like that?"

What was the catch?

Because there's no way there wasn't one.

The look he fixed me with was perfectly level, and it still had me wanting to back up on reflex alone because it felt as if he knew exactly what I was thinking.

"We both know there's much, much more to the story that you haven't told me."

Crap.

"But answer me this: are you an enemy of mine?"

"What? No!"

"Did you plan or anticipate us crossing paths in any way? Are you going to find ways to take advantage of my generosity?"

"No," I repeated, more firmly this time. "I told you, I'm still new to this mess."

In more ways than one.

"Then I won't ask for more now." Chiron shook his head, looking satisfied and either not seeing or at least pretending not to see the look on my face this time. "There'll be time enough for that later, if or when you're willing to share. In the meantime, we might as well greet my other temporary guest."

...What?

Before I could ask, a familiar voice beat me to it.

"I wasn't spying, I promise."

My eye twitched.

Seriously?

I glanced back as Sairaorg stepped out from behind one of the pillars on the edge, a sheepish look on his face.

Come to think of it, he had been invited back here with me and Courage, hadn't he?

"Oh, I know you weren't - I heard you coming." Chiron didn't look put out at all by his presence. "Have you had trouble sleeping as well, young devil?"

"No. Well, kind of." The literal devil grinned excitedly. "I was just excited!"

"For?"

"I want to train with you!"

For the first time since our conversation began, Chiron sighed.

"You're not going to give up, are you?"

"Not a chance!"

"Why?"

Sairaorg blinked.

"What?"

"Why do you want to train with me?"

There was a shift in the air as Chiron looked him over, a rising tension so abrupt even I felt it. Courage let out a low whine and nudged my leg in something that might've been warning.

Sairaorg's persistent smile finally dimmed, and he visibly hesitated.

"Well?" Chiron's tone was expectant in the same way a stern teacher's was - not loud, but you couldn't ignore it if you tried.

"I have a few reasons," Sairaorg said at last, his face cycling through a whole reel of emotions, before settling on something determined "But the first one is important, and the one that I've held onto the longest."

"And that is?"

"I need to be strong."

It would have sounded shallow and uninspired if anyone else had said it, but the way Sairoarg spoke that one word was something all on its own.

For a moment, Chiron looked unmoved.

"Why?"

"Because I was born weak, and I was told I was worthless because of it." The devil admitted with an easy shrug "I refuse to accept that, so I'm going to grow as strong as I can get, and then some."

"To get revenge?"

"No." Sairaorg didn't even hesitate, fists clenching at his sides pointedly "To prove that I can, and that anyone else can too."

...

"... Interesting." Chiron mused out loud, and the tension lifted.

I got the sense that he'd passed some kind of test.

And then I forgot all about that as Chiron turned back to me.

"What about you?"

"... What?"

"If I offered to train you as I did the heroes of ages past, would you accept?" He seemed to tower over me as he spoke, and my throat suddenly felt drier than that. "And why?"

Would I-

....

"Yes."

I didn't know if he expected me to hesitate, or take some time to think about it or something, but I didn't.

The question he just asked me was the one thing that came my way in the past twenty-four hours that I didn't need to overthink a thousand times over before saying a word.

He nodded, like he'd expected that out of me.

"And why?"

"Because I nearly died," I answered as honestly as he expected me to. I didn't even have to think about it. "And it sucked harder than anything in my life ever has, and I never want to feel that way again If I can help it."

Even ignoring how I wanted to figure out a way back home, and how I also wanted to get strong enough to look after the others, I needed to get strong enough that I'd never have to beg for anyone to step in and save me while I lay in a pool of my own blood.

God or otherwise.

I gritted my teeth just thinking about it.

And Chiron didn't miss a single detail as he glanced over me, then to Sairaorg and back again.

Then he sighed, one last time.

"Every time I put my foot down." The trainer of heroes snorted under his breath. "Every time... come along then."

Confused, me and Sairaorg exchanged a look before we glanced back to see him already trotting away across the courtyard.

"Where are we going?"

"To see what I'm working with, of course."

...​

A few hours later, the sun began to rise in the distance.

When it did, the sunlight lit up the clearing the four of us were in with rosy gold hues, and even the grass seemed to glow with a healthy luster.

I stood on end on my own, bow in hand and quiver slung over my shoulder, while Sairoarg stood across from me and started stretching his arms.

Chiron was far off to the right, with Courage sitting up next to him and huffing impatiently as the second ticked by.

"So just to be clear," I asked out loud, still reeling from how fast everything was happening. It was surreal. "You want to see us to fight?"

"I want to see what you two prospective students can do," Chiron said, crossing his arm across his chest. "And I haven't seen anything yet."

Well, that was pointed.

I turned back to Sairaorg, who looked like he was about ready to start bouncing in place out of sheer excitement, and began nocking an arrow.

"So this is wild, huh?" I tipped my head his way. "Nice meeting you, by the way."

We hadn't really talked. At all.

In hindsight, that might've been my fault.

"It is!" His energy was borderline infectious. "I'm looking forward to-"

My hands blurred as I raised the bow and fired at point-blank range. The arrow shot forward at speed, the celestial bronze tip glinting in the sun-

"Hah!"

And Sairoarg plucked it right out of the air.

Oh, he had to jump back half a step and a little to the left before snapping out his arm to grab at it, but he'd still caught an arrow and made it look effortless.

For a second, neither of us talked.

"...That wasn't fair."

"...In my defence, it worked on the cyclopes."

His expression brightened.

"You fought cyclopes?"

"Oh yeah, three of them. Dumb as bricks - oh, and a couple of hellhounds too."

"Really? Where-?"

I fired the second arrow I'd nocked it in the split, the drawing motion so quick and smooth you'd think I'd been training at it half my life and not less than two days - and Sairaorg still managed to surge out with his free hand.

For some reason, the absurdity of it struck a nerve.

"Stop catching my arrows!"

"You're the one shooting at me!"

"Because talking isn't a free action!"

"Good point!"

And then he lunged at me and I promptly regretted all my life choices up to now, because he charged forwards faster than the arrows he'd intercepted.

The first punch I managed to duck under, and his fist sailed over my head with a rush of displaced air that I could feel all the way down my spine. I tried to scramble back to put some distance between us, but he was relentless, driving forward and nearly taking my head off with a sudden kick that came out of nowhere - one minute his foot was on the ground, and the next the sole of his trainer was flashing past my eyes.

Then the third strike landed, a straight cross right to my chest, and the impact felt like the end of the world had come early.

"Got you!"

I didn't respond - mostly because I had no more air in my lungs as I went flying back some fifteen feet before tumbling down to the earth like a sack of potatoes.

"You aren't done, are you?" Sairaorg yelled, shuffling on his feat and jumping from side to side like a "Because ready or not, here I come!"

Despite the words, he was waiting until I staggered up to my feet before coming at me again.

Small mercies there.

I'd had no illusions about who was coming out on top here right from the beginning - I knew firsthand what kind of monster he'd be in a few years, but to think he was already this strong?

When he was around my age, maybe only a little older?

And this was probably barely a warm-up for him.

Or was it me who was just really weak?

That possibility made something bitter curl up in my stomach, even if I knew it was unreasonable.

And then I glanced up to a Chiron.

As our eyes met, the centaur raised a brow.

I could almost imagine his voice in my head, asking the question I knew was on the tip of his tongue.

Is that all?

The bitter feeling in my stomach suddenly transformed into something inordinately angry, and then it quickly grew into something more than even that, a pulling sensation that was hot and twisting and almost on the edge of painful as it spread through my chest and right up my throat.

Use it, some instinct me seemed to urge, and it sounded like the best idea I'd ever heard.

When I leaped up to my feet, it was just in time for Sairaorg to close in one me, and I screamed.

It was like a flash bang went off, only a hundred times worse - the sound that came out of my throat was an unholy screech that was a crime against eardrums everywhere, and it struck with physical force. I could see it disrupt the air and stagger Sairoarg, bringing him to his knees with a pained expression as his hands shot up to protect his ears.

And that was just the half of it.

The split-second burst of golden, fiery light was just as bad, blinding to look at and leaving the grass around us in a wide circle as nothing more than ash scattering in the wind.

The eruption of power only lasted for about five seconds, give or take a couple more, and it only managed to knock Sairoarg off his stride for just as long - but it was enough.

By the time he got up, I'd already released my third arrow, and it lanced out far faster than the ones before, wreathed in a faint golden glow that the devil in front of me couldn't dodge in time.

Not completely.

It disappeared over his shoulder and left behind a slice in his shirt and a graze maybe half a step above a paper cut, the kind that would sting a little at the absolute worst.

It was still something, though, and I felt a rush of achievement as I saw Sairaorg looking at it like he couldn't believe his eyes.

"You-?"

"What?"

I knew I wasn't going to beat him.

The burst of power I'd just used was already slipping away, and my brain was dropping out of the instinctive rush.

I didn't even know how to go about pulling something like that again.

Despite that, I still managed to crack a grin that probably looked a little too crazy for comfort as I stared back at him, because you know what?

If I was going to lose anyway, I was going to get at least a couple more hits in before I clocked out.

I was always competitive when I wanted to be.

"You aren't done, are you?'" I watched his shock melt right back into delight as I threw his words at him, and a grin that matched my tit for tat went right back up on his face "Because ready or not-"

"-here I come!" Sairoarg finished, and then we were going at it like total maniacs.

...​

Meanwhile, Chiron watched from a comfortable distance away, and exhaled wryly.

"I already have my work cut out for me, don't I?"

...

#164
So, I'm going to be honest.

I totally lost the fight - or I would have, if Chiron hadn't eventually called the spar to an end.

"That'll do - I've seen enough."

The words and the clap that followed came with a burst of strangely gentle power that washed over the field like tidal wave, non-threatening but so obvious you couldn't have possibly missed it, and Sairaorg and I broke apart before we even realized what was happening.

A part of me appreciated that.

We hadn't been going at it for too long, really, but my arms and legs had already begun to feel like lead weights, my head was ringing and I had the beginnings of a nasty shiner and what felt like an entire patchwork of blooming bruises running down the right side of my face and scattered across the rest of me too.

Even breathing hurt a little- my chest felt too tight for my lungs and every gulp of air I took felt a little too short for comfort.

Chiron may not have announced a winner, but I think we all knew how things would have gone if we'd kept going.

It wasn't surprising - Sairaorg was absurdly strong, I knew that going in.

He wasn't anywhere near the peak of what he could be, and he'd probably still be able to go up against nearly every 'ordinary' demigod I could think from back home off the top of my head just the way he was now and still have more than even odds of coming out on top.

But that didn't mean he'd come out unscathed, either.

When he stepped back, he was slightly favouring one leg on account of the nasty graze on his other's outer thigh, courtesy of the gold-tinted arrow he'd been too slow to dodge, and he was rubbing his side where another would have given him a terrible day if he hadn't angled out of the way and avoided being skewered in exchange for another glancing cut.

The worst hit, though, didn't even come from an arrow - it was the first-degree burn in the rough shape of my fist that trailed up his lower jaw and half his cheek like a bright angry red welt.

I couldn't even tell you how it happened - one second he was ten feet away and I'd had no arrow nocked, and the next he was right there and cocking back his fist with enough force to break my jaw, and I panicked.

It felt like punching a brick wall and my fingers were left numb and twitching from the impact, but the force of it still snapped his head back and staggered him out of his charge. The quicksilver burst of searing light that wreathed me as I struck did the rest, and while it barely broke his stride, you could tell that it hurt.

I also wouldn't be surprised if I hadn't given him some kind of temporary tinnitus with that unholy screech I'd let out - and like everything else, I hadn't even known I could do that.

For a second, we just stared at each other and caught our breath while Chiron came over.

Then Sairaorg nodded.

"You're tougher than I thought," He said, and his smile was bright and infectious despite the fact that the expression pulling at that burn had to sting like nobody's business. "It was a good spar."

Then he raised his fist at me, and I couldn't help but grin right back as I bumped my own against it.

"Heck yeah it was."

It wasn't a win, but it wasn't a failure either - not really.

And given how new I was at this, that was a point all of its own.

"Yes indeed." Chiron threw in his two cents as he stopped to tower over us, a pensive look on his face. Courage was hot on his heels, padding over quickly and giving me a happy nudge with his snout. "It was an interesting showcase."

"Yeah?" I stared up at the centaur expectantly. It was the moment of truth. "How'd we do, teach?"

"Well enough to demonstrate your strengths." He said, and then his gaze sharpened a little. "And also poorly enough that after the first few minutes in which I ascertained your capabilities, I started to entertain myself by making a list of all the ways a skilled opponent of similar potential could have killed either of you near-effortlessly. I lost count after the first two dozen."

I deflated, and going by his wince, Sairaorg's pride took that about as well as mine did.

"Still," Chiron said, and his tone gentled again as he held his arms out, palms splayed open "I have seen great warriors start from humbler beginnings, so I suppose we'll just have to put our backs into it."

The air over his hands seemed to shimmer, the light reflecting off of them oddly, and then a pair of metal flasks materialised into either grip between one blink and the next.

He handed one over to each of us, and I'll admit I stared a bit - casual magic was still new and trippy to me.

"Drink."

Sairaorg and I exchanged a look as we took them, and he shrugged first and began uncorking his. I took a sniff of my own, and there was something tangy to it - like lemonade, only it didn't taste like the stuff at all.

Instead, the first mouthful was sweet and earthy and mixed in with something warm that seemed to seep down my throat and all the way to my toes in no time flat.

The pounding in my head abruptly stopped, and I stood up straighter. My limbs felt stronger, and my breathing evened out in one sigh.

Even my vision seemed to sharpen, and I saw Sairaorg stiffen and raise a hand to gently trace his cuts and burns.

They were mending too, slowly but thoroughly.

"Woah." I even sounded different, fresh and raring to go. "This is-"

"An alchemical herbal remedy," Chiron answered. "Mixed in with a few drops of nectar."

Awesome.

"Though I wouldn't drink too much of it."

Oh, right. That was a thing with the food and drink of the gods, wasn't it?

"Cause we'd spontaneously combust, right?"

Chiron gave me an odd look.

"Of course not. Why would you assume that?"

Um.

"Stupid guess?" I offered lamely, and he seemed to accept that even if he kept looking at me funny. Sairaorg snickered under his breath, and I turned to glare at him half-heartedly.

Great.

Not five minutes in and I was already the class clown.

"It's a supplement," Chiron said. "It greatly bolsters healing up to a degree, but past a certain quantity it won't do anything besides give you a stomach ache. It's also mildly intoxicating in large amounts."

Intoxi-?

I blinked.

"...Is this magical booze?"

Chiron smiled again, amused, and then he snapped his fingers right after and both flasks disappeared straight out of our hands.

"...You know, that wasn't an answer."

The centaur's lips pulled up some more, and he gestured back to the house in the distance.

"You boys need to go get cleaned up. I'll put things straight here."

I winced when he pointed a the garden, because we'd made one heck of a mess out of it.

Half the grass I could see was ash after my first little light show when we'd kicked things off, the earth was pockmarked with shallow craters courtesy of Sairaorg stomping around like he was playing a demented game of whack-a-mole and winning, and there was even an enormous tree at the end of the field that had a whole chunk of its trunk carved out via ballistic fist and looked about five seconds away from toppling over.

"Sorry?" Sairaorg rubbed his head sheepishly, and Chiron chuckled.

"There's no need to apologize. This is nothing compared to what I expect of you in the future." He shooed us away absently. "Now off you trot."

"...Was that a horse pun?"

I swear, I only heard it after I said it. My brain-to-mouth filter was such an uncooperative jerk.

Sairaorg snorted, and then his eyes went a little wide when Chiron frowned.

"A what?"

Would centaurs find horse jokes offensive?

From the panicked look he gave me when I turned to him almost desperately, Sairaorg didn't know either.

"Well?"

"..." "..."
In that moment, Sairaorg and I connected - like our brainwaves just synchronized and allowed us to think on the same wavelength with perfect clarity.

He nodded solemnly.

I nodded right back.

It was profound, really.

"Nothing!" "Bye!"

As one, we noped right out of that conversation like we owed it money and started hightailing it back up to the house.

I think I might have heard Chiron laugh at us as we sprinted away, but that could have just been the wind.

...​

I was only just stepping out of the shower and wrapping myself up with a towel before I remembered an important little tidbit I hadn't thought about before.

I had no clothes.

As in, literally none, except for what I was wearing when whatever it was that happened went down and I ended up here, and at this point those were totally gross.

Luckily, Chiron must have noticed that a lot sooner than I had, because there was a pair of jeans, a shirt and a jacket plus a whole bunch of extra stuff folded up on the bed in little piles when I got back to the room.

There was even a new pair of trainers at the foot of the bed.

"Huh."

... I'm really going to end up owing him a lot, aren't I?

It was an uncomfortable feeling that I pushed down quickly - it wasn't like I had much of a choice, not right now - and I got dressed in record time.

The others were already there when I went down the stairs and turned a corner - Sairaorg was sitting at a counter and waved me over cheerily, and Chiron was idly laying out plates from the other end, and the smell of baked goodness and stuff I was suddenly way too hungry to tell apart hit me like a freight train.

"You're just in time for breakfast."

It just got better when I took the seat next to Sairaorg - There were bread rolls and puffed pastries, butter and jars of jam, yogurt cups and plates of fruit, eggs and sliced sausages, and even a couple of salad bowls in the middle of it all, besides a pot of tea and pitcher full of orange juice.

I was halfway through my first plate before I remembered to breathe, and I went for seconds and thirds before I even looked up.

Sairaog was inhaling his food just as fast, and even Courage looked like he was having the time of his life across the room with the bowl that'd been put aside for him.

"All done then?" Chiron asked when we cleared our plates and started stacking them off to the side. "Good. Then let's discuss your training."

I sat up and downed the last of my orange juice.

This sounded important.

"I said I would train you, and I will. Your physical conditioning will begin tomorrow," He promised both of us, and something about the way he said that was downright ominous. "But for today, I want to see how you handle basic arms training."

"Weapons?"

I may have perked at that, but Sairaorg sounded hesitant.

"I don't use weapons."

Chiron raised a brow.

"You don't, do you?"

"I-" He looked like he was having a hard finding the right words. "I want to be strong without relying on anything but my bare hands. That's my dream."

The way he said that last part came out so fierce and determined I almost leaned back on reflex.

In response, Chiron nodded and smiled almost supportively.

He walked around the counter and raised his hand hand, and pulled the same materialising magic trick from before, only this time instead of a flask it was a long, polished wooden staff that appeared in his grip, ash-colored and rounded at the end.

Then, without missing a beat, he leaned over and smacked Sairaorg over the head with it.

"Ow!"

"What was that about weapons again?"

Sairaorg's eyes widened, and I winced in sympathy.

I think I knew where this was going.

"I don't-"

Crack.

"But-"

Crack.

"I-"

Crack.

Every time he went to answer, the staff landed. There's no way the blows really hurt - take that from me, because I knew firsthand just how hard Sairaorg's skull is, but that couldn't have been fun to deal with either.

Eventually, they fell into this stalemate where neither of them moved or spoke.

Sairaorg opened his mouth.

Chiron wiggled his staff.

Sairaorg closed his mouth, a frustrated look on his face, and the one on Chiron's softened.

"Foolish child." His voice was still quiet, but now he sounded almost nostalgic. "The kind of strength you seek is admirable, and your dream is a worthy one. However-"

He wagged a finger when Sairaorg's expression brightened hopefully.

"-That doesn't mean you have to be a fool about it. Many a warrior have fallen because of false or over-inflated pride."

"It's not pride!" The devil protested vehemently. "I just believe in my body, that's all!"

"And when you are exhausted or outmatched, and have only a weapon you don't know how to use to bridge the gap?" Chiron chided "Or when you face an opponent who can only be defeated or countered by certain specific tools, and you don't have the skills to use them?"

Sairaorg's eyes went a little wide, like the idea had never occurred to him - or maybe he'd just never focused on it much - but the centaur didn't ease up.

"What will your strength be worth then?"

No answer.

"I'm not telling you that you must use a weapon. Only that, while you train under my roof, you must learn to passably wield at least two. It's better safe than sorry, as the saying goes, and I will accept nothing less."

"...Okay." Sairaorg sounded reluctant, but he nodded, and Chiron leaned back in satisfaction.

"Good. Consider it additional training - I also expect the same dedication and conditioning you've taken to strengthen your body to continue as well, and increase in time. No student of mind will fall behind in any way as long as I have anything to say about it."

Sairorg started at that, and then he beamed and clenched a fist.

"Yes!"

Chiron chuckled warmly, and then he turned to me.

"The same applies to you."

"I figured."

"Though in your case, it'll be three weapons including your bow."

I frowned.

"What, that doesn't count?"

I wasn't complaining or anything, but Chiron still leaned over to put a hand on my shoulder. He smiled at me the same way my old history teacher would - the sickly sweet look she'd give me right before sticking me with a week's worth of detention.

"You are a child of Apollon, Daniel. Of course it doesn't." His smile got a little bigger, and I swear it felt like I was staring down a tiger for a split second. "If you cannot master your bow to the extent that you put mortal Olympic champions to fail with the overwhelming advantages your heritage gives you, there won't be a single word in any language to describe how utterly inept you are."

"..."

Then he turned and strode out of the room.

"Now come, both of you. We're wasting daylight."

The two of us just watched him go for a second.

"...Holy crap," I muttered eventually. "He's got no mercy."

Sairaorg nodded quickly. "Right!?"

We stared at each other a bit, and then we started laughing.

...​

I won't bore you with all the details of what came next.

Cliff notes version?

Chiron led us to this gardening shed out back behind his house - only it wasn't so much a gardening shed as it was a small armory, with rows and rows of weapons of every kind you could imagine mounted on the walls like something straight out of a movie.

He even had a few guns, for Dad's sake - and he only winked conspiratorially when I saw them and gaped at him.

I picked out a blunted sword - couldn't tell you what kind, only that I could probably swing it around one handed if I tried - and a spear off one of the racks and followed after him when he led us back out to the field that we'd sparred in just that morning - only it looked spotless now, like we'd never been there at all.

The tree was gone though.

Chiron paced forward a bit, turned around and drove his staff into the soil, point first.

Before I could ask him what he was doing, I felt it.

His eyes glinted with a flare of power, and a burst of green light suddenly surged down the staff and into the ground. The earth immediately began to rumble and shake, and then the dirt in between us bubbled up and parted, and figures clambered out of the hole Chiron carved out for them.

They looked like stone mannequins but they were all disproportionate, faceless and just barely playing the part of humanoid, like boulders with limbs stapled on, and each of them towered over me at six-foot-something.

Worse, nearly all of them were holding onto enormous greatswords sculpted from the same dark rock that made up the rest of them, and a few in the back of the quickly growing mob had spears that were just as ridiculous-looking as the rest.

"Lesson zero!" Chiron said, and he actually sounded excited. That was about the point Sairaorg and I figured out exactly how screwed we were, and we both paled. "A demonstration of your current skill level - start!"

Every one of them raised their weapons and pointed them right at us.

"Oh come on!" I backed right the hell up. The sword in my hand suddenly felt like it weighed a thousand tons, and I itched for my bow. "Can we talk about this?"

"I don't know." Chiron hummed conversationally as the first rock-faced monstrosity started towards me, raising its sword and swinging it in a wide arc. "Can you?"

"Heh." Sairaorg laughed nervously, awkwardly angling the spear he clearly had no idea how to use. "This is going to hurt, isn't it?"

My day got progressively worse from there.

...​

So.

We got the crap kicked out of us.

I'm not going to describe what lesson zero was like either - I don't ever want to talk about it again.

Let's just say that Chiron's golems - that's what he called them after we were done, ignoring both our reproachful looks like an expert - had a whole bunch of fun wailing on us and knocking us around left, right and center.


The only time they'd let up was after they managed to disarm us, and they waited just long enough for us to pick up our weapons again before they charged us again.

I guess it was supposed to be a learning experience, probably. Their moves were repetitive and steady, and maybe we were supposed to take something from that, but I didn't think it was working.

In my defense though, I'd like to see you getting hit with an impact that feels like you're being run over by an eighteen-wheeler going a hundred miles an hour over and over again and see what you manage to learn about driving from it.

They eventually stopped beating on us and started actually teaching, sort of, slowing down their moves enough that we could copy them clumsily and actually try and pick up a trick or two, but by then I was already regretting ever born.

When Chiron called an end to practice a few hours later, I didn't even wait for his minions from hell to collapse back into inanimate stone before I dropped flat on my back and tried not to throw up.

My chest heaved with the effort it took just to groan.

Swords suck. Bows are god.

Lesson learned - I'm not even going to talk about the spear, even though that had kind of gone better until it didn't.

I had the fresh welts to prove it.

A shadow fell over me and blotted out the setting sun.

"I honestly expected worse." Chiron seemed chipper, and a part of me wanted to throw something at him for it. "You have good instincts for an absolute beginner. You both do."

I groaned some more. Sairaorg might have tried to thank him, but it came out more like a garbled wheeze - he'd taken a lot of hits that I'd managed to dodge.

"Regardless, well done! Next time, we begin specialized instruction." He clapped his hands, and the ground began to shift and put itself back together, though I couldn't even lift my head to watch the magic happen "Now get up, and refresh yourselves before dinner. You'll have to turn in early tonight - you'll need it for tomorrow."

Wait, what?

That didn't sound good. Hadn't he said something about 'physical conditioning?'

"What happens tomorrow?"

I started to panic when he didn't answer.

"Chiron, what happens tomorrow?"

He hummed noncommittally, which did frankly terrible things for my blood pressure.

"A word of advice? Sleep with one eye open." He said that in the same kind of voice you'd use to talk about the weather, and by that point even Sairaorg was looking worried again. "You never know what manner of threats can catch you unaware."

And with that terrifying comment, he called it quits and left us in the dirt.

...​

Despite knowing that it might be a bad idea, I still fell asleep.

Yeah, I know it was dumb, but I'd come out of the lesson feeling like my everything from the neck down had been tenderised and then pitched into a meat-grinder for good measure.

Honestly, I blame the probable brain damage.

That, and the part of me that thought that there were still lines that shouldn't be crossed.

I mean, come on - our beds had to be some kind of unanimous time-out zone, right?

Sleep was sacred, after all.

That's what any reasonable person would think.

Then I blinked awake a whole half hour before dawn as I felt something wrap around my ankle and go tight enough to make my foot go numb.

The room was still dark, obviously, but there was enough residual light for me to sit up, still half-asleep and rubbing the blurriness out of my eyes, and frown in slow confusion at the apparently sentient rope that wrapping it's way around my leg of its own free will, and trailing all the way off the bed, across the floor and out my bedroom door.

Wait, that didn't sound right-?

The second I started waking up properly, something on the other end of the rope yanked and I went flying off the bed in a tangle of blankets and pillows with a half-aborted curse on the tip of my tongue. I slammed down on my back hard, and then I was dragged across the floor and out the room like a fish on a hook so quickly I almost got friction burns trying to hold on for dear life, but it was useless.

Then we started hurtling towards the stairs.

"Oh for-!"

Bang.

By the time we made it down all the steps, my head had bounced off of them so many times it might as well have been a tennis ball and I'd landed in a heap so painful you'd think I was trying to mimic an origami crane.

When the rope was finally done tugging me around, I found myself parked right in front of Chiron's feet.

Well, hooves actually, but you get the idea.

The centaur looked amused by the way I stared up at him, mouth flapping uselessly as the rope vanished with a wave of his hand.

"Good morning, student of mine."

"Why!?"

"Because it's time for physical conditioning, of course, and a part of that will involve working on your situational awareness, which is currently abysmal. Now, give me a moment, and-"

On cue, there was a startled yelp somewhere upstairs and a loud thump, and a few seconds later Sairoarg was hurtling down the same expressway I'd taken to get here, rope and everything.

"Ugh!"

"-There we go."

Chiron took a sip from the mug of tea he was carrying and nodded like he hadn't just almost broken both our necks, and I suddenly realized something very important.

Our new teacher was absolutely nuts.

It may have taken a while to sink in, but better late than never.

"Now that we're all here, it's time to get to work."

...Or maybe not.

"What work?" You'd be worried too if you saw the gleam in his eyes. "What are we doing?"

"Oh, nothing much." The lie was the most bold-faced one I'd ever heard in my life. "The two of you will be going on a run, right about... now."

The marble flooring we were on lit up with a brilliant green hue, and my ears popped as it felt like the room around as depressurised and my stomach went oddly weightless, and then the world shifted around us like the fastest scene change in history.

The air got colder. The ground beneath us became rough and uneven rock, and the walls melted away into a view of this steep, enormous valley that stretched out far, far below in the shadow of two mountains and opened up to an entire landscape of sprawling green wilderness and stony terrain that went covered thing from my feet to the horizon.

It was the kind of view you'd only see on untamed nature documentaries. and advertisements.

"Teleportation circle?" Sairaorg murmured, and I inhaled in surprise. Those were a thing here, weren't they? "Where are we?"

"My favorite mountain trail," Chiron answered... nothing at all, actually, not that I exactly paying attention right that second. Teleportation was crazy distracting the first time around. "I want you both to run it from start to finish, and I won't give you a time limit. Not for this first go around."

He lifted his hands and brought them together like he was cupping a handful of water, and more green light pooled in his grip. The little spark rose out a second later and bobbed in the air like a miniature floating lantern, circling his head and flitting about this way and that.

"Follow the wisp, and it'll keep you on the trail."

Chiron lifted a finger and tapped it, and it shot over and started orbiting around us in a wide arc.

Sairaorg blinked.

"Wait, that's it?"

I would have smacked him upside the head myself for a tempting fate like that, but Chiron smiled again, and I immediately knew to brace for impact.

"That's it," He agreed, before leaning forward all of a sudden. "Though there is one little thing."

And there it is.

Sairaorg didn't have enough time to look confused before Chiron put his hand on his shoulder.

"Lesser Curse Of Atlas."

One second, he was standing upright.

The next, the magic hit him like a gunshot, and his knees dropped to the ground hard enough that you could hear the little pebbles underneath him splinter from the force of it.

"Just to make it more challenging." Chiron didn't seem bothered by the way he was struggling to lift his head off the ground at all. Instead, he turned to me. "Clench your teeth."

When I tell you the alarm bells started going off like crazy, I mean it.

"Why-?"

"Lesser Curse Of Atlas."

Oh. Because I nearly bit my tongue off in the landing. That's why.

See, that makes sense.

"How does it feel?"

I couldn't answer him, because I was flat on my face and struggling to breathe before I even realized what was going on.

It was like the dream I had last night, only a thousand times worse - Every muscle in my body turned to fire. My bones felt like they were being ground into dust. I wanted to scream, but opening my mouth would have taken energy I didn't have.

"Sairaorg, go. Get started." I heard Chiron say, but it sounded like he was a million miles away. I heard a sound I think might have been Sairaorg finally getting back to his feet, but at this point pain-induced hallucinations were definitely on the table so who even knew anymore. "The wisp will guide you."

"But he's-"

"He'll join you in a minute," Chiron promised. "Or maybe not. That's up to him."

"...I won't go far." I heard him say stubbornly, and it might have been aimed at me, and then his too-heavy footsteps went thudding off down the mountain path.

Then Chiron was speaking to me.

"Terrible spell, isn't it? It's intended for enemies, ordinarily, but this isn't the first time I've used it as a training tool instead."

I didn't try and say anything. All of my brainpower was going into focus on how I wanted to not be utterly pulverized.

"I wouldn't have cast it on you if I didn't think you could handle it. You are a demigod, Daniel."

I wanted to yell at him.

No, really!?

I guess it must have shown on my face - whatever part of it that wasn't tomato-red from the strain, at least, because he chuckled.

I was starting to hate that chuckle.

"I don't say that to be pedantic." I could see him stride a little closer to me as he spoke out of the corner of my eye. "You possess within you a fraction of the power of a god - divinity incarnate. Your strength is dependant on your faith in yourself, and I mean that quite literally."

My vision was starting to go black at the edges and everything else was tinting red, but I still latched on to that last bit and the odd way he phrased it like a lifeline.

What does that mean?

"You exist on the line that separates mortals from godhood." Chiron idly explained like he wasn't watching me get flattened into a pancake. "You can do more than any mortal - you are more than any mortal. If you want to learn to use your power, you have to accept that the extraordinary is your natural state of being."

That sounded...
How was that helpful?

"You have no comprehension of the limits of your potential, and you'll never learn them until you start striding towards them. Stop waiting for your power to burst out of when you need it most and command it too."

I wanted to ask him what the hell that was supposed to look like, but I was pretty sure I was on the verge of blacking out now. I reached out for that urgent, burning sensation from before, trying to make it work for me.

Come on, give me a hand here!

What was it that Chiron said again?

Command it?

I'm the demigod here, I thought, trying to force some uncooperative godly corner of myself to get with the freaking program, and I'm telling you to get out here right the hell now!

For a second, the part of me that wasn't flailing wildly like it was being tortured - which It kind of was, now that I think about it - felt like an absolute moron.

I can fight cyclopes and hellhounds and not completely lose my mind when hopping worlds for the second time in the entirety of my existence. I am not tapping out now!

My fury fed into itself in a loop until I was nearly screaming through gritted teeth.

"Get. Up. Now."

Then I felt it - the tugging in my gut, and then the spreading warmth lancing up through my veins like reflected sunlight about to erupt-!

"No!" He said sharply, and I lost my focus. The warmth I'd been calling up slipped and vanished, and it was like the force crushing me down doubled in power. I nearly choked trying to cry out, and my spine felt like it was on the verge of snapping. "Do it again, but slowly. Carefully. A candle that burns twice as bright lasts half as long, and a candle that burns a thousand times brighter won't hold its flame for even a blink of an eye. Bring it back, but steady it. Control it."

What do you think I'm trying to do!?

But despite the frustration, I think I kind of got what he was trying to say anyway.

The next time I tried to pull on that power, I... grabbed onto it, almost. Forced it to pour out slowly, instead of all in one rush - like I was adjusting the handle on a water faucet.

The warmth spread through me again, and this time I made it work for me.

Steady. Don't burn out.

This was different from before - I could feel it. Instead of surging out in one burst, it built up steadily and lingered until it felt like every atom that made me up was suffused with it, and suddenly I could breathe again.

Slowly, the pressure from Chiron's curse began to decrease, forced back bit by bit from unbearable to crushing to just plain old heavy, and with a grunt, I managed to get my hands out underneath me and heaved myself back up to my feet.

"That's the spirit!"

I was ready to tackle Chiron when I got up, consequences be damned, but then I caught the geniunely proud smile and it stalled me. He was looking me over from head to toe, and I belatedly noticed that I was glowing a little - a soft golden aura that reminded me of the outdoors at the height of summer.

"Now we're getting somewhere."

He even sounded proud, the way my uncle would when I walked into the house with an A on my report card, and I felt that anger slip away before I could even try and hold onto it.

The fact that I felt borderline invincible and ready to leap off the ground and fly from sheer euphoria and relief probably helped too.

Wait, hold on, can I actually fly?

I shelved that gleeful thought off to the side for a second as I tried to glare at Chiron.

"That was a nightmare. You could have warned me."

He took that in for a second, and then tipped back his head and laughed.

"There would have been no point. It's about to get a whole lot worse." A bow materialised in his hands, with a quiver over his shoulders - neither of them mine. "I'll give you a head start to catch up to Sairaorg and make whatever ground you can before we start working on your awareness and evasion."

The grin he gave me was downright menacing.

"Good luck, student. You have ten minutes."

"...my god." I whispered, already stepping back. "You are evil."

His eyes narrowed, and he started nocking an arrow.

"And now you have one."

Crap.

...​

Sairaorg grinned up at me when he saw me sprinting down the mountain like the hounds of hell were after me - and where was Courage anyway? - and looked ready to high-five me on the spot, curse be damned.

"You did it-!"

Then he choked as I grabbed him by the collar faster than he could blink, yanked him into the run with me and started following after the wisp of light bobbing in the distance.

"TALK LATER!" I roared just as the sound of arrows through the air whistling through the air began to chase after us - and how I heard that was anyone's guess. "RUN NOW!"

This time, I definitely wasn't imagining it

Chiron was definitely still laughing at us before it started raining pain, and things just went crazy from there.

...
