#204
The last 'slow' chapter that sets some stuff up, foreshadows some more, and gets us into the flow of things.

I never thought there'd be a day where I'd miss my basketball coach's teaching methods, but here we are.

Sure, Coach Williams had a lot of fun making anyone and everyone on the team run suicides until they dropped the second they put so much as a toe out of line, but at least he never actually threw the basketballs at us while we were at it.

Or, in Chiron's case, send enough falling arrows after us to blot out the sky.

You think I'm kidding?

The first few volleys that came streaking down were the easiest to avoid, even if the arrows were falling by the dozen, because I could almost feel them coming.

I'd call it a sixth sense, but that wouldn't be doing it justice - We ran, and suddenly it was as if I had some kind of inbuilt radar that kept pinging at the back of my head every time one was loosed into the air, and I forced us to weave and zig-zag across the rocky path we were charging ahead on even as they peppered and pierced through the ground around us and missed by feet - sometimes inches - without ever looking up to check.

I might have stopped to question it if I could, but I don't think Chiron was the sort to give time-outs and Sairaorg was more than happy to follow my lead on this one, so I rolled with it - and things had been going well, too.

"LEFT, LEFT! GO LEFT!"

"MY LEFT OR YOUR LEFT!?!"

"SAIRAORG, MY LEFT IS YOUR LEFT!"

"THAT'S WHAT YOU SAID LAST TIME!"

"JUST DO IT!"

"FINE!"

"WAIT, NO, I MEANT RIGHT!"

"SERIOUSLY?!"

"SORRY!"

...Okay, maybe not that well, but cut me a little slack here - I like to believe that I can think fast under pressure, and I usually can, but you could have crushed coal into diamonds with the kind that I was under right then, and a few teensy near-misses here and there on my first go-around with yet another fresh new power I didn't even know I had going for me until five minutes ago totally didn't count.

Still, I'd had us pretty much covered.

Then I guess Chiron must have stopped warming up or something, because things went from 'pear-shaped' to 'oh god why' in the blink of an eye.

I almost tripped over my feet and fell flat on my face when I felt the next volley of arrows coming - not an even dozen anymore, but twice that, and then triple that, and then they were just too many to count and all closing in on us fast.

"INCOMING!"

Sairaorg didn't question me this time - he had his own gut instincts too, and they were plenty sharp - and we kicked it up a notch as one.

And I mean that.

Woosh.

We'd already been going at it like we were training for the Olympic sprints despite the Lesser Curse Of Atlas weighing us down like a sack of bricks tied around our ankles, but the burst of speed we put on in that split-second was nothing short of insane - and right on time, too.

The moment the first of the arrows hit the ground that we'd just been treading over before, it was like the apocalypse had come early.

See, they weren't just regular arrows anymore - clearly, that would have been too easy.

Instead, nearly all of them had their own gimmick.

Some burst into blistering flames. Others blasted out waves of stifling frost. A few erupted with gale-force winds, and a handful more let loose with crackling lightning, complete with peals of thunder and everything, over and over again.

Every last one did something, and the combined flare of power hit like a cataclysm and nearly flung us off our feet, which would have gone even worse than you'd think because at no point did Chiron actually stop firing- oh no.

I didn't even know how he was doing it - we should have left him behind and a million miles away, but he obviously didn't get that memo.

More arrows landed - fire and frost licked at us painfully, daggers of wind stabbed at our eyes, and I came this close to getting the worst tasing in history more times than I could count.

Even the ground seemed to go from solid terrain to a living minefield out to get us - It was a complete nightmare.

So it probably said some stuff about me that I was having the time of my life.

Yeah, I said that.

It was terrifying, but once we hit our stride, I couldn't help but fall backward into that same feeling I got the first time I fired my bow and killed that hellhound, only this was even better - like riding the fastest roller coaster in the universe, only it was you in the driver's seat pulling off all the crazy twists and flips without even a lap-bar holding you in place - just sheer strength.

I felt unstoppable, on top of the world even, and I wasn't the only one.

The sounds of the forces of nature coming after us with a vengeance may have been stupidly loud, but even they couldn't drown out Sairaorg's booming laugh, or the wild grin I could see out of the corner of my eye.

And once he got started, I couldn't stop myself either, and so there we were, laughing like we'd lost all our marbles and bolting after the floating sprite like there was no tomorrow while everything in sight went to hell in a hand basket.

It was amazing, in all the worst and the best of ways.

We didn't shut up until the sprite finally changed course - it took a sudden sharp left and flew off towards the mountainside, and we were forced to veer after it as it went, scrambling over uneven ground that was quick to shift into something that much harsher and more jagged and abruptly leaping through the mouth of a darkened cave neither of us realized we were coming up to until we were already there.

The arrow fire didn't stop for a few more beats, the impacts sending tremors through the cave, so neither did we - we followed the sprite through a winding tunnel that sloped further down with every step, the air growing cold and damp and the light getting dimmer until it was only the soft green glow our magical guide radiated and the shimmer of golden aura coming off of me that lit up the path we were on and made the limestone-grey walls look alive with our shifting shadows.

We went far enough down into it that we eventually had to slow down, even if I still had enough adrenaline rushing through me to kill a dragon.

The sound of the arrows finally petered out a little after that..

A few minutes passed in tense silence, but Chiron didn't come charging in after us, and the wisp kept gently bobbing in our line of sight as it waited for us to catch up.

Sairaorg bit his lip "Is it over?"

"...Maybe?"

We both shared a look and immediately grimaced.

Okay, no.

Something stank to high heaven here - I'd only met Chiron three days ago and I already knew enough to understand that there was no way he'd let us off that easily.

Of course, because the universe had a sense of humor, that's when the tunnel opened up into the massive underground cavern and we walked right into the lair of the scorpion.

Before then, whenever I thought of these guys, I'd remember this old poster we had hanging in my biology class a few years back - a close-up diagram of an eight-legged arachnid with a black-brown carapace, a gnarly-looking stinger at the end of its segmented tail, and a lower body that was half burrowed in between the stalagmites it deliberately dug it's way into to take a nap.

This one looked almost exactly like that... only it was also the size of a small house.

Feel free to picture that for a second.

Its head was almost as big as a minivan all on its own, and its pincers looked like they could snap tree trunks in half with one clip. It had two oily black eyes on either side of its face and six more symmetrically divided underneath the first pair, all of them so dark I would've mistaken them for great hollow pits if I looked at them from the wrong angle, and its tail was wider than me at its thinnest point and was propped over its back like a carry-on bag, the tip gleaming dangerously in the green and golden glow.

Worse, there were ... leftovers scattered all around it.

Discarded swords and spears stabbed into the ground or haphazardly tossed aside, broken pieces of armour and scraps, and what had to be at least a few piles of bones that I had to try very hard not to think about for too long.

Looking up at it from just a few feet away was... well.

I wasn't even scared at this point - just done.

No, nope, nada and no thank you.

I had no open slots in my calendar for this - Please try again sometime between the seventh of never going to happen and the twelfth of in your most unholy dreams.

Turning around to catch Sairaorg's eyes in the relative dark - and let me tell you, he looked just as enthused about this as I was - I jammed a thumb over my shoulder and soundlessly mouthed the words at him.

Time to go. Right now.

He nodded very quickly, and we both started very carefully backing up. The scorpion stayed unmoving, dead to the world and totally oblivious to us being within striking range, and we put the first few feet between us without a hitch.

At this point you're probably already thinking to yourself: Hey, I've seen this movie before! One of these dashing morons is about to step on a stick or a pile of dried leaves or something and wake that thing right the hell up, right?

If that's what went through your mind then congratulations, because you're exactly right.

As soon as stepped back a little more, my foot landed on an inconspicuous patch of dirt that I knew had been flatter than a sheet of paper right before, and it let out a loud, ear-splitting crack.

I froze

Sairaorg froze.

Even the light sprite seemed to stop bobbing in the air, and the sound continued to echo and reverberate off the cavern walls and in between the stalactites above us, sharp and brittle like ice snapping under pressure.

The scorpion stirred.

"...Really?"

My exhausted sigh was drowned out when the thing's eyes lit up with a rising hiss - and when I say lit up, I mean that they flashed like neon-blue searchlights the size of large basketball hoops as they came alive, and Sairaorg and I's collective life expectancy curdled faster than a week-old milk carton when they locked onto us half a second later.

For a moment, nobody moved a muscle.

Then I smiled brightly.

"Good morning sir. Do you have a moment to speak about your vacuum cleaners' extended warranty options?"

It hissed, audibly confused, and its tail began to sway from side to side, like it was getting ready to lash out but couldn't decide whether the bite-sized snack in front of it was actually serious or if it was just hallucinating out of hunger.

That, or maybe it really did want to talk about vacuum cleaners.

After the last couple of days I've had, every kind of crazy had a place on this bandwagon.

"Ah, you don't have one? I can see how that's been a problem for you. This place could really use a good spring cleaning. In fact, we should just leave and come back at better time, right, Sairaorg?"

"Already gone!"

Now, see, that right there is why he and I were going to get along.

The hiss that came after us as we turned back and bolted quickly shifted into a screech of pure, uninhibited murder as the scorpion began to rip itself out of the earth it was partly submerged in - probably because it didn't appreciate the dig at its home - and we broke apart in either direction an instant before the stinger to end all stingers landed between us and pierced through solid rock like a toothpick sinking into wet clay.

"Holy-!"

It didn't slow down as it tore its tail free with a spray of crushed and pulverized limestone, and I had to duck my head low to dodge a chunk of the stuff the size of a mini-fridge.

We scrambled towards the cavern tunnel - only the scorpion wasn't having any of that. Instead of chasing after us in a straight line though, it went off to the side, towards the cavern wall.

Have you ever seen a spider flit from one spot to another too fast for your eyes to track?

The resident rage monster decided to pull that trick as it clambered over the nearest wall sideways and tore forwards with terrifying speed to catch up, clearing the distance and coming back in from the side just in time to cut us off and lunge with its pincers.

Sairaorg yelped and flung himself out of reach before it could get its claws on him, but it was a near miss by the skin of his teeth, and then he did something I hadn't seen from him before.

With a burst of displaced air, a pair of leathery bat-like wings exploded out behind him and he rocketed straight up and out of the way of another deadly swipe.
Right - Devil.

I couldn't afford to stop and stare the way a part of me wanted to, but that little display still clinched it for me.

I am so figuring out how to fly after this.

Until then, though...

My eyes narrowed as I caught sight of the discarded weapons across the cavern, my mind firing of a mile a minute, and several things came together up there in the vague shape of a plan.

"Sairaorg!" I yelled as I started sprinting, hoping that he could pay attention in his "Cover your ears!"

I gave him five seconds, then I opened my mouth and... roared?

Screamed?

Both?

In the end it didn't matter what the right word for it was, because this time the eruption of horrendously cascading noise that I let rip on command was entirely intentional and a thousand times worse than the last - the air visibly vibrated from the force of it, the walls and stalactites shook and rattled like they were on the verge of coming apart at the seams, and the scorpion stopped swiping at Sairaorg - who had his ears shut and could have broken a few teeth if he gritted them any harder - and instead seemed to lock down, shuddering all over in silent agony.

It bought me the time to reach over to the discarded weapons, yank up the nearest spear into my grip and turn to take aim in one movement.

I knew what to do now - After all, archery may come naturally to me, but the instinctive near-perfect marksmanship that came with that package wasn't exclusive to just my bow and arrows.

Or at least I hoped.

The world seemed to slow down as I inhaled sharply, eyes closing for the span of one breath as I reached deep for the power I was only just starting to truly figure out.

Work with me here.

And it did.

The aura surrounding me brightened as I exhaled, sunlight surging through my veins with renewed intensity, and I heaved forward and launched the spear with more strength than I'd ever used before - more that I'd ever imagined I could use - and watched it flash through the air, puncture and bury itself in the first of the scorpion's eyes like a hot knife through butter.

The warbling hiss it let loose as its eye burst into goop and viscera running down its face was awful, and it got worse when Sairaorg got his head back in the game and flew down over its skull from above, cocked his fist back and punched it hard enough that I could swear I felt the impact rattle the back of my teeth.

Then he did it again.

It tried to swat him away with its pincers and stab at him with its stinger again, but my training partner was just as fast in the air as he was on his feet, and by the time it went for another lunge, Sairaorg's fist had lashed out a third time, and my second spear took out another eye.

After that, it went berserk - even managed to tag Sairaorg just slightly enough to fling him back a little and use the chance to thunder forward, gunning for me with a guttural screech of a war cry.

Crap.

I cursed under my breath before flinging the next weapon at it - a sword this time, but if it was pointy and could be thrown it was fair game as far as I was concerned.

I think it might have tried to dodge, but it only ended up catching the blade in the eye next to the one I'd been aiming for, and the pain broke its run into something uncontrolled that ended with it ramming head-first into the wall behind me after I got right out of the way.

When it turned around again, it was much more sluggish and slower to recover, and its tail kept swinging around erratically - On the defensive now instead of trying to go for the kill

Not that it helped - I grabbed another spear, Sairaorg dove in from above, the two of us closed in and things just got messy.

Five minutes later, it had no eyes left, the joints between its armored segments and the vulnerable spots across its tail were littered with whatever else I could throw at it before I ran out, and there was a genuine patchwork of cracks spiralling across its carapace and leaking things that made me appreciate the fact that I was doing all of this on an empty stomach, because I'd have probably had a hard time keeping anything down otherwise.

Eventually, it just slumped, its legs giving out underneath it and letting its weight hit the ground with a deep thud. I almost felt a little sorry for it as it gave us another hiss, this one barely just a whisper, before its tail curled in on itself and it went still and silent.

...

Slowly, we put some space between us, and then Sairaorg dropped down next to me.

When the scorpion didn't get back up - didn't so much as twitch - we relaxed.

"We beat it."

"Looks like it."

I glanced at him.

"Wings, huh?"

He blinked, surprised, and then folded them away like they weren't ever there at all.

"Didn't you know?"

"Oh, I did. You just never used them."

They looked strange - almost too thin to hold up his weight, but they seemed to work for him just fine.

He scratched his cheek and shrugged.

"I didn't need to."

Fair enough.

We stared at each other for another second, looked back down at the fallen scorpion, and then we grinned.

"That was-!"

"I know right-?!"

"Ahem."

We froze, and Chiron waved cheerily.

Neither of us had heard him coming.

"It looks like I'm going to have to drill better awareness in you quite thoroughly for the lesson to stick - a thought for later." He clicked his tongue as we twitched in place. "Still, well done. Better than expected once again, though next time, my foolish students, make sure your enemy is truly defeated before you start celebrating."

There was a rumble behind us, and the scorpion suddenly reared up blindingly quick, pincers raised to strike - one last ditch attempt at revenge when our backs were turned - but Chiron only flicked a single finger in its general direction, and it died.

No, seriously.

One minute it was trying to lunge, and the next it was a total goner as an entire column of explosive wind and magic so dense you could finger paint with the stuff shot past us and bored right through it, splattering its insides across the back wall in a display so grisly you'd think it was pulled straight out of one of those cheap monster flicks people loved rewatching on Halloween.

It was dead before it dropped the second time, and we stared.

"Right then. We'll have a talk about what you did right and wrong after you finish your run."

".."

You could have heard a pin drop.

"... we're not done?" Sairaorg sounded faint, and my ability to talk outright glitched while my brain stuttered and tried to reboot.

The look Chiron gave us both for that one was the kind you'd give a little kid asking to be president of the moon - indulgent and amused and a little condescending in that 'aww, aren't you just adorable' way - and then he raised his bow out of absolutely nowhere, and we were suddenly back in a world of hurt.

...​

Hours later, sometime near noon, after chasing us ragged up and down the mountain path until we were on the verge of either dropping dead or spontaneously combusting just to call it quits, Chiron finally let us stop.

Thank my dad.

We collapsed side by side onto the soft grass of the field he'd run us into like puppets with our strings cut.

"I think I might die," Sairaorg croaked, voice muffled by the earth beneath us, and I rasped something that might have been an agreement before rolling over onto my back and gasping in relief.

The sunlight should have been blinding, but all I got from it was a slow warmth that felt like it was seeping right through me. The ache in my everything dulled and went soft, and the exhaustion turned into something drowsy instead of painful.

Turns out sunbathing was good for me - Who'd have thunk it?

I basked in it for a little while, taking in the sound chirping of birds and then the cool breeze, then I flickered my eyes to Sairaorg, who kept twitching like he was fighting off the aftershocks of getting struck by lightning.

Come to think of it, he nearly had been.

Chiron did not mess around, even when we started slowing down.

An idea came to me as I looked at him, and I leaned over with a grunt and put my hand on his shoulder.

Apollo was the god of healing too, wasn't he?

Sairaorg jolted when the light wafting off of me began to pour over and into him.

"What-?"

"Don't question it," I warned him. "It might stop working."

I didn't know what exactly I was doing here, but my gut said that it felt right, and it was working - not by much and not for long, because my tank was well and truly near empty - but it was enough for his muscles to unlock and his breathing to even out, even if it did hitch at the start with surprised wonder and something else I was too out of it to focus on.

"Well, isn't that an interesting sight?" Chiron stepped over to us as I let my arm drop, and he sounded pleased. "It's about time."

I was tempted to throw something at him, but I had nothing on hand but dirt and I think he could sorta tell, because he gave me an 'I dare you' look and raised an eyebrow my way.

"..."

Dang it. I'm not suicidal enough to try.

Chiron laughed at my disgruntled expression and then turned to trot away.

"Come along then."

I propped myself up on my elbows and stared after him incredulously.

The Lesser Curse of Atlas had been... if not dispelled, the at least greatly reduced the second we'd stopped running, but even that still felt overwhelming right now.

"You think we can still move?"

"You can't? Oh well. I suppose I'll have lunch on my own, then."

"...Evil." I whispered under my breath and let my head drop back to the ground. "So damn evil!"

Sairoarg just groaned in agreement.

...​

Luckily we didn't have to go far before Chiron delivered up on the offer of lunch - he just snapped his fingers once, and a low table materialised right there in the clearing, loaded with plates of roasted vegetables, stuffed grape leaves, skewers of meat and wild greens along with a whole bunch of other stuff.

"Are you making the food with magic, or just bringing it here?"

"Who knows?"

Real helpful, that.

I didn't have the patience to ask him again, so I just focused on cramming down bits of everything in sight - With how hungry we both were, it's a miracle Sairaorg and I didn't go on to eat the table when we were done clearing off the plates.

Chiron waited for us to finish up before he waved a hand and banished it all away

"Satisfied?

"Thanks for the food." Sairaorg smiled, and I tossed him a thumbs up.

"Good. Now then," He locked his fingers together and shifted a little to stand more comfortably. "Questions?"

Finally.

"I get the arrow fire, but what was up with the scorpion?"

Because there's no way his sprite just happened to lead us into its lair by accident - pigs would fly, hell would freeze over and Apollo would come down from Olympus to play catch with me before I believed that.

"There are many organizations that like to breed certain magical beasts and creatures. For weapons, entertainment, or what have you.' Chiron said, and I could tell he was winding up for a lecture. "I came across that one in particular after it decimated the group of fools that bred it and started rampaging across the mountainside."

Sairaorg frowned, confused. "And you didn't kill it?"

I got where he was coming from - Chiron had basically eviscerated it with a thought right in front of us, so why bother keeping it around?

"It was my first impulse." He agreed. "Something went wrong in its creation, and it was not quite self-aware."

I coughed.

"Seemed plenty aware when it was trying to eat us."

"A degree of basic intelligence and deliberately engraved instincts are no substitute for true life - that malformed chimera had no capacity for growth, and so I found a location that was well out of the way and sealed it under wards designed to keep it in perpetual slumber. You broke them when you stepped inside."

"But why not just deal with it back then?

"I thought it might be useful somewhere down the line."

"Useful? The thousand-ton murder-bug?" I asked dubiously, and Sairaorg started snickering into his palm. "For real?"

The centaur shrugged.

"You'd be surprised. I am many thousands of years old, and when you live as long as I have in this great world of ours, you learn that anything has the potential to come in handy under the right circumstances at some point down the line." He smiled. "Case in point: it helped me test my new students, didn't it?"

"..." "..."

Sairaorg and I exchanged a look, and he shrugged too.

You know what?

Fair.

"But what about the weapons and the bones we found in there?"

Chiron laughed.

"Props. I set them up in there for dramatic effect."

I blinked.

That...

Huh.

Now I was a little underwhelmed.

"I have a good grasp of what I can expect from you, now." Chiron continued when neither of us said anything else "Still a few tests to run here and there-"

The panic on our faces must have been obvious, because he grinned widely.

"-but I know by and large where to focus my efforts with both of you. Soon, we'll get started on the basics of hand-to-hand combat. It's been quite a while since I've instructed anyone in classical Pankration."

I didn't know what that was, but the way his eyes glazed over with nostalgia wasn't exactly comforting, and Sairaorg perking up didn't do wonders for my confidence either.

"Tonight, however-" Chiron's tone melted into something softer. "You'll be going off into the city."

That came out of nowhere.

"What?"

"You'll be going off into the city." He repeated gently - not that it helped much.

"Why?" Sairaorg beat me to the punch this time. "What are we doing?"

"Whatever you want, I suppose."

"..."

"..."

"Okay, you win." I threw my hands up in frustration. "I'm lost - what's happening now?"

Chiron chuckled.

"Exactly what I said - you're free to go into the city and do whatever you'd like for the night, within reason. Or stay on the grounds, if you'd prefer that, so long as you do something restful." He idly stroked his beard as we stared at him, trying to figure out the game this time. "You've earned a few hours of recovery for the day, and you'll need it for tomorrow."
My eye twitched.

"What happens tomorrow?"

Naturally, he winked and ignored me.

"Go into the city, explore, and get to know each other and enjoy yourselves a little. Pick up a few groceries " His eyes twinkled a little as he looked us over. "And if you need a suggestion on where to go and what to do after that, I have a few."

And that was that.

...​

The last time I'd gone bowling had been ages ago now, so when I found the name of an alley on the list Chiron had given us right before he'd booted us out of the front door I figured it might be fun.

Sairaorg hadn't minded either, and the place was pretty cheap all things considered - I did have a bit to spend after all, from that stack I'd found from in the backpack Chiron had left me.

I'd tried to return it to to him a while ago - I would have felt sleazy trying to keep it without a word - but he just smacked me upside the head with the heavy end of his staff and gave me another for good measure when I tried to argue.

"Foolish student, it's rude to return gifts."

It took ten minutes for the ringing in my ears to stop after that, so there were no more arguments from me.

Koralli Bowling was a dingy little place on the outside, with a faded sign and lighting that was a little crappy, and basically empty when we walked into the building a few hours later, but it was good enough to shrug off if you were just there to have a little fun.

Bonus - the clerk at the stand let me bring in Courage after I promised he'd stay the sidelines and not make a mess.

My dog hadn't been happy that I'd nearly left him behind and had made that very clear when I tried.

"Courage, damn it, let go of my shoes!"

"Grrrrr!"

Yeah, let's not talk about it. I grabbed him a couple of snacks from Chiron's kitchen and let him munch away while Sairaorg and I minded our own business.

The air was thick with the scent of old leather, stale popcorn, and the faint whir of the ball return system when we got to our lanes, these long stretches of glossy dark wood banged up by scuff marks and the occasional dent.

Neat.

I grabbed a ball from the return and I gave it a little twirl, grinning at the way the weight of it settled in my hands before I glanced over at Sairaorg.

"You ever played before?"

"No, but I know how." He paused. "I think."

"Knock yourself out."

He took a step forward, cocked back his hand a little and tossed his hand at a slight angle. The ball went zipping across the lane just a little too fast for a throw like that - if you weren't in the know, at least - and all but three pins went scattering with a loud crack.

"Hah!"

"What, you think that was good?

I mean, it totally was, but I wasn't about to let him have that before I leaned forward and took my own shot, and the ball sailed forward with a heavy rolling and a thwack that ended with a clean strike.

I grinned.

"Score!"

Sairaorg's smile turned competitive.

"Oh, it's on."

We got through some two dozen throws each before we slowed down enough that we could talk again.

"So, Sairaorg."

"Yeah?"

"How come you've come to train with Chiron?

I was just making small talk, but he almost missed a step in surprise and I frowned.

What was up with that?

I only asked because I didn't remember much of his story besides the basics- I don't think there was much of one, to be honest, but I think I would have known about him training with someone so famous if it had ever come up, and he looked uncomfortable at the question.

"...He's Chiron," Sairaorg explained, but it was slower and more hesitant than before. "If anyone can make me as strong as I want to be, or even stronger, it's him. And-"

I put my hands up when he glanced at me.

"You don't have to tell me if you don't want to."

"No, it's fine." He sighed and put the ball he was holding back onto the rack. "The thing is, I'm a devil."

"...Yeah, I got that. Hate to break it to you, but the bat-wings were a bit of a giveaway."

He snorted, and I grinned a little as he relaxed.

"Devil don't really have a good reputation with any other faction. Our ancestors really messed up back in the day, and even if things are better now, there are still plenty of devils today who are nearly just as bad." He said carefully, and I think I picked up what he was getting at pretty quickly. "Most people despise and want nothing to do with us, and I figured being a student of Chiron would make me strong, and help me with that too. He doesn't train just anyone, after all."

"So you want his stamp of approval," I said, and he nodded. "Is there a reason why?"

Because he was still hesitating, and nothing he'd said so far seemed to explain it.

"I want to make a deal with someone."

I blinked

A... devil deal?

Those were a thing, weren't they?

"Someone?"

"Maybe a Greek god."

I choked and nearly dropped the ball I was holding on my foot.

"Are you insane?"

I blurted it out before I could stop myself, but in my defense, that came out of nowhere.

I didn't know anything about the Greek gods in this world, but if they were anything like back home, then you couldn't just go up to them and make deals.

That's how you get sent on deadly quests or errands that have a ninety percent dismemberment rate, and that's assuming they didn't punish you for the audacity of trying to haggle with them like that anyway.

"I know it sounds a little crazy." A little? "But I don't have much of a choice, and it's just an idea I had."

"Crazy doesn't cover it, dude. Have you just not read Greek mythology?" I know he was probably just as impulsive as I was on a good day, but this just takes the cake. "Why would you want to-?"

"Do you know what the sleeping disease is?"

I paused.

"The what?"

Sairaorg sighed again, only the sound wasn't tired.

Just sad.

"It's a very rare magical disease that plagues devils. It makes them fall asleep and wither away until they die, even if takes centuries for them to reach that point - you can see the signs early if you know how to look for them, but once they close their eyes they never open them again."

"What, like sleeping beauty?"

He gave me an odd look.

"No, I think that was someone else."

"..."

I'm just going to ignore that bit for now.

"No one's ever been able to cure it, not even Ajuka Beelzebub. But there's never been records of a god trying to do something about it, either." Sairaorg clenched his fists. "The ones that could try have never had a reason to try and help, but I have to find a way to change that."

He inhaled deeply.

"I have to."
Something about the way he said that...
It dawned on me.

"It's not for yourself, is it?"

He shook his head.

"It's for my mom."

And just like that, I couldn't quite meet his eyes anymore.

"She's sick?"

Now that I thought about it, that was vaguely familiar now, wasn't it?

"She has it, and she's already asleep." He answered, and he sounded gutted about it. "But I'm going to find a way to help!"

"Sounds risky," I said half-heartedly, and he shook his head.

"Doesn't matter." He insisted. "I was born useless in the eyes of the Bael and half the Underworld. My mother is the only person who's ever believed in me, and she got shunned for it. Even when she knew she didn't have much time left, she never stopped believing in me or making me promise to become the strongest devil I could be, so I'm not going to stop believing in her either. No matter what it takes-!"

"I get it."

He stopped mid-rant, which was a good thing because I'm not sure he wouldn't have started yelling at the top of his voice if I'd let him go on.

"...huh?"

"I get it. You want to help your mom." I waved my hand in his general direction. "You don't have to justify it. If my mom was still-"

Woah.

I cut myself off and slammed my mouth shut so fast I nearly bit through my tongue.

Pump the freaking brakes - where the hell had that come from?

Did Chiron's staff rattle something loose in my skull or something?

I don't talk about my mom with or to anyone - I don't even think about her most of the time in the privacy of my own mind.

Haven't in years, and I wasn't about to start now.

"-doesn't matter." I switched tracks lamely, not that it helped. Sairaorg may hit like a juggernaut and charge like one too, but I doubted he wasn't smart enough to figure out what I'd nearly let slip. "Your mom sounds awesome. Only makes sense that you'd find a way to help."

"... She is pretty awesome," Sairaorg said softly, and when I glanced at him out of the corner of my eye, he was deliberately looking anywhere but at me. "Thanks, Daniel."

He definitely knew, didn't he?

Damn it.

"It's nothing." I cleared my throat, trying to move past the stiffiling awkwardness "What are friends for?"

Sairaorg shrugged.

"Wouldn't know. You're the first one I've had in a while."

...Seriously?

Now I gotta get invested.

"One-second thought, I might be reconsidering the friendship." I pointed at the digital scoreboard. "I can't hang out with someone who can't keep up, and I'm three strikes ahead so far."

"Oh really?" His eyes flashed dangerously "Watch this!"

Thwack - boom!

...​

That was how a ten-pound bowling ball broke one of the pinsetter horribly and got us both banned for life after a screaming rant from the angry owner.

I'm pretty sure we would have gotten arrested too, but Sairoarg and I clocked on to where things were heading quickly and had Courage knock over a popcorn cart as a distraction, then we hightailed it out of there before the cops could get us, laughing like absolute idiots the whole time.

We'd probably never be able to show our faces anywhere near the place again, but hey, I made a friend out of it, officially, so everything worked out alright in the end.

Or at least it did, until we got back to Chiron's, and found the old centaur waiting for us in the garden, mug in hand and expression half-way between amused and expectant.

"You're late."

"We made curfew!" Sairaorg protested, and I nodded vigorously.

"It's barely nine!"

"And yet you're still late." He glanced down at "By thirty-five seconds."

"You're kidding right?"

"Punctuality is important."

Oh god, he wasn't kidding.

"Does that mean we're grounded?"

"I suppose we'll see tomorrow."

For the love of-!

"Chiron, please, what happens tomorrow!?"

He just laughed some more.

...​

When I wasn't dragged out of bed by an enchanted rope and flung about like a rag doll, I let myself hope that today was going to be a good day.

But I was wrong.

I was so, so wrong.

Slowly, I looked away from the desk I was sitting at, panning my eyes around the stack of books nearly as tall as I was - On mythology and history, sciences and languages, maths, and about a hundred other things too.

Just looking at them was making my dyslexic instincts scramble back and seize up in terror.

Sairaorg looked like he might actually tear up as he met my eyes, a haunted look in his own.

Slowly, we turned to stare at Chiron, who was up at the chalkboard and scribbling out a few lines.

Homeschooling 101 - The path to success."

"No students of mine will remain uneducated." His tail swished as he turned around. "I expect straight grades from here on out, or there will be consequences."

I thought I escaped Algebra, but like a poisonous viper it slipped back into my life and stuck when I least expected it.

"...This is the worst thing you could have done to us."

"Give it time."

"That wasn't a challenge!"

"No, but the pop quizzes will be."

"...Can we fight another scorpion instead?"

"We'll cycle back to that in a few more days."

I tipped back my head and groaned.

...


Slowly but surely, the first few weeks began to tick on by.


...

#250
We may have kicked things off pretty slowly, but as soon as we hit our stride, there was no stopping.

Every morning we started with classes. Chiron ran us through the regular stuff, like maths and science and essay writing, but there was also mythology - or history, I guess, since it was all real.

We learned about the big highlights - the great and relevant pantheons and factions of the world, the different realms they governed, the way they all dealt with one another and the mortal world in between, but we covered the smaller things too - common threats, common magics, and anything that could give either of us a bad day or was important enough that Chiron decided we had to know about it.

And as it turned out, there was enough random trivia there to fill half a dozen libraries.

"I thought I could skip the books when I was disinherited," Sairaorg muttered to me this one time, halfway through another one of Chiron's lectures on inter-pantheonic diplomacy - which was exactly as fun as it sounded "This would make half the Pillar heirs I know cry."

He probably wasn't wrong - what we were going through was basically a crash course on everything supernatural, only our teacher didn't do anything by halves.

And he wasn't kidding about the pop quizzes either.

I leaned across my desk to pat his back in sympathy, then I yelped as Chiron's staff materialised and whacked my hand and his head in quick succession. He loomed over us as we winced, and I couldn't even tell you if he'd teleported or moved there from the front of the room, because he was just that fast.

"Any questions, my students?"

"I'm good." "What questions?"

"Wonderful." He smiled pleasantly, and that's how I usually knew we were in danger "Then when you're done reciting the major points we've covered today, you can start running laps around the estate. Clearly, you have some energy you need to burn off. A thousand should do for a start."

We groaned, but neither of us tried arguing - I'd learned that lesson after the one time I'd tried, and he doubled the number.

Honestly, I was just glad that all his classes were in Greek, because otherwise I'd have fried my circuits and had whatever was left of my brain melting out of my ears trying to keep up through my dyslexia.

After the regular lessons, we'd cycle through outdoor activities - a different one every day.

Sword and spearmanship practice against the rock golems was going well. Chiron liked to drill us until my arms felt like they were going to drop off and my legs stopped moving altogether - and that was on a good day - but it was paying off quickly.

It only took a few spars before I could hold and train with a sword without feeling like an idiot waving around a Halloween prop, and I got even better with a spear that much faster - I think the fact that it doubled over as a throwing weapon helped me take to it more.

Physical conditioning got more intense, too. Sometimes we'd go for laps around the house and go through enough calisthenics reps - push-ups, sit-ups, crunches, and all that - to make a professional bodybuilder cry, and other times Chiron would teleport us out into the middle of the wilderness and have us run through different terrains until we collapsed in breathless exhaustion, every time.

No monster scorpions with anger issues since the first one though, so that was a plus, but that didn't mean he'd stopped shooting us

Oh no - Not even when we were done training.

Whether we were in the house or within a hundred miles of it, post-training or right smack dab in the middle of it, the old centaur liked to spring in sneak attacks out of nowhere, just to keep us on our feet.

That, or he just enjoyed smacking us around.

I prefer not to think about it.

"One must always be prepared."

"We get it!" I yelled as we desperately hopped out of the way of his staff - five minutes after we were finished running and getting pelted by the aftermath of his arrows. "Stop hitting us already!"

"Stop getting hit." He countered reasonably, then he whacked me in the face and sent me sprawling into the dirt right before he swept out Sairaorg's legs and launched him into the nearby river before his back even hit the ground. "It's quite a bad habit, but I'll break it out of you yet."

"Please don't." I hissed, nursing the welt running down my face and the beginnings of a swollen jaw - they'd heal by the tomorrow, but they still hurt. "And I think Sairaorg might be drowning."

No, seriously.

He hadn't come up yet, and it's not like Chiron ever really removed the Lesser Curse Of Atlas from us - he just dialled the intensity of it up and down depending on what kind of training we were doing.

Or what kind of mood he was in.

"Indeed he might be." Chiron nodded and stroked his beard thoughtfully. "Well, go help him then."

And then he flicked a finger and threw me into the river after him, which, really, I should have seen coming.

Turns out Sairaorg was just holding his breath and taking an underwater break, the absolute genius, but I guess Chiron must have figured that out before I did, because he waited just until we clambered back onto shore before grabbing us both by the scruffs of our necks and tossing us right back in again.

Then he froze the water solid behind us.

On the bright side - literally - I figured out how to emit sunlight and warmth that quickly spiralled up into scorching heat in my panic when the air started running out, and Sairaorg had his fists, so between the two of us we managed to get out real quick, and with only a teensy bit of hypothermia for the road.

Success!

Sure, we had to go through it three more times before we were allowed to collapse, each tougher than the last, but that was just Chiron being Chiron.

Case in point - Sairaorg and I didn't always train together. Sometimes, we'd get pulled apart for individual practice.

For me, that was archery.

Chiron would use his magic to animate all kinds of different targets for me to shoot - floating scoring boards, more golems, and little miniature creatures constantly skittering about whatever field he took me to train in.

And they didn't exactly just still still and let me take them out, either.

The first time we practiced, Chiron didn't even give me a heads-up that they hit back, so I'd barely drawn back my bowstring before I had to duck underneath the honest-to-dad javelin that had come sailing for my face like its owner had a score to settle.

"Crap-!" I turned to Chiron, wide-eyed. "A little warning next time!?"

"Of course not."

Then he smacked me over the head.

"Ow!"

"Don't ask stupid questions. No enemy will sit still and let you take aim at them."

"I just wasn't ready for it."

"You won't always be. Learn to adapt or suffer the consequences."

Fair enough.

"I got it." I rubbed the top of my head gingerly and eyed his staff warily. "You know, that thing is going to give me permanent brain damage one of these days, and then you're going to feel really bad about it."

Or at least I hoped

"I'll try to find some way to live with the pain." Chiron said dryly "Then again, seeing as you don't seem to use that brain regardless, damaging it shouldn't make much of a difference at all."

"..."

"..."

"... I'm just going to start shooting now."

"I'd be disappointed if you didn't. Are you ready?"

I turned around and glanced at all the targets just waiting for me to make a move.

The closest were hundreds of meters away, the kind of shots world champions would only manage to make once in a blue moon, maybe, and the farthest were so distant they might as well have been a mile off - heck, some of them were probably farther away than even that.

Chiron raised a brow expectantly when I glanced back at him.

A while ago I'd have said that pulling them off would be impossible, but I was a demigod who was finally figuring things out, so I just grinned up at him and nocked an arrow.

"I said I got this, didn't I?"

"That's the right attitude." Chiron nodded approvingly, which made me puff up a little right up until I heard the next words coming out of his mouth. "Try to keep it up for what comes next."

I took a step back, but I didn't even have time to ask before the clouds gathered up above us and darkened like the beginnings of an ominous thunderstorm.

"Chiron..."

"I'd start running in three, two-"

"Oh, come on!"

"-one."

I was already moving right as the clouds shuddered and started raining hail stones the size of golf balls, and that would have been bad enough, only the stupid things came down in a torrential downpour and exploded like miniature grenades the second they hit the ground, pelting me with blasts of condensed force and shards of ice even as I ran around avoiding them and trying to fire my arrows off like an absolute lunatic.

"A good archer should seek a vantage point, but never sacrifice mobility! Never hold a single position for too long!"

"Why are you like this!?"

I yelled at him some more as I scrambled around, and he just laughed.

...​

In other breaking news, Sairaorg started training with an axe.

It wasn't actually that big a deal - We'd been talking during one of the rare afternoons where Chiron let us go off into the city to mess around, and after we hit the cinema and caught a movie, I ended up ribbing him over the fact that I was training with three weapons and he was falling behind at only two.

I was only joking, but it lit this competitive fire under him, so the next day he marched right up to Chiron and asked for another weapon, and our teacher just shrugged and told him to pick whatever he wanted from the armory - though I think he was a little please about it too.

Sairaorg came back ten minutes later with this mean-looking double-edged axe held in his hands, determination gleaming in his eyes and everything, and from then on whenever I was practicing my archery he was going at it with the rock golems and getting scarily good at using the thing just as quickly as I was picking up the spear, even if he still preferred his fists over everything else.

Heck, even Courage was getting in on the training action - My canine buddy started joining us on our runs and dodge practice a few mornings in out of the blue, keeping at it even when it looked like he was going to croak a couple of times, and after a while the little menace was holding his own and matching our pace just fine.

As the days turned into weeks, and then the first couple of months passed by, my senses got sharper, my skills grew, and I was getting stronger, faster, tougher - just all around better than what I was before.

We all were, and it was all coming up golden.

And then things kicked up a notch.

...​

It started during one of our Pankration lessons.

If you don't know what that is, think mixed martial arts, only it was brutal - it was part of the Olympics in Ancient Greece, and the only rules in its time were no biting and no eye-gouging.

Anything else was fair game if it meant taking down your opponent, and even back then people thought you were either desperate for glory or straight nuts for stepping into that ring even if they loved the spectacle of it - people regularly came out of it with broken limbs and mangled body parts, and that stuff was a lot harder to treat back then even if you had healers who knew what they were doing or were rich enough to afford them.

For regular mortals back in the day, there was a very fine line not to cross even if you were in it for the fun of it - Get hurt past a certain point, and nothing short of magic or a god taking pity on you was putting you back together again.

We didn't have that problem.

I darted forward, throwing a left hook, but Sairaorg powered through it, ducking low and coming up with a quick jab to my chest. I stumbled back and recovered quickly, flashing him a grin as we circled around each other.

"Stay light on your feet." Chiron's voice rolled over us from where he was standing off to the side, supervising with Courage plopped down beside him for a nap. "If you're pinned down, the odds of you slipping your opponent's hold drop abysmally."

No need to tell me twice.

I'd done a lot to bridge the gap, but Sairaorg still packed a meaner punch than I did, and he was absolutely the better grappler. I kept making the mistake of getting too close during the first few spars we'd had, and he'd taken me down and forced me to eat so much dirt it was a miracle I wasn't half-plant and growing roots already.

I was better at playing keep-away, though.

"You're getting comfortable, Sai." I ducked out of his range as he swung for my head again. "Slowing down there! Are you even trying anymore?"

He grinned right back, cocking his fists.

"What, like I have to? When you keep running away?" He abruptly charged ten steps forward and nearly managed to tackle me off my feet. "Why waste the effort!?"

"Hah!"

His next charge brought him right into my space, and the details blurred a little as we locked into the fight.

See, Chiron walked us through all kinds of basic moves, but Pankration wasn't about just the moves - once you got going, it was all one part reflex, one part control, and just the right sort of timing.

Deflect, dodge, slip and strike.

Sweat beaded my brow and my knuckles started going numb as we kept at it. I feinted a right hook after eating a particularly nasty punch to the gut, only to slide a quick uppercut under his guard and graze his ribs, and his eyes narrowed.

He lunged towards me again and would have toppled me over for sure if I hadn't backpedaled hard, and then he tried to leap after me before I could put up my hands again.

And that's when it happened.

Sairaorg cocked back his fist, and the air around him suddenly shimmered like a heat haze in a desert, glowing with an off-white shine that charged even the breath in my lungs with pressure - like the staticky feeling of Chiron's magic right before he dropped lightning bolt arrows on us or lobbed fireballs our way on a whim, but not quite right.

Everything seemed to slow down glacially as my instincts blared like a car horn at the back of my head, and I only had a split second to react, which probably saved my life.

I dropped flat - not a dodge, but a full-on sprawl to the grass as Sairaorg threw out his fist with a yell, and the world promptly exploded.

The air displaced with a crack and a howl, the ground trembled, and a cone of pure force blasted out in a fearsome pulse and carved a trench through the garden behind me. Soil and formerly solid ground rained down from above as the aftershocks of the blow threw them so high into the air that they just about replaced the clouds for a few seconds there, and when it was all over and done with, the two of us just stared, slack-jawed.

It was like looking at the aftermath of a meteor strike, not a freaking punch.

"...Sairaorg, what even...?"

I couldn't even get out the words, and it wasn't fear - stuff going boom in my immediate vicinity was nothing I hadn't already gotten used to around here - but utter disbelief instead.

Where the hell had that come from?

"I don't know?" He sounded as stunned as I felt, glancing at down fists like they were strange and alien creatures he'd just discovered attached to his wrists. Then he clenched them and inhaled sharply when they flared with that faint white glow all over again. "What is this?"

"The next step in your training." Chiron cut in, and both of us turned to him as he trotted up to us - and even if his expression was pretty level, I could tell that he was excited just from the sheer focus in the look he gave us. "It seems that it's time to push onto a new frontier. Today is a good day."

I've said it before, but it's worth a repeat - whenever Chiron does or says something like that, it's usually a sign that we were about to be introduced to some new-fangled and absolutely terrifying method of training I'd be feeling all over for the next week, but given that Sairaorg had just come way too close to knocking my head off for comfort, I was a little distracted.

Sue me.

"You have ten minutes to freshen yourselves up." He clapped his hands decisively, and we were both startled as he gestured back up to the house. "It's time for a rather special lesson."

...​

"Magic - what is it?"

Sairaorg and I sat on the ground, cross-legged on the grass as Chiron slowly settled into full lecture mode. He didn't look surprised when both of us gave him clueless looks.

To be fair, what exactly was I supposed to say?

It's the stuff that lets you make food appear out of nowhere and teleport and shoot arrows that explode at us?

He'd totally whack me for that one.

"Magic, magical energy, or mana among a thousand other words roughly refer to the same concept," Chiron said, pointing at the familiar chalkboard that materialized in front of us at the gesture. As he spoke, the words scribbled themselves out in neat little lines. "There is a great deal of debate between various different schools of thought, but the most commonly accepted - if vastly simplified and incomplete - theory centres around the belief that magical energy is the innate potential of any living being to alter the world around them made manifest, crystalized into tangible power through the inner workings of the soul."

He stopped there for a second to check that we were keeping up, which we... kind of were.

"Whether that potential is derived and watered down from the greater world itself or from other mechanisms within it is also up for debate, with wildly different answers depending on who you might happen to ask, but that level of thesis is irrelevant to either of you at this point."

That was good to hear - this was already threatening to get confusing fast, and we'd barely started. From the way he shifted next to me, I could tell that Sairaorg was just as relieved.

"One thing to keep in mind for future reference is that the exact properties and workings of magical energy can vary by species - different beings generally express that potential in different ways."

"I know about that!" Sairaorg blurted out and sat up a little. "It's why angels have their Holy Power, and devils have Demonic Power - they're both magic, but they're total opposites."

Chiron nodded with a smile.

"A good example, though the exact natures of the Abrahamic Holy Power and its counterpart are more complex than just that."

"Eh?

"Don't worry about it - it's a discussion for another day." He turned back to the chalkboard "While the magical arts cover the most widely used form of intrinsic power in the supernatural theatre, they are not the only source of it. Far from it, in fact."

A new couple of words appeared right on top.

Life-force

Chiron seemed amused by our blank looks.

"Any guesses?"

"..." I squinted up at him suspiciously. "...If I say 'it's what keeps us alive', are you going to hit me?"

"I'll let it slide just this once, because you're technically correct."

I'll take it!

"Think of it this way - If magic is the energy used to change reality around oneself, life force is the energy used to sustain oneself. It does, in fact, keep you alive, but that's the very least of what it can be used to achieve under the right circumstances. The soul is an efficient machine that runs on the bare minimum of a living being's life force, and this leaves a wellspring of untapped power in reserve."

He gave Sairaorg a very pointed look.

"A reserve that, once discovered, can be used to bolster and reinforce the soul, and in turn the body, resulting in an explosive growth of physical strength and capability - and that's simply to begin with."

Sairaorg's eyes lit up.

"Is that what I did?"

Chiron nodded

"You told me that you were born with an abysmal degree of Demonic Power, yes?"

My friend grimaced, but he didn't flinch away from the truth.

"I have reserves so pathetic I'll never be able to use them for anything useful. It's why I got disinherited."

... and now I wanted to punch someone, but that's really a thought for later.

"It's fine though!" Sairaorg smiled and clenched a fist fiercely. "I've gotten strong without it!"

"Indeed." Chiron agreed and matched his smile. "The absence of interference or distraction by inherited magical power likely contributed to it - you pushed your body to the brink for years, always searching for more strength, and in doing so you managed to become tangentially aware of the shape of your soul, in part, and your own base of life - Touki, as it's commonly known by the avid practitioners of the east."

"Touki." Sairaorg had stars in his eyes as he memorized the word, and I grinned a little as I nudged him with my elbow.

"So you figured out how to use your life force by accident... and the first thing you do is nearly end my life?"

"Ah." He laughed sheepishly. "Sorry?"

I pretended to scowl at him before shrugging it off.

"What's a little near-murder between friends?"

"Oh, that strike would have hardly killed you. You're more durable than you think." Chiron said absently, then he paused. "Though I will admit that it would have almost certainly done terrible things to your skull... and very likely your spine."

"...It was funny five seconds ago," I said flatly. "It's not funny anymore."

"You'd have walked it off eventually." Chiron hummed dismissively, and then he turned back to Sairaorg before I could start protesting and brooding over my mortality. "Moving on - tapping into your base of life is only the first step. With the proper training, you can cultivate that reserve and grow it to even further heights. By reinforcing your body and soul, you will also learn to shrug off the effects of conventional and certain greater magics, and heal physical wounds depending on their severity. In time, you can even begin to draw in and manipulate ambient life force from your environment, and disrupt that of your enemies to cripple them - this and more fall under the art that is, once again, most commonly practiced in the East and referred to as Senjutsu."

Forget about stars - by the time Chiron was done talking, Sairaorg had entire galaxies seared into his eyes, and he was vibrating so hard you'd think he was about to bounce up into orbit.

"How do we start!?"

"Don't get overexcited." He cautioned. "This new achievement can lead you to great heights of power, but it can and has been the downfall of many. There are cautionary tales of practitioners who damage their bodies and even sacrifice their lifespans in an effort to grow too quickly.

"Yikes," I muttered, and Sairaorg simmered down a little.

"I understand. I'll be careful." He promised, and then he shrugged a little and grinned again "And besides, I'm a devil! Even if I lose a little lifespan, I have tons to spare!"

"..."

It was about five seconds into the silence that followed that Sairaorg realized he may have said something stupid.
"Wait..."

In his defence, I'm pretty sure that was a joke, but from the look on Chiron's face, I don't think he cared.

"Um..." Sairaorg swallowed nervously when Chiron's stare didn't soften. "I mean-"

"It seems," We both froze at the way our teacher's tone came out - totally level as was usual, and yet somehow still the stuff of nightmares. I wouldn't be surprised if he practiced that in the mirror. "-that I must teach you self-preservation as well."

He smiled.

"Very well."

"It's time to start training your base of life, student." He snapped his fingers, and Sairaorg hissed sharply and nearly buckled over as the strength of the Lesser Curse Of Atlas increased so sharply I could see him starting to sink into the ground from all the extra pressure. "Start running laps for now."

"... How many?"

"Oh, let's start easy. Twenty-"

Sairaorg perked up hopefully.

"-thousand should do."

"Hrk!"

"And they had better be completed inside of an hour, or else..."

"...Or else what?" Sairaorg whispered as he trailed off, like he was rightfully afraid of the answer but couldn't help but ask anyway.

Chiron leaned forward to loom over him a little, still looking downright genial.

"Use your imagination."

Sairaorg thought about that for a second, paled, shot me a terrified look and then took off so fast I swear he left flashing afterimages behind as he disappeared into the distance.

"Now then." Chiron turned back to me after nodding in satisfaction, and I had to resist the urge to scram and run after Sairaorg. "Let's talk about Divine Thaumaturgy."

"...What in the what now?"

"I imagine you want to follow along in his footsteps and find your own base of life."

I opened my mouth, then closed it again with a nod.

Because... yeah.

I wasn't stupid - Sairaorg had just leveled up, big time, and even if it meant that Chiron was going to start upping the ante too, I wanted in on that.

"It's not going to be easy, is it?" I sighed, but I wasn't really put out by it. "Where do I start?"

Like hell was I falling behind now.

"The method he used is unlikely to bear the same results for you - not in a reasonable time frame," Chiron said bluntly, and I frowned. "Pure physical stress is an unreliable tool as a matter of principle, and even more so for a demigod. Hence, Divine Thaumaturgy."

"Still don't know what that means."

"In essence? It is a subtype of the magical arts reserved almost exclusively for demigods and those empowered by divine means - priests, godly messengers and the like." He explained. "A god's divine grace isn't simply potent magical energy - It carries within it imprints of that god's domains and authorities, and mortals blessed with such power can use it to mimic their properties in the form of spells and lesser magical phenomena."

The chalkboard cleared itself out as he waved a hand and another word appeared in their place.

Faith.

"A child of Zeus, for example, might call down lighting and storms with nothing but sheer will and instinct, but they can do more than that - they might sing hymns, dedicate prayers, and use words of belief among other tools as catalysts to resonate with the divine power within them and bring forth greater or more esoteric feats of power into the world even in the middle of a battle."

He glanced down at me.

"Are you with me so far?"

"I think so?" It wasn't that hard to keep up, just yet, even if he was starting to branch into headache-inducing territory. "God power likes to do god stuff, and you can use prayers and things like them as... magic words? To pull off crazier or weirder stunts?"

"Essentially. I told you before that faith in yourself makes you stronger, but faith in your father and the inheritance you derive through him will let you achieve things I doubt you can even imagine. Tell me - what are lord Apollon's domains?"

I blinked.

Didn't we just cover this a couple of weeks back?

"The Sun." That was the obvious one. "Light. Archery and Marksmanship. Prophecy and Divination. Youth, Healing and Plagues. Music, Arts and Poetry. Some kinds of Truth and Knowledge, and some other stuff too, right?"

"Correct."

Fun fact?

My dad has a stupid number of divine domains - so many that even the Greeks were probably getting really confused about it back in the day.

Hey, Joe, whose the god of basketweaving again?

I dunno, man. Isn't it Apollo? It's always Apollo!

Man, I kinda hate that guy.

Shut up or you'll get us smote, you idiot!

You get the idea

"But how does that help... oh."

It hit me like a freight train.

Divine power from a god can be used to mimic that god's domains... and I had a boatload of stuff to choose from there.

"Oh."

"Now you're getting it." Chiron laughed at the look on my face. "You've barely scratched the surface of your potential even if you've begun to manifest intrinsic abilities tied to it - supernatural marksmanship, the ability to sense projectile weapons heading your way within a growing range, an instinctive if untrained capacity to heal and the power to emit and manipulate sound and sunlight to various degrees."

I felt myself sit up in excitement as the implications started catching up to me.

"I can do more."

"Far more." He agreed.

"And this'll help me use my life-force the way Sairaorg is learning to?"

"Daniel, your divine power is your life-force - or part of it, at the very least. Demigods are born from divinity, which means that inheritance occupies a grey area between ordinary magical potential and life force and blurs the line between both. Train it, cultivate it, and you'll elevate every aspect of yourself with it."

...

Well, then.

My grin was starting to hurt from how wide it was getting.

How about that?

"Where do we start?" I asked again, and this time Chiron held out a hand towards me. An enormous book appeared over his palm, leather-bound and little dog-eared at the edges, and I grunted at its weight when I caught it.

"Get to reading."

"...Seriously?"

Chiron chuckled as I deflated.

"That is a compendium of old and relatively new recountings focusing on Lord Apollon's great works, as well as examples of applications of Divine Thaumaturgy commonly used over by priests in service to him - even a few of his children from centuries long past have relied or contributed to some of them."

I perked up again.

That sounded awesome.

Sure, they weren't actually my siblings - Apollo and Apollon were technically different beings, but only by degrees.

This could be huge.

"Learn them, and take inspiration from the feats within, and we'll see just how far you grow."

"Right."

"But first, join Sairaorg on his run."

"Wait, what?" I panicked. Don't blame me, half the people my age I know would run away screaming if someone tried to make them run twenty thousand laps around an estate as big as Chiron's."But you just said-!"

"Unless of course you think that you simply can't keep up, now that Sairaorg has moved on to the next level of his training."

"..."

"..."

My eyes narrowed.

Chiron smiled back.

"...See, the thing is, I know you're playing me." I scowled. "But damn it, it's working."

He was still chuckling when I took off after handing him the book and letting him turn up the curse until it was just about ungodly in it's force, but what else was new?

...​

Of course, it wasn't all smooth sailing from then on.

"SAIRAORG, I'M GOING TO KILL YOU!"

"YOU ASKED ME TO HELP!"

"NOT LIKE THIS!" I yelled over the screaming winds, and we started tumbling down to the ground... which was some ten thousand feet below the clouds underneath us.

Let me back up a bit.

Chiron gave me the book and told me to train with it.

So naturally, the first thing I did with it was try and figure out how to fly.

What?

Flying is cool, my friend could do it and I wanted to as well... only it turned out that just wanting to spring up into the air really hard isn't enough to make a son of Apollo pull a Peter Pan.

So I asked Sairaorg to help me out with it - and I meant help me brainstorm ways to figure it out.

The compendium Chiron had given me had all sorts of stories, prayers, hymns, and songs dedicated to Apollon that could be used as inspiration to pull off every trick you could imagine, from bringing the 'grace of the sun' from above - whatever that meant - to spreading plagues - which was kinda cool in a horrifying way - but nothing explicitly about flight, and I'd gone through a fifth of it by the time I started trying.

"Look deeper," Chiron advised when I tried to ask for his help. "And don't be afraid to get creative with your interpretations. The words are secondary to will and faith."

Will and faith - he kept going on and on about those, but something in my mind hadn't clicked yet, so I had the bright idea to turn to Sairaorg for a hand.

In hindsight, the sly look on his face should have clued me in on the fact that he was planning something, but I was too eager to try something new to defend myself.

"I can show you what flying is like for me, if you want?"

"Yeah, that might help, actually," I said, then I faltered. "Wait, show-?"

Too late.

I couldn't turn around fast enough before Sairaorg cackled and tackled me, unfurled his wings, and shot up right into the sky with me, dangling me over the ground by the ankles.

"GOT YOU! NOWHERE TO GO THIS TIME!"

"SAIRAORG!"

It was like rising up a drop tower at a carnival upside down and doing it a thousand miles an hour, so I was perfectly justified in setting his clothes halfway on fire and giving him a nasty sunburn the second he got us back down again.

It didn't stop him from laughing and running all over before I managed to chase him back into the house - and then Chiron caught us tracking dirt and soot into his living room, and made us clean the entire place, top to bottom...with toothbrushes.

Seriously, I couldn't make this up if I tried.

Even Courage wanted nothing to do with it - he padded into the room chewing on a bone Chiron must have given him, took one look at us hunched over and scrubbing down spots on the marble floor with the little things and zipped right back out again.

"Traitor!"

...​

I kept at it for a week, with no results... until I had the bright idea to wake up early one day and sit outside in the garden to watch the sunrise, and see if that did anything for me.

I'd like to say I had a plan going going for, but honestly?

It was totally just a whim - most of the things I was learning now on using my powers were more spiritual and abstract and just plain old weird instead of logical, so it couldn't hurt to try something like this, right?

Right?

...

Okay, fine, I'll admit it - I felt really dumb in the first half-hour leading up to it, and then I started reciting some of the lines from a few of the poems in the compendium I'd memorised under my breath for the heck of it.

"Glittering, Wise, Father of Light."

"Behold Burning Warmth, The Fire Of The Rising Sun."

I was throwing around anything out at that point - and then the first rays of sunlight started rising in the distance, and it was like a flip had been switched.

I jolted so sharply you'd think that someone had hooked me up to a car battery, my instincts went into overdrive, and the ordinarily subtle glow that covered me when I used my powers burst out in a megawatt flash of radiance so brilliant that for a second, it was as if another dawn had come out to match the one on the horizon.

Holy crap.

"Gleaming In A Sea of Orange And Rose"

"Thy Chariot Rises... And Now So Will I"

That last part wasn't part of that poem, or any other.

I didn't even know how that poem ended - I made those words up on the spot, based entirely on what I wanted.

Will and Faith, right?

I looked up the sun, rising in the distance.

Constant, steady, and inevitable.

I'm the same, I told the little piece of a different kind of sun I imagined was burning away inside of me, and I want up.

The world held it's breath with me for a beat... and then it finally decided to play ball, and my feet began to rise over the ground.

"Yes!"

...​

Another quarter-hour later, and Sairaorg walked out the front door, ready for his morning run.

But he sure wasn't ready for me, and the squawking sound he made as I flew in from behind the house and slammed into him so hard he face-planted into the dirt was hilarious.

Or maybe that was just my sheer euphoria doing the heavy lifting, but who even cares?

I could freaking fly!

He came right back up a second later, expression scrunched in disgust as he spat out a mouthful of dirt before it went slack in shock when he stared up at me and realized what he was seeing.

"Dan!?"

I hooted down at him from above, wreathed in a shimmer of pulsing, glowing light, laughing like a total basket case - and man did it feel good.

"Got you back, sucker!"

For a second, there was only stunned surprise there, and then his eyes lit up in matching delight.

"Oh, it's on."

His wings unfurled, he leaped up after me, and we were both dots rising into the morning sky again by the time Chiron padded out, fresh mug of tea in hand and a bemused look on his face.

Courage came out after him, head turning this way and that in search for his master, and then he caught sight of him up above and did a double-take.

"Impressive, isn't it?"

The hellhound barked in disbelief, and the centaur shrugged.

"I suppose you wouldn't know, would you? Take it from me - their progress is quite remarkable, especially in this softer day and age. That aside, they do seem to have forgotten about their morning classes." He clicked his tongue. "Foolish students. I'm going to have to teach them another lesson for that."

Or so he said, but his smile didn't abate.

They'd come down eventually - he could let them enjoy their flight before he smacked them back down to reality.

Just this once.

...​

At the same time, deep in Daniel Winchester's soul, a nascent ember crackled, popped, and slowly grew into a S̵̻͐̔̾̈́̕p̸͉͂̓̅a̸͙͓̋̀̕̚͘r̷̫̭̦͖̅͝ḵ̸̰̑͂̑

...

Chiron to his students: The Most Important thing is not to get hit.
