#843
The next couple of weeks were the most ridiculously painful ones of my life, and I mean that in pretty much every possible definition of the word - but mostly the physical kind, because if Sairaorg and I thought Chiron was intense before?

Hoooooo boy.

The higher gear he literally manhandled, kicked and outright blasted us into was a whole other kind of ball game.

We still went through our regular training, the classes and the basic spars against each other, but from the second he decided it was time for us to actually stress test those skills - 'stress' being the big and shiny operative word here - Chiron started pulling us away from them every day without fail and teleport us back out to that valley.

And then he'd take us apart - and again, just so we're entirely clear here, I mean that literally.

It turns out that when your magical know-how is so far out there that you can heal mangled limbs and semi-pulverised insides in a few hours without even breaking a sweat, you have no problem pushing the limits of regular sparring a teensy bit more than usual.

Sounds fun, right?

Chiron thought so too, and maybe I would have laughed about it with him if I hadn't nearly had my jaw broken three times in as many days before I learned to shut up and move fast enough to dodge the blows he sent my way, over and over again.

Some of them, at least.

"Keep at it!" Our teacher half-encouraged and half-demanded just about every time he wailed on us all across the valley, and with all the energy of a man with a thousand-year-old grudge. You'd think we'd burned his house down or something. "You've cultivated the skill, now comes the strength!"

Naturally, that was easier said than done, because the first time he did say it was immediately followed up by him clocking me in the side of the head hard enough that I spent the rest of the day tasting colours.

Sairaorg had it just as bad - breaking his arm the first time around was basically just the warm-up for the next few days, and Chiron seemed to take it as a personal freaking mission to make sure we came out of every other go-around barely able to stay on our feet and looking like hell warmed over.

Assuming we could even stand at all - I'm pretty sure I nearly ended up paralyzed from the waist down that one time he drop-kicked me off a cliff... and then dropped the cliff off after me.

Yeah, that was a rough six hours.

The craziest part though?

It was working.

Over the span of fifteen days, I came up with and tested four-and-a-half new spells just to keep up and not wind up in a full-body cast.

I pushed myself to move faster, to hit harder, to multitask between my bow, spear, and the magic until I could sling from one to the other in the blink of an eye.

Chiron always blinked faster, of course, except for those rare times when he felt like tossing me a bone and humoring me, but the change in pace of our fights was still something that not even a blind idiot could have possibly missed - and I'm not just talking about the way I used my powers.

It was like I'd gone from a slow and steady march over the last few months to a wild sprint in no time flat - No matter how badly I got folded in the end, every time we went at it was a little different, a little better.

I didn't just feel like I was improving - For the first time since all of this started, I felt genuinely powerful.

And I wasn't the only one, either.

Sairaorg?

Senjutsu reinforcement was still brand new to him, and he hadn't done anything relatively more impressive than dipping his toes into the shallow end of a pool the size of the Atlantic, but just the sheer, stupid power he was able to cram in underneath his skin now was something else entirely.

Sure it was just the basic stuff - Senjutsu wasn't just about punching harder, but controlling spiritual and natural energies to pull all sorts of stunts and phenomena out the wazoo - but the classics were exactly that for a reason.

If he was already strong before, then the things Sairaorg was learning to do with just his fists now were getting downright cartoonish - like someone decided to stuff an earthquake or three in a five-and-a-half-foot frame with an attitude and zero concept of chill before letting it loose on the world.

It was awesome.

Didn't save us from getting the crap beaten out of us on the double, but we were slowly climbing up that mountain no matter how many times we got knocked off of it.

...

And then a goddess decided to drop by for a visit.

...​

Okay, let's back up a bit.

It was two days before we were set to go down to the Underworld to visit Sairaorg's mom - that was happening both sooner than I expected and right on time, because the wait had been killing both of us.

I don't know why Chiron picked that day out of all of them, but Sai had been quietly ecstatic, and he'd rushed off to send a message to his butler through one of his bat familiars pretty much immediatley.

The guy was set to show up via teleportation circle to pick us all up the day after tomorrow.

And yeah, finding out Sairaorg had a genuine butler waiting for his calls was, like, the highlight of my week.

Much rich-kid teasing ensued - though I'll level with you here and admit that I don't really have much room to stand on anymore, what with how rich I'd gotten practically overnight.

Between the six shipping containers worth of solid gold, the other loaded with gems and trinkets - each - and the few dragon leftovers from Smaug that Chiron wasn't going to be keeping to make all kinds of alchemical tricks that we'd be store up our sleeves to use down the line...

Well.

We hadn't gotten around to sorting it all out and getting exact numbers for how loaded we both were by now, but odds were it was a number some people wouldn't even know how to pronounce.

Still processing that bit, honestly.

Moving on now - before my day jumped off the rails so quickly you'd think someone had blown them to kingdom come, Sairaorg and I had been hanging out in the garden.

If that sounds boring, good.

That was the whole idea - it was one of those miracle Sundays where Chiron would give us the afternoon off to do whatever, and we were milking that breather for all that it was worth.

Sairarog had been sitting against a tree and playing fetch with Courage, occasionally tossing a stick for him so far out that an ordinary dog would have croaked trying to run after it and back more than a couple of times, and I was cross-legged on the grass a few feet away and strumming the strings of my new harp.

The thing was a total score, by the way - my fingers barely had to touch the strings for the silvery metal to sing, the notes going from low to high and back again.

"You're getting pretty good at that." Sairaorg offered, and I shot him a thumbs up.

"Thanks, man"

I wasn't an expert, and having the instinct to use the harp didn't mean that my brain came pre-loaded with the instructions or the sheet music for songs or anything, but piecing together how to play just by strumming at the thing and practicing with old nursery rhymes and ear-worm tunes was a lot easier than it would have had any right to be if I'd been a regular old mortal.

Also, it was just plain fun.

I'm no Mozart yet, and I still hadn't figured out how to play the hymns of Apollon Chiron had suggested without cheating off the manuals he pulled for me from his library, but my 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' was already the gold standard of bedtime lullabies everywhere.

It might have even made the man shed a tear himself.

We spent a little time like that, enjoying the fresh air and the sunlight - that was kind of my thing and all - and it was all very bright and scenic.

Until I got bored.

What?

ADHD was still a thing for me.

"Sai?"

"Yeah?"

"You want to go into town? Get some lunch?"

He perked up and stopped tossing Courage's stick, which was probably for the best.

If he put any more strength into his throws then that thing was going to disappear over the horizon, and my dog would be miffed about it all day.

"Cheeseburgers?"

I shrugged and started packing up my harp.

"Sure."

If we left then, we might have even been able to catch a movie before heading back. It'd been a while.

Course, as it turned out, that really wasn't in the cards for us that day.

We stood up, took about five steps forward, and then the air around us changed.

Nothing dramatic, or even obvious, but something suddenly made my skin prickle hair and at the back of my neck stand right up.

Sairaorg and I didn't even blink as we spun on spot so we were standing back to back, knees crouched and senses peeled sharper than razor blades.

Chiron has snuck in enough surprise attacks on us at this point that being ready to go at a split-second's notice was as close to second nature for us as you could possibly get.

Only, I didn't think this was Chiron.

Call it a gut feeling.

"You see anything?"

"No." Space twitched a little as I sent a spark of magic trailing down my arm and into the band on my wrist, and my spear popped into reality and settled into my grip like a fifth limb. "I - there!"

A narrow streak of shining silver quickly burst out of the treeline and hurtled right towards my center mass so fast the air seemed to be screaming around it.

A month ago, it would have given me a crazy bad time - now, though, I just had to swing my spear at the right angle to intercept it.

Silver met red gold and bounced off with a sound that was somehow both a heavy gong and a shriek of metal against metal so tortured it made even me wince, but it wasn't Serpent's Downfall that came out of it malformed and misshapen.

The arrow hit the ground behind us, and I had just about enough time to realize what it was before five more came soaring out, each just a little bit faster than the last.

Fine. Bet.

Swing, swing, swing - I deflected three in short succession, ducked under the last, then Sairoarg outright yanked the last one out of the air before hissing and tossing it aside.

"That stings."

I'll say - for a second, his palm actually seemed to smoke, and the skin turned bright red like he'd accidentally pressed it against a hot stove and didn't pull away in time.

Nothing major, but it ticked me off something fierce as I glared back at the tree line and raised my spear a little higher.

The blade began to crackle with pulsing flames.

"Show yourself!"

"Yes, please."

Neither of us jumped when Chiron shimmered into being right next to us, steaming mug in hand and an almost exasperated expression on his face as he looked out past the trees himself.

We didn't relax either.

"Preferably before my precocious student sets my flower beds and woodlands on fire."

He paused and gave me the stink eye.

"Again."

"Hey!" I spluttered indignantly, even if I didn't pull my eyes away from the spot I was busy glaring at. I was not getting shot by an arrow today - once was enough, and no, I'm not going to talk about it. "That only happened one time! And you made me shovel it all away and re-plant everything myself!"

Sairaorg had laughed himself to tears, the jerk.

Chiron ignored me with the practiced ease of a teacher who was having absolutely none of your crap, before taking another sip and clearing his throat politely.

"Had I known you were coming, my lady, I would have prepared them both for such a meeting."

My lady?

I would have asked - heck, I opened my mouth to - but someone beat me to the punch.

"There's no need for that Chiron."

The woman materialized right in between the three of us between one breath and the next, without a flash of light or even a shift in the breeze.

She was wearing cargo pants and heavy-duty combat boots, and a black leather jacket over a white shirt. A necklace capped with a particularly gnarly-looking tooth hung around her neck, and her face was both youthful and familiar in a way that tickled at something near the back of my head.

I didn't swing my spear at her head at the sudden appearance, but I didn't lower it either - not that she seemed to notice.

Her long white-blonde hair shifted against her shoulders with the breeze, and her silver eyes barely flickered to Sairaorg and me before they panned back to Chiron - not quite dismissively, but more like she'd clocked our general existence and immediately acknowledged the fact that we were about as threatening to her as a pair of particularly fearsome gerbils.

I could believe it, too.

Something about her was different to Apollon - namely, the fact that I didn't feel like I was standing next to a ticking hydrogen bomb about to go off right in my face, but was somehow still leery as anything of getting too close.

It was hard to describe.

"There's no need for formalities. I'm just dropping in for a quick visit."

Even her voice was familiar, and I figured it out before Chiron inclined his head in a respectful half-nod.

Silver arrows. Familiar face.

Sheer presence.

"How may we help you, Lady Artemis?"

And there it was.

"Isn't it obvious?"

I wasn't even a little surprised when those silver eyes locked back onto me with real focus.

Then again, I don't think any of us were.

The goddess's slow smile was very careful, and way too assessing for comfort.

"My twin shared some interesting news with me, and I've come to see what all the fuss is about. Hello, nephew. You have impressive reflexes."

Needless to say, we didn't go out to lunch.

Spoiler: AI Artemis

...​

"Let's take a walk."

What was it with me, Olympians and walks?

I mean, I was only two for two on those, but as far as most sane people were concerned, that was two too many - if it happens again, I should get a free ice cream sundae or a coupon or something.

Until then, it wasn't a request - gods didn't really do those.

Even if they phrase something like one, most of the time you'd have to be dumb as bricks not to get that it really, really wasn't.

Or maybe an actual brick.

Let's be honest here, stranger things have panned out in this pantheon.

Regardless, Artemis wanted to talk to me.

She spent thirty seconds chatting with Chiron in a voice that was probably deliberately too low to follow, ignored Sairaorg entirely - which was more than fine with everyone present - and then turned back to me with a raised, expectant

"Well?"

"Sure?"

What else was I supposed to say?

Chiron and Sairaorg just shrugged at me when I glanced over at them, the goddess of the hunt didn't seem upset or in any way peeved, and I had two different ways of getting the heck out of dodge if any of that changed.

It was a done deal.

And I was having such a nice day too.

I sealed my spear back up again and reluctantly made to step up behind her as she turned away t and began to walk back in the direction her arrows had come from.

"Good luck," Sairaorg muttered, and I sighed.

"I'll need it."

"No kidding. Don't get smote."

That got a wry grin out of me.

"That's the hope."

"You already know what to do." I was less nervous and more tense -ready to spring into action at the slightest hint of danger, even -but I'll admit that the fact that Chiron didn't look bothered at all as he downed his tea was doing wonders to keep me calm. "She's here to observe you and likely nothing else. Treat it like you would a visit from your father."

"Those aren't really good for my blood pressure either, teach."

He snorted and vanished his mug.

"Tragic."

... I think he was still upset about the flowerbeds.

"Nephew."

Artemis's voice snapped me back into focus, and I yelped and took off running after her - she was already disappearing between the trees and her pace hadn't cooled one bit.

"Come."

"Where-?"

I didn't get to ask.

Abruptly, without warning, she started running.

The transition was seamless - she stepped right into the sprint and took off across the woods like it was the most natural thing in the world.

As a goddess of wilderness on top of a whole bunch of other domains as well, it probably was.

I followed after her at a focused sprint, trainers crunching against the grass and piles of dead leaves underfoot, and something strange happened.

The forest began to stretch and warp like something was twisting it around us as we ran. The air caved in like a tunnel with no beginning or end, and tiny silver motes began to light up all around us whole glowing shade so bright that when it hit her hair, it shone like pure moonlight.

Then things got really weird when the outside world started to... melt, almost.

It flickered and sunk into the background, phantom images bobbing and vanishing with every passing second like we were running through a train car that was also moving a thousand miles an hour and leaving everything behind it in the dust.

I didn't flinch or stumble in my run, because I could feel how much of an all-around bad idea it would have been, but it was still the second oddest form of teleportation I'd ever experienced - and yes, I knew what was happening pretty much instantly.

Kind of an expert at this point.

At least it was over quickly.

Artemis's run slowed out of the blue, and the tunnel of air and shifting imagery began to fray at the seams. The second she slowed to an outright walk, it faded away entirely - and just like that, we were somewhere else.

The first thing I noticed was the cool air, tinged with the smell of thyme.

Actually, scratch that - the small hill overlooking the forest we appeared on reeked off the stuff, to the point that it nearly overpowered the pine and fruit underneath it. A mountain rose in the distance, part of a range that stretched out to the right of the horizon and kept going and glinting green in the mid-day sun.

Actually...

I kind of recognised the place.

Chiron had a portrait of that exact range hanging in the house and somehow, Artemis seemed to know what I was thinking.

"Mount Pelion."

She stepped up next to me, and the footsteps were so light I swear you'd think she was walking on air.

"Where once your teacher lived and made his home, thousands and thousands of years ago. He still keeps a holding there, as is his right, but he occasionally visits from time to time."

Huh.

"Cool."

In hindsight, I could have worded that better considering who I was talking to, but she didn't seem to mind.

If anything, she was a little amused. The corners of her lips even quirked up a little.

"I suppose it is."

For a second, neither of us talked.

I didn't fidget as her eyes bored into me, but that was because I had this niggling feeling that it would give the wrong impression more than anything else I could do.

Heck, I even tried not to blink on pure instinct, and did a damn good job of it too.

The silence stretched on.

And on.

And on.

Eventually, I gave up.

"Why did you bring me here?" Then I coughed and added, quietly "My lady?"

"I told you, didn't I?" Her expression didn't change, but her eyes finally left mine and flickered down towards the forest. "I was curious. My brother has not claimed a child in centuries."

I stiffened a little at the way she stressed the words, and even though she didn't look back at me...

She knew.

No doubt about it.

She understood that something fishy had gone on there - whether that was because my dear old new dad had told her, or because she was spitballing at some version of the 'truth' was anyone's guess, but she knew something.

Great.

"And?" I didn't freak out, even internally - I'm proud of myself for that. "What happens next?"

"We shall see." She started trecking down the hill with the easy grace of someone who's done it a hundred thousand times before, and I had no choice but to follow. "Apollon's words were enough to answer my questions, but sometimes actions are of greater value."

My brows furrowed and I hopped after her as she leaped over a row of jutting boulders and landed on the balls of her feet.

"And that means...?"

"It means I want you to look at these and tell me what you see."

I blinked as she gestured down.

Tracks.

Heavy tracks.

Chiron had taught us enough about hunting that I could immediately tell they didn't come from a deer, and for plenty of reasons too - the obvious one being that they were anywhere from five to ten times the size they should have been.

I crouched down to give them a good look before glancing back up at Artemis, who'd gone back to watching me silently.

"Well?"

"They're not deer tracks." She didn't say anything, so I crouched a little further down and pointed to the claws. "Whatever these things came from, it had hooves, but they're too round at the base, and the claw imprints are shorter and stubbier than they should be."

She raised an eyebrow, and I could almost hear her telling me to get on with it.

"And see here?" I was getting a little warmer know as I pressed my palm into one of them, and it sunk all the way up past the wrist before it hit the dirt at the bottom. "The earth here is rough and rock solid almost all the way through, but the tracks are still too deep. Whatever made them is big and heavy."

Which meant they were strong - the supernatural kind of strong.

"What else?"

I almost started when she finally spoke, and for a second, she almost sounded approving.

"Uh..." I followed the tracks with my eyes before pointing awkwardly and trying not to cringe. "It went that way?"

I was expecting a flat look or some more judgemental staring, but she only just raised her eyebrow again and crossed her arms over her chest.

"Is that right?"

"...Yes?"

"Are you asking me, or telling me?"

"...Telling you?"

"Then what are you waiting for?" She tilted her head expectantly, and I realized she was expecting me to lead the way. "Go hunt your quarry."

And you know what?

I went and hunted my 'quarry' - because I had one of those now, apparently.

...​

We followed the trail for the better part of an hour, even though it looped in on itself multiple times - like the owner was a tourist who just couldn't figure out which they were going and had to double back again to look for famous landmarks.

The closer we got to whatever it was waiting at the end, the rougher things got - and I'm not just talking about the environment.

The ground got steeper, and more torn up. Plenty of the heavy pine trees were leaning the wrong way, and the bark was looking a little... crushed, like something absolutely massive had steam-rolled past them and nearly torn them right out of the ground.

Ah, who am I kidding?

That's exactly what happened - I could almost smell the thing from the tracks it left behind. This nasty scent that reminded me of this one time Uncle David took us on a road trip to Cold Spring for the weekend.

We stopped at a public gas station halfway there to use the bathroom, and the place reeked to high heaven and back in a way that made my eyes water and my nose start filing out retirement paperwork.

Fun times all around, you know?

Artemis followed behind me effortlessly, even if we didn't talk. She seemed content to observe me as we cleared the ground, and eventually I think I just managed to mostly tune her out.

Somehow.

"There."

I heard a heavy, huffing exhale of a sound as we got closer, we found it right as we crested another small hill, nestled in between a glen along the middle of a circle of toppled trees.

That was the good news - I found my quarry!

That was also the bad news - I found my quarry, and dear dad was he ugly.

The monster boar was twice as big as a minivan, some twenty feet higher even when slumped over in sleep, and covered in a coat of bristling, shaggy fur so thorny I nearly pricked myself just staring at it. Its tail was short and stubby, and two oversized horns jutted out from the sides of its jaws like giant ivory swords of pure doom.

And the smell - did I mention the smell?

It was about a hundred times worse straight from the source, and if you could bottle the stuff up from the air you'd have a chemical-grade weapon on hand whenever you wanted - only I didn't think anybody would want this.

I tried not to gag as the boar shifted in its sleep, letting out a snore that sounded like a chainsaw blade sparking against gravel before petering back out again.

"An Erymanthian boar, then." Artemis hummed beside me, arms uncrossing as we both knelt down to see it better. "I thought as much."

I blinked.

"The one Heracles captured?"

I wasn't super read up on all the mythologies yet, and especially not the true mythologies Chiron was teaching us firsthand, but the Twelve Labors were basically the alphabet of the Greek hero stories.

Everybody and their grandma knew about them.

"No. That was the Erymanthian boar. This is merely one of its descendants." She pursed her lips. "They don't ordinarily range this far south, but this one has been making a nuisance of itself. It's disrupting the local ecosystem and threatening to cause problems with the mortal settlements nearby."

Right.

Messing with the natural balance and threatening the masquerade would prickle at her domains and sensibilities like nobody's business, wouldn't it?

"So you want me to...?"

I trailed off leadingly.

"What do you think?"

"Right."

It was pretty obvious, wasn't it?

Granted, I wasn't sure why she wanted me in particular to do it - she had a whole crew of people up to the ask - but I figured I was better off not asking.

With a crackle and a flare of light, Serpent's Downfall reappeared in my grip, and I hefted it up and over my shoulder.

The boar rumbled in its sleep some more, which was my cue to take aim for its head and reach back to take it out before it woke up. - A bit brutal to start with, but I wasn't fighting Porky the murder-swine if I could avoid it.

I had better things to do with my time.

"Wait."

I paused and stared at Artemis in confusion.

"Correct your posture."

What?

Her boot inched forward and nudged my foot back a little, and her hand pressed against my back lightly.

"Your aim is near-perfect, but you're too stationary. You need to be ready to move the moment that spear is out of your hand." The reprimand was clear. "I know that Chiron's taught you to stay light on your feet, so don't let the temptation of an easy shot break you out of the habit. That's how you get killed in predictable and often pathetic displays."

...

... Was she actually giving me advice?

Good advice too?

I don't know why that surprised me that much, but the hesitation cost me.

With a heaving grunt, Porky woke up.

His fur bristled even more as he sluggishly rose to his feet and pawed at the ground, and his red eyes flickered on like enormous LED lights. He snorted heavily, nostrils flaring, before he angled his tusks first and stared right at us.

At me.

"...Good nap?"

Those eyes narrowed before he let rip another crackling growl and started furiously tensing up like someone waved a red cape in his face and dared him to have a go at it.

"Rhee!"

I stared at Artemis, but she didn't seem the least bit concerned.

She was still waiting for me to make a move.

"Rhee!"

Okay, fine.

We're not doing this today.

The second Proky put one ugly hoof forward, I was already gone.

Reach Of Sunlight.

I vanished in a flare of sunlight and reappeared right next to Porky, too close for him to turn around and gore me with those tusks, and with nowhere left to retreat to even if I chose to give him the time to back up.

Spoiler alert - I didn't.

"Ignite."

Like the dragon it came from, my spear didn't do subtle.

The moment I hurled it forward and up into Porky's side, Serpent's Downfall lit up like a second sun.

The shockwave of superheated air followed suit, blowing back the fallen trees and incinerating the grass underfoot before it slammed into the boar before it could even squeal.

The force behind it was so insane that it actually lifted the three-hundred-ton monster off its feet at about the same time that half its fur caught fire, and it was dead before it the ground again like a pile of overcooked barbecue.

...

For a second, I just stared at it a little.

Huh.

That was easier than I thought it be.

The smell of burning fur and grass hit me, and I crinkled my nose before recalling my spear. I turned back to Artemis, who was looking down at me with an unreadable expression.

"...Mission accomplished?"

Excessively and with probably insulting degrees of overkill, but that was usually the best kind, right?

Artemis stared some more, and I was starting to get worried that that was a default state for her or something.

Then the expression melted away, and the goddess tipped back her head and actually sighed in resignation.

What?

"You..." She sounded as exasperated as Chiron had been, and also... fond? "...Are absolutely my brother's son."

Somehow, that wasn't what I was expecting either.

...​

Things moved quickly after that.

Artemis leaped from her perch to assess the still-smoking Porky's corpse, before she clicked her tongue and snapped her fingers.

"Some of the meat is salvageable. I'll send a portion to Chiron, and the rest to my hunters, who'll treat it and donate it to a few women's shelters across the area." She glanced my way. "Your hunter's share is accounted for."

Well then.

"Thanks?"

Guess I knew what we were having for dinner today.

Then I yelped as she grunted and reached over to flick my ear.

Why even!?

"Don't abandon your courtesies, but don't make a habit of thanking people for your due either. Some may take it as a sign of weakness and seek to take advantage of you."

I hesitantly nodded, and she seemed satisfied.

"Time to go."

Like before, there was no warning.

She snapped her fingers, and the forest melted away - only this time, the sound of car horns and bustling noises hit us first as we appeared right in the middle of a busy street, framed by small buildings on either side and the early afternoon crowds.

"Where are we?"

"Volos." Artemis was already walking down the street like she owned the place, and I followed after her as she stepped into the crowds.

It was still Greece, I could tell that much easily, but it wasn't Athens either. "The nearest port city to Mount Pelion."

That was an answer.

I'd have asked why we were here too, but I didn't need to bother.

We wasted no time turning across the street, past a sign, and right into the open door of a small apartment building off to one side.

Three flights of stairs later, she reached for a warm wooden door and rapped her knuckles against it three times, while I stepped back and looked it over carefully.

Magic.

Faint - very faint - but still there.

There was a familiar sound or three from behind the door - pots banging, a TV running, and all the other kind of stuff you'd expect to hear at a little apartment before a pair of running feet overshadowed them and the door clicked open with the slide of a deadbolt.

There was a little kid who couldn't have been that much older than Alex behind it, curly-haired and bright-eyed and chewing on a wad of bubble gum like his life depended on it.

Then his jaw dropped as he took one look at Artemis and lit up like a firecracker.

"Aunty Temis!"

That's when my jaw dropped too.

I didn't - read: couldn't - say a word as he shot forward and slammed into her legs, desperately trying to climb her like a baby koala on a mission, but Artemis just laughed.

Laughed.

"I missed you!"

"Hello, Elias." Her gentle smile was just jarring as she lifted him up and pulled him into a hug. She even pressed a kiss to the top of his curls. "I've missed you too. Have you been good for your Mama?

"Mhm!"

She patted his hair fondly.

"Good sprout."

Okay, what?

"Elias!" A woman appeared at the doorway, bronze-skinned and curly-haired just like he was. "Artemis!"

"Hello, Elena."

This time, there was no way I was imagining the fondness in her voice.

Then she lunged forward just like her son and hugged the goddess too, who welcomed her with open arms like it was the most natural thing in the world.

That sparking sound you may be hearing would be the wires in my brain short-circuiting.

Genuinely terrible sensation - Zero stars, would not recommend.

Eventually, Elena pulled back.

"Are you going to be staying?"

"No, unfortunately." Artemis patted Elias's hair a little more before she carefully handed him back to his mother. "I only came by to tell you that the 'wildlife disruption' the locals were having has been dealt with. A stray Erymanthian boar."

Elena's brows furrowed.

"This far south?

"Curious, isn't it?" Her eyes flickered to me, and Elena followed suit and finally seemed to realize that I was there too. "Something drove it far out of its normal range"

"Who...?"

"This is Daniel Winchester. Son of Apollon."

Elena inhaled sharply and leaned back in surprise.

"Truly?"

"Indeed."

I raised a hand akwardly and gave her my best smile as she looked back at me.

"Afternoon."

She bowed her head my way in a gesture that was a little formal to be a normal greeting, and I tried to keep my surprise off my face.

Along with everything else I was feeling.

"An honor."

There was something about her that reminded me of Artemis herself - a faint aftertaste of power that was obvious with both them standing nearly side by side, like a candle placed next to the star that lit it.

...I had an idea about that.

"We'll be off then." Artemis smiled at Elias one last time, and nodded to Elena. "I have to put this one back where I found him or I'll never hear the end for it."

Elena laughed. "Please come visit again soon."

"I will."

"Bye, Aunty Temis!"

"Goodbye, sprout."

Then we turned around and let the door shut behind us as we headed back down the way we came.

...

What was that?

"Was she-?"

"One of my former huntresses?" Artemis nodded "She left my service years ago."

I nearly missed a step.

"They can do that?"

"Let me guess - you've heard that my hunters are locked into my service and their oaths forevermore after they swear them, and any attempt to leave or break them is punished most severely."

"Uh..."

Damn it, I knew this. Chiron had covered it lightly, but the details slipped my mind when it mattered.

She rolled her eyes as we stepped back onto the street.

"I don't even know where that belief continues to come from. My hunters are permitted to leave at any time they please, so long as they inform me beforehand. Yes, things were once different and more complicated, but..." She sighed lowly, and her voice took on a tinge of... something I didn't want to touch. "Time is a powerful teacher, even for us gods, and regret is a crueler one that often goes hand in hand with it. I've learned from that personally."

"...Ah."

Yep.

Not going anywhere near that one even if you wrapped me in an air-tight celestial bronze suit and paid me to do it.

I'm rich now anyway.

"She felt like you." I didn't want the genuine edge of sadness in her voice to linger and choke out this conversation even more, so I went for the obvious bait. "Her power, I mean. It felt similar."

"I imagine it did. It's a remnant of my blessing on my hunters. Less potent, but still powerful. A gift and a warning both."

"Warning?"

She looked at me then, and something about her gaze made me lock up fast.

"I have enemies, nephew." Her words were slow, and calm, and somehow menacing despite that. Her eyes sparked pure silver again, shining in a way that nearly hurt to look at "There are many who hold grudges against me, both valid, exaggerated and everything in between, and they are welcome to challenge me as they wish... but should any dare lay a hand on my hunters, former or otherwise, or their children and loved ones after them..."

She didn't have to finish the threat.

It was at that exact second that I finally realized what the real difference between Artemis and Apollon.

Both were gods.

Both were ridiculously powerful.

But Apollon's strength was effortlessly obvious. Just existing in his general vicinity made you feel small and at risk of spontaneously combusting.

Artemis was like an apex predator - a coiled hunter ready to pounce, and one you didn't truly know was there until she was already going right for your throat.

Then she blinked lazily, the moment passed, and I felt like I could breathe easily again as the air between us went back to normal.

Woah.

That was...

"You really care about them, don't you?"

It was glaringly obvious, but I still had trouble processing it as we continued to walk and talk.

That reaction seemed a little too... human for an Olympian.

I mean, these guys were my extended relatives, and I'll still be the first to admit that they are the poster-children for why gods and mortals mixing has a minimum fifty-fifty chance of exploding spectacularly in everyones faces.

Artemis blinked again.

"Of course I do. The hunters are my friends, my sisters, and even my daughters. My family." Something in the way she stressed that word was very deliberate. "And I value my family greatly, nephew."

There was meaning in the way she said that too.

I just didn't quite know what it meant, or what to do with it.

"What do you want from me?"

I know that blurting it out probably wasn't the smartest thing to do, but at this point I already made it nearly an hour and a half without saying something reckless.

As far as I'm concerned, that was a new record - and for a reward, I wanted a straight answer.

"To take the measure of you. " She offered freely. "And ask you a question. That devil friend of yours..."

I tensed a little, and I think she caught onto it pretty much instantly.

"Yes?"

What did she-?

"Do you intend to join his peerage?"

...

...

...

Oh.

Her nose scrunched as the word rolled of her tongue, like just saying it had grossed her out, but I barely paid attention to it.

"Sairaorg doesn't even have a peerage yet."

"That's not an answer."

It wasn't.

Probably because never even thought about it before,I hadn't even thought of it before, and I'm... ninety percent sure Sairaorg didn't even have Evil Pieces?

He certainly hadn't told me if he had, and it wasn't something he'd have to keep secret from me.

But now that I thought about it...

...

...

...

"No."

It wasn't the 'devils are nasty, why the hell would I?" answer she might've been expecting, but it was the truth.

I was a demigod, and I already had enough powers to go head-to-head and toe to toe with Sairaorg - and even then, I was barely getting started.

I didn't need to permanently switch to another species to get stronger, or for their magic, or for any of the other reasons people would accept a deal like that in the first place, never mind all the downsides that'd come my way from getting tied to the one faction nearly everybody else despised so completely it was almost hilarious in hindsight.

That just wasn't me.

"No, I wouldn't." Artemis seemed quietly pleased by that, or at least satisfied, so of course I had to risk bungling that up by opening my mouth again. "But that doesn't mean that I would turn my back on my best friend, or that I'm not going to have his back if he needs me too."

Her silver eyes narrowed, but I only swallowed lightly and nodded firmly.

"I won't."

And that's my quota for dumb things to spit out mid-conversation, met and exceeded.

Go me.

Strangely, though, Artemis didn't get upset.

Instead, she snorted.

"Fair enough."

"..."

"..."

"...Wait, for real?"

"I told you that I came to take the measure of you, and I do believe I have." She smiled my way, and the expression seemed almost normal. "Loyalty to a questionable companion is not ideal, but until it becomes a problem, at least the principle behind it is admirable."

And proud, in a calm sort of way.

"It's far from the worst thing you could have inherited from your father."

Then she leaned forward and tapped my forehead with her index finger.

Something shifted, and I reared back a little as my senses seemed to flare out - I could smell the exhaust from the nearby cars, feel the breeze heading my way, and feel the movement of every other person on the street in ago - before settling back down again.

"What was that?" I blinked silver spots out of my line of sight. "What did you do?"

"Consider it a gift. A little edge for you to sharpen and hone, as a welcoming gift into this family." She turned away with something that might have been a smirk. "You'll need it."

"What was that?"

"Nothing."

...

Yeah, and I'm Zeus.

Though I probably shouldn't make that joke out loud. With my luck, he'll drop out of the sky next to take me on another stroll.

...

...

...

Okay, discarding that line of thought, right freaking now.

I shuddered, and Artemis raised a brow.

"Something to say?"

"Not a one."

"Good. Then we're done here."

I... paused.

"We are?"

"I said so, didn't I?"

The 'keep up, you moron' was loudly implied. But it still sounded gentle, almost teasing.

"But what about the Erythmanian boar? You told Elena that something had pushed it out of its hunting range."

"Yes? And?"

"...Aren't we going to look into it?"

With the way she'd looked at me back then, I'd thought that's were things were going.

She seemed to consider that for a bit, before nodding lightly.

Like she'd just made up her mind about something else.

"Tell you what. I won't - I still have responsibilities and duties pulling me away, and the immediate problem has been solved." Slowly, she smiled again. This one was distinctly sly. "But you can."

...

I pretty much asked for whatever comes next, didn't I?

Man, Chiron was never going to let me hear the end of it.

"I can?"

"Indeed. Return here sometime within the next month, and investigate on my behalf. If you can find whatever it is that's causing these disruptions and point me towards it, or even handle it yourself for that matter, I'll consider offering that devil friend of yours a reward as well." I started, and her smile stretched even wider. "Yes, I daresay he'd be the first of his literally damned kind to ever receive such a token in recent memory, if ever at all."

When she put it that way, I only had to think about it for all of three seconds.

On the one hand, she'd just asked me to run an errand.

Potentially a dangerous one.

On the other hand, Sairaorg, so...

"We'll do it. Or try to, at least."

Technically I should asked Sai beforehand, but let's face it, that one wasn't even a question - he'd probably riot if I refused on his behalf.

"Good." She nodded approvingly. "Then it's time for you to return."

She waved her hand, and I lit up with a silver glow as space began to fold around me - None of the mortals around us seemed to notice, though.

"Watch yourself, nephew." I would asked why, but she stunned me when she leaned forward one last time and ruffled my hair. The look she gave was measured, but warm enough that I could almost feel settle into my bones like the wave of magic that followed. "Your existence has made my brother very happy, and I'm not unimpressed myself. Do keep at it until we meet again, won't you?"

"I-?"

Too late.

Her hand pulled away, and I was suddenly gone.

...​

I reappeared inside Chiron's house, right outside the kitchen.

Naturally, they were already inside and waiting for me.

"Dan?" Sai looked me over carefully as I stepped into the room. "Are you ok?

I didn't answer.

Instead, I went over everything that had happened in the last hour and a half, from start to finish and back again, before slowly nodding to myself as I reached a conclusion I never would have guessed at a week ago.

Then again, unexpected surprises were basically my bread and butter at this point, so go figure.

"I think." They both stared expectantly "That my aunt might actually be cool."

And wasn't that something?

For some reason, it was Chiron that started cracking up first.

...​
Extra:

Back in Volos, Artemis stared at the spot that her latest nephew flickered away from before sighing and rolling her neck around a few times.

The gesture was more of a habit than a strict need, but nobody worthwhile would judge her for it.

Then she cleared her throat and spoke, sounding just about done with everything today.

"He's already gone, brother. You can stop hiding now."

For a moment, there was no response.

Then Apollon shimmered into view, hands in his pocket and easy smile on his face. He stepped onto the street from thin air, literally, and as always not one of the mortals surrounding them perceived the change at all.

"I wasn't hiding."

Artemis rolled her eyes and began to march in the opposite direction.

"I'm sure. Was there something you wanted to say, or did you just come to watch over the boy like a mother hen?"

"I would never." He lied breezily. "I just wanted to see what my dearest twin thought of my son."

She snorted.

"You already know what I think."

"Humor me."

"The boy is fine. Better than, even. He's quite impressive for his age."

That might have been an understatement.

Artemis knew talent, and power, and those who had both in ages long since past.

For a child of a softer, calmer era, Daniel Winchester was coming along nicely indeed.

"He is, isn't he?" Apollon's pride was warm, his grin delighted. "You should have seen him eight months ago. Barely more impressive than an average mortal, and now look how far he's come."

Oh, and here they go again.

"I'm not blind, Apollon. I blessed him for a reason."

She didn't just give handouts, not even to her brother's children.

Especially not her brother's children - fleetingly rare as those had become.

As a goddess who valued grit and perseverance, Artemis knew when to grant a boon, and when said boon would only be a crutch that led to inflated the ego and arrogance bordering on a death wish.

This one, however, she could not see herself regretting.

At least her brother was proud of his new son - that, she couldn't begrudge him. It had been centuries since she'd last seen him like this.

"And to kill a dragon at his age."

Her eye twitched.

On second thought...

"Will you ever shut up about that?"

She'd seen that spear. She'd seen the memory.

It was an achievement worthy of songs - but she'd already gotten the damned message, and her twin was nothing if not excessive when he wanted to be.

Apollon just laughed.

"Hardly."

Wonderful.

"Did you ever find out where the dragon he's defeated came from?"

Because Smaug the Bane Of Dwarves was not a name she was familiar with, and curiosity had been niggling away at her for some time now.

"I have some theories. Some more valid than others." He shrugged nonchalantly. "Chiron's already helped them claim the corpse and is preparing to sell the excess. I'll get my hands on a few pieces and see what leads they turn up."

She nodded.

"And the boy himself?"

Because she was perhaps one of the few people aware of his existence who also knew that he was not Apollon's son by birth.

At least, not the ordinary kind.

"Irrelevant." Apollon didn't miss a beat - not that she expected him to. "He is my son, indubitably and inarguably. I'll find out more in time, but the most important matter has already been settled."

That was the absolute truth, and they both knew it.

"And his devil companion?"

"..."

"..."

"What about him?"

Artemis shot him a flat look as they continued walking down the street. The mortals parted away from them like a wave splitting against a rock cliff, still unable to see them but stepping aside anyway out of sheer instinct.

Ants scattering away from a boot that had no interest in crushing them, but could still do with ridiculous ease.

"Fine." He huffed and adjusted the cuffs of his suit. "It's too late. If I wanted to separate them, I should have done it sooner. They've trained together and fought together and bonded."

His expression didn't change, but the subtle displeasure was obvious.

"Their friendship is less than a year old, but it might as well have stretched on for centuries. I can't pull them apart now, by force or otherwise."

Because Daniel Winchester would never forgive his father for it, and Apollon would not be harming his son for the sake of one devil.

Some would disagree with that plan.

Others would refuse it outright.

The last time a Greek demigod had gotten close to a Abrahamic devil had been centuries ago, and that situation had spiralled into an utter disaster so absurd there was still gods who felt the impact of it to this day.

Apollon was one of them - but he didn't need the reminder, and Artemis wasn't inclined to bring up bad, bloody history, so she just nodded and let the matter drop

"Is that why you're keeping your distance?"

"Hardly. He's uncomfortable in my presence, and that will take time to change." He shrugged easily. "Let him train and grow stronger for now. It'll make him more comfortable, and I can be patient."

If nothing else, it was a good plan.

Daniel Winchester was growing stronger, and Sairaorg Bael was, for now, not a problem. For a devil of his age, and lacking in magic as well, his spiritual presence was growing rather notably, but that was a footnote for the moment.

For now, all was well.

"So tell me, sister, have any of your hunters killed a dragon recently-?"

She scowled and took off into a sprint faster than Aeolus's winds themselves.

"Oi! Temis! Where are you going?" Her infuriating twin just laughed and followed in pursuit. "We were just talking!"

A second later, the two gods disappeared into the fading sunset.

...​
