#1,683
There was once a time when Chiron - scorned and unwanted son of Kronos the Crooked One and Philyra the Oceanid, Wisest and Justest of all Centaurs, and famed and mythicised Trainer of Heroes - thought that he would never take on another student again.

To be clear, the sentiment itself hadn't been any sort of instant, immediate realization. He hadn't woken up in the morning one day, looked at his reflection in the nearest mirror and suddenly decided to consider retirement.

Oh no.

The temptation to step back from the mantle and role he'd forged for himself - and quite happily at that, thank you very much - tended to come and go over the centuries and millennia.

It couldn't be helped, truly.

Greek heroes - and the small number of others he'd taught outside of that circle, who'd been comparatively rarer but hardly unheard of where it counted - tended to, on average, lead very... interesting lives.

That was about the kindest word Chiron had for it.

Asclepius, Peleus, Heracles, Jason, Achilles, Patroclus... the lists - plural, naturally - went on and on, and even when the inks ran dry and there were no more pages left to fill, Chiron could still readily offer more and more names from heart and memory.

And those were just the classics.

There was a pattern to a great deal of them, one that played out in different contexts from era to era even if the highlights and the greatest hits stayed the same at the roots.

Struggle and conflict, pride and glory, a path fraught with danger and crowned with either triumph or failure in legendary degrees... it was all a coin toss from the moment they left his care - some even before that - and after training them to the best of his ability, all he could do after the fact was sit back, hope dearly for the best, and wait to see which way the quarter landed.

But hope didn't always pay dividends, and those stories - their stories - were never just stories.

Not just tales to entertain the masses, or moral lessons in the making for scholars and children and everyone in between to pore over and pick apart looking for meaning that was decided with perspective and was often liable to shift under the right prompting.

How could they be?

Instead, to Chiron, they were wounds.

Bittersweet - and sometimes just bitter - always scarring and soul-deep in a way that left the path he'd chosen for himself a hopelessly drawn-out life sentence.

Death by a thousand cuts - only immortality rather handily took death out of the equation, but the pain remained, long-lasting and more poisonous than any arrow dipped in Hydra venom could ever hope to be.

Still, he'd made his peace with it.

Change was inevitable, and the good outweighed the bad. The joy he experienced as he raised each student to the height of their potential -or setting them on the path to do just that, wherever necessary - far surpassed the tides of grief that washed over him as they met their ends, even if it hardly ever felt so in the moment.

Such was his way in life, and all had been well.

And then Ajuka Beelzebub of the Abrahamic Devils brought forth his Evil Pieces into a world that always seemed to balance on a knife's edge and be only a few right prods away from carnage, and Chiron - along with anyone and everyone with even a shred of sense and terrible foresight - immediately smelled blood in the water and nightmares on the horizon.

The one 'great' faction that was almost universally despised by most all others - and plenty of those that were lesser but still existed in their own right for good measure - suddenly possessing a means to reincarnate other beings into more of themselves?

A way to take - by carrot or infernal stick - the best and brightest they could reach from among their many, many enemies' ranks to swell their own, all the while dressing it up as a means of repopulation or what have you?

Please.

Waving the red cape at the charging bull was one thing, but this was akin to one marching up to said bull, slapping it in the face with said cape, and then immediately tying it in a bow around its horns and hoping for the best.

Chaos ensued.

Political disasters - the kind that tended to end in tense, drawn-out negotiations or landmass reshaping cataclysms - spawned overnight.

The supernatural theatre as a whole seemed to brace for impact, and with good reason - but no amount of bracing could have prepared Chiron for what came next, and that day was still burned into his memory in meticulous, utterly devastating detail.

The day he arrived too late to a battlefield scoured by gods and mortals alike, torn apart in a battle he'd known would come in some shape or form.

A battle he'd cautioned against, warned against, and tried so desperately to prevent, but the effort failed all the same.

That day, Chiron's hooves sunk down into blood-soaked mud on the edges of a hellish tragedy, the ground blackened and ruined around the broken bodies of an entire generation of his students - and more besides - and all the while, the gods raged against one another in the sky and tore it apart between them, just as they had done with everything below.

Eventually, it ended as things do - but, again, all too late.

When the dust settled, and the screaming stopped, when only regret and shame remained to fill the void they left behind and the silence more damning than the trails of Tartarus itself... Well.

There was nothing left - none that mattered, not to him.

Chiron left that day, after seeing to the rights and final dignities of those he'd taught and cared for in life, and let the gods of Olympus bear the weight of the fallout, the price of the consequences they had reaped for themselves.

They were of no concern to him, and it was only fair, wasn't it?

It was they who had allowed their mistakes to fester and rot until the maggots crawled out with teeth and claws, looking for their pound of flesh - and rightly so.

Even the gods recognized that much, but only after the bill had come due.

And as for Chiron?

The centuries that followed were... difficult. For a time, he secluded himself from the world entirely, returning to his home in Mount Pelion and sealing himself away in his grief.

Mourning was never easy, and mourning losses so easily preventable - at least in hindsight - was that much harder.

In time, however, he emerged. Not at the behest of any gods - though plenty had tried and failed - but in his own time, when he was well and ready to and not a second before.

He returned to his homes across Greece, shifting from one to another in an old, easy routine as the decades passed, and then the centuries that followed after them.

Even then, he made no move to take on new students, even when many of various worth attempted to seek him out.

He was, for the most part, simply quite... with that aspect of his life.

For the foreseeable future, at the very least, even if the temptation to take up his craft grew stronger and stronger with every passing year.

You can't teach an old dog new tricks, after all, and ancient centaurs were much the same when it came to the important things in life.

Still, he had been living in quiet isolation, passing his days in lazy, even-tempered peace, and as far as this era was concerned, everything had been nice and quiet for a change.

And then he'd go out one day, and promptly be ambushed outside his favourite city-grocer by a devil with gumption and drive in spades, and none of the attitude that would have soured it.

"Hello!" The boy had beamed, looking like he'd sprinted a marathon or three to find him and still heaving for breath on every other word. "I'm Sairaorg Bael! Please train me!"

So he said.

Loudly.

In the middle of a crowded street.

Chiron had only blinked.

The presence of a devil in his vicinity didn't faze him, even with the history involved - he'd sensed the child coming from well over halfway across Athens, and with not a speck of malice to be found in his presence - but that question...

Really?

Really?

"I am regretfully retired."

The boy had paused, taken that in for all of a second and then nodded more to himself than to Chiron.

"Can we talk about that?"

"What is there to talk about?"

"I don't know yet, but I'm open to negotiations!"

Goodness, the audacity of this child.

Not just bold as brass, but determined and heartfelt in a way few would ever expect from a member of his kind - especially one with that particular name - and absolutely refusing to take no for an answer.

Even when Chiron up and left him there, and then watched in no little amusement as the tenacious young devil spent the rest of the day zipping to and from across the city trying to find him.

And the next.

And the next, and so on and so forth.

It became a little game between them, and that's how it started.

Then, some time later, he'd 'stumbled' upon Daniel, heavily wounded but held in a stasis spell - almost certainly god forged - that shattered the moment he got close enough to make sense of it.

Essentially leaving him with another child he all but had to take some measure of responsibility for, even if only because of the weight of his own conscience.

Potential hero or not, abandoned children in need were more than a sore spot for him.

How very... deliberate.

Conniving and clever, too. Certainly well played on Apollon's part in hindsight, even if Chiron knew full well that it had stemmed from a place of calculating caution, practicality, and no small amount of cold, demanding wrath.

The impossibility of his newfound son's existence warranted investigation, after all, and there were few places better to keep in sight than in Chiron's care.

That particular plot would have fallen apart had Chiron chosen not to play ball, so to speak, but really, that was never truly an option, and anyone who knew him well enough would have expected as much.

Chiron's resolve lasted all of a single night after that.

"Why do you want to train under me?"

"Because I was born weak, and I was told I was worthless because of it. I refuse to accept that, so I'm going to grow as strong as I can get, and then some."

"Because I nearly died, and it sucked harder than anything in my life ever has, and I never want to feel that way again if I can help it."

The rest, as they say, was history.

Two new students under his care at long last.

Both determined, strong-willed and brimming with absurd potential.

They were also hard-headed at times, reckless, and apparently cursed with an incredible ability to land themselves in some of the most ridiculously convoluted spots of trouble imaginable, but then again, how many of the past heroes who'd trained under his aegis hadn't ended up with a track record that read like the fates themselves had a grudge and wanted to pay it back with spite and interest?

A measly few?

If even that?

Sairaorg and Daniel's shenanigans were simply par the course, really.

And now here they were.

Ten, nearly eleven months later - some of the best he'd had in recent memory - and Chiron found himself in a familiar position once again.

Down a pair of students - and one particularly irritable Nemean Lion, as a last-minute bonus - and waiting with just the right blend of expectant pride and patient hope for their return.

"The more things change," He whispered to himself hours the evening after they left, wry and tired as he sat back in his chair out in the garden and enjoyed the cool, crisp breeze under a pleasant wash of moonlight. "The more they stay the same."

The quest for the Golden Fleece - and what an intriguing artifact that would be to study in time - was a noble one, and Sairaorg and Daniel's skills were well honed, their rate of growth astounding by the standards of this calmer era.

Even when measured with the metrics of ages long gone past, they were still impressive, if only because Chiron would have accepted nothing less.

Still, a teacher worried.

He'd allowed the quest because they had the capability. They needed to learn how to come into their own without his hand on the scales, but regardless of how endlessly fascinating - and very, very dangerous - the concept of other worlds remained, the idea of threats he couldn't quite account for outside of what were, at best, educated guesses didn't sit well with him.

Not at all.

That was why he'd played his cards just right and added a third to their party just before they took off.

Prodding Regulus into joining the boys on their quest had been a last-minute decision, entirely for Chiron's own peace of mind, and also remarkably straightforward, as simple as outright telling him about the quest just over the horizon and letting the lion's interest do the rest of the work for him.

He had made no secret of his growing boredom, after all, and that made it all too simple to rope him into the affair instead of letting such a golden opportunity go to waste.

Granted, Regulus was no fool and had known full well what Chiron had been doing, but it wasn't supposed to be much of a secret to begin with.

What would have been the point?

No, the part that he had kept deliberately concealed, naturally, was where they would be going in due time - and for more reasons than just the obvious too.

Revealing his student's secret without his say so, even for his own good, was something Chiron had precisely no interest in outside of the direst of emergencies, and even then he would exhaust all other reasonable alternatives before even considering violating his trust in such a manner.

That was a hard set rule.

...And, as a side benefit, Daniel likely enjoyed the chance to spring his harrowing world jumps on Regulus himself, and while Chiron wouldn't normally encourage that kind of squabbling pettiness, there was no true mean spirit behind it on either end as of yet, and that lion was more than capable of giving as good as he got and then some.

...

Eventually.

After recovering from what was patently the worst - or at least unrefined - form of magical transportation Chiron had ever experienced, bar none.

His lips twitched in light amusement, before smoothing out again into something more contemplative as he considered the other reason he hadn't clued his temporary houseguest in on Daniels's ability.

It was Regulus himself - Or rather, what he was and possibly represented.

The mightiest Nemean Lion to ever live, yes, and by a great and as of yet unsurpassed margin as well, but also the only recently incarnated soul once trapped in and actively powering a biblical Sacred Gear, and therefore connected to - formerly, or perhaps not - the Biblical Heaven's System.

And that particular absurdity...

Chiron found himself sighing tiredly just thinking about it.

The God of Abraham possessed, as many deities did, a great number of claims to power and transcendence, but what elevated Him far above all but a few others was not simply his nature as a monotheistic deity - though that did, of course, have it's own weight - but his sheer and undisputed authority as a Creator.

And in that, there was no greater example than His System.

An autonomous, all-encompassing metaphysical framework that permeated perhaps all layers of this world - even the domains and realms of other pantheons and divinities, up to and including the Dimensional Gap - allowing Him to exert his presence and influence in varying degrees regardless of the whims of most other influences.

Sacred Gears, Spirit Inheritors under the biblical aegis, as well as the prayers, faith and miracles of His religion before all else... all of it determined and managed by that one overarching creation.

How truly ludicrous, but it only grew more so when one connected the dots and realised that the System in itself likely acted as a technical means of omnipresence - though again, only to various degrees - and, essentially, as a direct result, a tool of His 'omniscience'.

In short?

Chiron suspected that Sacred Gears were, or at least could be used by the System as an external way to observe and learn from the world by way of their hosts.

Granted it was only a theory, and one with holes in it given what he knew about the nature of the gears themselves from experience, observable accounts and events in the last few centuries going unanswered where Chiron would have thought they would necessitate a response - Any kind of one.

But there was nothing.

More immediately recent happenings also conflicted with his theory that much more, given that Daniel had outright taken Incinerate Anthem with him across worlds and not garnered so much as a wiff of response from the Abrahamic faction.

Not a one.

That was suspicious in of itself, and while it could be in part due to his lineage bieng what it was ad the sheer disaster that would ensue if they so much as touched a hair his his head without due cause - or with any kind of cause at all, valid or not - the silence was part of a pattern that brought to mind certain... rumours that had been slowly gaining traction in the supernatural world over the past number of decades, held back only by sheer disbelief...

But those were thoughts for later.

The takeaway here was that Chiron hadn't told Regulus what to expect beyond the vaguest details simply on the off - and exceedingly unlikely, but not impossible -chance that that knowledge might somehow carry over across Heaven's System and prompt another kind of mess entirely.

Taking the risk with Incinerate Anthem was already inevitable from the moment the gear bonded to Daniel, but it was better safe than sorry with yet another Longinus thrown into the mix.

Particularly after the... riveting little tidbit Dan had shared with him after he'd jumped back from his family visit the day before.

Yet another significant thought for later.

He massaged his scalp with one hand and slowly shook his head.

Much later.

For now, he could only wait for his students to return, content as can be given the circumstances and with the knowledge that they were armed with just about everything he could have provided them with in the time they'd had to prepare.

He'd even say they were overprepared, but there was no such thing.

They might even manage to get through their quest without too much trouble.

...
...
...

He lasted a few more seconds before breaking out into relatively quiet laughter he just couldn't hope to hold back.

Who was he trying to fool with that false optimism?

Those two firebrands of his were going to sow all manner of chaos before everything was said and done, and everyone involved knew it well before they'd set foot outside the house.

Hah.

Chiron was looking forward to hearing all about it, but first things first...

He tilted his head to the side and waited patiently as the presence he'd sensed moving throughout the house made its way in his direction.

Two of them, actually.

A few seconds later, the door to his left opened with a carefully muted click.

Sarah Winchester stepped out into the moonlit night, immediately startled after catching sight of him out of the corner of her eye and let out a soft, embarrassed sound as she settled back down again.

Quite jumpy, but that much was understandable - It had been a long day, in more ways than one.

"Sorry." She held her youngest daughter in her arms -Alex - propped against her hip, deeply asleep with her head tucked into the crook of her neck and with a small blanket thrown over her and Sarah's arm. "She woke up a little while ago and had a hard time getting back to sleep, and I thought we could both use some fresh air. We didn't mean to bother-"

"No, no, please." He gestured, and another sun lounger appeared a few steps away with a barely perceptible shimmer of green-tinted power, large and inviting. "Join me if you wish. There's plenty of room to go around."

Her eyes widened at the casual display of magic, and she sucked in a sharp breath. Her mouth and jaw worked soundlessly for several long, stunned moments..

For his part, Chiron settled for smiling politely and letting her adjust at her own pace.

It had been a deliberate move, after all. The better to begin easing her into an aspect of her life he doubted she had much familiarity with.

For a moment, his senses also brushed along the spark her child carried with her - a strain of inherited power, diluted but still clearly present for those who knew to look for it.

Then he dismissed it as well.

A problem for another day.

"...Right." She said at last, and it was with a hint of wonder and something like exhausted hysteria, but wonderfully lacking in manic energy. "Magic."

"Indeed."

Her lips quivered like she wasn't sure whether or not laugh at the dry - but kind - delivery.

Then she moved, slowly and carefully lowering herself and her child into the chair beside him, as if she was afraid it would disappear under her the moment she committed to sitting on it.

When it didn't, she relaxed just a little and breathed a sigh that sounded much too heavy and paradoxically fragile for one so young - relatively speaking - but, again, Chiron supposed it was only to be expected given everything she had and would keep experiencing for quite some time before the novelty of it all faded away.

The Winchester clan as a whole was in for quite the adjustment period, and the hours long conversation - seminar, really - that Chiron has sat them through for the better part of a day after their arrival was only just the tip of a single ice berg in the middle of the Antarctic.

For a few minutes, neither. The sounds of coming from the grass shifting against the breeze up ahead and the woodlands in the distance filled the silence between them, and the air was calm and peaceful.

"The stars are beautiful tonight," Sarah whispered at last, slowly brushing back Alex's hair as she looked up at the sea of twinkling spotlights splayed out across the heavens. "I've never seen them so clearly before."

"Those would be the astrological wards."

"Ah?" She blinked. "Astrological...wards?"

Hmm... how best to break this down?

"In this case, think of them as a type of magical boundary line - a mystical electric fence, if you will - that can be 'programmed' to allow and carry out certain functions within a specific area." His hand swept out easily, motioning across everything within their line of sight. "The ones surrounding my home have many functions, but a fair few are responsible for filtering out light pollution and magnifying the viewer's perspective of the stars. Hence, astrological wards."

She seemed to digest that in pieces, before nodding slowly.

"I think I.. understand that, a little. Not as much as I maybe should, but..." She shrugged, and to her credit, the gesture was only a little hesitant. "At least it's a heck of a view, right?"

Fair enough.

Chiron smiled, and she noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing at all, and I agree." His smiled warmed some more. "And so does your nephew."

She blinked again.

"Dan?"

"Yes. He and Sairaorg like to camp out and spend the night under the stars, every once in a while."

Granted it had only happened the first few times because they'd been too exhausted to drag themselves back to the house after some particularly arduous training - and Chiron regrets nothing there - but they'd gotten into the habit of spending some of their time that way and it was far from unpleasant.

Though why Daniel tried to use Serpent's Downfall of all things to light a campfire that one time just after he'd started mastering its use and ended up taking out half his flowerbeds in one go was anyone's guess.

Keeping a straight face after that one - and Sairaorg's resulting debate on whether or not cursed dragonflame could be used to safely roast s'mores if they were purified with natural energy after the fact - had been the challenge of several lifetimes, and trust him, he would know.

The more interesting was his demigod student's burgeoning interest in Astrology, even if it was likely only cursory.

Nothing concrete, barely a few ideas, really, but it was a very valid thaumaturgical field to look into with some experience, and what was the sun if not the star with the greatest immediate relevance over their day-to-day lives?

Food for thought.

"That's good to hear." Sarah's smile was bright with relief. "Sairaorg is a great kid, and I'm glad they're such good friends."

"As am I."

Those two had grown as close as family in so little time, and what a wonderful truth that was to reminisce over.

There was a short pause.

"Thank you." Sarah spoke up again, wetting her lips nervously as she tried to find the right words. "I know we've said it before, but David and I are... so, so far out of the loop here, and catching up is taking up time."

"There is no shame in that."

"I know, but... again, thank you."

She met his eyes earnestly.

"For taking care of Daniel, and his friend. For looking after him when we couldn't. For helping us out and letting us into your home. I know words alone can't possibly be enough, but thank you, for all of it."

Chiron nodded gently when she was finished.

"I appreciate the sentiment, but it is unnecessary. They are both my students. Looking after them?" He smiled and shook his head. "That is my duty and my privilege, and my home is always open to them and theirs."

She took that in for a minute and the smile she gave him after it was that much brighter.

"I'm glad my nephew met you. You're good people - the best of them all, and Dan thinks so too. Tells us all about it whenever he comes home, even if he only just gave us your name the other day."

How charming

"I do try."

Sarah laughed, and Chiron considered it a minor victory when her shoulders relaxed a fraction, and when her reaction to him summoning a pot of tea and two mugs a few moments later was nothing more dramatic than a small, surprised flinch.

"It shows." She said, shifting Alex in her arms as Chiron poured them each a warm, steaming drink. "I don't think I've ever seen Dan so... happy before. It's amazing."

Chiron paused.

The way she lingered on the word, the way her voice warped around it... there was an implication there.

"Was he not before?"

She looked at him blankly.

"Happy?"

Her eyes widened.

"Oh, no, that's not what I meant! Dan's always been an upbeat kind of kid. Outdoorsy, makes friends at school easily, the whole list. Everything a boy his age should be. It's just..."

Again, she hesitated, mouth opening and closing like she was picking and discarding words with every motion.

"If it's a personal matter..."

Curiosity aside, Chiron wouldn't push.

"No, it's not that." Sarah shook her head slowly, before sighing and running her free hand through her hair bracingly. "It's a long story."

He didn't say a word, letting her gather her thoughts at her own pace. His lips did quirk up, hover minutely, when Sarah took a sip of her tea and startled, looking at her mug with an appreciative glance.

"This is incredible."

"Thank you. I'm quite proud of it."

"Mhm." She set the mug down, looked at him once more with something parallel to hesitation, before closing her eyes and clearing her throat. "Dan's mother... did he ever get to telling you about her?"

Chiron raised a brow.

"In no great detail, and I knew better than to press."

Sarah breathed out lightly, and the sound was soft and rather tellingly sad.

"I'm not surprised. It's been six years, and I can probably count the number of times he's even mentioned her name out loud with both hands and still have fingers to spare." She opened her eyes as she spoke, glancing down to where her sleeping daughter was slumped against her chest. "Her name was Evelyn, and she was David's twin. The older one too, but not by much, and she was... a real character - Not in a bad way, though."

A ghost of a smile pulled at her expression, before fading away again quickly.

"She was kind. Smart. All kinds of witty. Real brave, too."

"Like mother, like son."

"Oh, absolutely. Dan takes a lot after her. But the thing is... David told me that the kid was born wired into the crazier parts of the world, right from the get-go. No choice or way to get away from it or anything like it, not with his dad being... what he is."

A god

The word was unspoken, but it echoed between them all the same.

"Evelyn, though?"

Sarah shook her head lightly.

"Before Dan was born, she was practically swimming right in the deep end of that pool, and all on her own too. Magic, monsters, and wild dangers straight out of the storybooks... Evelyn was all about that kind of life. A real swashbuckling adventurer type, you know?"

"I can imagine."

And he very much could, given that Evelyn Winchester's description was already reading like an excerpt of the lives of many am audacious mortal he'd trained, been acquainted with or even simply heard of over the course of his very, very long life - to say nothing of the similarities she already shared with her son.

Nothing particularly noteworthy in the grand scheme of things, but it lined up neatly with what he already knew of the woman.

"She did a lot of good too, helping out at this place...David said it was called Camp Half-blood?"

"I'm aware of the concept."

A summer camp for demigods.

How... decidedly novel.

"Yes, well, it wasn't all sunshine and rainbows. Everything she was doing... David was against her going at it the way she was since before we ever met, and it caused a lot of friction between them over the years until she had Dan and decided to settle down." She said quietly "Some of their rows were messy, and before my little nephew showed up, they only got a little better after they clued me in on the big secret."

"That must have been difficult to come to terms with."

She snorted loudly.

"Oh, horribly."

That very much tracked.

"I thought David was joking, at first. Then I thought that he was having a nervous breakdown when I realized that he was being dead serious. My sweet, hard-working Fiancé to be talking about monsters and things straight out of a children's bedtime story like they were right around the corner and waiting to pop out at us - it scared the life out of me." She took another sip of her mug and blinked slowly. "I'm not... I think the term is 'clear-sighted?' I can't see through the Mist."

She paused.

"Or at least, I normally can't. Evelyn... she was there because David begged her to be, and she did something to me. This temporary trick, and suddenly..."

She stopped again and inhaled shakily.

"I didn't see any monsters, but she made me see enough. To believe, at least."

...

Well then.

That was a very interesting way to put it, wasn't it?

Chiron was aware of the Mist as a concept, but this supposed ability Daniel's mother had possessed... a conceptual ability of some sort?

Most likely.

A power tied to her heritage, perhaps - Hecate was the Goddess of magic... and Mist.

More questions for later.

"The point is, things settled down after Dan was born, and we all had a great time of it. As good as can be. Until six years ago, when an old friend called Evelyn, asking for help, and she decided to drop Dan off at our place and take off. 'Just for a week', she said."

Ah.

So that's how it was.

Sarah smiled sadly when their eyes met again.

"She never made it back - not.... not alive, at least. We held her funeral just a little while later." Her grip on her daughter tightened, nearly imperceptibly. "Dan... it tore him apart. He wouldn't eat and sleep. He didn't even talk for days after we broke the news to him, and barely spoke more than a few words in our direction at all for weeks and weeks afterwards. Grief counselors and all that... none of them helped. It wasn't until I had Alex months down the line that he seemed to come back to life a little, but it still took the better part of a year for him to act like himself and he never brought up Evelyn on his own again. Not once."

The imagery there was potent, and Chiron closed his eyes and leaned back in his chair as he took her words in.

"Grief is a very powerful thing."

"It is, and it was." Sarah agreed, swallowing painfully. "And I don't think I made it any easier in the first few years."

"...How so?"

To that, she laughed again.

This time, it was distinctly more miserable.

"My friend and sister in law had just died, and my husband was a wreck. I had three children - babies - under my roof, one of them a newborn, the other a toddler, and the third was a ghost-" The word caught in her throat, and she looked about a second away from slapping her palm against her mouth to stifle it away. "No, I'm sorry, that was cruel. What I'm trying to say is.... it was all one big mess."

Her eyes began to glisten as her voice wavered, and she wiped at them furiously in between quick, sharp breaths.

"The worst part was that, for the first few months after Dan came to live with us full time, I was so scared." The admission sounded like it was gutting to let loose. "I'd just given birth, and everything seemed so... fragile, and all I could think about was the stories David had told me over the years, about demigods attracting every kind of blood-thirsty monster under the sun. Monsters I wouldn't have even been able to see coming, because I'm just mortal."

And didn't that sound like a trial pulled straight out of the olden stories?

"I can only imagine." He leaned over and placed a hand on her shoulder fleetingly, just long enough to send a burst of steadying warmth through her frame.

She jolted back as he moved away, but the relief in her expression was genuine, and her breathing quickly grew more even.

The look of pain and old regret in her eyes?

Not so much.

"I didn't... reach out to Dan the way I should have." The admission was heavy and impossible to push down once it hit the open air between them. "Not at first. I wasn't quite neglectful, god forbid, but between the girls and the fear, I didn't reach out to him the way I could have - the way I should have. It took time for me to get my head back in the game, and I'll always regret how much of it I wasted before I did."

"Daniel thinks the world of you."

It was merely a statement, not an excuse or forgiveness - if those were necessary at all.

Still, it served its purpose.

Sarah Winchester finally smiled again.

The expression was weak, but it was there all the same.

"Things did get better, eventually. And like I said, he's a sweet boy. Kind. Maybe a little wild here and there, and sweet Jiminy Crickets can he be mouthy when he gets going-" They both snorted in mutual commiseration there. "- but he's got a heart of gold, and now he's with people who can appreciate every part of him. The normal, the supernatural, and excessively too snarky."

Chrion huffed in amusement.

"We're addressing the snark."

"How's that going for you?"

"Moderate progress as of yet. I'll have to get back to you on that one."

They laughed again, before she adjusted the girl sleeping in her arms and sighed peacefully.

"That's what I meant, before, when I talked about happiness. He was always happy, but now he feels... more whole, if that makes sense?"

"It does," Chiron assured her, entirely truthful. "More than you'd expect."

Daniel Winchester

Sairaorg Bael.

When compared to their own reflections from a year past - give or take a couple of months - they were both more whole.

Still plenty rough around the edges. Still scratching at the surface of great potential.

But happier, more capable, and simply more by nearly every metric than they were before.

In a way, so was Chiron, and wasn't that just something special?

The silence stretched, once more companionable, before Sarah shifted in her chair and reached for he mug one last time.

"Phew." She downed her drink and set it aside, trying to brush off some of the lingering weight from their conversation. "That got a little too heavy for my tastes. Sorry about that."

"There's no need to apologise."

Both her and her husband would likely need time to come to terms with everything they learned - even now, Chiron suspected that the true scale of it all hadn't quite sunk in yet.

This evening?

Just a pressure valve going off and letting loose some steam, but he would be ready to entertain their questions whenever they came.

He had promised to take care of them, and he had no intention of going back on his word.

In the meantime, though...

"How about some stories?"

Sarah shifted in surprise... and interest.

"Stories?"

"My students have had a very eventful year of training, and a few adventures to match."

"Really?" Her eyes gleamed with interest. "Oh, David's going to love this. Hit me."

And Chiron smiled.

"Let's start with the dragon."

"..."

"..."

"Dragon."

"Yes."

"As in... Dragon."

"Indeed."

"Giant, fire-breathing murder lizard - that kind of dragon."

"The very one."

"..."

"..."

"Oh, dear God, I'm going to ground them both until they forget what sunlight feels like."

"That's the spirit."

And they went from there.

...​

Regulus felt it the moment the sun-brat did... whatever it was he did that had them being flung across a sea of screaming chaos the likes of which he'd never seen before, and that was saying something, because throughout his existance as both a mythical terror of Ancient Greece and the power behind a Longinus after that, he'd seen a damn lot.

And by it, he didn't mean the method or the power the snarky punk used to pull off that stunt - and make no mistake, he had questions there - but the other, more eerily hackle-raising sensation he'd clocked a second too late to call out in warning.

Nestled deep in the brat's soul, just a split-second before they leaped into something Regulus wasn't even going to pretend to understand, Incinerate Anthem... jolted, almost.

Jumped.

Or maybe just acted up in general.

He couldn't tell for sure.

Couldn't be helped - He'd only come across that semi-sentient and almost always embarrassing hissy fit of a Longinus a few times over the years, and it was always trouble to put up with.

It's wielders?

That much more annoying, with all the charm of splinters lodged in his nigh-invulnerable paws.

Case in point?

Daniel Winchester.

Kill-stealer?

Him?

Hah.

Regulus would teach him some manners and feed him enough dirt that he'd grow roots and thank him for the opportunity, but in his own good time.

Until then, priorities - The kind he could already tell were shaping up to be dangerous in a way that had his soul stirring and rumbling in the confines of his recreated vessel.

This quest...

The centaur had warned him about what to expect, but only in the vaguest sense, their brief conversation toeing the line between interesting and irritating with precision the old horse had probably honed down to an art form.

Brace yourself. Give your expectations room to breathe... and prepare.

At the time, Regulus had only narrowed his eyes at the immortal who'd trained the fool who'd gone on to kill him and growled in acknowledgement.

Not that he held a grudge there, mind you, because he didn't.

His pride was beyond that kind of pettiness, and a win was a win. The only anger leftover from that story was because he never had a chance to get a rematch at his peak afterwards.

Still, he'd known full well that pushing the point wasn't going to get him a straight answer.

If that was on the table, the Trainer would have just come out and said as much, and he hadn't cared enough to press for one either.

That was supposed to be the point of this, wasn't it?

A surprise? A change in routine?

A little fun to step over the crippling boredom he felt outside the spars he had with the other brat, Sairaorg.

Apparently damn-well not.

He'd had just a split-second's worth of sharp warning when Incinerate Anthem's presence flared subtly, the feeling pinging straight up to and off the backs of his teeth and throwing him off his game just enough to make a difference, and then everything careened off the rails and his expectations for the day went off to die in a ditch in hilariously violent ways.

Only Regulus wasn't laughing.

First the fall, if the trip could even be called that.

Really, he wasn't sure it should - falling made sense, after all.

That hadn't.

Then, one after the other, the plot twists started hitting like they had something to prove, starting with that thing in the void they tumbled into, human-shaped but as blatantly overwhelming in sheer existence as any god could ever hope to be, but not one itself.

Himself.

Whichever way that coin landed, if it did at all.

However that played out in the end, he knew one thing for sure - that creature wasn't divine, or even right in any sense of the word.

When he'd stared up at those crimson eyes, somehow immobilised just the same as both brats despite the difference in power, Regulus had felt something so utterly other leering down at him from that perched throne that, had he burst free right then and there - and he had been trying - he would have gone for its throat without so much as blinking.

Not out of anger, or offence - just pure instincts, and his had been screaming in a way that demanded action.

How long had it been since anything had triggered that kind of fight-or-flight response in him?

A genuine threat, the kind that didn't just rile him up and make him itch for a good fight?

He could barely remember.

Then it moved, casting them out of the incomprehensible void of realm with a wave of its hand and a burst of kaleidoscopic light that seared Regulus's eyes in a way he found mildly infuriating - or maybe that was just the frustrating whiplash, either or - and away they went.

When the lights faded and the concept of space itself stopped playing Twister like a human toddler on a nasty sugar rush, they were somewhere else, and again, they appeared somewhere far outside of his frame of reference.

The enclosed garden spreading out around them and towards the walls of the mortal construction was nothing special, and the faint pressure of paper-thin magic didn't raise its value any, but the air itself...

Hmm.

It felt stale - nearly dry in a way that had nothing to do with moisture. As though something critical, fundamental, was missing from the world itself.

Another surprise that felt unflinchingly wrong - and then there was the company this time around.

"Do not fear, master."

The boy who stepped out of the latest light show and couldn't have been that much older than either of Regulus's brats - physically and in appearance, at least - spoke, and there was geniune power in his words.

Enough that the two nuisances in his life shifted to ready stances at once.

"I am Saber, a servant who will protect you. Against any and every threat."

His eyes flickered over the three of them meaningfully, before looking past them to track down the other one the sun-brat had blasted away on sight - and of course, Regulus had already sensed him recovering and getting back to his feet, and that was telling all on its own.

Both of them... they looked like young humans, and felt like it too, but only vaguely.

There was a presence to them that ordinary mortals didn't and couldn't have, and no, it wsn't about the fact that the blue-haired spear wielder was some flavour of demigod, or the more pressing issue in front of him.

Regulus's pupils dilated as he growled warningly at the would-be-knight in shining armour, who, credit where credit was due, met his gaze and his warning flare of power unflinchingly.

But he had good reason too, didn't he?

He would recognise that kind of scent anywhere.

Dragon - at least in part. And that invisible weapon he was brandishing...

Dangerous.

Very dangerous, even by his standards.

"Woah." Sairaorg suddenly raised one hand and kept the other curled into a deceptively loose fist, just enough to imply harmlessness without lowering his guard. Good. "Not a threat. We don't even know who any of you are - or where we are."

True.

"What he said." The sun-brat muttered, but he was angled away, keeping a wary eye on the spearman who'd gotten to his feet between one blink and the next, face assessingly blank even as his red eyes burned with battle-honed intensity. "Just took a hell of a wrong turn at Albuquerque."

The knight's eyes narrowed, but his gaze shifted over to the spearman again, who kept up the blank facade for all of a few seconds, before his expression broke out into a mask of pure bloodlust right after Regulus's own heart.

"I am a threat." He declared, and the knight's face hardened in response. His gauntlets tightened audibly around the grip of his hidden weapon "But not tonight - I know when I've missed my shot."

His gaze darted past the knight, towards the girl who'd been all but cowering behind him in qual parts fear and stunned disbelief. Regulus could tell that she was the weakest person present, and by far.

So completely outstripped that she should have been insignificant in comparison, only a step or two above a bog-standard mortal, but the spearman still looked towards her and she all but trembled as their eyes met.

"Looks like you get to live another day, little lady."

"Hold. Your. Tongue."

The knight stepped forward, just the once, and the air charged with power.

Enough that Sairaorg's aura rippled as his Touki surged closer to the surface, and the sun-brat's presence shifted as his spear's glow began to flicker warningly, like live ordinance about to blow.

Come to think of it, the spiteful little thing was probably reacting to the feel of dragon in the air as well.

For his part, Regulus just watched, and waited in a way that would have had most anyone with anything resembling a brain heading for the door.

After all, he was loud when he wanted to fight.

He was silent when he wanted to kill.

The spearman didn't seem concerned - if anything, his answering grin was delighted.

"So you're the Saber of this Holy Grail War, eh? And you have some fire to you as well." The grin sharpened. "Good. I want this to be fun. Here's hoping that you don't disappoint when the time comes."

Holy Grail?

Then he turned back to the sun-brat, the puzzling words already left behind.

"You."'

The fiery spear rose an inch.

"Me?"

"You're not a servant." Those red eyes flickered to Sairaorg. "And he sure as anything isn't."

"What's a servant?"

"Heh. Nice try, but lying to me is worthless even if you put in the right effort to try." He twirled the spear in his grip, and everyone shifted in preparation - bar the girl, who was still a friend, but Regulus wouldn't expect prey so feeble to move in a field where any errant swipe of an attack could likely utterly eviscerate it. "I've been around enough demigods and druids in my day to recognise them on sight - or anything close enough to count."

His eyes narrowed some more.

"Thing is, I thought people like you - like us - weren't supposed to exist anymore. Not in this pansy era. You especially...what kind of absurd circumstances do you have going for you that the World would have allowed you to be conceived, much less continue to exist?"

Regulus stayed silent, even as the words settled and prickled in his mind.

What was any of that supposed to mean?

"Dude, we have no idea what you're talking about. Sai?"

"What's a demigod?"

"See?"

For a moment, Regulus resisted the urge to huff in exasperation.

Why did he let himself be saddled with these idiots again?

The spearman seemed unbothered.

"Fine. Have it your way, for now. I'll drag the answers out of you when I get back at you for that cheap shot." Then, without another word, he turned back to the knight. "Til next time, Saber."

Then he moved - not fast enough that Regulus couldn't track the motion, but at a speed that was more than respectable for any mortal as he leaped and rocketed towards the roof, bursting through it without an ounce of resistance and an explosion of dust and crumbling debris.

The girl whimpered even as her protector stepped in front of her neatly and swung out a single arm, shielding her from the worst of it without a single word.

"My home."

Regulus saw the knight twitch, like he wanted to give chase - only that would have meant leaving them behind with the girl, and he had yet to take more than a single threatening step away from her.

"So in case that didn't make it abundantly clear, we're not with him."

"..."

"..."

Seriously?

The knight's gaze was stony in silent answer.

"What business do you have with my master?"

"None." Sairaorg offered. "We don't even know who your master is."

"And while we'd love to find out, I have just one question first." The sun-brat, a cheerful smile on his face that was about as genuine as any well wishes Regulus would ever offer him. "You're Arto - Arthur Pendragon, aren't you? The King Of Knights."

...

What?

"What!?"

"What!?"

The girl and Sairaorg voiced the incredulous thought in his place, only just, and the knight stiffened, his stunned silence answer enough.

"You... how?"

Regulus shared the sentiment, looking over the knight - and wasn't that a more fitting title, now - with new eyes.

That power. That presence.

It tracked.

But how... a spirit inheritor?

No, that wasn't it.

What fresh clown show was this?

"I'm going to take that as yes." Oblivious to his thoughts, the sun-brat just kept smiling. "And on that note, I'm going to thoroughly prove that we aren't your problem... by getting right the hell out of your way. Sai, grab the kill-stealer."

And of course, Sairaorg did at once, trust in the loud mouth absolute even in the face of this absurdity.

Regulus almost tore his hand off as it brushed against his mane on sheer principle, but even that fleeting touch was enough.

"Ciao!"

The knight - Pendragon, because why not? - made an aborted move towards them.

Or at least tried to.

His expression cracked upon with more shock, but before he could so much as open his mouth, much less move again, the sun-brat latched on to Sairaorg's shoulder.

Space shifted-

And then they were gone.

...​
The second they dropped down into Dan's home over at Maple - the place they'd planned to end up in in the first place, Sairaorg was rounding on him with enough questions to play competitive bingo like a professional.

"What-?"

"Hold that thought."

Naturally, his best friend didn't answer any of them.

Instead, he stumbled, shook his head, and immediately turned the corner around the living room, stepped into the kitchen, and went straight for the fridge.

"I need a soda pop."

He didn't come back with a soda pop.

Instead, he came back with an entire six-pack, which... honestly?

Fair enough.

Sairaorg grabbed one too... and if his grip was a little unsteady, and his heart was beating loudly enough that he could hear the rhythmic backdrop over every other sound from and around them...

Well, that was his business.

"What was that?"

He winced.

Regulus had beaten him to the punch, and his voice was quiet, which is how Sairaorg knew that he was really unhappy.

Dan didn't answer until he'd cracked open a can of coke and downed it all in one go.

Then he shrugged.

Crap.

"Who knows?"

"Talk."

"You heard me ask for a minute, didn't you?"

"You can have an entire afterlife if I rip you in half, how about that?"

Yikes.

Sairaorg didn't think for a moment that Regulus actually would, but his voice was just a little too sharp for comfort.

That last ten minutes... they hadn't been fun.

Or made sense.

For any of them.

Did I just meet King Arthur?

What even-?

"I'm taking a minute, kill-stealer. Trust me, we just dodged a bullet the size of a tank shell." Dan stopped and tilted his head to the side. "Or a nuke, probably. Yeah, nuke sounds better."

Then he grabbed another can and almost exploded it in his grip.

Somehow, that didn't help his mood any.

"Stupid unreliable power. Stupid magic old man. Stupid sword of mass destruction - why does everything always level up when I'm not looking?"

The words were a hissed whisper, tinged with as much raw panic as Sairaorg had been pushing down from the moment they'd seen... that man, sitting on his throne in the middle of very literal nothingness, but he heard them just fine.

That didn't mean he understood them.

"Dan."

He looked up, face carefully calm in a way that told Sairaorg that he was having a fit and a half beneath the surface, and for good reason too.

Which, again, was perfectly cool. He was in the same boat and everything.

He just didn't know where that boat was sailing too, and Dan did - somehow.

Another son of Apollon gimmick?

Or was it something else?

"...I'll tell you later." His eyes flickered to Regulus, and then he grunted grudgingly. "The kill-stealer too. We can bring him up to speed on everything else on the way, too."

"Why not-?"

"Sai."

His voice stopped that question dead in its tracks.

"Sai, we're here."

He sucked in a sharp breath, cold realization replacing incredulity as the reminder came rushing right back.

Dan saw it for what it was pretty much instantly, and he grinned.

"It's quest time, buddy. First things first, though."

He dropped down to a knee, let his spear drop as he sealed away his armour and unslung his backpack... and then he pulled out a flip phone.

If he wasn't having a teensy bit of a crisis at the moment, Sairaorg would have probably snorted at how anticlimactic that was.

"Somehow, I don't think we're living up to the classic Greek hero questing manual."

"Of course we're not." Dan didn't look up as he punched in the numbers they'd both memorised by heart, just to be safe. "Most of those guys usually had prophecies, ominously disturbing deadlines, and had, like, two to three violent and tragic detours per quest. At minimum. My modern-day relatives around here aren't that much better, either."

This time, Sai's lips did twitch, just a little.

"Guess we're not following the script, then."

Obviously, and he already knew it, but their goofy back and forth always helped centre his nerves.

"Duh." Dan's eyes gleamed almost manically as he grinned back up at him, before putting the phone to his ear as it started to ring. "Screw all that noise. We're speed-running the hell out of this thing."

...​
Gleeson Hedge startled awake as his phone rang, kicking up racket in his coat pocket so loud he nearly pitched halfway across the street away from the bench he'd been using to catch some shut-eye while he had the chance.

"Damn..."

Fumbling with it was a trial and a half as it was, and he already looked like he'd been through two dozen of them and some change.

His head hurt. His horns and hooves ached. His limbs felt worn and his clothes made him look like he'd been homeless from birth, but that's just what happens when you spend the better part of a week dodging hungry monsters who thought that Satyr was a great source of protein.

The bags under his eyes alone were practically a cry for help - Not that he needed it, really.

He had his trusty baseball bat - spiked through with celestial bronze nails, naturally - and he'd shown that sleazy dracaena and a good bunch of her friends that he wasn't afraid to use it.

Mama Hedge didn't raise no wimp!

... course he'd bolted after more of them showed up, but if they weren't going to fight fair, he wasn't going to stick around and give the dozen or so ravenous snake women with terrible breath and uglier teeth a free meal.

Mama Hedge didn't raise a suicidal moron, either, no matter what the stunts he used to get up to back in the day.

Still, as stiff as his spine was and as clearly capable a satyr he was... It had been a rough few months.

Ever since David Winchester had called, half out of his mind and begging him of all people for help...

Damn it.

He hadn't thought he'd see the day when Evelyn's brother called him for anything, ever.

He didn't like David. David didn't like him.

Or, actually, that's how it used to be.

These days, it was more that he didn't like David, and David hated him with so much fury it was a miracle he hadn't ended up dead the last time they'd met.

He'd even gone into the thing expecting to be stabbed at least, because he knew that Evelyn had given him some celestial bronze keepsakes over the years.

Some worst stuff too - and he wouldn't have blamed him that much for trying, especially not on that day.

After what had happened... what he'd had a hand in causing...

He swallowed roughly even as he hit the call.

Years later, and the guilt still rolled like poison in his gut, and when David had called and told him that Evelyn's son was missing...

Well.

He'd made a few calls, dropped everything he was doing and - after making sure he wasn't looking for a dead kid in a way he was never thinking about again, ever - came running right over.

And now...

It had been a rough few months, but he could have a depressing spiral over coffee and enough banana bread to send him into a food coma as soon as he could get his hands on it.

For now, though... he had work to do.

He grunted and accepted the call.

"Hello." The voice on the other end was young, but confident like it had no choice but to be. That was standard fare around these parts. "Is this Gleeson Hedge?"

"That's me." His voice sounded raspy and out of use even to himself, and he almost winced before pushing past it and licking his dry lips. "Who's asking?"

Then his brain finished waking up, and he sniffed suspiciously.

"And how did you get this number?"

He didn't hand this one out to just anybody. Phones were a tricky business in this gig.

"My uncle gave it to me."

Unc-?

And suddenly, Gleeson was wide awake - so wide that his eyes nearly popped out of their skull, and his heart scraped against the roof of his ribcage with how furiously it jumped.

No.

He was never that lucky.

No damn way-

"I'm Daniel Winchester. I think you knew my mom?"

"..."

"..."

"..."

"Hello?"

Too late.

The phone had already slipped out of his grip and clattered against the pavement.

To Gleeson, the small impact may as well have been a meteor strike, and it echoed in his head in way that was three times as loud and cataclysmic.

"Hello? Anyone still there? Cause I just dropped a super dramatic one-liner, and I'm going to look real dumb if things don't pan out the way I planned."

...

...

..

Oh, what the Tartarus was this?

#1,912
Thought this chapter would take me a good bit longer to write. Then I got hit with some truly terrible rl circumstances.

Zero stars, would not recommend.

On the plus side, writing helped take my mind off of it and meant I finished this earlier than expected, so it all worked out at the end lol.

The last 'slow''chapter of the quest - thought it speeds up quite a bit near the end - before we start ramping up in the coming chapters, and this arc isn't a super drawn out one, so due with that what you will.

"Daniel Winchester."

It might have been the static, the background noise on his end of the call or even my own judgment fritzing after the brush with hilariously, hysterically stupid danger we'd just dipped out of on the double, but Gleeson Hedge's voice…

It wasn't what I expected it to be.

I mean, to be fair, I wasn't sure what I expected there to begin with, given that I didn't know all that much about the guy in the first place.

According to Uncle David, he'd known my mom.

They'd been friends and everything, and they'd even worked together over on… let's call it the other side of the Mist.

That was already hard to put into context or think about at all for reasons as plain obvious as the nose on your face, but I also knew - remembered, only relatively recently and real vaguely at that - he wasn't just another background nobody in the grand scheme of things.

Because of course it wouldn't be that simple.

Instead - and take this with a grain of salt or three, because I'm the furthest thing from confident here- I was pretty sure that one day, he'd wind up helping a handful of quirky demigods on a classic 'do this, this, and that pronto or the world as you know it is toast with a side of Tartarus' type quest... and that was about all I could come up with there.

I'm not kidding, either.

It took a long while, but after racking my brain for any details until the inside of my skull felt like a pressure cooker ready to go off, the best I could come up with was a handful of shaky names and the idea - and calling it that is me being generous - that that the whole circus there had something to do with... Hera?

And...wolves, maybe?

For some reason?

Either way, whatever that was all about was just a whole other thing entirely.

Or will be a whole other thing, I guess.

…Will have been?

Eh, who even knows anymore - and, no, that wasn't a rhetorical question, because the answer was just flat out not me.

I had way too many things on my plate now to worry about stuff that was probably - hopefully - primed to go off years and years down the line, and even if all I knew about that fiery mess in the making didn't basically boil down to a list of unreliable footnotes with more holes in it than a block of swiss cheese, I still wouldn't go looking for more trouble ahead of time.

Modern Greek heroing 101: Unless you're all out of options, even the terrible ones, avoid the crap out of any prophecies.

Seriously, just don't.

Eight and a half times out of ten, they were the ultimate monkey's paw, where the paw comes back to life, resurrects the rest of the monkey for good measure and then they both set out into the world with the express purpose of making your life miserable - however long the rest of it lasts afterwards anyway, and good luck getting a healthy average on that one.

Really, good luck getting a healthy anything once you get involved with one of those.

My dad may be the god of oracles and future knowledge, but that didn't mean those things wouldn't screw me over just as badly as the next dude down the street and then some, so... yeah.

Let's not - not right this second, at least.

But back to Hedge now: his voice wasn't what I would have expected it to be, knowing all that I did.

Rough and keen, sure, but also a little haggard, just enough to be noticeable, and I could hear his breaths, all slow and deliberate like he wasn't quite in tiptop shape and was powering through it through sheer force of habit.

Sairaorg and I both knew the feeling.

"Daniel Winchester." He repeated, and there it was again - that same careful tone. "Evelyn Winchester's boy?"

I was too wired up to flinch at the name, even if I did inhale bracingly before breathing out just as quickly.

You know. For luck.

"That's me." I agreed, and he didn't have anything to say to that just yet. "I hope this isn't a bad time?"

"..."

"..."

The silence that followed didn't fill me with confidence, and wasn't that a great note to start off with?

"...Are you kidding me?"

I blinked.

"What?"

"I-You-" He cut himself off, hissing a sharp breath into the phone in a way that me resisting the urge to wince and pull away from it. "Back up. Back all the way up."

"Sure?"

What was there to back up to?

"You say you're Daniel Winchester."

"I... do." I said slowly. "Because I am."

"And say I believe you-"

"Why wouldn't you believe me?"

"Because life, the world and the three fateful old hags that run it all from the top are never that good to me," He said bluntly, voice crackling over the line, and only a moron wouldn't have understood who he was talking about with a hint that ham-fisted. "That, and a whole dictionary's worth of words I won't be spitting out on the off-chance that you actually are a fourteen-year-old pipsqueak."

"I'm nearly fifteen, and pipsqueak? Really?"

"...Say I believe you." He repeated again, and some of that sharp skepticism bled off into something I didn't quite recognise. "I have questions."

Well, alright then.

"'Hit me. I'm an open book."

Which was a bold-faced lie. Without the right context, my existence probably read like and made about as much sense as a half-baked bedtime story that an asylum inmate jotted down on the back of a bunch of used napkins with finger paint and spaghetti sauce, but hey.

It was the thought that counted, right?

Right.

"Where are you?" He cut that line of thought right off and got right to it. "Are you safe?"

"Pretty much. I'm home." I answered, before clearing my throat. "Back home, I mean. My uncle's place."

I knew why he was asking - Uncle David had mentioned something about tipping the man off all the way back when I first 'disappeared', asking for help finding me, and that made sense.

I knew that one of the big things satyrs around these parts were responsible for was finding and guiding rookie demigods, even if that obviously went absolutely nowhere where I was concerned.

"That's...good." He seemed...surprised. "Good. How long have you been back?"

"It's been a couple of-"

Hold it.

The word died in my throat as I suddenly remembered one teensy, tiny little tidbit that had nearly slipped my mind mid-conversation - I'd told my uncle to keep my coming back a secret.

From my... father specifically, sure, but that gag order ballooned out to cover pretty much everyone else on the spot, because who the heck would Uncle David talk to about me that wouldn't become a total security risk the moment an Olympian looked at them funny?

Long story short?

Gleeson Hedge knew I'd up and vanished off the face of the planet - literally - but he didn't know I'd been 'back' for a good long while at this point, and I had a gut feeling that letting it slip and telling him as much would come back to bite me with a grudge if I wasn't careful.

Awesome.

Naturally, I did the mature thing and promptly clobbered my potential problem over the head before pitching it into a ditch for later.

"-days." I finished a little lamely. "Couple of days."

There.
That was better… but not really good, either.

I could tell, because the second stretch of silence that followed was somehow all sorts of loud in that special way these things tended to get after someone screwed up hard enough.
I could put two and two together and understand why, more or less, but you could nearly hear the awkward cricket noises anyway.

"...Two. Days."

I almost winced at the tone.

"Give or take, yeah."

A second passed.

The another.

And another.

And then-

"...David Winchester, you insufferable, thickheaded, lamebrained little-"

I saw it coming, but this time I did wince as the guy broke out into a tirade of... let's call them words - either that, or war crimes against polite language - so fiery they were probably a health hazard to anyone within twenty feet of him.

Call me crazy, but I don't think he liked my uncle much, and the last time we talked I got the impression that the feeling was entirely mutual, and real personal too.

Didn't know why, and there was a story there, but I didn't go looking for answer I didn't need, even if I was curious - I could figure all that out in my own good time.
Still…

"...Had one job, you complete and utter bag of-!"

Guess he wasn't kidding about that dictionary, and man was he nettled. I didn't even know you could use some of those words like that, and I'm not talking about the Greek ones.

Credit where credit was due, though, because he got a hold of himself real quick a few seconds later and rounded back on me so fast I could almost feel him glaring at the phone through the other end of the call.

"Where. On Pan's Good Earth. Have You Been?"

"Well, see-"

"No, wait, don't answer that. Not right now."

Don't gotta tell me twice. I wasn't going to give him a straight answer anyway.

"We'll get to that later. First things first - You said you were at your uncle's?"

My brow rose an inch.

"Yes, but-"
"No buts. Sit tight. I'll be there in a few hours."

"Come again?""

"You heard me. Unless you're in danger, and I know you know the kind I mean-"

"Hold on a second-"

"Kid - If that's who you are, because I'm still not entirely sold on that one." He said, very, very seriously, and also as dryly as a desert at the peak of summer. "I've been' holding on' for the better part of a year."

I opened my mouth… and quickly closed it again, because rats dang it, that was actually a fair point.

"Even longer if you count... ah, to the Pit with it. Just stay where you are. I'm getting a good look at you today and getting you somewhere safe if it's the last thing I do."

Master or Servant, and sometimes Master and Servant both.

The point is, they did it, it happened, and the spell I weaved tried to piggyback of the idea of it all - the concept of something greater appearing mundane in the eye of the beholder.

Completely normal

Nothing to worry about here, no siree

Shadow Travel, man.

It sounded ridiculous, and looked terrifying and especially unholy - one of the most dangerous monsters of all, even at their weakest.

And with her on one side and the Dracaena on the other…

He grimaced and shifted on his hooves.

All in all, not the best spot he's ever been in.

And only a block away from the spot he'd expected to meet the kid at.

Evelyn's kid.

Damn it all.

"We found him firssst!" The leader of the dracaena hissed, hefting up a worn, rickety-looking spear tipped with a blade of bone. The others flashed claws and barred their teeth in warning. "Thisss isss our territory!"

"Do you think I care?" The empousa's voice was cold and mocking, but it did nothing to hide the rabid hunger beneath it - this one hadn't fed in a while, and that made her dangerous enough that four on wasn't enough to tip the balance for sure. "We're close enough to the border that no one would look twice, and I'm the one that chased the little goat and tired him out first!"

True.

She'd also backhanded out a first story window and onto the hood of a car, but who's counting?

"He ssstill belongs to ussss!"

Gleeson's nostrils flared, and his bat rose a little higher.

He'll show her belong!

… Hopefully on his way out of this mess, once the freakshows started tearing one another apart.

If they didn't…

He swallowed and gritted his teeth.

He'd figure it out, or his name wasn't monster-thumping Hedge!

"Think, you fools!" The empousa snarled, and her burning hair flared so sharply he could feel the searing heat of it twenty feet away. "He's a satyr!"

"Yesss!" The leader nodded. "Lot'sss of meat."

"Good eating!" A second agreed.

"For the love of the Lady, think!" The empousa snapped. "What do satyrs do, when they're not wandering off into the sunset looking for their pathetic Pan?"

Gleeson's angry curse died in his throat when the demented blood sucker rounded on him, radiating malice like a cloud of cheap cologne.

"They play protector," She sneered. "For demigods."

The dracaena froze.

So did Gleeson.

"Demigod?"

"Halfling?"

"Much better eating!"

The empousa rolled her eyes.

"Finally! Killing him comes later - first, we find out where the real prize is at. Now then, tell us where they are, little goat." Her fangs gleamed as her mouth opened far too wide. "Where's your charge."

… Pan curse it all.

He didn't - couldn't - stop to think before he was crouching at the knees, already winding up to break out into a dead sprint.

One good hit - that's all he'd need to make an opening.

So he opened his mouth to tell the third-rate reject exactly where she and her new friends could shove it-

"Right here!"

And then he heard that, and his blood turned to ice on the double.

The monsters recoiled and made to turn around, but they never had the chance.

"Hurghk!"

The empousa died first, a golden blur sliding in from across the corner of his vision and lunging straight for her with such ridiculous speed that Gleeson didn't even see the moment the glowing spear was shoved halfway through her mouth and punching clean through the back of her skull.

Her eyes widened stupidly, and then she was exploding in a shower of dust and scattering absolutely everywhere.

All in under a second.

The spear retracted, and the blonde haired kid who owned it swung it over his shoulder and slowly turned away from the frozen Dracaena, to the equally dead-still Gleeson.

And then he smiled breezily, and oh, Gleeson would know that half-smirk anywhere.

"Yo!" He waved casually, like he hadn't just taken down a monster that could kill scores of unprepared demigods with a swing of its arm in the time it took him to blink. "I'm Daniel. We talked on the phone?"

It was so nonchalant, so unhurried, that it gave the dracena the time they needed to reboot.

Then the air was filled with wary, enraged hissing, and the first of them lunged, spear aimed at Evelyn's son and his unprotected back in a way that had Gleeson's heart doing high-speed jumping jacks on its way up his throat.

"Look out!"

He didn't.

The kid didn't even have to turn around.

A second blur shot out of absolutely nowhere, and the spear shattered like brittle glass a split-second before the dracaena's spine followed suit.

It died without even a whimper, dissolving into dust that went hurling off to batter the leftover three like a gust from a particularly pathetic sand storm.

That, or something more embarrassing, but Gleeson was too busy playing catch-up to throw proper shade when it was called for.

Daniel Winchester's impossibly fast tag along stood still only long enough for him to realize that it was a second kid - of course, of course - and then he turned towards the remaining enemies and smiled.

His purple eyes almost crinkled and everything.

"Hello."

Then he cocked back a fist.

"And goodbye."

Then he punched forward, once.

And the air itself seemed to explode.

The force of it slammed Gleeson back against the brick wall, the noise deafening, the ground under his feet tremoring, and for a beat, it was like the entire alleyway was coming apart at the seams.

Is this how I die?

What a crappy way to go - He hated it!

Luckily, the universe chose to play ball, finally, because the air settled a breath later, the howling stopped, and careful silence came drifting back down again like a baby being soothed back to sleep.

All that… in about twelve seconds, more or less.

When it was done, and he blink through the stinging in his eyes to, he clocked the fact that Evelyn's boy hadn't so much as twitched from the impact.

His hair wasn't even ruffled.

If anything, he looked mildly irritated, like somebody had poured the milk in his cereal before he sat down at the table.

Or worse - poured the milk in before the cereal.

"Sai, for real?"

The other kid shrugged sheepishly, rubbing the back of his head.

"Sorry. I toned it down, but I didn't think they'd be that weak."

"... yeah, they were flimsy, weren't they?" He agreed, blue eyes tracking the last of the golden dust before he shook it off easily enough. "Guess we got lucky on the first go around. Good thing Regulus didn't follow us, or he'd never shut up about it."

"Probably."

…What the-?

That's when he finally locked on to it.

The scent.

Not Daniel Winchester's - oh no.

His friend's.

One whiff, and his spine turned to stone, and everything got much, much, much more complicated.

"Anathema."


...


Sai and Dan, gearing up to blast their brand of bullshit straight into the unsuspecting Gleeson's Life.
