#7,565
Surprise!


A pure-blood devil, an Olympian demigod, the Greatest Nemean Lion Of Old, and a witch in training to round out the lot.

Three of the Thirteen Longinus Sacred Gears between them, renowned the world over.

All crossing his path in one way or another, ending up under his roof - in under a year at that.

In so quiet an era as this, such omens could cloud even the most level-headed mind with suspicion, and why would they not?

The Creator of the Gears was well known for His grand machinations, and having such raw potential appearing to concentrate in one spot was a red flag if there ever was one.

Naturally, that alone wasn't all Chiron was left to contemplate.

Of course not.

The conversation he'd had with his students after their quest for the Fleece took such paltry, mundane misgivings and doused them in copious amounts of kerosene and dragonflame - and that was putting it lightly.

God is dead.

Three short words, with a potential enormity that betrayed most any language in existence.

Almost ludicrous to entertain. Cataclysmic if true.

Yet, paradoxically, it was a revelation of such weight that it immediately looped back into near-uselessness when one considered its sheer scope and the simple reality that it was nearly impossible to verify discreetly.

Not without triggering consequences best left in the depths of the nightmares that spawned them.

Heaven had no shortage of enemies, after all, and it was far from powerless in return.

The Angelic hierarchy yet remained.

The Great Seraphs endured.

Michael the Taxiarch existed — and that alone was enough. He had likely Mantled His Father's Throne.

To say nothing of the Heavenly System itself.

That power…

For all of its infamy, few could even guess at the full breadth of its function, and the fact that Daniel simply hadn't - or couldn't - bring up what he somehow knew before was... disquieting, to say the least.

...

Nevertheless.

He took a quiet sip of his tea, eyes briefly flickering to Lavinia Reni, who had remained silent after making her impassioned plea, and shelved the entire line of thought for another time.

There were priorities at hand.

Though speaking of said student... Any second now-

Sunlight bloomed off to the side, and Daniel reappeared in the courtyard in a flare of golden brilliance.

"I'm back."

"I'm aware," Chiron answered dryly, utterly unsurprised.

He'd sensed Apollon's descent and subsequent departure in real time - the prompt return was expected.

Lavinia, on the other hand, had risen halfway out of her seat in startled wonder.

"How did you...?" Her brows furrowed. "No teleportation circle. Something more complex? But there was no structured dispersal phenomenon... maybe the light?"

Daniel blinked, and Chiron raised a brow.

"Uh, no. That wasn't it." His student gave the girl a sheepish smile. "I only went across town, and using a geometric transportation array for something like that is kind of a waste - and that's just for circles. Going with anything more complicated on a short solo trip is-"

"Elaborate, unnecessary, and more performative than useful." Lavinia agreed without missing a beat. "Using circles as a base is so commonplace precisely because they have the best balance of stability and utility, and-"

"-if you know what you're doing, you can go for broke and upgrade them into something fancier when you need to." Daniel finished with a grin. "Like when you've got passengers hitching a ride. Or baggage. Or both."

"Exactly." The girl began to match his smile tit for tat. "But your light-?"

"That's... more of an inbuilt thing. Similar result, different method." He rubbed the back of his head and shrugged. "Way different."

That was about the point when Chiron chose to step in.

"Ahem."

Both froze, remembering themselves, before whirling to face him and valiantly pretending they hadn't been seconds from going off on a tangent of their own.

A brave attempt. Points for effort.

"As fascinating as this conversation is, there are matters to attend to." Chiron said. The pair flushed, and he repressed an amused smile in favor of focusing on Daniel. "Did your stroll prove productive?"

"It did," his student confirmed, and his expression quickly sobered. "Glenda Silverbrook is definitely in Cocytus, and I don't think that's changing anytime soon."

Lavinia's attention snapped back to him in alarm, but the demigod only paused to offer her an apologetic look before refocusing on Chiron himself.

"Dad says that the appeal is a no-go on his end, and that Aunt A won't bother either. Not yet." Daniel explained quickly. "But he will let us go down there for a visit if you're there to play chaperone, teach."

Ah.

Immediately, he knew to expect unpleasantness on the horizon.

Regardless of 'supervision', Apollon would not allow his son anywhere near the Underworld for something so 'paltry'.

Not unless he intended to capitalise on an opportunity and make a lesson of it.

Given the subject matter at hand...

Chiron's gaze turned to Lavinia, and he frowned faintly.

This would not end well.

The girl didn't notice the reaction - her eyes had yet to leave Daniel's.

"Your 'Dad?'"

"Right. I guess we should finish our introductions properly." The demigod breathed out once before raising a hand in polite greeting. "Daniel Winchester. Son of Phoebus Apollon."

And there it was.

The young witch stilled, and Daniel's smile dimmed.

Just a touch.

"Nice meeting you. Said it before, but it still applies on my end."

The moment stretched.

Tellingly so.

Then-

"... Likewise." Lavinia eventually agreed, and though the expression she wore was stilted with politely masked wariness and apprehension, the attempt had value. "I've never met a demigod before."

It was a clumsy olive branch, but the attempt was there, and Daniel was smart enough to take it for what it was and go from there.

"Yeah? Then I'll try not to disappoint." He turned back to Chiron. "So... field trip?"

Field trip, he says.

To a prison realm of eternal torment, deep within the Underworld itself.

Chiron almost snorted.

Greek heroes. A pretty girl smiles, and they're ready to leap headfirst into hell.

Always a classic.

Still.

Both his students were at that age.

He'd have to run a few remedial classes on the importance of clear heads and common sense - a modern-day Orpheus would be downright embarrassing - but in the meantime...

"Why not?"

Daniel blinked.

"Wait, really? Just like that?"

"I see no reason against it, and there's no time like the present." Chiron agreed. "Unless you have an objection or two you'd like to share with the class?

"Objections?" He looked to his right, caught one glimpse of Lavinia's poorly muted, barely hidden hope, and quickly shook his head. "Nope. Not a one."

"I thought so."

"Just give me, like, five minutes." He threw a thumb over his shoulder and took a few steps back. "I have to pack a bag."

"I see. Give Sairaorg my regards."

"Will do."

At least he knew better than to deny it before he vanished with that uncharacteristically eerie displacement that heralded his slip into the chaos between worlds.

The better to travel into Misla Bael's estate with minimal fuss, and tactical applications of that gift were as marvelously chilling as ever.

"Thank you." Lavinia suddenly spoke up, drawing his gaze once again. "For agreeing-"

"That can come later." He stopped her gently. "For now, it's best to steady yourself. No aspect of the Underworld welcomes the living with any grace, and Cocytus is more trying than most."

And that was the understatement of the millennium.

She swallowed and nodded firmly, and he resisted the urge to sigh in sudden weariness.

The girl was strong, and she had heart.

He could only hope that it held fast in the face of what he suspected was to come.

For her sake, if nothing else.

...

The son of Apollon returned six minutes later on the dot, no bag in sight and raring to go.

"Ready."

"Evidently."

"Welcome back." Lavinia offered, and he subtly perked up.

Children, honestly.

"So how did we get this started?" Daniel asked, before pausing in thought. "And do we have to pray to Hades or something? Because we're showing up in his backyard?"

"When in doubt and under most other circumstances regarding the Underworld?" Chiron nodded. "Certainly."

Showing proper respect to the Lord of the Dead within his domain was the bare minimum any intelligent soul - living or otherwise - was bound to fulfill, lest they earn his ire in a harebrained, pitifully avoidable way.

Or his Dread Queen's for that matter, but that was another concern entirely.

"That said, Cocytus is a special case. The will of the river extends not only through the metaphysical territory it was once 'limited' to, but through the many realms of torment it has since subsumed."

"Subsumed?" Daniel frowned warily. "It can do that? It's done that?"

"It can, and it has." Or 'he' has, technically, but semantics were unnecessary here. "The exact principles behind it are complex, but suffice it to say that Cocytus's reach has overwhelmed multiple lesser domains of punishment in the time since the boundaries between the pantheonic aspects of the world degraded."

It was why the devils and the Fallen angels of the Abrahamic pantheon - among others - could imprison their worst in a frozen hell without causing one political incident after the next.

They were only ever using a lesser realm under Cocytus's control.

The river itself remained as it always was - an infernal stretch of endless lamentation.

"The boundaries of the world, huh?" Daniel took that in slowly. "Dad mentioned something about that once - about how the world used to be bigger back in the day?"

Even Lavinia seemed fascinated by the implications therein, fascination momentarily overtaking the apprehension that had never quite left her all throughout her time in their presence.

Chiron welcomed the change, even as he snorted and shook his head.

"I imagine he would, but that is a story for another day."

As were the tales of the godswars that followed.

"Now, prepare yourselves."

Both of them stiffened at his change of tone.

"We leave now."

They nodded in unison.

"Yes!" "Right!"

Good.

Without another word, he raised a hand.

The effect, as precisely calculated, followed instantly.



*̷̛̰̪̖̟̔͋̄̀͝*̷̧̨̢̛͖̺̱̹͔͖͔̃̀͆̅́͋̎̔͊͛͝*̴̛̭̌̓̃̔͆*̴̘̯͈̤̯͈̹̳̳̣̼̝̯̲͍̄͋̈́̑̂͐̆*̸̢̧̢͍͔͎͍̪͉̹͉̘͙̲̦͓͓̅͗̓̄̽̇̅̒̿͘̚͝*̸̲͗̉͑̑͌͑͂͝*̷̢̱̻͕̤͛͐́̊͆̌̏͗͊͊͠*̴̢͓̯̩̦͉̱̟̝̓͛*̶̡̪̰͓̥͙̻̟̱͇͚̏̏̀̌̿͘*̷̡̜̦̰̤͉̬̊̃́́̔̈́͘̕͠*̶̨̳̱͈̯̜͚̮̙̇͗̒̿͑́̓̌̏̏͜*̴̯̙͚̭̼̲̪̥̓̐̍̋̎͝*̷̧̹̼̯̖̫̠̻͔̂̏̃͛̈́*̷̬̹͇̻͎͌̓̒̒̋̈́̓*̷̢̨̡̨̪̻͍̥̮͚̟͕̰̝̥͉̆͛̂́̆̂͗̈́̒͒ͅ*̷͕̓̏̆̀​



Space compressed, folding and layering in impossibly symmetrical patterns. Power leaped outward like a bolt from a thundercloud, nearly staggering both children in a single sweep. The air charged with static, cooling until their breaths misted and hoarfrost began to creep over the marble underfoot.

Then he brought his hand down, and they vanished with a single rush of displaced air.

...​

No matter how seamless the transition, descending to the Underworld from the mortal realm was jarring on a fundamental level.

The living were not meant to tread where the dead dwelled.

Reappearing on a stony outcropping overlooking the riverbanks of Cocytus amplified the dissonance several times over.

It was not a welcoming sight.

No true radiance existed here - just a thin, sour glow seeping out from a colorless sky, and mist clung low over the banks, a veil of cold silver-grey that blurred depth and distance until every detail faded into the immaterial and the uncertain.

The river itself lay beneath the fog, appearing black as pitch and stiller than death in places where the pall seemed to thin, but that was only a trick of perception - The darkness there swallowed what little light reached it and rushed all the while, hungering for more.

Every few heartbeats, shapes flickered on the edge of clarity: shredded spirits drifting in and out of the haze, formless wraiths no less bound to the waters beyond the murk than the rest of its victims.

And they all whispered.

The waters, the mists, and the souls of the damned echoed with unintelligible mutterings and hoarse screams, pleas for mercy and cries of maddened despair, and a thousand things besides, all swelling into a gestalt presence of absolute, unforgiving misery.

Even with Chiron actively shielding them from the worst of it, both of his charges - temporary and otherwise - could feel it.

Lavinia held out a hand, almost unconsciously, fingertips crackling with the faintest hint of magic before she seemed to remember herself and clenched it into a white-knuckled fist.

Daniel held himself steadier, but just for an instant, his eyes flared gold - with hints of purple - and the air around him steamed as warmth rose to ward off the glacial chill.

"Calm," Chiron advised. They had good instincts - and they would need them - but even still, they could not sense as he did within this realm. "Drawing attention here would be unwise."

The realm's rulers most certainly knew of their arrival.

So did the will of Cocytus, slumbering as it was.

Aside from the looming attention, no other response was warranted.

Yet.

That would change at the first reckless misstep, no matter how innocent the intention behind it.

"Gotcha." Daniel offered a tight smile. "No funny business. What now?"

"Now-"

Something familiar shifted at the edge of his perception - something drawing closer, at speed - and he resisted the urge to sigh tiredly.

Of course.

"-We deal with that first, apparently."

"What-?" Lavinia paled as she picked up on it. "Oh."

"Chiron-"

"Calm." He repeated as Dan tensed, no doubt twitching for his spear. "He means us no harm."

"Who's-?"

The words were drowned out as a rhythmic, hammering beat vibrated through the rock underneath them, followed by a wet rumble that strained the air in their lungs with pulsing force.

The mist swirling along the riverbanks to their side shifted, stirring unnaturally, twisting and churning as something disrupted it from within.

Then the silhouette within took shape, dark and gargantuan, before it began to break through.

"Oh, sweet mother of Dad."

A fair reaction.

A massive head pushed forward first, level with the edge of the cliff they stood on, wide-jawed and with eyes like molten gold. Strings of silvery mist clung to black fur, dripping and wafting off its canine snout like smoke.

Then the other two followed through the fog, rising further up as clawed paws the size of boulders slammed down against the base of the cliff, and such was the impact that fractures splintered and spiderwebbed their way up through solid stone, groaning and heaving all the way.

The air reeked with the scent of iron and sulfur and something altogether sharper, and the warmth Daniel radiated was rendered unnecessary under the sweltering furnace that was the newcomer's presence.

Three heads. One enormous form.

Power enough to reshape the landscape with a single swipe.

Both of the children hardly breathed.

Chiron only smiled and stepped forward, unbothered by the three sets of blazing eyes glaring down at him.

"Hail, Kerberos." The name resounded with appropriate gravitas. "How do you fare on this good day?"

The Hound of Hades growled.

Not loudly, or with particular malice, but the sound of it still erupted outwards like the shockwave of an explosion, blowing back the mist and washing over them like a tidal wave.

Clearly, he was in an excellent mood.

"Kerberos." Lavinia whispered. "Cerberus. The Gatekeeper of the Underworld."

"Chiron." His student started, very carefully and very quietly. "Getting flashbacks to the last time three hellhound heads looked at me like this. Newsflash: It didn't end well."

"As I said." Chiron hummed, ignoring the gusts of hot air hissing out of the Stygian Beast's nostrils. "He means us no harm. In fact, I'd wager he's only here to satisfy his curiosity."

Kerberos growled again, as though in agreement. His lips pulled back - all three sets - and bared mouthfuls of gleaming fangs in tandem.

"…Okay then." Daniel nodded amiably and looked only mildly incredulous doing it - really, the twitching eye was very subtle. "What curiosity?"

"Give it a moment."

Lavinia drew in a short, sharp breath as the hound's heads lowered further, the scent of fiery brimstone curling on his breath as they did.

Soon, he was close enough that any outstretched hand would've met a snout - as absurdly ill-advised as such a notion would be - and that's when it happened.

The shadows at Daniel's feet stirred in a rather familiar, predictable manner, and Courage slunk out a beat later, padding ahead with wary, stilted steps.

"Do not interfere." Chiron murmured when his student started violently. Lavinia's reaction was much the same. "Watch."

"But-"

"Watch."

Kerberos's heads sank even lower, nostrils flaring in a single unified inhale. His six eyes brightened ominously, and another booming rumble rolled out of his chest as they did.

Courage went statue-still.

Given the sheer difference of scale, one could hardly blame him.

The smaller hellhound's head remained bowed as the Guardian inspected him with towering, unimpressed judgment, stiffening further only when a single snort of warm air buffeted past him and blew back his fur.

Even then, he held his ground.

A beat passed.

Then two.

Three.

On the fifth, the light in Kerberos's eyes changed.

His next growl was a lighter thing - less dangerous, and more restrained.

The change was enough to prod Courage into movement, stillness breaking as the younger pup exhaled a small, cautious puff, ears still flattened and pulled tightly against his head.

Then, ever so slowly, he began to creep forward.

Daniel almost reacted at that, but one glance from Chiron stopped him, and for good reason at that - Kerberos would not appreciate the interruption.

The hound's three heads circled Courage slowly, sniffing in unison, before all paused and let out a low, reverberating chuff.

Not quite a declaration, and more akin to acknowledgment.

"Curiosity, as I suspected," Chiron explained as Courage's tail twitched uncertainly. "Like calls to like, after all, and Kerberos goes wherever he pleases within his master's domain."

The Hound of Hades had no doubt sensed his lesser kindred the moment they arrived, and followed it to the source.

It had no other reason to be here, and paid the rest of them little mind regardless.

Courage continued to creep forward, small and wary, and one of Kerberos's moved in to meet him halfway.

A pause followed - a split-second instance where Courage hesitated - before closing the rest of the distance and tapping his snout against Kerberos's own.

A light, deliberate greeting, and the size difference made the very sight of it comical, but it was enough.

Kerberos huffed in satisfaction, and slowly began to retreat - though not before bestowing them with a final, sweeping look.

One head at a time.

The leftmost focused on Lavinia with a slitted stare that left her motionless through sheer force of will and nothing else.

The rightmost drifted to Daniel, who held his ground and followed suit.

The center head lingered on Chiron the longest, snorting once more in another bout of gracious acknowledgement.

Then, with this curiosity sated and his business concluded, Kerberos pivoted. His fur rippled as his heads flowed in perfect synchronization, and the great beast drifted back into the fog from whence he came.

The mist swallowed him in moments, and the thudding impacts of his footfalls quickly faded, leaving only silence and the lingering scent of sulfur in his wake.

"..."

"..."

"..."

"...Well." Daniel croaked eventually. "That happened."

Immediately, Courage deflated like a balloon, whining pitifully as his legs gave out underneath him.

"Hrrrrrr."

"I hear you, buddy." He nodded lowly, wincing in sympathy. "Scylla and Cetus had nothing on that guy, but hey - at least this one didn't try to eat us, right?"

Lavinia's startled splutter was entirely justified.

Courage, on the other hand, didn't bother dignifying that with a response.

Instead, he darted back and leaped into Daniel's shadows, melting away in an instant.

"...Well. We won't be seeing him for the rest of the week."

"He deserves his rest." Chiron offered, though for just a moment, his attention diverted to the lingering touch of Kerberos's power melding in with Courage's darkness.

Interesting.

"I-" Lavinia paused and let out a slow, measured breath. "I was not ready for today."

That she didn't ask about the smaller hellhound was telling.

"I don't think any of us were." Daniel agreed, and the girl almost smiled. "But at least it's not boring, right?"

"...It's not boring, yes."

Perfectly diplomatic. Chiron was impressed.

All the same, he cleared his throat - just enough to draw both of them back to attention.

"It's time to continue."

The weight of his words shifted the air, and both of them straightened in response.

He didn't say a word more - not to them.

Instead, Chiron turned his attention outwards and peered into the mist.

Then he spoke.

"By the authority of Lord Phoebus Apollon, we seek a path to a mortal prisoner within."

His voice rolled out, suffused and resounding with power.

"Lead us to Glenda Silverbrook."

The mists stopped swirling. The chorus of misery stilled.

The silence was absolute.

Then it began to part, opening a narrow, winding passage in its midst. Silvery tendrils reached out in the same beat, extending towards the cliff and layering over one another as they took shape and cooled the air that much more with their very passage.

Soon, the surface of the make-shift bridge solidified, crystallizing into fracture-patterned ice that gleamed eerily in the low glow of the Underworld, stretching all the way back into the unknown.

Chiron only inclined his head - a necessary gesture of respect - and motioned forward.

"Our path is open."

Lavinia took one look at it and blanched.

"That's not... I'm very familiar with ice. I know it." She eyed the deceptively clear surface the way another would a pool of bubbling hydra venom - and he would know. "But I've never felt anything like that."

"I imagine you wouldn't have."

Absolute Demise's power - filtered through the limits of a young mortal -was one thing.

Cocytus was quite another.

"Stay close, both of you, and follow my every step."

She nodded uncertainly, and Daniel did the same, grimacing all the while.

"This feels like walking into the Lonely Mountain all over again."

Hah.

"Don't be foolish, student." He patted him on the back. "Should the worst come to pass, this will be far worse."

"...Awesome."

"Isn't it just?" The ice crackled and held as he stepped forward and took the lead instead. "Shall we?"

A rhetorical question at its finest.

The bridge groaned softly beneath them as they followed, starting off into Cocytus's hold.

...​

Even by Chiron's standards, the passage was unpleasant from start to finish.

They moved through the mist, pressed in on all sides, yet the path ahead remained near-endless for a time - both claustrophobic and far too vast for comfort, all at once.

Space itself was distorted within, compressing and unfolding with little rhyme or reason, and the cold deepened with every step, bordering on malevolent.

Nothing that exceeded his tolerance - not even close - but oppressive all the same.

He could feel Daniel's instincts recoil against it, however.

The aura of light and warmth he gave off increased exponentially the farther in they went, pushing back against the prison realm's crushing weight even though the effort was, in the end, misguided at best.

There was no battling this aspect of Cocytus.

Still, it served a purpose.

Lavinia certainly appreciated it more than he, given how close she veered to the boy - rather unconsciously at that, but Chiron suspected that his student wouldn't protest the closeness if he were in the right headspace to process it.

As it was, they had greater concerns than personal space.

The whispers - faint and distant, echoing in disjointed patterns from every which way - only added to the creeping pressure weaving its way around them.

Then, at last, the passage yielded into something with more substance.

The invisible walls boxing them in expanded. The ice underfoot hardened, more crooked and jagged, and lost its sheen.

The whispers dulled until they were nothing more than an itch, scraping away at the back of one's head.

And there, kneeling a little distance away, was the reason for the sudden change:

A woman.

Greying, haggard, dressed in plain, ragged robes that hung loose on her frame. Her head was bowed, shoulders slumped, and her limbs hung limply at her sides - like a puppet with its strings cut.

This was-

"Glenda!"

The scream had barely torn out of Lavinia's throat before the girl was hurling herself across the intervening space and dropping to her knees beside the woman.

Her arms reached out, trying to prop her up, but all she achieved for her efforts was a lolling head - at least for a moment.

"Glenda..." Lavinia sounded on the verge of tears. "Glenda, pleaase. Look at me."

The sound of her plea made Daniel flinch.

"Chiron, should we-?"

"No." He cut him off firmly. "There's nothing we can do."

Nothing they should do, for that matter, besides standing witness for what was to come.

Soon, Glenda Silverbrook's head began to rise - and it was as haggard as the rest of her.

Sallow, lined skin stretched tight over sharp bone and covered in traces of hoarfrost and rime. Her black eyes were sunken and unfocused, and her lips moved quietly, spilling broken, indecipherable murmurs.

"..."

"Glenda?"

The murmurs stopped. The eyes fluttered with something parallel to burgeoning awareness.

"Can you hear me?" Lavinia's voice trembled. "Glenda?"

Her eyes flickered, then sharpened, before settling on Lavinia with slow recognition.

"...Lavinia."

The whisper was hoarse, but Lavinia beamed with near-manic joy at the sound of it.

"It's me. I'm here."

The reunion should have been touching.

It wasn't.

Chiron knew better than to trust it, and from the uncertain stance he took to his right, Daniel had picked on it as well.

For all his recklessness, his senses were razor-sharp.

"This is... Cocytus. Why..." Glenda's gaze sharpened some more, and her voice gained a touch of strength. "How are you here?"

"I came to see you."

More clarity returned to her those eyes.

"You came..." She croaked out. "...to see me."

"After the news about Oz spread, I looked for you." Lavinia tried to explain, almost stumbling over the words. "When I found where you were, I wanted to appeal to the Olympians. I went to Lord Chiron for help and... it all led here."

Glenda's attention lingered on her, glacial and full of incomprehension, as if the words were beyond understanding.

Then, her eyes drifted first to Chiron, lingering on him with a sharp, jolting recognition, and he returned it with expressionless calm.

"Chiron...Trainer of Heroes..."

Her glance shifted to Daniel, and to his mild surprise, there was a hint of recognition there too.

Then again, for those who've experienced it once before, the divinity the demigod was putting out was difficult to mistake.

Then, the older witch turned back to Lavinia, and her expression creased with incomprehension once again.

"You…" she whispered, the words dragging out with incredulity. "Came for me?"

"Of course I did." Lavinia's brows furrowed, and she quickly reached up to wipe her blinking eyes. "You're... I had to. How could I not?"

For a moment, there was silence.

The words lingered.

Then...

"...Hhh..."

The laugh began.

Low at first, undercut by a brittle rasp that scraped against the non-existent walls of cold mist surrounding them, before curling upward into an ear-rattling, twisted chorus.

Lavinia reared back in stunned disbelief, but the laughter didn't peter out.

If anything, it swelled before finally collapsing into wet, ragged coughs that rattled the witch's entire husk-like frame.

Even then, her breaths rang with what was left of it.

Chiron remained impassive as the witch pulled herself back together again, content to observe in silence.

Daniel was far from content, but even he held still despite the sound clearly making the skin at the back of his neck crawl.

"'How could I not?' " Glenda's lips slowly curled into a smile that was more teeth than emotion, and the sight of it made the girl pale well before her mentor was finished speaking. "You must be joking."

"G-Glenda?"

"Four years under my care... and Grauzauberer after that..." Her glare could have stripped flesh from bone in its savagery. "And somehow, you remain a pathetic, naive little fool."

And there it was.

Chiron was not surprised, even as Daniel's jaw dropped.

Lavinia, though...

"What?"

Her voice came out flat and almost numb with disbelief.

She didn't step back or raise her hands, but simply stared instead, mind refusing to parse through that reaction.

Glenda didn't waste the opportunity in that silence.

"Stupid girl." She sneered, and began to rise, her movements sickly and disjointed. "What sentimentality possessed you to follow me down here?"

"I-"

"What did you think would happen?" Glenda went on, cutting and deliberate. "That you would comfort me? Save me, perhaps?"

She was towering over the girl by the time she was finished, a half-frozen scarecrow with dark, spiteful pits for eyes.

"To think the torments of this accursed realm were not enough." She spat, and every word made Lavinia flinch. "Now I'm to endure you as well - truly, those gods laugh at us all."

This time, Chiron had to physically stop Daniel from stepping forward.

It earned him a stunned, mutinous look, but he only shook his head at his student's vehemence.

It wasn't the time to interfere.

Not yet.

Lavinia and Glenda didn't even notice the near-intervention.

The former was staring up in the beginnings of dazed horror... and the latter was the horror itself.

"Well?" She snarled. "Nothing to say? No hopeful drivel to pile onto my misery?"

"What?" Lavinia managed a repeated whisper - and even that was strangled almost beyond repair. "Why… what are you-?"

Then something seemed to occur to her.

"Cocytus - this place." She swallowed and unsteadily rose to her feet. "That's why. It's making you-"

Again, Glenda burst into laughter.

"That blind, boundless faith again." Her smile was mirthless and venomous. "Perhaps this is fitting - to come face to face with the fruit of my labours in this hell. I cultivated it for a reason, and yet... to experience it once again, now that the game is up... how pitiful."

...

Lavinia opened her mouth, but words failed her.

Her hands twitched at her sides, trembling, and she took a half-step back - then another, and Glenda pounced on the perceived weakness like a beast scenting blood.

"This realm did not make me what I am." She hissed, before the pointed cruelty drained in favour of something quieter, but no less sharp. "I am not addled, nor a victim of this place - though I have had many in the lifetimes I've lived."

A short, frozen pause.

"I have slaughtered warriors. Eradicated armies. Burned entire bloodlines to cinders, and when I was done with the enemies on the field, I found my way to their homes and finished what was left - and even that was a mercy, compared to the rest."

She took a step closer, uneven but filled with terrible purpose.

"I have taken what I wanted, twisted what I pleased, and resorted to means that would make the blood in your veins curdle; not out of malice, or for the sake of the slaughter, but for power - the only currency that matters in a world ruled by gods and monsters. The very reason so many turn to the path of magic to begin with."

Another step.

"I am Glenda Silverbrook, and I am as I have always been. Long before the Olympians came to Oz. Long before you ever learned my name."

Finally, she looked Lavinia dead in the eye.

"I am not changed, girl - merely stripped of a pretense that has already served its purpose."

Her slow smile was a mockery of the gesture.

"Or did you think you were different? Special?"

Each word seeped out like poison.

"The little orphan with the God-killing weapon embedded in her soul that I just so happened to take in?"

That, finally, earned a reaction.

Lavnia sucked in a breath.

Once, but with terrified finality, because the girl was far from stupid.

She knew exactly where this was going.

"You were not meant to save me, Lavinia Reni. That's not why I spared you from a life of mediocrity, or trained you when you demonstrated talent worth bending to my will." Her lips curved up once more. "You were a curiosity - an experiment carried to term."

"...No."

"A source of valuable data on an invaluable resource," Glenda finished without pause. "And an opportunity that could not be wasted. Had Augusta not taken an interest in you, I might very well have never sent you to Grauzauberer in the first place."

"No."

"Better to keep a tool close at hand, regardless of the effort-"

"No!"

Lavinia's scream was visceral.

"That's not- I don't believe you!" she tried, voice cracking in desperation. "That's not why you-!"

She couldn't even get the words not.

Not with her breaths so shallow and uneven, her chest heaving with every beat.

The air changed again.

A faint, flickering silver of light bled out across her fingertips, and the cold surrounding them quivered with a different, more subtle quality.

The first stirrings of Absolute Demise.

Glenda only smiled again, and this time, the expression was almost gentle.

Within a blink, she crossed the remaining distance and seized Lavinia's chin in a faint, easily breakable grip.

"If your parents were not dead when I found you, I would have killed them myself."

The magic died.

Absolutely and instantly.

So did Lavinia's very breath.

"All you have ever been worth." Glenda finished in a low, final whisper. "Is that Sacred Gear you possess. A blade forged blunt so that it may never cut the hand that wielded it - and now that my story ends in this prison, you have no value to me at all."

Chiron could almost see it - the moment where Lavinia Reni's heart was torn from her chest, and the light in her eyes blinked out.

Apollon had truly played this one marvellously, in that he hadn't lifted a finger at all.

"Now begone from my sight."

And Glenda pushed her.

Not hard. Not with much force at all.

The girl toppled over all the same, silver sparks scattering from her fingers as she hit the ice.

Or she would have, had a pair of arms encased in golden light not spared her the fall.

"You."

Even as he knelt down to steady her, Daniel still managed to look up at Glenda and meet her cold, cruel glare.

His eyes burned gold and purple in sheer, apoplectic fury.

"You absolute monster."

Glenda only sneered.

"Bold words, Demigod."

How about a slow, emotional chapter, too really pace out our character interactions?

...

Nah, fuck that.

"You absolute monster."

"Bold words, Demigod."

Glenda's ugly sneer didn't waver an inch as I caught Lavinia in my arms, breaking her fall and glaring up at the older witch with all the pure, unbridled murder I could muster.

Right then, I had oceans of it to spare - only it didn't seem to faze her.

If anything, the hateful contempt in her eyes seemed to froth and swell that much more as she looked down at me.

At both of us.

"What a pathetic sight you make now, Lavinia."

Even halfway into a nervous breakdown, with her eyes glazed and so very away for comfort, Lavinia still managed to flinch in my hold.

Naturally, I took that swimmingly.

"Shut. Up."

The words tore out of me in a violent snarl, reverberating in triplicate echoes. Fire burned under my ribs and flared with them, a wave of heat surging out against the crippling, soul-deep cold of Cocytus - pushing it back, just for a second, and setting the frozen mists to a steaming hiss.

"Oh?"

Glenda didn't back down, even as her full focus snapped right back onto me again. Her neck craned low as she leaned forward, angling her frame into the bubble of growing warmth in an excruciatingly disjointed motion.

"Do my words displease you, little godling? Do they make you angry?"

Her face twisted as she bared her teeth, frozen skin pulling and cracking in an expression that was utterly wrong.

"How arrogant."

I almost choked.

"Arrogant!?"

"Arrogant!" She roared back, and it was as if her vocal cords were splintering like breaking ice. "Where does this rage come from, demigod? Do I offend your sensibilities? Do I disgust you? Hah!"

She laughed, demented and unhinged, and it snuffed out whatever it was I'd been about to spit at her before I could even think the raging answer through.

"What right does one like you have to fury?"

Her lips curled, blue and near-dead.

"You, who were exalted above countless others through nothing more than the simple virtue of your birth. You, who were born with more power coursing through you than most humans will ever know, or dare to imagine."

Her cracked smile widened as I grit my teeth hard enough to ache, and the fiery disbelief burned through my veins like gasoline.

"And yet you look at me with such disgust, when you understand nothing of humanity's weakness in this world - of true helplessness, or struggle, or strife without end."

The cackle that followed was raw and razor sharp.

"Unlike you, child of divine tyrants, I was born with the burden of mere mortality... in a world ruled by monsters who laugh at such pitiful limitations."

She trailed off slowly, before abruptly lunging forward to loom over us, head tipping low, eyes locking on mine.

"Your kin are no better... and so I ask you this, Olympian-spawn..."

A beat passed, frozen and eerie.

"What right does someone - something - like you have to judge me?" She whispered, low and vicious, with a gaze so dark it could have passed for hollow. "And how dare you look at me with such shameless audacity?"

I-

...

...

...

Breath.

Breath.

Breath.

...

Heracles. Meleager. Achilles.

So many others that trying to list them all was like counting sheep, and those were just the highlights, not the sum total.

All of them had been great heroes or warriors who'd had good things going for them - or could have had them, at least - but ruined it all by blowing their fuses and letting anger take over the steering wheel at just the right moment to destroy everything.

Chiron had drilled it into us himself.

Keep calm, and if you move to act out of anger, stop dead in your tracks and run it back until it stops making sense.

Words to live by, and in my defense, I tried.

A distant part of me already knew that I shouldn't be letting her get to me - that I shouldn't be this angry to begin with.

I'm an idiot on a good day, but I'm not stupid.

Cocytus was messing with my head.

The cold, the aura of misery and despair...

The slow, glacial pressure that's been building up inside my skull since the second we'd set foot into the mists, impossibly subtle right up until the moment it was noticed - then it was suddenly a mountain trying to crush everything underneath it, ramping up with every passing second making it impossible to think straight.

Even then, losing my cool wouldn't help.

I knew that.

Accepted it.

Embraced the logic with gusto.

...

Unfortunately, logic as a whole was currently overshadowed by all this unyielding rage!

"How-!?" The growl building up in my throat sounded damn-near alien. The things she was saying. The things she was implying, as if she knew anything about me. "How dare I-!?"

Glenda's teeth shone in the building glow coming off of me, because she was still smiling.

"Was it something I said?"

That's it.

My hand snapped out, and a miniature blaze flared into existence along my palm, gold and purple flames warping in on themselves as the mist around us went from hissing to screaming.

Finally, Glenda's smile vanished, replaced with stunned surprise - but not for long.

"Augusta..." She whispered, before her lips curved up right on over again. "So that's how it was."

Within a blink, her ear-scraping laughter was back, sounding out over the recoiling frost and the rush of welling flames.

"One beast to kill and usurp another." The delight there was loud and unashamedly genuine. "How fitting."

I almost blasted her right then and there.

Calling it a close call wouldn't do it justice - I was seconds away from cremating the deranged hag and calling it a day.

Then I looked at her.

Really look at her, I mean.

Past the venom and bile, and right into that one glint in her eyes that had been there since the beginning.

Something I only caught by pure chance - or close enough to it that the difference didn't matter.

Not anger. Not satisfaction.

Anticipation.

What?

The flames in my palm flickered, before quickly being snuffed away as I clenched my fist and pulled it back through sheer force of will.

The cold of Cocytus snapped back against the fading heat like a rubber band with teeth.

Savage, but the way Glenda's smile instantly died managed to take the worst of the edge clean off.

It also clicked a piece or three into place.

"You want me to kill you, don't you?"

She didn't skip a beat.

"I am already in the Underworld, you stupid child."

But even through the scornful look, something in her expression slipped.

Or maybe it was her stance - the way she leaned forward.

Either way, it was tiny.

Just this one little ghost of a shift, so small it was pointless to describe, but now that I was looking for it, it was also impossible to miss.

Even if I had, I knew a technical truth when I heard one.

"That doesn't mean you're dead."

The immediate silence after that - jilted and furious - was all the answer I needed.

But it wasn't the only one I got.

"No, it certainly does not."

That's when Chiron finally stepped up next to us.

I hadn't forgotten he was there - always look out for your surroundings - but the last minute and change had nearly blanked him out of my perception anyway.

...

I'd almost acted out like a reckless moron in front of him, and I'd probably pay for that later.

Right then, though-

"What do you see, Daniel?"

His voice was perfectly level as he glanced over at me, before gesturing over to Glenda.

"Well?"

I... blinked at him for a minute, before slowly glaring over at the older witch as I gently propped Lavinia up.

What do I see?

"The scum of the earth?"

She glowered back with all the vitriol to match, but she did it without so much as a breath, and Chiron only smiled humorously.

"Quite, but beyond that."

He snapped his fingers, and the sound echoed like a thunderbolt, complete with a wave of green light that surged out and washed over Glenda like a tide.

"Observe."

They appeared all at once as the light broke over them, spectral, fused chains of off-gold circling her wrists, connected with a length of links, half-slack but only just, with another running up and anchored to a thick, double bolted collar wrapped around her neck.

Thorough, and completely miserable from the first look alone.

That, and they felt familiar, too.

My eyes narrowed.

"My dad did this, didn't he?"

It made sense, even before Chiron nodded.

The divinity ringing off of them was more than second nature to me at this point.

"Cocytus is a prison few can dream of escaping, and those chains are an added sentence made manifest. Lord Apollon always did have an affinity for bitter ironies."

"An irony?" Glenda's face did… something that was no less hideous than everything I'd seen so far. "A mockery, more like."

"Hardly. From your own admissions, you were always a mockery and a shame to all that is good and decent, entirely of your own making." He replied effortlessly, unbothered, and the look on her face folded into something priceless. "The Sun Lord only added the finishing touches and a teaspoon's worth of accountability."

What did Dad-?

"Healing banishes pain, and the truth can set one free." Chiron didn't wait for me to ask. "Quaint, simple truths, but these chains you see before you, my student, are the inverse of both."

The collar on Glenda's neck seemed to glimmer as he spoke - maybe in acknowledgment, or pure coincidence.

"A divine binding that draws out the unforgiving truth regardless of the speaker's will, and a barbed blessing that enforces healing and recovery on a living mortal trapped and suffering in a realm of the dead - the better to suffer that torturous dissonance all the more..."

The kind of thing that made you think - except, when you were in the middle of hell, literally, with the pressure of the realm constantly grinding you down no matter how hard you tried to push back against it, that was all you could do.

Think, and feel everything.

Dissonance - wrongness

That's what the witch had been sentenced to.

My eyes snapped over to her, and Glenda said nothing.

She didn't have to.

"That's why she's baiting me." I turned back to Chiron as it dawned on me. "She wants to die, for real this time, because that's an out."

I freaking bet.

I'd been here all of twenty minutes - maybe more, maybe less, because time got weird in the mists - and I already wanted out.

Glenda Silverbrook had been here for months, as a living person in a place where the living categorically didn't belong.

Except there was nowhere else to go: this was the end of the line, even when she did die properly.

The chains just dragged it out that much more.

That's...

"Is that why...?"

The thought derailed when Lavinia stirred, hesitantly shifting away from me and rising up to her feet.

He didn't deny it.

"Most certainly. I would not have permitted it - a divine punishment must not be so easily averted - but her intent in goading you both was unmistakable."

For the hundredth time over, Glenda only sneered.

Lavinia... didn't react to that.

Not violently, or loudly, or with anything worth writing home about, really.

"...I see."

For a moment, I could almost feel...

Something.

A flicker of sensation ghosted over the strings of mists curling around her, but it vanished before I could sense it out properly.

Glenda didn't seem to miss it, either.

She looked over at Lavinia, and for the first time since all of this started, the contempt on her face folded into something different.

A flat, almost resigned grimace.

For the love of-!

"If nothing else, you are all that remains of my teachings, and this is a final lesson on the consequences of naive stupidity. You would do well to carve it into your heart."

Lavinia didn't answer her - didn't even react, after all that, and Glenda huffed and turned away at last.

"Now leave. Those are the last words I will ever waste on you."

You've got to be kidding me.

"Really?"

She paused, pulling back out of the mists she had been retreating into and turning to stare at me with a fresh, glimmering sprinkling of hoarfrost already spreading over her skin.

"You had to twist the knife in deeper?" I ground out lowly, desperately trying to ignore the temptation to reach for Incinerate Anthem's flames again. "You couldn't spare us all that horrible screech you call a voice?"

Then an idea came to me, and I let myself smile.

It wasn't a nice smile.

"Then again, maybe you couldn't." I tipped my head forward, towards the slowly fading chains - losing corporeality, but still inescapable as far as she was concerned. "Dad does good work."

She stilled.

"What?" I let my smile grow bigger, until it was half-teeth and growing. "Was it something I said?"

I'll tell you this much: Throwing that back in her face?

It felt good.

Viscerally

Of course, it didn't last, either.

"Is that right?"

I expected her to lose it.

Maybe froth at the mouth a little, because from everything I'd seen, see was exactly that kind of lunatic.

"Proud of him, are you? And proud of yourself too, I expect?"

"Why wouldn't you be. Demigod that you are - but don't you forget my words, either." The words came out like knives, complete with a stare that could cut through bone. "You have no right to judge me - or any human, for that matter, when you are not and will never be one yourself.

I...

"What the hell are you talking about?"

She repeated it so matter-of-factly that it took a second to parse through, and then I bristled, mostly out of pure incomprehension.

She spat 'dirt' out like the syllable was made of pure acid.

Just desperate garbage all the way through

I don't understand how she was getting to me, again, but the answer didn't come quickly, even as Cocytus swallowed her, hungry and impatient.

"What else?"

"Satisfaction."

I hate her.

I've only known her for one conversation, and I hate her.

"Chiron?"

"Daniel?"

… I'd have probably said something too - many somethings,

"This is over." I managed, after I was done working my jaw back and forth uselessly. "Can we leave now?"

Lavinia said nothing, but neither of us expected her to.

"Please?"

He nodded, looking at me with something I didn't want to parse through right now.

"Certain-"

Some kind of call full of authority, strong enough to make the mists blow back a foot and a half.

An enormous teleportation circle.

Stupidly elaborate, loaded with so much power I could feel it in my teeth, and already active.

Son of a-!

No time to move. No time to call out.

By the time I'd locked onto what it was, everything was already dissolving into refracting patterns, and we were whisked away into the light.

...

Time since battle start: 6.5 seconds.

...​

We're not in Kansas anymore.

When the world reappeared, I was already moving.

The red-purple sky and the violet clouds didn't matter.

Neither did the new terrain - A desert that stretched out in every direction, but the colors were wrong. Rust-red sand bled into sickly ash, broken by endless rows of jagged stone. Boulders and spires jutted upward in violent, uneven lines, climbing high enough that the tallest of them could give skyscrapers a run for their money.

I was standing on one of those.

Lavinia wasn't.

I could feel her, far, far out and off somewhere to my left, but that was about the first thing I noticed.

Well, that, and the wave of recognizable hooded figures coming at me from all angles, blades out and porcelain masks glinting as they dropped out of the air and onto the boulders and spire-peaks surrounding me.

Lovely.

"Hold!"

One of them stood out above the rest - figuratively and literally.

He stood on his own peak above the others, blade raised high, and instead of a blank mask like the rest of them, his was more elaborate, with inked scale patterns and a shape I wouldn't even pretend to be surprised at, considering my track record.

A red and purple-black dragon.

Because of course it was.

What even is today, and why is it always dragons?

"You. Interloper."

He pointed his sword at me, edge-first, and a menacing pulse of aura rose out of him and seeped into the air, thick with wild bloodlust.

"You interfere in matters that do not concern you." His voice was a low, garbled growl, and I could tell that he was orders of magnitude more powerful than the ones I'd just taken down. "Surrender, or die."

...

"...Can I get a minute to think about it, or-"

"I will not ask again."

Of course you won't.

I almost laughed.

Not even thirty seconds in, and I had no earthly idea what was happening anymore.

Who these idiots were, and how in the hell they had the guts to pull something like this right outside Chiron's home.

My teacher would flip.

Dad would probably go apoplectic.

But right here, right now...

Priorities.

Questions and answers could wait.

Lavinia first.

"Look, buddy." I raised Serpent's Downfall, and all of them bristled. "I don't know who you are - or who you think you are... but by all means..."

The heat I'd been holding didn't spike.

It detonated.

Light bled out of me in a hard, gold-white surge, with just a hint of purple in to set the scene.

The air jumped up to a thousand degrees.

Stone beneath my feet groaned, cracked, and began to glow red-hot.

A concussive wave rolled out in a perfect ring, kicking dust and shattered rock off every nearby spire.

And me?

"If you want some-"

I looked up at the apparent leader and grinned like an absolute lunatic.

"COME GET SOME!"

He shot down towards me, blade extended, and I dove right in and became a firestorm.

...

The young witch of the hour was trapped with an old friend - in theory.

The unexpected interloper was making a mess of everything - and everyone.

"Well, damn."

And all the while, another pair of eyes observed everything from above, black wings fluttering in the breeze.

Soon enough, their lips curved up in sheer delighted surprise.

"Would you look at that?"

...​
