Other than that, voila: our first look at a couple of devils a little closer to home.

Misla Bael:

Another day dawned over Lucifer's Underworld, and for Misla Bael - Vapula by birth, thankfully - it began in her solar.

The room was as well-kept as ever, with polished wood floors that gleamed under the morning light, and warm carpeting in shades of brown and gold.

Bookshelves lined one wall, filled with neatly organized volumes - mythology, magic theory, and even the occasional novel tucked between heavier tomes.

She'd always been an avid reader, and if some of those volumes happened to be a touch more… romantic and risqué than others...well.

No one should be begrudged their guilty pleasures. Frankly, she refused to apologize for having good taste.

Her desk was wide and orderly, missives and papers stacked in neat piles over glossy oak, a picture frame at one end, and a half-empty cup of tea steaming at the other.

There were a few other touches here and there - a pair of high-back chairs, a dormant fireplace, and a number of little bits and bobs - but they were passing details for now.

She walked to the massive double window that dominated the far wall and idly rested her hands on the frames, watching the sunrise.

The light crept slowly across the Underworld, deep and soft, painting the horizon in a way that was beautiful as it was perfectly artificial.

Truly, the New Satan's creation of the false firmament was a feat in itself.

Hark! Lo and behold, for we your rulers have shaped even the heavens to our will, and gifted them unto thee.

Or maybe that wasn't quite it, but the point stood regardless.

Whether as a gift to the reincarnated, a declaration of pure satanic power, or simply a change of pace to mark a new era, it was a statement that spanned the length of all the territories held by the Houses of Seventy-Two, and more besides.

Subtle, yet paradoxically on the nose - or over it, quite literally.

The politician in her approved.

The rest of her was content to enjoy a dawn she didn't have to journey to the mortal realm for. She took it in for a few long, calm moments more, before sighing contentedly and stepping away.

There had been a time when she thought her sunrises were numbered -artificial or otherwise.

Nothing like an impending death sentence - or as good as - to make you appreciate the little things in life.

Misla may have been saved from the Sleeping Disease in the end - a miracle in every sense of the word - but some habits the specter of it had formed were there to stay.

Still, duty called.

On cue, there came a knock at the door. Exactly three, precise and evenly spaced as always.

It opened a moment later to reveal Anton, offering her a polite smile as he stepped inside, guiding a small wheeled cart before him. Silver gleamed softly atop it - fresh tea, a covered dish, and neatly arranged cutlery.

Right on time.

"Good morning, my lady."

"Isn't it just?" she returned the smile, pausing halfway to her seat. "Anton, you know full well that formalities are unnecessary behind closed doors."

"As you say, my lady."

Right.

Some might have mistaken it for stone-faced adherence to protocol, but she knew her older cousin well enough to catch the faint thread of amusement beneath it.

She rolled her eyes fondly as she took her seat, and he set about placing the dishes before her with practiced ease, movements smooth from practice.

Sliced fruit, neatly fanned across a small plate, a scattering of candied nuts beside it, and some rather lovely-looking cake slices joined it a moment later. Buttered toast followed, along with the pot of tea, a dish of honey, some cold cuts and assorted cheese, and a little jar of dark marmalade set off to the side.

A wonderful spread.

"Join me?"

"If you wish it."

"Please."

Anton's presence would always be welcome.

He was, after all, the closest thing she had to an older brother worth a damn - far more reliable than her father or any of her uncles, and certainly better company than her younger brothers.

That had always been the case.

Her cousin had been born half a century before the Civil War, a little over five hundred years ago now. His father had been the head of a branch line of the greater clan, and his mother had been a human mage who'd been captured in some skirmish or another in the human world.

Her treatment as a prisoner was... not kind, nor fit to be spoken of in decent company. It resulted in Anton's birth and her death, and that was all that needed to be said about it.

The Lord Vapula of that time had been furious. Not over the circumstances of Anton's birth - such things had never troubled devils of his disposition - but over what he perceived as the sullying of the bloodline.

A half-breed child was a stain on the legacy of their Pillar, and if Misla's father hadn't taken Anton in, he would have been cast out into the dirt - or worse.

Not that her father had done it out of any sentiment whatsoever, mind you. He'd laugh in the face of the very thought.

Anton was not his shame - not directly - but he was of their blood.

A servant of potential, free of charge

It was the same sort of ruthless thinking that eventually carried her father to the head of the Pillar, earning him the title of Lord Vapula after the main line was wiped out in the Civil War.

Nevertheless.

Anton had been a part of her life since the day she was born, and she wouldn't have it any other way.

They ate in silence for the first little while, letting the morning pass them by, before his eyes eventually strayed to the piles littering her desk.

"Quite a bit to get through."

"Don't remind me." Just looking at them made her cringe in distaste. "What endless delights I've woken up to."

Life hadn't stopped for anyone but her when the Sleeping Disease had finally taken her, and the Underworld had kept turning - and so had its devils.

Territories under her oversight were eyed like prized cattle.

Business interests she had a stake in found themselves suddenly - and oh so conveniently - contested.

Contracts were poked and prodded, tested for any give.

Anything. Everything.

If it was worth something and not locked down tighter than the Vatican, it drew eyes and claws alike.

Par for the course, really.

Any hint of opportunity, or weakness, or both, and Misla's so-called 'peers' swarmed like locusts.

They'd probably started sharpening their knives before she'd even closed her eyes, and even Sairaorg hadn't been spared.

The thought made something sharp and venomous bristle in her chest, before she forced it down with a careful inhale and another sip of tea.

It was also to be expected, in some sense.

Her son was a noble twice over, and a Bael before all else.

Failure or otherwise - another flare of loathing she had to swallow at the thought alone - he was valuable.

By the same token, he was protected. To a degree.

Whatever her contemptible husband's opinion, Zekram would forgive no great overstep against a descendant who bore his name.

The Ruin Lord had sown carnage and destruction far and wide for far less, and though he rarely stood in the public eye, the specter of him loomed all the same.

But Zekram Bael also did as he pleased.

When he chose to act, he moved those beneath him like pieces on a board - toward prosperity or misery as it suited him - and thought nothing of it so long as the ends aligned with his will.

That was why there no relying on him.

Not truly.

His reputation was a shield, but his attention was a blade that cut both ways, and then a third for good measure.

"Something the matter?"

Anton's sudden question derailed that line of thought, and Misla blinked, startled by how far her mind had wandered.

"The usual."

She wiped her hands with a napkin before reaching over to pat the nearest stack of papers.

"Years of pileup. So much to get through, and every line on the checklist is just as tedious as the rest."

"I see," Anton said, voice even. "How troublesome."

"Absolutely."

"..."

"..."

Silence.

He sipped his tea.

She stared at him.

A moment passed.

"...Well?"

"Is there something you require, my lady?"

She gave him a flat look. "Anton."

"Yes?"

"I know full well you've read everything in that stack."

In every stack, more like.

"Hardly. I would never act with such impudence." He set his cup down with a soft clink. "I merely skimmed a handful."

Skimmed.

Misla couldn't quite stop the twitch at the corner of her mouth.

Of course he'd read them. He couldn't leave dangerous 'offers' lying about where Sairaorg might get at them before he had a few more years of experience - and she loved him all the more for it.

"Well, since you've skimmed…" She gestured to the mountain of papers expectantly. "You can help me sort through the chaff."

"Of course, my lady." His expression didn't twitch an inch, but it was all in the eyes if one knew to look for it. "If I may?"

He waved a hand, and the stacks obeyed, lifting into the air under the spell. Papers floated and swapped in tandem, sliding neatly into place before finally settling into three separate piles once more.

She hummed and leaned forward to look them over.

"By category or by priority?"

"By intent." Anton corrected, before pointing to the first pile. "Offers made in 'good faith'."

They both nearly snorted, though he hid it better than she did.

Good faith in affairs like this almost always meant not actively malicious, for now.

Even then, be wary.

He gestured to the second pile.

"Ambitious overreach, but well-mannered.'

And the third-

"Deliberate insult, or genuine idiocy. More the former than the latter, I hope, or else one could truly weep for the state of our nobility."

This time, she did snort.

"Never change, Anton." She reached for the top letter from the third pile, cracking the seal with a flick of her fingers. "Never-"

The words died in her throat as she read over the lines.

A missive from one Elvira Flauros - a conniving little pest from a branch family of said Pillar, and a woman Misla had never had much patience for to begin with.

Too indolent and hedonistic by half, and a widow thrice over despite their shared age - and everyone with a shred of intelligence to their name knew that at least two of those untimely deaths she had likely had a hand in herself.

But the letter wasn't addressed to Misla.

It was to Sairaorg.

Worthless condolences over the state of Misla and her fall to the Sleeping Disease. An empty promise of help, however way she could. An invitation to-

...

"Ah." She smiled serenly. "I'm going to rip her spine out through her throat."

"Please don't, my lady." He didn't miss a beat "The consequences would be irritating at best."

"Don't worry. I'll feed it back to her when I'm done."

So she could rinse and repeat, as many times as needed.

Or until she grew bored, whichever came first.

If the hideous little vulture was bold enough to circle her son - angling for a debt, or a favour, or something altogether more perverse - then she was bold enough to weather a little correction.

If she wasn't, the problem would still solve itself one way or another.

"The point stands," Anton said, dry and not especially concerned. "If you must, I humbly request that you do so somewhere that won't stain the carpets."

Misla... paused.

"That happened only the once."

"Three times, my lady."

"Two and a half," she protested immediately. "The last one doesn't count, and it was eighty years ago at that."

She hadn't even been the aggressor there - those deranged cultists had been attacking her.

"It cost us a tapestry," he reminded her flatly. "The gold-threaded Assyrian was one of a kind. Beyond repair."

Misla waved a hand dismissively. "It was hideous."

"It was ancient."

So she was ever reminded.

"Ancient things can still be ugly."

"And the west wing of the castle?"

"...It was in the way."

"My lady."

"Fine." She slapped the letter down and took a deep, calming breath. "We can shelf all talk of Elvira Flauros's entirely hypothetical evisceration for the moment."

They could always circle back to the specifics once she knew exactly how much violent disembowelment was due, and on whose account.

"That is all I ask."

Anton seemed pleased.

Positively stone-faced, but pleased.

"Don't be smug, cousin."

"Certainly not." He lied smoothly. "I only advise patience. There are plenty more matters left to test it."

She eyed the stacks waiting off to the side, and her nose wrinkled.

"Lovely."

...​

The next hour and a half was an exercise in restraint the likes of which would have driven saints to heresy.

She spent it sifting, skimming, and occasionally muttering curses under her breath at the sheer - and growing - audacity of what seemed like every conniving parasite under the false sun, and more to spare.

The gall of these animals.

Anton hovered nearby, ever the picture of polite attention, occasionally placing a fresh cup of tea within reach and offering the rare bit of commentary when she prodded him for it.

By the time she was halfway through the lot, her mind was threatening a migraine and she could hardly blame it for the mutiny.

Finally, she groaned and quietly pushed the remaining paperwork aside, leaning back in her chair with a posture that could generously be called 'reposed' - noble women do not slump, of course - and idly massaged her temples.

"It's as if half of them have given up on dignity entirely," she muttered, eyeing the leftover paperwork like a decanter of bubbling poison . "And most of the ones left are too stupid to recognise it."

Not that that excused them from her eventual vengeance, but, Satan below, what a pathetic mess.

"I did warn you. That aside, however…" Anton waited until she met his gaze. "There is a silver lining."

She raised a brow.

"The news of your awakening and subsequent return will send them all into hysterics of a most satisfying sort, and you won't have to lift a finger to enjoy them."

Hah.

The laugh bubbled out of her before she could stop it, because he wasn't wrong.

The estate had been on lockdown from nearly the instant Misla had awoken. No one in, and no one out, save for Anton, her son, herself, and one exception - the single linchpin who had set all of this in motion.

Nobody knew that Misla had 'bested' the Sleeping Disease - no devil ever had - and that was entirely by design.

Once the word broke, the fireworks would be spectacular, and she had every intention of timing the revelation for maximum impact.

October thirty-first.

Samhain.

The Night of the Thinning Veil, or so the mortal myths went.

It was also the night of one of the Bael family's grand annual balls, and everyone who was anyone in the Underworld would be invited, theatrics and all.

The perfect stage.

"A little over a month to go."

"Indeed."

A few weeks more, and Misla and Sairaorg would make their triumphant return for all to see and seethe - along with a special guest or two, circumstances permitting.

It would be magnificent.

Dangerous too, in all likelihood, but danger was only relative.

Nothing worth doing had ever been easy, after all. Nor safe at that. And for the crime of dismissing her son as worthless?

A reckoning was long overdue.

"Heavy thoughts?"

"The heaviest."

...

Though maybe it was time to switch tracks, if her mood was so clearly starting to show.

She rose from her chair and threw her arms up in a lazy stretch, letting her back pop as she arched.

Oh, but that felt good after hours in place.

A little pacing helped get her blood flowing, and Anton stepped aside with a small smile as she drifted past - he knew her habits well.

Eventually, she stopped beside a marble pedestal.

One of a handful scattered throughout the solar, each holding up some trinket or curiosity gathered over the years.

This one, however, carried something altogether more striking.

A gem, nestled on a raised cushion.

No bigger than an apple, perfectly cut, and absolutely alive with its own inner light - and what a glow that was.

White at the heart, with shards of fractal color flickering along the edges, and all the more brilliant for it.

Calling it radiant didn't quite do it justice.

Misla had never seen anything like it - not without magic at play, obviously, and that often defeated the point.

Not here.

Then again, when she really stopped to think about it, the beauty was the least relevant part of its value.

The fact that it had been a gift from Sairaorg - a little treasure he'd picked up on some adventure with his friend - made it truly priceless.

And speaking of said friend...

Her thoughts inevitably drifted back to Daniel Winchester.

How Sai had managed to not only end up under the legendary Chiron's tutelage, but also strike up a friendship with a Greek demigod - an Olympian one, at that - still baffled her.

Greece was off-limits to the lords and heirs of the assorted Pillars, on account of that diplomatic cataclysm of an incident a few centuries back -the stupidity there had been positively breathtaking.

Official relations were beyond non-existent - even the hope of them was dead and buried, the ground salted, and always one minor provocation away from open disaster.

For her son to get as far as he did, unopposed and unharmed...

She'd almost suspect foul play, only that didn't quite fit.

There was no point in sight, no hidden snare she could see, and Sai had flourished beyond even her wildest expectations.

The pinnacle of High-Class already, and he'd done it in less than a year.

Ludicrous growth even by the standards of the Great War - and in this era of relative peace…

He'd eat the competition alive, and dive right back in for seconds.

Misla's pride burned so fiercely at the thought she had to smile.

There was much she didn't know - secrets her son and his friend kept that she could only guess at, refusing to pry - but the results spoke for themselves.

Even still…

Her mind kept shifting back to the logistics of what came next.

Sairaorg's strength. Her reawakening.

The connection to the Olympian Pantheon through the world's most famous centaur, and the only other student he'd picked up in a very, very long time.

All of it would shine the spotlight on them, and there'd be no going back after the fact.

Serafall Leviathan alone would take immediate interest - and frankly, Misla wouldn't put it past her to camp outside their door in search of answers.

The woman had always been too eccentric by half - nor would she be the only one.

Not by a long shot.

"Things are going to get quite loud."

"I imagine so." Anton agreed readily enough. "Does that displease you?"

"There's no point in being upset over the inevitable," she said. This was always going to happen. "But a mother is allowed to worry."

To that, he inclined his head.

By Anton's standards, that was almost a shrug.

"Lord Sairaorg is capable."

"That he is."

"And the meeting today will be good practice for the future."

She blinked.

"Oh. That."

Despite the estate being sealed off for the time being, Sairaorg was expecting guests.

Though expecting might be a strong word.

'Politely resigned' fit better, and as for the guests themselves...

A girl from the Abaddon Clan, and an attendant who bore the name of Andrealphus - for whatever that was worth, given that the Pillar was officially extinct.

Human-blooded, then, or something of the sort that barred her from heirship if the name and lineage were genuine.

Other than that, they were unremarkable, if apparently quite persistent.

Good for them.

Misla would have still had Anton turn them away with one excuse or another, had he not suggested otherwise himself.

Something about settling the matter once and for all.

Sairaorg had reluctantly agreed, and here they were.

"Tell me about them again?"

"There's not much to say, my lady." He adjusted his cuffs with practiced ease. "They are obviously rather dogged, and set on making their case to Lord Sairaorg. But I do not believe you'll find them unworthy of the attempt."

The emphasis there was pointed, and her eyes narrowed.

"Meaning?"

"From all that I've seen, sparse as that has been..." He paused, picking the words carefully. "They are precisely the sort of young devils the current regime approves of."

Which... told her many things, and nothing at all.

Typical.

All the same, her interest was piqued.

"This should be interesting, isn't it?"

Her cousin gave another rare smile.

"That is entirely up to the youth."

...​

Kuisha Abaddon:

Kuisha wasn't sure whether she wanted to laugh or cry.

The grand hall of the Vapula estate loomed above her, and for all that it was warmly lit, the glow bouncing off the walls might as well have been searing.

The coach beneath her was plush and comfortable, and the furniture was polished to near-gleaming. A few pieces of art hung along the walls, and those were more tasteful than gaudy.

Even the air smelled nice, with a scent that was one part wax, old wood, and something pleasantly floral that hit just right.

All in all?

Perfectly civilized.

Somehow, that made the urge to fidget worse.

Of all the times to come down with nerves!

Coriana sat beside her, hands folded in her lap, mirroring her posture right down to the polite, very carefully rehearsed smile.

And right across from them - past a coffee table loaded with refreshments she'd never be able to stomach under this kind of pressure, and another couch to boot - sat Sairaorg Bael.

He just sat there, dressed in half-formal wear and stared at them placidly, and something about that focus was... intense.

In a way it hadn't been before, and Kuisha would know.

It wasn't the first time they'd met.

Not the second or even the third, either, but given that he didn't look half a second away from storming off mid-conversation, this was already shaping up to be a better encounter than the last.

"Lord Sairaorg-"

"Hold on."

Or maybe not.

"I'd like to say something before we get started." He added, before the sickly feeling of defeat - another one - could start pooling in her gut. "Just to get a few things out of the way."

"Of course." "Please."

Coriana's answer quickly overlapped with her own - she was just as nervous, poker face or no, and it showed - but the Bael barely seemed to register it.

"Great." He clapped his hands together lightly and leaned forward an inch. "First things first: you can drop the 'lord' bit. Everything about this is already a bit much without the added formality stacked on top. Just call me Sairaorg - Sai, if you want."

Over my dead body.

"If you prefer it, Sairaorg."

"And that goes both ways." Coriana added with a muted flourish, which got a nod out of him for the effort.

"Thank you. I'll take you up on that." He let that hang for a second, before nodding again. "Moving on now - what do you want?"

"...Pardon?"

"You want something from me." He said, and the honesty there was so raw she almost flinched. "I know you do, and you both know I know, and I'd rather not play twenty different word games dancing around the point. That'd be a waste of everyone's time, so let's just skip through all of that and get right down to it. Deal?"

...

Too blunt. Way too blunt.

For a moment, Kuisha scrambled.

She could just about feel Coriana doing the same.

The etiquette lessons and the rules of decorum she'd memorised back to front flashed through her mind, it took her a second longer than she'd have ever liked to force her thoughts in order.

"What we've always wanted." She answered with confidence she didn't truly feel. "A position in your Peerage, should you be open to granting us the opportunity."

The solid truth, but in as few words as she could put it.

When in doubt, keep it short.

Sairaorg raised a brow.

"My currently non-existent peerage, you mean?"

"Currently." Coriana latched on to that. "That's the operative word, isn't it?"

"...Maybe. Maybe not. What's it to you?"

The words were perfectly mild as he looked from her to Kuisha and back again.

"Why would either of you want to join my peerage?"

It was a fair question.

Direct, just like he promised, and unapologetically pointed.

Of course, Kuisha couldn't answer it with the first thing that popped to mind.

Because he represented a chance at something great.

Cast out or not, Sairaorg was still a member of the Great King's bloodline. He had resources, connections, and power to spare, even if it wasn't of the kind a Pillar noble was expected to have before all else.

He'd never claim heirship over the house - that position was well and truly supplanted by his brother, Magdaran - but given enough time and even a smidgen of drive, he could still reach heights most devils could only ever dream of.

Higher than anything she or Coriana could realistically aspire to, even.

Even discarded, a failed Bael was worth more than a successful Abaddon.

The thought made another unpleasant emotion curdle in her veins, before she crushed it down again.

Extra Demons were largely irrelevant in this day and age.

Outliers like Roygun Belphegor and Bedeze were just that - exceptions to the norm.

Getting worked up over the facts was a waste of time.

She'd much rather do something about them, and Sairaorg was still waiting for an answer.

"I believe we can all help each other."

The boy crossed his arms and leaned back.

"That right?"

"Yes." She held her hand out to the side, far enough away that it couldn't be mistaken for anything even remotely threatening. "I possess my Clan Trait: Hole."

A flicker of demonic power was all it took for space to warp and twist across the room, before collapsing into an obsidian rift.

Perfectly spherical, and perfectly controlled - for storage or spatial travel or whatever else in between - before another flick of her fingers dissipated it like it never was.

Without missing a beat, Coriana raised her hand to take her place - just like they'd practiced.

"And I possess my Clan Trait: Frostflame."

A torch's worth of fire blazed across her palm, blue and ghostly, and the temperature in the room plummeted instantly. Even the lights seemed to flicker and dim, until she clenched her fist and snuffed it out.

Sairaorg was staring patiently when Coriana turned back to him, and Kuisha had never looked away.

He wasn't impressed.

Not unimpressed, either.

Just patient.

She tried not to let it get under her skin as she spoke.

"We have power, and you have standing - more than we'll ever have, even now. "

Strike while the iron's hot.

"As one Peerage, we can pool all of that together. Cover our bases and carve ourselves a place in the Underworld that no one would be able to deny, with you as the King you should have been regardless."

...

...

...

The immediate silence was deafening.

The seconds after it were glacial and painful in a way that made Kuisha's skin feel three sizes too tight and counting.

Miserable with sheer expectation.

Did I overdo it?

She tried not to look at Coriana.

Please tell me I didn't overdo it.

Then Sairaorg cleared his throat.

"... Well." He leaned back in his seat, crossing one leg over the other as he went. "That was interesting."

Neither of them said a word.

They didn't even consider it.

"It was a good pitch, really. Very straightforward, and not nearly as condescending as it could have been, so props for that too. I'm impressed."

But?

Kuisha knew it was coming.

"That said... it was still pretty flawed."

And there it is.

"Flawed?"

"Absolutely." Sairaorg smiled, and the way his eyes seemed to glint had something at the back of her neck spiking to attention as fast as it could. "See, the thing is... I don't lack for power."

That was all the warning they got, before a wave of pure pressure slapped down over the room with all the subtlety of a hurricane.

Boom.

The floor trembled. The walls shook. The crystal chandelier kicked off an orchestra of shivering glass.

And they were the lucky ones.

The force hit them, and the air evacuated Kuisha's lungs faster than she could blink. Coriana's fist nearly speared through the couch as she clawed at it with a sudden jerk.

Her bones alone felt like they were quivering from the inside out, and when she looked up, wide-eyed-

"Sorry about that."

-everything cut off.

The pressure vanished, and the tremors died with it.

Instantly.

"My bad." Sairaorg offered breezily, uncrossing his legs and leaning forward again over the sound of settling glass. "Guess I didn't tone it down enough."

"Tone-" Coriana's voice was only halfway strangled, which was better than what Kuisha could have managed right about then. "That was toned down."

"Sure." There was no lie there. He didn't need one. "A little under a tenth of my output, give or take a smidge."

...

A tenth.

...

That overwhelming pressure.

...

One. Tenth.

...

...

...

I made a mistake.

Or maybe the Baels did.

Either way, when she met Sairaorg's eyes again, she held her composure.

How, she had no idea.

Her blood was probably more adrenaline and concentrated incredulity than it would ever be in her life, but she managed it.

Then she echoed his words.

"I'm impressed."

"Thank you." He said graciously - and maybe with a little finality - but she wasn't done.

She couldn't be.

Not after all this.

Not a chance in hell.

"I'm impressed," She repeated again. "But not discouraged!"

Sairaorg...

He stopped.

"No?"

"Not at all."

"... Go on."

That time, she heard it.

Saw it, too, if only a little.

For the first time since their conversation began - since they'd met, period - there was a different light in his eyes when he looked at her.

Amusement? Acknowledgement?

A sliver of respect?

...

It didn't matter.

Full speed ahead.

"Speaking of power is one thing, and small demonstrations like this are all well and good, but if you want to make an informed decision, you might as well see us at our best - or do you disagree?"

Take the bait. Take the bait. Take the bait.

"...Where are you going with this?"

Yes!

"To its natural conclusion, obviously."

Kuisha was aware of many things then.

The rush of blood in her ears. The pounding of her heart.

The look of ludicrous disbelief Coriana was nailing to her head with all the force of a supernova - or itching to, at least.

Even the voice of self-preservation in her head that was cursing her out in several dozen languages and in ways that defied devil comprehension to boot.

She ignored all of it.

The only thing she focused on then was the expression on his face as she stood up and steeled her spine with all the determination she could muster - and plenty of spite, too.

All or nothing - and I'm not giving up.

"Sairaorg Bael?"

She looked him dead in the eye and smiled, trying not to die on the inside all the while.

"I challenge you to a duel."

...

#10,538
Ever played with a magnifying glass on a hot summer day? Held it up against some cheap plastic junk or something?

Yours truly did that this one time growing up, and I ended up melting a hole clean through my favourite toy truck.

Getting grilled by Apollon after the fiasco of a morning I'd just had felt a bit like being under a magnifying glass myself, so…

Yeah. I could relate to that truck now.

Parental concern was scary stuff.

Olympian parental concern was a whole different kind of problem.

On the bright side - pun, forever intended - Chiron was on the job.

He waited just long enough for me to recount the story to Dad - from the trip to Cocytus, to the kidnapping, to the fight with Ezren Vale - and then he stepped in.

The next thing I knew, the two of them were breaking out into rapid-fire Greek, and the strangest part?

I couldn't understand them.

My translation spell was always running in the background, to the point where actualising it was pure, consistent instinct at this point, but it didn't help me any here.

I recognised… some of the dialect, vaguely, but the rest?

It might as well have been Martian.

The tone was easy to place, though.

Dad was furious.

I could feel it, even with every word flat and perfectly level. Like the pressure that builds up in the back of your ears right before they pop.

Which was… comforting, sure. The fact that he cared.

Also intimidating, for entirely obvious reasons.

Or maybe intimidating was the wrong word.

Serious fit better.

Deadly serious.

Either way, Chiron was clearly in the same boat, and just as good with his poker face. The two of them went back and forth for a minute -two tops- before Dad's attention snapped right back to me again.

I straightened up on reflex.

"Hi?"

He didn't say anything, at first.

Just looked at me instead, all pointed and intense, and snapped his fingers in my general direction.

Warmth washed over me from head to toe, bright and fast as a flicker. My busted lip knit together, the bruises littering my face faded, and a jolt of energy ran through me like a double shot of caffeine straight to the veins.

"Woah."

I'd already been healing on my own, and I would've been fine in no time at all, but this made that look like amateur hour.

I felt incredible.

"Better?"

The word came out with all the emotional depth of a cinder block.

"Downright peachy." I patted myself down and grinned. "Thanks, Dad."

He didn't buy it.

"Don't thank me for that, you chaos-prone menace of a child."

"Hey!"

"Are you going to argue the point?"

"…Well, no, but it's still mean."

That got a snort, and the pressure wafting off of him dropped a tad.

Just the one, but it counted.

"'Mean', he says. I should assign you a platoon of Hyperboreans for a personal guard. Even that might not be enough to keep up with you."

"Now you're just doubling down."

Then I blinked.

"Also, Hyperboreans?"

I knew who they were - Chiron had covered them once, way back when, and the library wasn't short on reading material.

The mythical, blessed people who lived 'beyond the north wind,' beloved by Phoebus Apollon.

But in this day and age...

"How would that even work-?"

"I would command it, and so it would be."

"..."

"..."

"... Not what I was asking-" And he absolutely knew it, no way he didn't "-but fair enough."

I could fish for answers later.

"I'm glad we agree."

Yep. Definitely messing with me.

"So?"

He gave me another long, careful look, and the mood shifted again.

"You're unshaken."

Unshake-?

Oh.

"Dad, I'm fine."

It wasn't the first time I'd gotten caught up in a tight spot, and - let's face it - it wouldn't be the last.

At this point, given everything, 'off-the-rails' might as well be my middle name.

Still.

Today hadn't been a walk in the park, but when was it ever?

"Things got hairy for a second, but I handled it - I won."

I always do...

Eventually.

Apollon took that in for another minute, and he didn't blink once.

Honestly, it was a little concerning.

The seconds ticked by.

Then, abruptly, he smiled.

"So you did."

And there it was.

The satisfaction and pride in that one expression took the leftover edge off the room with feeling, and hit me with an entirely different kind of warmth.

"Well done."

Boy, was that something.

"Yeah, well." I shrugged it off as best I could and finally dismissed my armour, shifting it back to its storage space in a flash of gold. "They totally had it coming."

That was about when Chiron cleared his throat and cut in.

"Quite." We both turned back to him. "And now comes the matter of retribution."

Apollon's eyes flashed.

"That was never in question."

It really wasn't.

Not with the slight against Chiron through Lavinia, and then me, and that was before the 'son of Apollon' bit got weighed in.

"When you say 'retribution'-"

He patted me on the shoulder.

Once.

"Let's not spoil the surprise."

Lovely

"For the moment, it's nothing to worry yourself with," Chiron threw in his two cents. "The matter will be settled. Approaching the Grigori for restitution is simple enough, and as for these Utsusemi-"

"All the simpler, given enough time." Apollon finished darkly.

Real positive vibes there, I tell you.

"Ezren said they were new on the supernatural scene."

Which may or may not have been a lie - I wasn't about to trust anything out of the undearly departed nutcase, may he rest in ashes - but my teacher rolled with it anyway.

"The connection to the Five Principal Clans is worth noting."

"If they are outcasts, it is irrelevant," Apollon countered. "The Kami will care little and less for the leavings of their mortal charity cases."

"Kami?" I stared between the two of them. "As in Shinto? The heavenly spirits?"

The primeval gods and divine spirits of Japan, basically, but there was more to it than just that.

Then again, that was true for every pantheon to ever pantheon, so there.

"The very same." Chiron agreed. "We've touched on the Clans before, briefly. What do you remember?"

"The basics?"

Five original families blessed by the powers that be to protect humanity from dangers galore, uphold the virtues of heaven, and all that jazz.

Except I couldn't say that with Dad right there and looking at me, so I cleaned it up a little.

"They're the supernatural overseers of... parts of Japan, right? Running on 'divine mandate?'"

"An interpretation of it, yes, though in reality, that only extends so far. Ancestral and inherited blessings are a given - the very root of their prominence - but direct involvement is rarer in this era, though not unheard of, and their collective favour with the deities they worship waxes and wanes with the centuries."

"And merit," Apollon added lightly. "Exceptional mortals will always draw more attention than the rest."

"Okay." That made sense. "So what does this have to do with the Utsusemi?"

"Optimistically?" Chiron stroked his beard. "Nothing at all. The Agency the Fallen spoke of exists - allegedly - as a gathering that splintered off from the Five Principal Clans sometime in the recent past. A rogue faction, so to speak."

It hit me in half a second.

"So the Kami have no reason to get involved."

"Correct." He nodded approvingly. "The Five Principal Clans have the backing of the Kami, in theory, but effectively stand on their own for the most part. Problems of their own making are not the concern of the gods who empowered them - doubly so when those problems apparently do not wield that vaunted power regardless. Therefore, this Utsusemi Agency is twice removed as a potential diplomatic risk."

"Which means they don't have to clean up the mess unless it gets out of hand," I quickly realized. "But it also means they can't complain if Dad decides to go all biblical on them instead. Not after this stunt."

Putting it together wasn't- Wait.

Pause.

I glanced at Apollon, and damn it, he was already raising a faintly amused brow my way.

"Er, I mean, not 'biblical'-"

"Of course not. I could do far better than that." He waved off my twitch with a faint, growing smirk - or something close enough to pass muster. "And the Kami won't be a problem. Granted, Takamagahara will use any pretext to act if given enough in the way of provocation, but I have no intention of having them interfere as I excise a rot they let grow in their own domain."

Chiron hummed. "Intermediaries, then?"

"For now." Apollon didn't deny it. "I have some ideas. Artemis's hunters are ever convenient, and they're already due for a trip to Japan. A little investigation on the side won't delay them overmuch."

"I see."

I didn't.

"Aunt A's sending hunters to Japan?" They both turned to look at me. "Why?"

Even if they were mortal worshippers - most of them - they technically counted as part of her retinue, and that meant just about everything about them reflected her will.

They had plenty of leeway to do whatever, but also wouldn't make a move without her say-so.

"A little favour I cashed in with my dear sister, but never mind that. You have bigger concerns."

"I do?"

He turned to look me right in the eye, and I felt a sudden ominous sense of doom.

Call it demigod instincts.

"You're grounded."

"..."

"..."

"....Come again?"

Chiron snorted.

"No, seriously, what?"

He waited just long enough for my jaw to drop before his lips quirked up again, and right about then, that was as good as hysterical laughter.

"Kidding." He reached over to ruffle my hair. "To an extent, that is. I'll be readying a response for the Grigori the rest of the miserable pond scum responsible for this-"

The vitriol there was quiet, but still plenty murderous.

"-and I would prefer that you stay somewhere inarguably secure for the next few hours. A day at most."

Which was... not that big deal at all, actually.

The surprise must have shown on my face, because he huffed an amused breath and took a step back.

"Not what you were expecting?"

I started at him funny.

"You want me to stay in the house all day?"

"No particularly." He shook his head. "Stay within the city itself, and that will be enough."

Even better.

Heck, Sairaorg wasn't here, and if Lavinia hadn't shown up, I'd have probably spent the day down at the arcade anyway.

"I'm not complaining, but why?"

"A precaution, nothing more."

But I could tell that wasn't it.

He was damn near radiating I-know-something-you-don't energy.

"Dad?"

"Ask me again when I choose to unground you."

I made a face, and it got one last laugh out of him before he turned back to face Chiron.

"The girl?

"Miss Reni is recovering. Given the circumstances, she remains my guest for the time being."

He didn't argue the point.

"Good. Then I leave it all to you."

"Always a pleasure, Lord Apollon."

Dad nodded once, tipping his head back just enough to catch my eye and wink.

"Stay safe."

Then he was gone - vanishing in a shower of golden sparks before I could get another word in edgewise.

...

"Well." Chiron was the first to break the silence. "That's that, I suppose."

I groaned and dropped right down to the floor.

"I'm done with today."

"Daniel, it's not even noon."

"And that's the problem."

"Hmm. Tea?"

"Uggggh."

…​

I took the tea.

Then I took a hike.

Lavinia wasn't awake yet, and according to Chiron, she wouldn't be for a while.

Fomorian beast venom was nasty like that - a poison ripped straight out of a chaotic sea monster or twenty that made life a nightmare for humanity in Celtic mythology.

Or history, I guess.

Not to be confused with the actual Fomorians, who held their leash and were locked in an arctic cold war with the Tuatha Dé Danann - the Celtic Pantheon - since the death of their Tyrant-King, Balor of the Evil Eye.

And yes, I'm quoting Chiron.

Sue me.

Point is, whatever got Lavinia was watered down to almost nothing, and that was the only reason she wasn't a lot worse off, Longinus or no.

"Any purer, and it would have been quite lethal," Chiron told me on the way out. "Crippling, at best. She'll need at least a day to get back on her feet as it is."

Which was kind of an understatement.

She was practically in a coma - a temporary one, sure, but still - and Sairaorg was still off handling devil business, so I went to the one place left that just felt right.

"Dan?"

Aunt Sarah blinked as soon as the door swung open and saw me standing on their new front porch.

"Hi. Can I come in?"

"Don't be silly."

Spoiler alert: The new Winchester Central was a teensy bit of an upgrade over the original.

The entryway alone was four times bigger than the original. Everything from then on was either polished marble and stone, warm wood, or clear triple-paned glass, and that carried through for all three storeys and the half dozen rooms between them - more, even - including the basement.

And there was the magic.

It was everywhere, surrounding the grounds and the gardens, and centered on the house.

Taking the first step in was like walking straight into warm honey.

Not enough to stop me, or even hurt - I was keyed into the wards before anyone else - but it still dragged, heavy and present in a way I couldn't have missed if I were half-dead and six feet under.

Good.

I wouldn't have had it any other way.

Getting my family moved into this place had been easy as anything. Chiron hadn't even waited for me to finish asking before stepping in, and bam.

Sparkling dream house with a view to die for and enough security to survive a supernatural war breaking out next door.

That centaur never did anything by halves.

I tried to make an argument about paying for everything myself - it was the least I could do, and it wasn't like I couldn't afford it a hundred times over - but he shut that down so fast I barely got three words in.

Cue the three-hour lecture on gift-giving, more home economics, appropriate financial management, and all the creative ways to call me an idiot without actually coming out and saying it.

Very educational.

It also made me die inside, just a little, but that's all relative.

Fast forward a couple of weeks, and here we are.

I snagged a seat at the counter as Aunt Sarah marched us into the kitchen, probably in an effort to avoid destroying whatever it was roasting in the oven.

"Everything alright?"

I shrugged, glancing around the kitchen.

It matched the rest of the house - all marble and stone work and fancy gizmos everywhere - and there were a few pictures magnetized to the fridge.

Katie and Alex, and then Uncle David and me, and a few crayon drawings to round off the set.

"I had some time, and a rough morning. Figured I'd check in… see how things are going."

And hey, if I happened to score some emotional support hugs from the cutest little cousins in the universe, who was gonna complain?

"'Rough morning,' huh?" Her brows furrowed, and she slowly slid into the chair across from me. "You want to tell me what that means?"

"Just the usual."

"Dan."

I hesitated.

"...Think about the life I've got going for me these days, then ask yourself whether or not you actually want me to answer that."

It took her a second to process that.

Then she winced.

"Ah."

Yeah. Thought so.

There was no chance I'd ever tell her, anyway - not everything.

I'd outright killed people today, and even if I was filtering that out through the 'live or die, us or them' part of my demigod lizardbrain, it wasn't the prettiest feeling in the world.

"Are you safe?"

Hah.

"When am I not?"

She gave me a suspicious look, and I smiled innocently.

Eventually, she sighed and let it go.

"Sometimes, I really do miss being able to send you to your room."

My smile turned smug, and she didn't miss it.

"Daniel Winchester, you wipe that look off your face or so help me-"

"Okay, okay, I give. Full surrender." I raised my hands and snorted. "Jeez, Aunt Sarah."

"Better."

She shook her head, muttering something under her breath, but the corner of her mouth twitched.

"Any other questions?"

"Would I get a straight answer if I asked?"

"I'll give you four in ten odds, and that's as high as it goes."

"You cheeky punk."

"It's part of my charm."

That got me a huffy ear pull before she got up to fiddle with the oven again.

"So… where's Uncle David?"

The girls were here - I could sense as much, out in the back yard - but him?

Nada.

"Job interview."

I...

Huh.

"Already?"

I knew that moving from one world to another wasn't as easy as just popping up - especially not if you stuck to the mortal end of things more than the supernatural.

Chiron had helped with all the finicky paperwork and the little details in between, but I'd thought they'd need a little more time to hit the ground running.

Apparently not.

"You know your uncle. Work gives him a schedule, and a schedule gives him peace of mind."

Fair.

She opened the fridge, grabbed a bottle of OJ, and poured us each a glass before settling back in the chair across from me. The orange scent hit my nose, bright and sharp against the faint smell of cinnamon in the air.

Just like home.

"Thanks."

"Mm." She took a sip. "We've started looking into schools for the girls, and I'm trying to sniff out a good teaching job on the side. Fingers crossed it all lines up and makes life a bit easier."

"So you've got everything figured out?"

"Oh, God no." She laughed like it was the best joke she'd heard all week. "But we're chugging along, and the sooner we get the ball rolling, the sooner things start to feel… normal."

"...Right."

Normal.

Of course.

Hard to blame them for missing it, after being uprooted from everything they'd ever known.

Because of me.

Aunt Sarah's eyes narrowed.

"What was that?"

"What?"

"That look, right now."

"What look?"

"..."

"..."

"...Dan, you don't feel- ugh, what am I saying, of course you do."

She closed her eyes and pinched the bridge of her nose.

Then she looked up at me.

"You shouldn't be feeling guilty about all of this."

"I'm not!"

"..."

"..."

".... Okay, maybe just a little," I admitted. "But it's only fair. This is happening because of me."

I wasn't going to wallow in it, because they were safe and things would get better than they ever were - I'd make sure of it - but all the danger had also kicked off because of me, no two ways about it.

That still weighed on me sometimes, and probably more than it should.

"That's..." She sighed again. "You sweet boy. Drink your juice."

I quirked a brow.

"Go on. It's getting warm."

She waited until I took a sip before speaking again.

"I'm going to tell you a story. One I've already shared with your teacher."

"Chiron?"

She rolled her eyes.

"No, Katie's old karate instructor."

"And they say I don't come by my snark fairly."

"Listen."

She was serious, this time.

"I once took a peek through the Mist, back home."

My eyes widened, and I sat up straighter.

"You did what?"

She was mortal.

"It's a long story, and a one-time thing I only managed because your uncle and... your mother-" I didn't react, but it was a close thing. "-did the heavy lifting for me."

I opened my mouth, then closed it again.

"Some kind of spell?"

A ritual, maybe?

"No idea." She shrugged helplessly. "There was this awful drink, and... I couldn't tell you the rest even if I wanted to, and back then, after seeing first-hand that my husband wasn't off his rocker - and neither was his sister - I wanted nothing to do with any of it."

"But you didn't have a choice."

"But I didn't have a choice." She agreed. "Once the genie's out of the bottle, there's no stuffing it back in. I spent weeks jumping at every shadow, terrified of things I'd never even be able to see coming, and trying to keep from losing my mind until I finally simmered down enough to roll with the punches."

...

Well.

I took a deep breath.

"Aunt Sarah…"

She waved me off.

"I'm not telling you this to get it off my chest." She leaned forward, eyes serious, making sure I got it. "I'm telling you because I want you to really listen. And believe me when I say this…"

She gestured around the kitchen, the house, everything.

"The new house, the new everything?"

I waited, and she smiled.

A real, genuine smile.

"It's good, Daniel. More than good. It's a huge adjustment, don't get me wrong, but better than anything your uncle and I could have hoped for."

I perked up.

Couldn't help it, really.

"Yeah?"

"Are you kidding?" She laughed again. "The protections, and Chiron… having people we can actually talk to about this stuff, especially with the girls growing up… no more damned Mist leaving me blind when danger comes calling. Even your Uncle is over the moon. It's why he's so excited to get back to work - He wants to go native, and I'm right there with him."

"And the girls?"

"Please. They miss some of their friends and a few of their favourite things, but they love it here already."

She reached over and patted my hand gently.

"Stop worrying. It's all a bit hectic for now, and there are a few bumps on the road ahead, but we're going to be just fine."

...

Coming here was the right choice.

"I'll take your word for it."

I couldn't keep the smile off my face, and she matched it tit for tat.

"Good. Are you staying for lunch?"

"I-"

"Nope. Rhetorical question. You're absolutely staying for lunch."

"I was going to say yes."

I had the time to spare.

"Atta boy." She nodded approvingly. "Now go see your cousins, and tell them to get in before they catch heatstroke or god knows what else."

I was already off my stool and halfway out the kitchen.

"Roger that."

I jogged out the back door and into the yard. The sunlight hit just right, bouncing off the manicured green lawn and the glassy surface of the pool, and the grounds were expansive enough that I had to turn a corner before I saw the girls.

Thunk!

They were duking it out with pool noodles they must have grabbed when Aunt Sarah wasn't looking, swinging them around with all the intensity of a duel to the death.

Accuracy was a pipe dream, though, but they had the spirit.

"Hya!"

"No, you hya!"

"That doesn't make sense!"

"I know!"

...This cuteness is bad for my heart.

"Room for one more?"

They froze midswing.

Or Katie did, at least, and Alex took the chance to whack her in the face one last time.

Crack.

"Hey!"

I nearly fried a blood vessel trying not to cackle.

Then they were on me - Alex first, ducking behind me to avoid Katie's justified vengeance.

"Danny!"

I grinned and hefted her up into my arms before reaching over to boop Katie on the nose.

"Miss me?"

"Mm!" She wrapped her arms around my neck, and I pretended not to see her stick her tongue out at her scowling sister. "I win."

"I'm going to get you later." She warned her, before turning back to me and smiling toothily. "Γειά σου!"

"Γειά." I greeted her right back. "You're picking up your basic Greek pretty quickly, huh?"

That pronunciation had been near perfect.

"It's easy!" Then she put her hands on her hips. "Did you bring Courage?"

Alex perked up.

"Can we play fetch?"

Yeah, they loved the little guy.

Met him a while back and he'd been all the rage with them ever since.

Of course, the first time it happened, I forgot to tell Uncle David that my dog was coming out for a visit, so when he came into the backyard and saw a crimson-eyed hellhound barreling after the girls with its jaws wide open…

It wasn't pretty.

Lots of screaming, and at least one swing of a celestial bronze sword was involved.

Totally my bad - but moving on now:

Go on.

I nudged my shadow with a little flick of power, and a part of it broke off, slipping under Katie's feet and pooling behind her own.

"Well, actually, Courage had a little message for you guys he wanted me to pass on."

"A message?" Alex tilted her head as I crouched until I was eye to eye with Katie.

"No he didn't." Katie crossed her arms, but she leaned in anyway. "But what is it anyway?"

Smart.

"He says..."

They leaned forward eagerly, and I smirked.

"...That you two are absolutely amazing at sword fighting."

They both beamed, and I nudged the shadow again.

Now.

"And to turn around."

The darkness behind Katie welled up all at once, taking shape before they ever saw it happen, and-

"Aarf!"

- Hold up.

Courage materialised the way he always did, and the girls squealed in delight as they whirled around. Aleck squirmed out of my grip so hard she nearly used my face as a launching pad, but I didn't even feel it.

Instead, I watched Katie hurl her arms around my dog, and...

Something wasn't quite right.

"Did you get bigger?"

No, that wasn't all of it.

He stood almost a foot taller than before, his fur darker, and his eyes were a deeper shade of red.

When he barked and let his tongue loll out, even the flash of his canines looked that much sharper.

How?

He'd had growth spurts before, but that couldn't be that - I'd seen him just this morning.

Some kind of side effect from the visit to the Underworld?

It was, technically, his natural habitat.

Or maybe Kerberos-

"He feels weird."

My eyes snapped down to Alex.

"What?"

She was staring at Courage, eyes narrowed as her hand pressed against his snout and stayed there. Her lip curled in... concentration?

"Feels weird," she repeated.

"He's fluffy?" Katie was already scratching behind his ears, looking down at her in confusion.

"Yes. No." Alex shook her head and patted his snout again, more insistent this time. "Feel!"

"I am-!"

Katie cut herself off.

Alarm bells started winding up in my head.

"Katie?" I asked carefully, glancing at Courage. He looked just as lost, even as he soaked up the attention. "What is it?"

"Dunno."

She'd stopped scratching him, but her hand kept moving through his fur, slow and absent, like she'd forgotten what she was doing.

Both of them had.

"Gonna need a little more than that, kiddo."

She frowned, thinking hard.

"He feels funny," she said finally, and Alex nodded her little head like it was the most important thing in the world. "Like… like… the old TV at Daddy's garage!"

"That old staticky thing?"

"Yeah!" She frowned, then shrugged and went back to petting him. "Maybe."

Maybe.

They were picking up on his… otherness. They had to be.

They shouldn't be - except…

Great-grandchildren of Hecate.

Just like me, on one side of the family tree.

Even Uncle David could use magic.

Small, shaky little gimmicks with the Mist, but still something.

The girls-

No.

The house.

I glanced around, tracing the invisible line where the wards wrapped the place up tight and turned it into a fortress.

Proximity to ongoing or strong mystical phenomena could increase your sensitivity to the stuff - that was magic 101.

And they'd been living here for weeks.

...

Noticing magic was the first step to using it, and their inheritance being what it is...

...

I took a deep breath.

Okay then.

I needed to talk to Chiron.

Aunt Sarah and Uncle David too.

While I was figuring out how that conversation would go, Courage finally had enough of all the stillness.

"Aarf!"

He lunged at Katie with no warning and gave her a quick, wet lick right on the cheek.

"Ah!" she yelped, staggering back, giggling like a loon.

Alex froze when it was her turn, stunned, before letting out a peal of laughter when my dog nearly bowled her right over.

Then he took off, barking up the storm, with both of them hot on his paws.

It left me snickering, even with everything going on in my head.

Fine.

I could wait until after lunch, at least.

Aunt Sarah had said it herself - the genie was already out of the bottle.

What's a few more hours?

...​

A Few Hours Later:

Daniel.

I blinked awake in a split second.

Zero to a hundred in no time flat.

"Dad?"

I'd settled down with Katie to watch a movie - Alex had gone off for a nap - and before I knew it, I'd dozed off right there on the couch.

Then Apollon's voice echoed in my head, and I was up like a light.

Return to Chiron's estate, if you please. Be quick about it.

It wasn't the first time we'd talked like this, and he wasn't so much talking as he was broadcasting the words into my mind, but I was used to it now.

The fact that he was calling me back so soon...

Something's up.

"I'll be right there."

I slid off the couch carefully, trying not to jostle Katie. She shifted in her sleep as I went, blanket twisting around here, and I pulled it back into place and smoothed her hair back while I had the chance.

"Sweet dreams, K."

Then I took off.

It took me all of a second to make it out the door, and then I was gone, teleporting back to Chiron's in a wave of gold.

True to form, Dad was waiting for me when I got there.

But he wasn't alone, and the company wasn't Chiron, either.

They were sitting on the lawn just past the edge of the woods, the setting sun throwing everything in red and orange. A small fire burned between them, rounded off with rough stones in a perfect circle—like something right out of a flashy camping manual—and sweet, pine-heavy smoke drifting up into the warm air.

It was all very scenic. Ten out of ten on the presentation.

"Son. Join us."

Dad didn't need an introduction, but the person sitting across from him was…

They didn't look like anything special.

They didn't look like anything at all, actually, what with the warm brown cloak and the hood over their face that somehow covered everything, even when I looked right at them.

But the power wafting off them…

Enormus.

Endless.

Not dangerous, or even threatening, but one hundred and ten percent out of my league, and then some.

Like meeting Dad for the first time all over again - only not as exestentially terrifying.

Not even close.

"There's no need to worry."

I started when the words came at me.

"I mean you no harm, child."

Strangely enough, I almost believed that.

Their voice came out low and soft, completely edgeless, and something about it made me just a little less wary.

Like I'd have been tempted to disarm and join them - her? - by the fire, even if Dad wasn't right there and patiently nodding at me to hurry it up.

Let's play this out, then.

I stepped over and dropped down onto the log next to Dad, and the cloaked woman seemed pleased enough, even though I hadn't said a word yet.

Before I could, she'd already moved.

Her hand rose up, all pale and slender, and she rolled her wrist right over the fire.

A pot blinked into existence above the flame, looking like it'd been around since the Bronze Age - red, rough, and almost a little ugly for it.

Then the smell hit me like a truck.

Holy Artemis.

Spices and meat, and something rich and smoky...

I'd eaten at lunch, but whatever was bubbling under that lid smelled amazing.

"It is said-" The woman started speaking softly, arms crossed over her lap as she waited. "-That when Phoebus Apollon first ascended to Olympus, he graced the home of the Gods with a new and magnificent heavenly radiance. The wind spirits carried the song of his arrival far and wide, and he marched in with his bow in hand, and the skull of the dread Python dragging behind him to showcase his might and prowess for all to see."

There was a pause, and I glanced at Dad out the corner of my eye.

His lips were pursed, but he didn't seem upset.

More... exasperating than anything else.

"That story is true." She continued, and this time, she sounded almost amused. "With a twist."

"And so it begins," Dad murmured tiredly, and so quickly I would have missed out if I wasn't hyper-aware of everything surrounding me right then.

"You see, though Apollon would go on to make a proper introduction to the then-incomplete Council of Twelve and all the gods who called Olympus home, the first time he arrived.... well, he chose a rather poor time to do so."

"Poor?"

It was the first time I'd said a word since I'd shown up, and neither of them seemed to mind the interruption.

If anything, she seemed pleased.

"Unfortunate might be a better word for it. The other gods were otherwise occupied. Poseidon was settling a dispute in his kingdom beneath the waves. Demeter was lounging in the mortal world with Persephone. Ares was overseeing a mortal war, and Athena was keeping to herself. Zeus and Hera, of course, were elsewhere, raging over one squabble or another, and the force of their fury had most of the other gods and nature spirits fleeing Olympus just to be safe."

"Smart." Apollon threw in, and I could almost feel her smile under that hood.

"You didn't think so at the time. You came hoping for a grand and brilliant welcome-"

"And I received no such thing." He huffed tiredly. "The mountain was nearly deserted, save a few terrified nymphs and a handful of lesser daimones. Must we retread this story?"

She laughed.

It was high and cheery, but there was nothing mean-spirited about it.

"Forgive me. It's a fond memory, is all." She sounded wistful. "You were so very young then, and quite mortified. I invited you to join me by the hearth, and for that first little while, you wouldn't even look me in the eye."

"Yes, well." Apollon sighed and gave me a look. "It was very awkward."

I don't know why that made me want to laugh, but I had enough self-preservation to reign it in.

It wasn't easy.

"Awkward, perhaps. But it wasn't long before you were regaling me with the stories of your adventures, and all the glory in between. We shared a meal, just like this one, and for me, that was introduction enough. It was wonderful."

Dad... didn't deny it, which said plenty all on its own.

Then she looked at me, and my breath caught.

"There is no great moral to this story - just nostalgia, and all the peace it brings."

I could see under the hood now, even as she went to lower it.

Her hair was dark brown, falling in waves over her shoulders, and her face was soft and kind. She had one brown eye, deep and warm, but the other was milky and clouded over.

Blind.

The scars were worse - deep and streaking, trailing across the side of her face and down her neck in patterns like sickly, reaching tree branches.

Lichtenberg figures - the kind you get from surviving lightning strikes.

That's it.

I looked at Dad, and he nodded. Once.

Then I looked back at her.

I know who this is.

And I could tell she knew too, because she smiled all over again, and the scars did nothing to take away from it.

"Once upon a time, it was I who was the first to welcome your father into the family."

She let it hang just enough to make a point.

"It seemed only fitting, then, that I do the same for his son."

...

...

...

Man, this day.

But when in doubt-

I swallowed down the nerves and tried for a grin.

"Thank you, Lady Hestia."

"Aunt Hestia, if you must."

The eldest and most beloved Olympian corrected gently, and then patted the pot at her side, flames and all.

"Now, shall we eat?"

...
