#10,991
Daniel Winchester's motto in life:

"Due to incredibly foreseen circumstances well within my control, I will once again be taking reckless actions within the next three-to-five business days."

jump-jump-out.gif

Hestia had always appreciated the quiet moments.

Not the grand feasts of Olympus, nor the clamor of gods arguing over pride and power, or even the respectful bustle of temples and bonfires filled with mortal prayers.

They all had their place… to an extent.

It wasn't quiet for quiet's sake, either.

It had its value in moderation, as many things did, but she was never one for numbing silence, and she abhorred emptiness.

Her father and his primeval cruelty had seen to that.

Stillness without rest. A hateful darkness without end. A place where nothing moved - where nothing could.

Certainly not the nascent gods they were, helpless and insignificant until the day of salvation came, and the war of reckoning finally began.

The memories would not leave her.

Hestia was the oldest, the one who had endured the longest, and she remembered it all.

She always would.

Even so, the past did not rule her.

The Titanomachy had come and gone, and the reign of the Titans was long ended. With the dawn of their era, the children of Kronos had each striven, in their own way, to cast off his ugly shadow.

Hestia was no different.

Hearth. Fire. Family.

Hence, the quiet moments - like this one.
 
The fire crackled between them, steady and warm.

The pot steamed over the flame, and the stew within had turned out well, if she did say so herself.

Kokkinisto.

Braised beef, slow-cooked and simmering in a spiced red broth.

A touch on the simple side, perhaps, but the smell was - and pardon the pun here - positively divine.

And then there came the company.

Apollon was as he ever was these days, radiant and tempered with age, his light no less brilliant for how tightly he leashed it.

Her lips curved up.

Goodness, how far he'd grown.

Though, admittedly, a good bit of his present restraint had to do with the child sitting to his right.

Daniel Winchester.

Hestia spared her newest grand-nephew a glance as she lifted the pot and began to pour, steady and unhurried, filling each of them a bowl.

Learning of the demigod's existence had been… a surprise, to say the least.

Well out of left field at that.

After the incident - for lack of a more fitting word - all those centuries ago, Apollon had been in no rush to sire another, and who could blame him for it?

Most of the family had been much the same.

Gutted - ravaged, even, in that especially vile way they could only inflict upon themselves.

It had taken decades to reestablish a measure of civility, and a dozen more for even the vague illusion of cordiality to take root.

Hestia's state at the time hadn't helped any, though she would claim no responsibility there.

Despite accusations to the contrary, she wasn't quite so much of a doormat as to apologise for being wounded - and she had been.

Horrifically so.

The scars and the physical marring were only half the story, if even that.

Still, once again, it was no great wonder that another Olympian Demigod had not been born in so long.

Once bitten, twice shy, and when one was bitten a hundred times - a thousand, over just as many years...

Well.

Enough was enough, at least for a time.

And now...

Here this boy was.

Hestia's smile didn't waver as she handed him his bowl, and he accepted it gingerly.

"Thank you?"

"You are most welcome."

He was wary of her, she could tell.

Not threatened, per se - that would be wholly unacceptable - but not entirely at ease, either.

Fair enough.

Her power was a vast presence, even when calm and restrained, and the touch of it he could sense was likely more than a little intimidating.

Patience here was no chore.

She passed Apollon his bowl, and he took it with a level nod.

"Thank you, aunt."

"Of course."

Then she looked back at the boy, and pretended not to notice the faint stiffening of his shoulders.

"And now for your companion."

Daniel blinked, caught mid-spoonful. "My-?"

Her eyes dropped toward the shadow clinging to his feet, shifting and stretching against the glow of the flames. To mortal eyes, it would have seemed almost entirely normal - just a dim smear of darkness - but Hestia knew better.

"Won't you come out, little one?" she asked softly, keeping the words low and gentle. "It would be quite discourteous for us to sit down for a meal and not invite everyone present."

The shadow stilled, and for a moment, nothing happened.

Then, as the hesitation passed, it slowly unfurled, spreading and deepening until it grew three sizes larger. A pair of crimson eyes blinked open in those depths, and the creature they belonged to silently crept out into the firelight.

"There you are."

The hellhound was a handsome thing, with sleek black fur and a healthy size for one so obviously young.

An interesting breed as well - she could sense Kerberos's lingering touch on it, and a flicker of something fainter and altogether stranger underneath, but the oddity was not overpowering

Curious.

"And who might you be?"

The hellhound, predictably, had nothing to say.

He only stood there at first, still and quiet, and a part of him clearly wanted nothing more than to melt back into the darkness and wait for her to disappear.

The rest of him was tentatively curious - smart enough to register the lack of ill will - and she didn't miss how the pup had angled himself just enough to keep Apollon's child behind him.

Brave and loyal, then.

Hestia greatly approved.

"His name is Courage," Daniel offered. "Pretty straightforward, I know-"

"Not at all."

She reached out and scratched lightly beneath his chin. Courage froze for half a beat, then a low, pleased rumble worked its way out of his chest. Her other hand ran through his fur, and his hackles fell that much more.

"It suits him very well, doesn't it?"

By the time she was done, the fur along his spine had settled, and his tail was wagging like it had a mind of its own.

"Better?"

"Aarf!"

"Excellent."

She pulled back, snapping her fingers with a faint flourish, and a giant tray of roasted meat appeared at the hound's paws. Courage's eyes immediately lit up, a happy bark escaping him, and his tail wagged twice as fast.

"Aarf!"

Daniel blinked, surprised, and Hestia arched a brow at him.

"I can hardly offer him the stew, can I?"

Mind you, she could - harmlessly - but that was beside the point.

Courage looked back at his master, practically bouncing in place with anticipation, and Daniel swallowed back a snort.

"Why are you pretending to be polite all of a sudden? Sic 'em."

That was all the encouragement he needed, and he was on the tray in a flash of fangs, snagging a juicy rib and crunching down happily. His tail thumped against the grass and dirt like a drum, and Daniel laughed.

Even Apollon seemed amused.

"Look at him go."

"He's always been a foodie." Daniel shrugged before following his own advice and finally taking a proper spoonful of his stew.

Then he stopped.

"Oh my god."

Apollon smirked.

"Goddess."

"Technically." Hestia agreed.

"This is amazing."

"I'm glad you think so." She winked. "It's all in the spice."

They dug in after that, though none of them were quite so voracious as Courage.

The excitement was flattering, really.

"However did you meet him?

Daniel paused and grimaced, like he'd remembered something unpleasant. He set the bowl down, shrugging again as if to shake off the memory.

"Ah. I've made you uncomfortable-"

"No, no." He hastily shook his head, "It just happened a while back, and I wasn't at my best when it did, that's all."

Hestia let him take his time.

What was the rush?

"I ran into some trouble with a few monsters," he finally admitted, "Back before I met Chiron. The real nasty kind, too. Courage was with them, but he stuck around with me when it was all wrapped up."

"I see."

She didn't.

That was hardly a story, but it had clearly been no happy encounter, and Apollon had stilled off to the side with the kind of silence that historically spelled nothing good, so she let the matter slide.

"Then he has good taste to go with that fitting name." She nodded to Apollon. "Though the affinity you inherited from your father likely helped."

That seemed to stump him.

"The what?"

Apollon tapped his temple when the boy rounded on him.

"Think about it for a moment."

To his credit, it only took a second for it to dawn on him.

"Oh." His eyes widened. "Apollon Lykaios."

His father nodded approvingly.

"Go on."

"'The Protector Wolf-God of Arcadia.'" Daniel's brows furrowed. "But that epithet translates to... like, ten different roles."

"More or less."

"So... an authority over dogs of all types, because of the conceptual line of descent from wolves to tamed canines?"

Hestia raised a brow.

He was well learned, but that was only to be expected. Chiron's standards had always been exacting, and her wise brother would settle for nothing less.

"Not entirely accurate, but you're thinking along the right lines."

She stepped in before they could spiral too far down the thought.

"In your case, affinity is the simpler word for it," she said. "A natural ease. Creatures like him" - she tipped her head towards Courage - " and those that share a similar 'archetype' recognize it, and thus are affected to one extent or another."

"It doesn't make them tame." Apollon added. "Not passively. At best, it gets your foot in the door, and nothing more."

Daniel glanced at his hound, who was still working through the tray with single-minded focus.

"...Right. So that's why he never tried to eat me."

Courage looked up from the tray, ears flicking, and gave him a look that was downright offended.

"Kidding, bud. I know you love me."

"He does." Hestia agreed. "Very clearly so."

The hellhound huffed, somewhat mollified, and padded over to nose at Daniel's side.

He earned a snort for his efforts.

"Yeah, yeah. I hear ya. Won't happen again."

Which was evidently the right thing to say, because Courage lingered just long enough to stand on the point, before turning back to his tray with renewed purpose.

"See?" Daniel looked to Apollon. "What'd I tell you? Total foodie."

"He's a growing beast, son. Let him have his proteins."

"If you say so."

"I do say so. In fact, I'm quite good at 'saying so'. It is one of my many impressive qualities."

"According to who?"

"Myself, of course. I need no other validation."

"... Dad."

"Do you have something to say, Daniel?"

"Nope." He mimed zipping his lips. "Not a word."

"Smart boy."

The bickering was heartwarming.

Truly it was - Apollon rarely made for morose company, but there was a certain joy to him now that had been blunted, and dearly missed.

The return to form made for an infinitely more satisfying sight.

Then Apollon's gaze lifted, and he met Hestia's eyes across the fire.

The air changed, and a small, nearly imperceptible nod passed between them.

Daniel almost missed it, but by the time he went to open his mouth, Apollon was already rising and brushing nonexistent dust off his trousers.

"A moment, please," he said, as if remembering something mid-thought. He reached out, ruffling his son's hair in passing. "I've got a bit of business to attend to. I shouldn't be long."

"But-"

Too late.

Apollon was already gone.

The space he'd occupied folded in on itself in a flicker of light, and then there were only two of them left by the fire.

Daniel's eye twitched.

"...He has got to stop doing that."

"It's a habit," Hestia said lightly, waving a hand to make the leftover bowls vanish as if they'd never been there. "The flair for the dramatic runs in the family."

He was off to speak to Chiron, no doubt. The better to plan out their response to this day's debacle - and yes, she was well aware of what had happened.

It was why Apollon had seen fit to hasten his son's "official" introduction to Olympus, through her, and she had no complaints.

It had been bound to happen eventually, and this pretext was as good as any to start with.

"So what now?"

"Ideally, I get to know you better."

"Sure." He said automatically, before hesitating - more out of consideration than any real nerves. "Am I answering something, or just talking?"

"Both. Neither. Whichever suits your whim."

She had her questions - plenty of them, and then some - but Hestia was hardly going to interrogate the child.

Not without good reason.

"Though I should tell you that I've already heard quite a few stories."

His eyes narrowed suspiciously.

"Stories?"

"Devils, dragons, murderous witches, Nemean lions, and Longinus Sacred Gears in between."

"..."

"..."

"..."

"...Alright then." He sighed, before rubbing the back of his neck sheepishly. "Those stories."

"I've only heard the highlights, but enough." Her smile didn't fade. "I must say, our pantheon's demigods have always led very sensational lives, and you're off to a stellar start there."

Positively stratospheric, given his age.

He raised a finger, mouth opening... before it closed again wordlessly.

"You know, in hindsight, hearing that from an Olympian is concerning on so many different levels."

Then he looked at her and winced.

"No offence."

That had her laughing outright.

He wasn't wrong.

"None taken - and I did say stellar, not tragic."

There'd been enough of the latter to last unto the end of time, no matter how romanticized the old stories tried to make it.

Heracles alone had been a case study in protracted misery - and that was without her sister's influence, vengeful and cruel as it had been.

Mythical fame was a poor consolation prize at best.

"Your father and Aunt have also told me other things as well." She shifted gears. Daniel perked up as she continued. "That you are clever, quick-witted, and most certainly kind. You are still young, and yet you have already made your father and Aunt quite proud indeed."

It was the honest truth, and the words made him flush - par for the course.

What distinctly wasn't, though, was the flicker of something else beneath the embarrassment.

Just a flash, there and quickly gone, but she caught it regardless.

Guilt.

How... troubling.

Hestia did not know this child nearly enough to cast judgment, but from what Artemis had carefully implied...

Her lips pursed.

"Let me ask this, Daniel Winchester."

He straightened, picking up on the shift in her tone.

Sharp.

"Yes?"

"What is your greatest ambition?"

That, she could tell, was not at all what he'd been expecting.

"Come again?"

"You heard me."

She smoothed the ruffles in her cloak and looked up expectantly.

"You have done and come quite far in relatively little time at all. Why? What is your motivation?"

What drives you so, little child of light?

"That's-" He cut himself off, leaning back and running a hand through his hair. "Huh. Okay. Nobody's asked me something like that since Chiron. Way back when."

A pause.

"I don't have one." He winced at his own answer, then rushed on. "Not some huge, world-changing dream or anything."

"No?"

"Not really." He admitted. "I started training because I needed to, and it only made sense. I mean, passing up on being a student of Chiron? Come on - I'm not crazy."

She snorted, and the act almost earned her a grin.

"It's been wild ever since. Way off the rails, twenty-four-seven, but also a total blast, you know? The stuff I can do now is nuts, and the magic... heck, I even came out of it with a best friend."

The devil, her mind whispered, Sairaorg Bael.

Artemis had mentioned that little development as well.

"But?"

"But… there's no finish line, if that makes sense? I mean, I'm always getting better - and not stopping anytime soon - but I'm not doing it for any special reason." He tossed his hands up lightly. "Not that kind of Greek hero, I guess. I'm just doing what feels right and rolling with the rest."

"..."

Hestia didn't answer right away.

The fire waxed and waned as she turned the words over, and Daniel clearly didn't know what to do with the silence.

If he weren't so drilled - Chiron's doing again, obviously - he probably would've started fidgeting.

She could see him suppress the urge before clearing his throat.

"I get that's not the most impressive-"

"Impressive has nothing to do with it." She cut that off before it could start. "There is no correct answer to that question."

Sincerity was the only metric that counted, and for all that he'd struggled to put it into words - and in a way, still hadn't - he'd passed with flying colours where Hestia was concerned.

"In truth, I'm rather glad."

"Glad?"

"Oh yes. There is no rule so great as to decide the scope of a child's dreams."

Nor would Hestia wish to hear one that did.

Drive and ambition were all well and good, but zealously following one or the other was ever and always the ruin of gods and mortals alike.

Theirs especially.

"Many are far too quick to mistake contentment for complacency." A foolish mistake. "You do not lack for talent, or will. So long as you do not lose your way, taking life at your own pace is no failing."

She folded her hands in front of her and nodded reassuringly.

"If anything, it is quite enviable."

Daniel took that in slowly.

"Then why ask-?"

"Why else? Curiosity."

It wasn't any sort of test, if that was what he thought. Nothing so contrived, but it was telling, and in a refreshingly promising manner.

As far as first impressions went, her grand-nephew's was a breath of fresh air.

"Though there is one more thing to address."

Daniel looked up.

"Your origins."

He stilled.

There it is.

Hestia wasn't a fool.

Between his abrupt appearance, Artemis's none too subtle insinuations, and that flash of guilt just now...

There was a mystery afoot, and its name was Winchester - but she wasn't here to solve it.

"Peace, child."

He barely seemed to hear her, and the intensity of his sudden gaze didn't waver.

Frankly, he had a terrible poker face.

Even Courage had looked up again, turning his head from him to her and back again.

Hestia sighed.

With a small motion of her hand, two wooden cups appeared between them, filled with a blend of nectar and squeezed fruit. One was rich and golden, and the other softened, diluted until it was safe enough to pass muster.

That was the one she picked and held out to him.

"Drink."

"..."

"Drink." She repeated firmly. "And for mother's sake, breathe. There's no need to brace yourself like you're awaiting judgment."

That seemed to get through to him, somewhat.

He took a cautious sip - startled - and then another, shoulders easing a tad as the warmth settled in.

"Good, isn't it?"

It was no Dionysian elixir, but it was pleasant in its own right.

"…Yeah."

"Wonderful. Then we can move on." She took her own sip and put the drink aside. "I won't insult your intelligence - or my own - by pretending I don't notice that something about your origins is… unusual."

He tensed, the silly boy.

"However," Hestia stressed the word. "You understand that it changes nothing, yes? Unusual is entirely relative."

Even that was a laughable understatement.

There was no norm for the birth of children under their Heavens.

Some were shaped from clay and given life. Others were born of gods alone, carved out of natural phenomena as daimons or nature spirits, or claimed long after their first breath, and no less valid for it.

And those were just the simple cases.

Humanity itself had been wiped away and remade anew when the old world ran its course - mostly - and that hadn't been a one-off, either.

What was one demigod's touch of strangeness in the face of all that?

"Apollon has claimed you for all to see, your divinity is his and yours both, and you are part of this family."

Artemis's blessing was also plain and present, but there was no further need to bring up the obvious.

"You are indubitably your father's son, and that is all there is to it." She declared with finality. "Anything beyond that is context and nothing more."

...

Daniel stayed still for a long beat, letting the words sink in.

Then, slowly, he took another drink, and a deep breath after it.

"I am going to tell him, you know."

The admission was quiet, but it rang with truth.

"Not right this second, maybe, but I will."

So did that. Pity that it was unneeded.

"You could hold your silence forever, and he wouldn't love you any less for it."

He jerked in place like he'd been struck.

Then, almost abruptly, he started laughing.

Half-breathless and faint, certainly, but the relief there was a good sign.

"That's pretty direct, Aunt Hestia."

"And all the better for it."

A great many of her family's troubles could have been mitigated or averted outright if they had simply spoken plainly when it mattered.

Some more so than others.

Her fingers rose absently, brushing along the scars across her cheek.

Daniel didn't miss the motion.

He'd made a solid effort not to stare at her disfigured side or the pale, blind eye, but the occasional glances were only natural.

"You may ask, if you wish."

"I... uh, already know." His thumb traced the rim of his cup. "Dad told me."

Hestia tilted her head consideringly.

"Did he now?"

She doubted he'd gone to any great detail. That day had been poison through and through.

"And do you have any questions of your own?"

"Not really." But he shifted all the same. "I don't want to be rude or anything, but those can't heal?"

"Not to any great extent, I'm afraid."

Wounds inflicted by one deity on another were never mere marks on flesh and bone, and she told him as much.

"This will sound irritatingly poetic, I'm aware, but such things have... a weight and depth to them that can imprint lasting harm."

Damage.

Gods can be wounded - they could be killed - and there was plenty of room for pain in between.

"Often the injury itself matters less than the cause."

Or the one who caused it, she didn't mention that part aloud.

Daniel was frowning heavily as it was.

"That's not fair. I'm sorry."

How sweet.

"No, it isn't." She agreed, before tipping her head back with an exhale and closing her eyes. "But I do not lament for it. I made a choice to prevent my family from tearing itself asunder, and this was the price paid. No more and no less."

Hestia did not relish her current state, nor was she happy to accept the role of the martyr - it should never have been needed at all - but she was grateful it had spared them all something far worse.

That was enough.

And perhaps, with a little luck, this child's arrival would mark the turning of a new era.

The thought was a pleasant one, and it would be remarkably fitting if nothing else.

She basked in it for a moment.

Then she opened her eyes - eye, really - and her gaze met something unexpectedly fiery.

Daniel's frown was tight, his jaw was set harder than ever.

Hm?

His foot tapped against the dirt once, twice, three times... and then he was up on his feet so quickly even Courage gave a startled bark.

"Forget that."

"Excuse me?"

The demigod didn't answer her.

The shape of him simmered with a faint outline of golden light, matched only by the stars above Chiron's estate.

"You wanted to get to know me, right?" He nodded at his own question. "Fine. Here's the cliff notes version: I'm Dan. I like spearmanship and magic and duking it out with my best friend whenever we feel like a spar. Spoiler alert: That's pretty much always."

Hestia's mouth parted in surprise, but he wasn't quite finished yet.

"I don't like waiting around, murderous cyclopes, and people who can't take a joke. A couple of other things too, like tragic endings, but let's not nitpick."

"Nit-?"

"But the most important thing you should probably know?"

He gave her a half-grin that was all Apollon.

"I have zero impulse control. Like, none at all, outside of the occasional blue moon. It's a problem, and a work in progress." The confession was utterly shameless. "But it also helps me keep moving and get things done, so everything balances out for now."

"Aarf!"

"Not a word, Cujo!"

Daniel didn't so much as look at him.

His focus was entirely on her.

"I'm telling you this because that story is just awful. All around professional-grade bummer-"

Pardon her?

"-And I've decided to try and do something about it."

Hestia blinked incredulously, caught somewhere between his choice of words and their meaning.

"'Do something about it?'"

His grin went full-blown.

"Taking that as a yes!"

"I-"

And then the words were robbed from her entirely as he held out his arms, and something gold and shining and truly a little ridiculous materialized in his hold.

A large tangle of gleaming wool, soft and pulsing with power, and shining gold down to the last brilliant fiber.

A divine artifact.

That much she recognised immediately, though the object itself she had no name for.

Not much in the way of power, but radiating... a great blessing of some variety?

The potency was impressive, she could tell with just a glance.

"What is that?"

This time, the surprise in her voice was well-earned.

"And how did you come by it?"

It was not a Sacred Gear - the obvious answer - and she doubted Apollon would have forgotten to mention a gift so grand if it had come from from.

Artemis and Chiron as well.

It wasn't the greatest she'd ever seen, not by far, but for a tool in mortal hands....

"Just a little something I picked up on a side-quest a while back. It's been pretty cool to play around with since, but here's hoping it actually works as advertised."

Her grand-nephew hefted his great prize and crossed the distance between without an ounce of hesitation.

"Daniel-"

He unfurled the golden mass in his hands, and the wool flashed, catching the firelight as it slid free and blazed all the brighter for it.

"Fingers crossed."

Before Hestia could react, the audacious child pressed it into her arms-

Courage barked again, rearing back-

-a̴n̴d̶ ̶l̴i̷g̶h̴t̸ ̴s̶p̷i̵l̴l̷e̶d̴ ̷a̴c̴r̷o̶s̷s̸ ̷t̷h̴e̶ ̸̧̘͖͂̂͘c̴͚͙̍l̸̯͇̠̘͙̓e̵̖̐̒͌̚a̴̢̹̟̾̑r̷̭̥̘͋̈́̀ȉ̸͕̝͝ņ̶̛͎̤͔̹̿͌̃g̴̡͔̗̟͚̽̓̌́͝


...

...

...


It would not have worked.

Not without time, effort, and a dozen other circumstances besides.

...

It should not have worked.

...

And yet…

...

There was a symmetry there to exploit.

Hestia Aidios - She Who Is Eternal - had been wounded in a clash between the King of the Heavens and the force led by his maddened, would-be successor.

The catalyst?

The murdered children of the gods.

So there was a kind of poetry - an intricate, undeniable symbolism - to another child of one of those same gods reaching out to mend even a fragment of what had been broken.

Daniel Winchester poured his power into the Golden Fleece, cradled in the Eldest Olympian's arms, and for a single, brilliant instant, the stars aligned

Just the one, but enough.

The scars did not vanish, but some faded, and more retreated where they had once run deep.

Their ache did not disappear, but it dulled, for the first time in as long as they had existed.

The attempt at restoration took root.

Most of all, as the light of the Fleece began to die, and the demigod dropped to his knees with a ragged, winded gasp, limbs steaming from the effort alone-

"What have you done?"

A dead, stunned gaze came to sudden life, and everything took off from there.

...

...

...​

Overhead, despite the clear, star-strewn sky, a low, looming rumble of thunder rolled across the heavens.

LET'S GOOOOOOOOO!!!!!!!!​


Chiron's Estate:

Daniel's power ignited like a star in miniature, flaring outward in a sudden, unexpected rush, and Chiron and Apollon materialised in the clearing mid-conversation, just in time for the lightshow to begin.

Of course.

The surge narrowed, drawing in on itself until it stood as a single pillar of light just ahead, self-contained and shining with brilliant intensity - and it held, banishing the dark and casting everything around it into a stark relief.

More than that, in fact.

The air warmed with the glow, growing sharper and purer. The grass beneath them followed suit, brightening with a pulse of colour and vitality, and then came the sensation of it all.

Soft and heady, with an aftertaste of sunlight and gold.

How fitting.

Apollon took it in with a blank, eerie stillness that was best used to hide one's sudden incomprehension.

Chiron just sighed and resisted the urge to pinch the bridge of his nose.

Five minutes.

That idiot student of his had been left alone with his aunt for all of five minutes - if that - and this was the result.

He wasn't even surprised, truly.

Exasperated at best.

I should have stayed in retirement.

Slowly, the power began to recede.

The light retreated like a tide, and the pillar flickered once, then twice and thrice, its edges fraying into strands of gold that unraveled into the air.

Then it flickered out all at once.

Daniel dropped to his knees before the last of the radiance faded away, hitting the grass with a ragged gasp made all the more theatrical by the haze of steam wafting off of him.

"…Okay," he rasped, voice wrecked, "That may have been a bit much."

Idiot.

He wasn't injured, but he'd all but emptied himself out. The Golden Fleece slipped from his nerveless fingers, landing on the dirt with a low, dull thump.

And that was only the start of it.

"What have you done?"

Hestia didn't wait for an answer, and Chiron couldn't fault her for that.

Her hand slowly rose to her face - not without a hint of stunned wonder - and brushed along her cheek.

The scars had changed.

The deep, jagged damage had drawn back, softened into pale, silvery lines that caught the firelight instead of breaking it. Faint and diminished, and the least of them had vanished outright, leaving smooth, blemishless skin once again.

Then her fingers traced upwards, towards her ruined eye, before stilling in disbelief.

He couldn't blame her for that, either.

"Hey, it worked."

She blinked, and both eyes - warm brown, steady, and restored - fixed on the ridiculous child in front of her.

"Awesome."

Daniel grinned, audacious as ever, but the expression was weak, and quickly fraying at the edges.

"Was only about sixty percent sure that would work - strong fifty, maybe-"
The slur in his voice made it all too clear where this was going. "And it would've been all kinds of lame to screw up after that whole sp..."

He trailed off, smiled at nothing in particular, and proceeded to faceplant directly into the dirt.

"No."

Or so he would have, if Apollon hadn't been there to catch him before he went down.

Even then, his head lolled to one side, eyes glazed and drifting, and the god's mouth drew into a thin, unhappy line.

"Depleted to the last."

"M'okay," Daniel mumbled, barely shaping the words. "N...need a minute."

"You need considerably more than a minute, and a stern talking to," He countered, and gently lowered him onto the grass. "And, as your outrageous luck would have it, you're in no state to hear a word of it."

He wasn't wrong.

Daniel was unconscious before his father was even halfway finished speaking, and that was rather firmly that.

The luck of the devil, and Sairaorg wasn't even here yet.

Granted, waking him would have been easy enough, but Apollon seemed more concerned with looking him over and frowning heavily.

Potentially to confirm that he would, in fact, stay where he'd been put.

Given Chiron's experience over the last year or so, that was a perfectly legitimate concern.

And very convenient, at the moment.

"Nephew…" Hestia knelt beside him, drawing another blank, careful look for her efforts. "What did your son just do?"

"I'd very much like to know myself."

His eyes shifted toward the Golden Fleece.

Understandably so, given its clearly divine nature, but the moment he went to reach for it-

A blur of black cut across the clearing.

They had all been well aware of the hellhound's presence, of course, and Courage had been trying very hard, on his part, to melt against the backdrop of the night...

But the little pup was also nothing if not a model opportunist.

"Aarf!"

Chiron blamed his students' influence.

The both of them.

He beat Apollon to the Fleece by a hair - purely on account of surprise - closed his teeth around it with a lunging, harmless snap, and sprang right back around and into Daniel's shadow without a second thought.

...

Another long, awkward moment passed.

Apollon's hand remained half-extended before he lowered it slowly, with an expression that edged somewhere between disbelief and thinly veiled irritation.

"...Really."

Chiron's lips twitched, and Hestia was clearly struggling not to laugh.

Apollon was less amused.

"Return that at once."

The shadow under his unconscious student didn't so much as stir.

"Hound."

Nothing.

Apollon's gaze tightened, and a pale glimmer of something fiery and distinctly warning flickered across his eyes.

Even the air grew a touch heavier.

"That was not a suggestion."

The shadow shifted precisely once, and then stubbornly remained exactly as it was.

Chiron commended the bravery, if nothing else.

Futile execution, but full marks for effort.

"You-"

Then the full indignity of arguing with his son's pet finally caught up to him, and Apollon stopped mid-word.

Hestia, on the other hand, gave up on a bad job and broke into open laughter.

"Where did you find this pair?"

They turned to stare at her, and that didn't help any.

She huffed out a breath that might've been an attempt to stop, failed, and promptly laughed louder, shoulders shaking with the force of it.

"Et tu, Aunt?"

She wheezed.

The glee was contagious, and Chiron felt some of the tension ease away.

His own, mostly.

Look at her go.

One should never grow too comfortable in the presence of gods - that was simply common sense - but joy suited his sister well, as it ever did, and with the state she was in now…

Well.

It was a good look.

And all too predictable, in hindsight.

Daniel had a heart of gold and compassion aplenty, melded with the attention span of a gerbil that couldn't help but sprint headfirst into problems of its own making.

Well-meaning, bull-headed recklessness at its finest.

Chiron would make him regret the habit - obviously, and in due course - but he couldn't argue with the results.

Not this one, at least.

Finally, Hestia's laugh began to peter out, and Apollon crossed his arms.

"Are you quite finished?"

"Just abouts." She giggled, wiping a tear from her eye. "Goodness, I needed that."

"And you have it at my expense?"

She snorted and sat back against her log, settling comfortably on the grass.

"I am enjoying being able to see properly again. I think I've earned this."

Apollon didn't argue the point.

He watched her carefully instead, looking over the smoothed lines of her scars and the unblemished eye with a focus that was one part relief, another fascination, and just as much suspicion to boot.

Then he cleared his throat.

"You're looking better."

"I am." She agreed brightly "Exciting, isn't it?"

"That is one word for it." Apollon turned to Chiron. "Well?"

Chiron raised a brow in return.

"Well what, my lord?"

His eyes narrowed.

"Chiron."

"That is my name, yes."

"You know something."

"I have an approximate knowledge of many things."

Hestia snickered under her breath - really, she was in quite a mood - but Apollon's eyes only narrowed further.

Now it begins.

"What is that artifact, where did it come from, and why does my son have it?"

"Currently, your son's hellhound has it."

What was life without its technicalities?

"And as for what it is… " He tilted his head meaningfully. "I'd advise waiting for Daniel to answer that himself."

No one present was under any illusion that Apollon couldn't strip it from Courage with the slightest act of will - the very thought was ludicrous.

Precocious as the hellhound was, he was no Kerberos, or anything close to impressive in the grand scheme of all things.

Not where one of the Twelve was concerned.

But he was Daniel's, and that made all the difference.

Apollon pursed his lips.

"Something to do with his origins, I take it?"

"I'm afraid so."

Though 'afraid' was likely the wrong word.

Chiron had very little doubt that Apollon would embrace his son regardless of his… extraterrestrial circumstances.

That wasn't the problem.

The logistics of that revelation would be, but those could be dealt with in time.

Daniel didn't quite appreciate how important he was in his father's eyes.

Oh, he was very much aware of it in the abstract, and had come to terms with it in some respects, but in others he remained quite oblivious.

It was a work in progress, if an endearing one.

In the meantime, however...

"Haste makes waste, as the saying goes, and you know it better than I."

Most Olympians did, given their track record, and Apollon's face twisted in displeasure.

Hestia sobered as well, staring between them with blatant curiosity.

"He's got you there, nephew."

"Doesn't he just?"

He let out a slow, even breath and turned back towards Daniel, who remained blissfully unaware of the headaches blooming in his wake.

A moment passed.

"I could simply pluck it from his mind," Apollon said at last, almost conversationally. "Him and the hellhound both, if need be. The devil likely knows as well."

Chiron's smile didn't waver.

"You could."

But he wouldn't, and they both knew it.

Centuries ago, perhaps, but these were different times, and an overstep of that magnitude would eviscerate the careful trust Daniel was beginning to place in him.

Naturally, that extended to Sairaorg as well.

For all that Apollon begrudgingly tolerated the young Bael at best, he was still Daniel's best friend.

And Chiron would not have accepted any sudden moves there regardless.

He had never much cared for divine meddling in the affairs of his students.

History had rather soured him on the concept.

"...Very well, then." Apollon turned away with a click of his tongue. "What's one more curiosity added to the list?"

Lovely.

"It won't be long now." Chiron offered pleasantly. "Sooner rather than later, I'd say."

He wasn't blind - Daniel had been working up the nerve to come clean for quite some time now.

This would only bring things to a head.

Apollon made a noncommittal sound, but Hestia leaned forward in interest.

"I'm missing quite a few things, aren't I?"

"You're in good company, aunt."

Then he snapped his fingers, and a little mote of pulsing light sparked with the motion and drifted down into Daniel's shadow. The darkness stirred as it sank in, rippling once, and settled just as quickly.

Chiron blinked.

"A blessing?"

"The little pup is impudent, but loyal, and the brightest lights cast the deepest shadows by nature. If he's to be my son's, he should be worthy of the honor."

Fair enough.

The favor of a god of wolves stacked onto Kerberos's touch...

The results would be interesting to study, if nothing else.

Hestia's lips parted-

"Don't."

Her hands rose in surrender.

"I didn't say anything."

Apollon gave her a flat look.

"You thought it."

That she didn't deny, and her answering smile was soft and fond.

"Grace is a good look on you, nephew."

"Everything is a good look on me. I'm the common factor."

Chiron would have rolled his eyes - honestly, the drama - but Hestia moved first.

"While we're on it, if we're handing out well-deserved gifts..."

She leaned forward and sank her arm into the fire.

Ah.

The flames barely flickered around her as she reached through them, and when she pulled back, she was holding a small coal in her hand - red-orange and gold, softly crackling, and almost deceptively unassuming for something so clearly powerful in its own right.

"Here we are."

She rose and crossed the short distance to Daniel's side, kneeling beside him and gently brushing his hair back with her free hand.

"I fully admit I understand nearly nothing of the circumstances at play here, and that's novel, truly it is." she admitted quietly. "Wherever and however this child came to be... it must be quite the story."

Her fingers curled slightly around the ember, and the glow of it grew that much brighter, flames coiling and licking at her skin.

"But he is family, and he has heart, and this is the very least of what he deserves."

Then she pressed it down against the demigod's chest.

The ember flared at once, spilling red-gold fire across his shirt in a sharp, harmless bloom that spread outwards like a tide.

Apollon and Chiron watched - Daniel didn't so much as stir - as the coal sank through him, the light of it melting beneath his skin inch by inch until it settled entirely into his frame.

Then came the pulse.

For the briefest instant, a faint purple glow flickered beneath his sternum and alongside the dying red-gold light, and vanished as quickly as it appeared.

A reaction from Incinerate Anthem.

Not entirely unexpected, that

Holy Relics didn't take kindly to pagan influences at the best of times, and the Cross was markedly volatile even when compared to the Spear.

Still, it didn't go any farther than that, and Hestia stood and stepped back a moment later, looking quite pleased with herself.

"There. All done."

"That was a generous gift, sister."

Very generous, in fact - that was no simple bestowal of grace - but Hestia only waved him off.

"A Foundation and nothing more. It's up to him to make something greater of it."

And Daniel wouldn't have it any other way.

That boy had an ever-growing fascination with anything even remotely magical, and it suited him well, for better or worse.

"Now then." Hestia's tone shifted into something more measured, and she tapped lightly at her cheek, just beneath the restored eye. "Shall we discuss this properly?"

The easy atmosphere in the clearing changed.

"Because secrets or no, this isn't something that can go unnoticed for long."

Likely it already has been.

She didn't have to say the words - none of them were fools - and slowly, all three of them turned to look up.

The stars were out, and the sky was vast and clear.

Not a thundercloud in sight.

Chiron wasn't reassured in the slightest, and Apollon's expression curdled like milk.

"Voyeur."

"Nephew."

"Tell me I'm wrong."

"Bricks from a glass house, my dear." Hestia chided, but for all that the banter was familiar, the undertone was strained. "There is no danger here, Apollon."

"So you say."

"So I declare."

Her voice firmed like iron.

"No one will harm your son, my grand-nephew, and a child of Olympus. I will not stand for it - and neither will the others."

"Hm."

"Any of the others."

The message there was so pointed it might as well have been an arrow, and Chiron closed his eyes and longed for a good cup of tea.

A Sideritis blend, just a dash of honey. Quite heavenly.

When he opened them again, Apollon's expression remained unreadable. His mouth had flattened slightly, and the tension hung in the air like smoke.

"...We shall see, Aunt."

The god turned back to Daniel without another word, waving, and a brief flare of light snapped into being around the boy, before folding in on itself and taking him with it.

Whisked off to his room - Chiron could sense as much - and it was a conversational sidestep if there ever was one.

The silence that followed was also telling.

He exchanged another look with Hestia, and a moment of resigned, weary understanding passed between them.

Two cups of tea, then.

Her lips quirked faintly.

"How is your guest?"

Now there was a question.

"Recovering. She's had quite a day."

A horrific culmination of increasingly miserable events that had begun with Augusta Hawthorne's stupidity and spiralled on from there, and she had borne the brunt of sins not at all her own.

The less said about this newfangled Utsusemi debacle, the better.

Was it any wonder he'd chosen to let the poor girl sleep while she could?

The waking world would still be there in the morning, regrettably enough.

"I imagine she did," his sister murmured, and the sympathy there was entirely genuine. "So... what is to be done about it?"

Many things indeed.

Daniel and Lavinia Reni had been attacked right outside his home, under his protection.

His guest and his student both targeted, and had they been any less capable - or any less fortuitously blessed with those Gears - the outcome might have been far less forgiving.

Chiron frowned at the very thought.

Amusing as it was to attribute it all to Daniel's propensity for boundless chaos, this was not that.

Instead, it was an overreach, a slight, and a crime all in one.

And it would be answered.

"I am going to ensure the children have a good night's rest."

Their comfort came first, and no one present would gainsay him on that.

Hestia waited patiently, and Apollon finally turned back to the conversation, his eyes glinting darkly - and all too knowingly.

They had discussed this, after all.

"I think I'll go for a little stroll."

And if he happened to find himself in the Netherworld while stretching his legs, in the company of a Fallen Angel or two…

Well.

Coincidence was a curious thing.

His smile could almost have been mistaken for gentle.

"It should be quite refreshing."

...​

Misla Bael's Estate:

Breakfast the next morning was pleasantly quiet.

Anton was already present by the time Misla arrived, composed as ever while directing the servants through the final preparations. Tea steamed gently beside her seat, rich and familiar, while the rest of the table slowly filled around it.

Sairaorg stepped into the hall several minutes later, smiling as brightly as he ever did.

He also looked like he'd gone twelve rounds with an earthquake, which - considering everyone in the estate had heard the distant explosions earlier that morning - should have been quite concerning.

There were bruises mottling his cheekbone and jaw, faint fading gashes along the side of his face, and his hair hadn't quite settled back into place properly. Even his knuckles were faintly scraped and reddened, as though they'd recently been split open and knitted back together again.

Misla just stared at him over the rim of her teacup, not quite letting her amusement show.

"Good morning, my love. Did you tumble out of bed?"

And into another made of knives, perhaps?

Sairaorg flushed and coughed into his fist.

"Morning, mother. I was sparring with Regulus."

"Ah, yes," she mused aloud. "The incarnated Nemean Lion - a living Longinus - who's taken to brutalising my son on a schedule."

What a world she'd woken up to.

"It's training." Sai shrugged as he took his seat across from her, then paused. "And I think he's still mad we forgot about him that one time, or just using it as an excuse to maul me whenever he gets bored. Either or."

"That sounds remarkably unpleasant."

And mildly horrifying at that.

"It's not that bad." He piled eggs and sausages onto his plate and poured himself a drink. "Fun, really. At least when he doesn't get mean about it. Those claws sting."

The small laugh bubbled out of her of its own accord, and Sairaorg brightened with victory.

Even Anton seemed to swallow a smile, and that one clung to decorum like a priest to gospel.

"So long as you're safe," she conceded. "Though while we're on the matter…"

He had already gone back to eating, half-distracted, before glancing up through his next mouthful.

"Hm?"

"Is that why you accepted the Andrealphus girl's challenge? For the fun of it?"

"Oh. That? No." A flicker of concern crossed his face. "Why? Do you think I shouldn't have-?"

Misla shook her head.

"You're old enough to be making decisions for yourself."

These for certain - Her son could be stubborn enough to headbutt a mountain if the mood took him, but he was clever besides, and more capable than many devils twice his age, noble or not.

Nobles especially.

"They approached you properly enough - if quite persistently - so you're free to handle the matter however you please," she said, setting her cup down with a faint tap. "Though I would like to hear your reasoning."

Call it a mother's curiosity.

"Sure?" He hesitated. "It might not sound all that impressive."

"Try me."

She didn't miss a beat.

"Right. Okay." He put his fork down and cleared his throat. "She's not strong."

That… was an interesting start.

"Kuisha Abaddon, I mean. She's not stronger than me, and neither is her friend."

"How can you tell?"

"Senjutsu."

Of course.

"Don't get me wrong, I don't think they're weak. They've both got plenty of demonic power and the Clan Traits to match, but unless they're really good at hiding their power - like, scarily good?"

He shook his head.

"I've got them beat by a mile."

"I see."

Smiling with fierce pride and reaching across the table to pull him into a hug would ruin the mood, so Misla settled for a raised eyebrow.

"And?"

"And they know that." Sairaorg leaned back in his chair and reached for his glass of orange juice, idly turning it in his hand. "I showed off, just a little, and I could tell it rattled them."

Her brow rose a little further.

"But Kuisha Abaddon still looked me dead in the eye and challenged me anyway." He finished explaining. "Her friend - Coriana - was just as nervous, but she was still ready to back her up right then and there."

He gave another small, sheepish shrug.

"I liked that."

And he would, wouldn't he?

A touch sentimental, perhaps, but if anyone could appreciate that sort of single-minded determination, it would be her son.

And still....

"That does sound admirable," she agreed, dropping a sugar cube into her tea. "But there's a fine line between bravery and desperation, and even the one standing on it can't always tell you which is which."

Even then, there were limits.

Spine was all well and good, but it only promised potential, not results.

"Maybe." He nodded right back, but a faint grin tugged at the corner of his mouth anyway. "But I guess we'll find out, won't we? There's a reason I set it for a couple of months from now."

The way he said that…

As the challenged party, it was perfectly within Sairaorg's rights to choose the time and venue - But now Misla was curious.

"Are you plotting something, my love?"

The idea of it was positively charming.

"Do tell."

"It's not a plot." His nose wrinkled. "It's more of a test, as pretentious as that sounds."

Misla laughed outright.

"You are a Bael and a Vapula both. Believe me, your ceiling for pretention is higher than most."

She would know.

Sairaorg wrinkled his nose even harder, and Anton suddenly became very interested in a patch on the far wall.

"That's not encouraging."

"It is what it is. Now go on. Don't keep me in suspense."

"The Samhain Ball."

Misla straightened a touch.

"It's in about a month, give or take. That's when everyone finds out you're back."

"We're back," she corrected reflexively, though it was distracted at best.

"Yes?"

"Whatever happens there…the entire Underworld's gonna hear about it inside of a week." He tapped a thumb against the side of his glass. "I just want to see if they actually follow through, or if it was all talk after all."

Not a bad idea, admittedly…

But that wasn't what stuck with her.

"Whatever happens-" She stopped. "Sairaorg, are you planning on making a scene?"

He looked up and smiled innocently.

"Nope. Why would I do that? It's going to be loud all on its own."

True.

"I just can't wait to visit home again. See some old friends."

There was a sharp edge to the violet of his eyes.

"Father too."

...

Oh.

...

Misla pursed her lips.

Sai looked unrepentant in the silence that followed, and she understood.

Didn't she ever.

Her own grudge against her husband was built on the same foundation, and it was a bitter, hateful thing by any measure.

Despising the Lord Bael came easily after what he'd done, and Misla had rained ruin down on others for less.

Even so, she wouldn't be a mother worth the name if she didn't rein this impulse in.

"Don't be rash." She cautioned, and Sairaorg sat up slightly. "Enjoy yourself. Let them see you and all that you've become, but remember to watch your step."

There were plenty of grudges to settle, in the end, and the circumstances were in their favour, but charging in headfirst with spite alone was foolish.

Embarrassing, even.

Her son would be better than that.

"I'm not going to do anything stupid."

"I didn't say you would." She smiled patiently as he looked away. "Just remember to pace yourself, and act on your best judgment."

Slow and steady would win the race, and they were already halfway there.

"…Sure."

"Wonderful."

The agreement was halfhearted, but it'd do.

Misla reached for a piece of toast and began buttering it, before splitting it cleanly in two.

"Now then… your aspiring Peerage candidates. Any more clever ideas?"

"Not really." He shook his head and drained his cup at last. "And I still think everyone's being just a little too optimistic there. I'm not even sure I want a peerage yet - or ever."

He threw his hands up in exasperation.

"For the love of - I don't even have Evil Pieces yet!"

Misla blinked.

That first part was... a conversation for another time.

Not every noble devil assembled a peerage.

She never had, despite having the opportunity.

Then again, times had changed.

With the New Satans' rule as strong as it is and the Rating Games as prevalent as they are, a young Pillar heir refusing to build one could be politically problematic, at best.

As for the second point…

"Actually…" She exchanged a sly smile with Anton and raised a hand. "About that."

Sairaorg's confusion didn't last.

He took one look at her face and his jaw dropped.

Then it dropped a little more when the polished chess box appeared in her hand - small, lacquered black wood with silver inlay.

Small and unassuming, for something quite so important.

"No way."

"Yes way." She laughed at his stunned disbelief. "You have just as much right to them as any of your other 'peers'."

"When-?"

"Oh, I've had them for a few years now."

Since before their exile, even.

Misla had made certain to pick up a set before it came to that.

The Underworld would freeze over and the Morningstar would rise again to thaw it out before she left her son empty-handed.

Though she had made sure Anton only knew to give them to him no sooner than his fifteenth birthday, just to be safe.

Sairaorg was a treasure, but granting children the ability to reincarnate any mortal not obscenely more powerful than they are as subordinate devils tended to result in anything from indulgent waste to diplomatic incidents, with endless headaches for a middle ground.

Best not chance it altogether.

"Go on then."

Sairaorg took the box a little stiffly, still just this side of gobsmacked.

He turned it over in his hands once, then twice, before awkwardly setting it down and cracking the lid open.

There they were.

Fifteen gleaming Evil Pieces rested in neat rows against dark velvet, each one polished to a mirror sheen and only faintly thrumming with dormant power.

For a moment, her son simply stared.

"...Seriously?"

She waved him on.

His fingers hesitated over the first row, ghosting across the pawns - almost skittish at first, but curiosity pulled him in.

Then he drifted to the next row, slowly tracing their shapes as he went.

Rook. Knight. Bishop.

He stopped at the Queen Piece.

The most powerful one of the set.

He drew it out carefully, holding it up to the light, studying it with startling intensity.

Then, to her surprise, he smiled.

"Something the matter?"

He didn't seem upset.

"Right now, there's only one person in the universe I'd even consider giving this to - and if I was stupid enough to ask, he'd probably punch me across the horizon."

Misla waited, and his smile widened in satisfaction.

"And I'd let him."

She didn't have to ask, and she was glad to hear it.

"You have a good friend, Sairaorg."

A very important one - potentially a very dangerous one - but a good one all the same.

Her son agreed.

"The best."

Of course, that was when Anton cleared his throat.

"Lord Sairaorg?"

Both of them turned to meet her cousin's gaze, and he quickly produced a folded letter from somewhere within his suit.

"You have a message, Lord Sairaorg."

Sairaorg blinked.

"From Mr Winchester."

"Dan?" He took it with a bemused look and unfolded it. "Why wouldn't he just-"

That was about the point where he started reading, and the words died in his throat.

His face immediately settled into long-suffering annoyance.
Then his brows furrowed.

Then he choked.

"Sairaorg?"

He didn't answer.

His eyes went wide.

Then wider.

They kept roving over the page, word by word, until they reached the bottom, and by that point his face had gone eerily blank.

The only signs of life were the spasming grip he had on the letter and the faint, sporadic twitch beneath his left eye.

"What is it?"

Wordlessly, he handed her the letter.

Misla accepted it with growing concern, and began reading.

To his eternally venerable and endlessly illustrious Lordship, Sairaorg Bael.

What're you still doing down there, loser?

Everything peachy?

Actually, don't answer that. I don't really care.

Remember that field trip I dropped by to tell you Chiron and I were going on? The one with his new guest?

It went off the rails.

Like, way off the rails - our kind of off the rails.

Stuff happened, I met a nice witch, things went down, and then we met another evil witch in Cocytus.

Yeah. That Cocytus.

Oh, and Kerberos too, I guess - Courage had a trip with that one.

That was the boring part.

Chiron sent us home when we got what we came for, and I nearly got decapitated not three minutes after we popped back.

Then the two of us got kidnapped - Me and the new girl, I mean.

I know.

New record, right?

Only thing missing was the confetti.

Anyway, long story short?

I fought - and beat - more homicidal Shinto-reject assassins than I can count, got stuck in ground zero of a Longinus-class Balance Breaker, and squared up against an Eight-Winged Fallen Angel.

Beat him too, by the way. I'm officially up a hundred points just for that.

New girl got hurt pretty bad by the end, and then things got weirder on my end for a bit - but I think it all worked out in the end.

If convenient, get back over here so we can talk about it already.

If inconvenient, please come anyway, you worthless hellspawn.

Love,
Chiron's better student.

P.S. - Say hi to your mom for me, and remember to tell her that adoption is a perfectly acceptable life choice in the twenty-first century. She doesn't have to put up with you if she doesn't want to, the poor woman.

...

Misla lowered the letter slowly, staring at it in silence.

Her lips parted, then helplessly closed again without a sound.

What?

"I'm going to end him." Sairaorg was muttering with a vacant, thousand-yard stare. "I'm going to end him, and then his dad will end me, and it'll be worth it."

She didn't know where to begin addressing that one.

On a whim, she turned the page over and blinked again.

"There's another postscript."

The muttering stopped.

Her son slowly craned his neck towards her, tension coiling through him like a wound spring.

Anton had to turn away entirely, and she had to swallow an incredulous snort and clear her throat.

P.P.S. - If you're wondering why I wrote this instead of showing up in person, it's because the look on your face must be priceless.

A second line followed immediately beneath it, the scrawl of it only slightly messier than the rest.

Also, I raided your Snickers stash. Bite me, sucker.

...

Three.

Two.

One.

Sairaorg leapt out of his chair so quickly he nearly upended the table.

"PAGAN BASTARD! I'LL KILL HIM!"

Chiron's Estate:

Three months since the Fall of Oz.

Two months since the offers began.

Polite invitations. Sly little proposals. Friendly conversations that always seemed to circle back to how they only wanted to help - for a price.

One month since some of them stopped being quite so polite.

Funny how quickly the smiles disappeared once they realized there was no one standing behind her.

No patrons. No sponsors. No backing.

She didn't even have a home anymore.

Grauzauberer had always been dangerous, but it was a deathtrap - or worse - for anyone without a strong enough shield.

Desperation and stress and fear kept growing until she couldn't tell where one ended and the next began.

In the end, that's what pushed her to Greece.

To Athens, and Chiron Philyrides - a legendary figure who might actually hear her out.

Somebody who could help.

And the rest was history.

...

Cocytus. The attack. A Fallen Angel.

...

Walburga.

...

Glenda.

...

...

...

When Lavinia woke up the next morning, she felt nothing.

Not pain, or hurt, or despair.

Not even the smallest spark of anger.

Nothing.

The emptiness was its own kind of weight instead.

An aching, hollow exhaustion that sapped the strength from her limbs and left her feeling impossibly light and unbearably heavy all at once.

Burnout really was an insidious thing.

Even when Chiron came to speak to her, she could barely bring herself to look him in the eye.

Balance Breaker backlash.

Poison.

No permanent damage.

He spoke, and she listened, but it might as well have been static for all the good it did.

Lavinia understood every word, but for all that she'd woken up in a bed more comfortable than any she'd ever slept in, she was just so, so tired.

Maybe the Trainer of Heroes could tell, because his next words were particularly kind.

"You remain my guest, at your discretion."

She nodded numbly.

What else was she supposed to do?

She had nowhere else to go, and even getting up off the bed felt impossible.

Chiron watched her for a moment longer than necessary, before exhaling gently.

"This is a conversation for another time. It's time for breakfast."

And there was no arguing with that.

"You need to eat."

That was how she ended up at a table alone - for comfort's sake, maybe - despite the generous spread of food laid out across it.

Cold cuts and sliced cheese, a jar of honey, plain yogurt, fresh bread, and a few untouched bowls of cereal beside juice and water.

There was nothing wrong with it.

Lavinia still couldn't stomach it.

She tried to lift a spoon to her lips, her hand trembled so badly she stopped halfway there.

She gave up on the third attempt, and the spoon settled back into the bowl with a faint clink.

Eating was out.

Unfortunately, just sitting there wasn't much better.

The moment she stopped going through the motions and let the silence wash over her, her thoughts would start wandering, and that was the last thing she wanted.

Everything that had happened-

Lavinia squeezed her eyes shut.

The emptiness inside of her was almost a blessing, then.

Her mind veered away almost instinctively, latching onto the first thought it could cling to.

The poisoning.

...

That wasn't much better.

The wound itself had been nothing. The dagger hadn't even left a scar.

She'd checked, if only in reflex.

But the memory of it still made her shudder.

The burning in her veins. The sickening wrongness of it-

Lavinia swallowed.

No.

That wasn't much better at all.

But...

It gave her something else to focus on.

One thing led to another, and before she knew it, a notebook was in front of her and she was scribbling away for the sake of it.

Just to drown herself in something familiar.

Scritch. Scratch. Scritch.

It worked a little too well, and she only noticed she wasn't alone anymore when something moved in the corner of her eye.

Lavinia jerked, and the room nearly flash-froze.

The air turned sharp enough to bite, and a thin layer of frost spread across the nearest window before she reined Absolute Demise back in.

"I'm sorry-"

By then, Daniel Winchester had already backed away three hurried steps, both hands raised in surrender.

"No, no, my bad. Should've knocked. Heard there was breakfast and I figured-" His eyes caught on the notebook. "-I'd... join... you...?"

He trailed off, staring at the page for a long second.

Lavinia found herself staring back.

She didn't know what to think of the demigod.

Given she'd known him for less than a day, and most of that time had been spent either unconscious or fighting for her life, the uncertainty seemed fair.

He seemed genuine enough.

Bright and warm, too, and nothing about him felt immediately wrong - but that didn't mean anything, did it?

Appearances were worthless, and trusting people at face value was one of the most dangerous mistakes anyone could make.

Even before everything that had happened, Lavinia had known that perfectly well.

She'd also seen him fight.

Or maybe seen was the wrong word.

Her accidental, uncontrolled Balance Breaker had been a cracked, ugly thing, but she still vaguely remembered flickers of awareness - some evolution of her Sacred Gear's power.

Battlefield Clairvoyance, almost.

She'd caught fragments through the haze of delirious pain - most of them had slipped away, but some still stuck with her.

A figure burning in shades of gold, tearing through the blizzard with a fiery spear in hand.

Another black smudge with shadowed wings, lunging after him.

Then a flash of searing, scorching purple.

They felt more like fever dreams than anything else - blurry and uncertain - and reconciling any of them with the boy standing in front of her was a trial and a half.

Still, Lavinia stayed wary.

She couldn't help it.

"What kind of spell is that?"

That... caught her off guard.

He hadn't looked away from her scribbles, but his attention wasn't sharp or dangerous.

Just fascinated.

"Spatial magic? Point-to-point teleportation?" She heard him mutter under his breath. "No, too complicated. And there's no receiver for an end coordinate - wait, no, there it is, but that's a closed loop."

His brows furrowed.

"And ward-lines… so only the caster can use it?"

She wasn't quite sure how he ended up on the seat next to her, but there he was, poring over the notebook between one blink and the next.

"But why is it structured to take more than one input?"

"Because it's not meant to transport people."

The answer slipped out all on its own, and his head snapped up to meet her eyes.

"Come again?"

Lavinia hesitated.

She hadn't meant to answer - hadn't meant to speak at all, really - but now that she had…

He was still looking at her.

"It's not complete, and it's not meant to transport people."

"Then what-?"

"It's a defensive spell I'm trying to put together." A half-baked idea at best. "The venom I was poisoned with-"

He winced immediately, before plopping onto the stool to her right.

"Right. That was nasty."

Then he seemed to put the pieces together, and his eyes widened.

"Wait, this is for that?"

He turned back to the page, looking at it in a new light.

"Defensive… you're designing a spell that purges poison from a human body by teleporting it out?"

"…Something like that, yes."

It was barely a model, and she knew it, but Daniel perked up before she could finish.

"Oh, that's clever."

Lavinia glanced back down at the notebook dubiously.

"And complicated," He admitted a second later, even if the admiration was still there. "Super complicated. You need a spell component that makes the purging effect automatic, unless you can multitask like a monster. And another one that makes sure the spell knows what to purge, and what not to. It's active inside the body, and that can go gnarly really, really fast."

It was her turn to wince.

He wasn't wrong - there were horror stories of self-targeted spells backfiring and violently disfiguring the caster and everything around them.

And those were the mild ones.

"The cost would be hard to work around too." Now that she was thinking aloud... "Something so expansive... the drain would be ridiculous. Unless it had a conditional activation. Another aspect of the spell that only triggers the whole thing when it detects a foreign toxin in the body?"

He nodded along slowly.

"Sure, but then it loops back to another... not problem, exactly, but-"

"I know," Lavinia agreed. "It's reactive, not preventative - and not a cure."

A spell designed to protect against poison still needed poison to work against.

The principle wasn't all that different from an antivenom.

Only no antivenom was perfect.

Daniel clicked his tongue.

"If it only activates after something gets into your system, you're already in danger. Unless the spell can purge every last trace of it before damage sets in, but that's-"

"Too optimistic to bet on." She finished, and he nodded again.

"Depends on what you get hit with, I guess. Some of the stuff out there only needs a second to ruin your day."

That, she'd learned very well.

"Then another aspect to protect the body?" She frowned in concentration. "Repair and reinforce?"

"Yeah, probably for the best."

A small yellow notepad simply flashed into existence in his left hand, followed by a pen in his right.

Then, before Lavinia could finish tensing, a bowl of figs - of all things -appeared on the table between them.

Figs.

What-?

"You also want to double down on these wards."

He was already writing.

"They're straightforward and all-around useful, but magic like this won't be subtle. If an enemy picks up on it, they could take it over, and considering what it does… somebody could literally turn your insides into your outsides at range, and that's just off the top of my head."

That mental image was enough to break through her bewilderment.

"That's morbid."

He finally glanced up from his notes, distracted, and gave her a charming little half-smile.

"I'm a Greek demigod. Morbid is relative."

"..."

Lavinia couldn't argue that.

Children's bedtime stories about Greek mythology couldn't argue that.

"Fig?"

She blinked.

He was holding out the bowl to her.

How does he keep moving so quickly?

"Trust me, they're amazing."

Her first instinct was to politely refuse.

Then she caught the scent of them - sun-warmed, honeyed - and the impulse wavered.

What could it hurt?

"Thank you."

She took a bite and nearly jumped.

Sweet and light, and the rush of flavour went straight to her brain.

"Oh my god."

"Right?"

Lavinia couldn't answer - she got nearly halfway through the fruit before coming up for air.

She hadn't realized how hungry...

...

Nevermind.

She took another bite.

"So about the reinforce-and-repair bit," Daniel went on, pen already moving again. "I asked, and when Chiron healed you, he did it by dispelling the innate magic in the venom, transmuting the physical substance in your blood, and transfiguring away any damage all in one go, which is just… so far beyond me it's not even funny. Not without cheating."

"Cheating?"

He shrugged.

"Son of the god of healing. Most of the injuries I get are things I can basically will away, with enough time and power. The more esoteric stuff is a problem, though. The venom used on you..."

He bit the end of his pen in thought.

"If I had to do it... potion, maybe? Everything comes back to alchemy in the end."

"Alchemy?"

The curiosity made her sit up.

"Is that your chosen craft?"

...

Idiot

She regretted asking almost immediately.

Too direct - It would have been bad form in Grauzerber.

But he didn't seem offended.

"As in, a magical discipline?"

She nodded carefully.

"Nope." He popped the 'p'. "I don't really have one?"

The confusion must have shown on her face.

"Don't get me wrong, some things are more interesting than others, and I'm really itching to look into Astromancy, but I'm not picking one thing over the other any time soon. Magic is just… magic, you know?"

Something about the way he said that...

It almost made her smile.

"I think I do."

He grinned brightly, then drummed his fingers against his notepad.

"And as for Alchemy… I'm reading up on some basics, but it's more of a 'waste not, want not' kind of thing for me."

And there was that curiosity again.

"What do you mean?"

"Me and a friend keep... sort of stumbling into situations that end with us getting our hands on some pretty nifty things. Having at least some idea how to use them just seems smart."

"Things?"

"Reagents, mostly. Magical sheep wool, dracaena scales, some thaumaturgically active metals... even dragon's blood."

Lavinia froze.

Wholly and completely.

"Dragon's blood?"

"Yep."

"Pure dragon's blood?" she pressed, because that was an important distinction.

Even if it wasn't their field, any witch or magician worth their salt knew how powerful - and valuable - something like that was.

Daniel's grin tugged a little wider.

"Straight from the source."

Ridiculous.

Dragon-sourced materials weren't impossibly rare, depending on the quality, but even the lowest grades could be hideously expensive.

Pure, genuine dragon's blood could ruin-

Straight from the source.

Her mind stalled.

...

No.

Surely not-

"When you say 'source'-"

"I mean the source is a giant fire-breathing murder lizard," he answered without skipping a beat, before pausing and tilting his head. "Well, was. We did a real number on him."

Lavinia stared in disbelief.

The demigod didn't look remotely sorry.

"Don't worry, he totally deserved it. In fact…"

He bit into a fig and twisted his stool to face her.

"Let me tell you a story."

...

And so he did.

…

"I… don't know what to say."

"I get that a lot."

She didn't know where to start.

"You and your friend had a teleportation mishap."

"Right."

"And you ended up in the middle of a supernaturally aware community you'd never heard of."

"Correct."

"Right next to a dragon lair - a lair that belonged to another remote community before that same dragon decimated them and stole their home for himself."

"Not seeing any holes so far."

Lavinia was trying, she really was.

"And after hearing all that, your first instinct was to… walk into the place and hope for the best?"

He must be joking.

Daniel seemed to think about that for a moment, before beaming chipperly.

"Sounds about right!"

He wasn't joking.

"But…" She shook her head helplessly. "That's so stupid."

Then she flushed crimson.

Too far.

"Sorry, that was rude -"

"No, you're right," he admitted shamelessly. "We got lucky, and it all worked out for the best, but man was the lead-up brainless. Chiron - and others - totally read us the riot act for it. Multiple times. In just as many languages."

He snorted under his breath, and Lavinia almost followed.

Shakily, but it counted.

"It also gave Teach the perfect excuse to punish us in the worst way imaginable."

"Worse than a dragon?"

It was half a joke, but he was dead serious when he leaned in to answer.

"Way worse."

Lavinia held her breath.

What could possibly-?

"You've heard about Smaug." His voice darkened ominously. "Now let me tell you... about The Chicken."

…

And so he did that too.

....

If she'd been at a loss before, now she might as well have gone mute.

"That can't be real."

"But it is." His eyes were haunted. "It is."

"..."

She wet her lips hesitantly.

"I'm so sorry."

"So were we."

He gazed off into the distance with a thousand-yard stare.

"We thought we were ready for the horrors of this world, but we were wrong. Chiron proved that. We were so wrong."

The last bite of his fig disappeared in a flash, and he finally turned back and looked her right in the eye.

Blue on blue.

Somehow, that made her lean in, until they were nearly nose to nose.

"Don't forget this warning, Lavinia Reni. Never forget. We couldn't put it down - it was too powerful."

He didn't blink once.

"It's still out there."

She swallowed.

"Beware The Chicken."

"..."

"..."

"I... won't forget."

"Good. I'm glad."

A moment passed.

Then another.

And a third.

Lavinia's nose itched.

Daniel's lips twitched.

They both sucked in a shaky breath.
