"Snrrk!" "Pffft!"

Daniel cracked up first, one hand shooting out to catch the edge of the counter before he toppled off the stool altogether.

Lavinia didn't even try to stay upright. She doubled over right there in her seat, one arm wrapping around her middle, the other bracing on her knee, giggling hard enough to make her eyes sting.

The tide of it was bright and completely breathless, and if anyone had seen them, they would've thought they'd both lost their minds.

How long since she'd laughed like this?

She couldn't remember.

The thought only made her laugh harder, muffling it into her sleeve as another helpless burst shook her shoulders.

Daniel was only a little better.

One of them would meet the other's eyes every once in a while, and that would set them both off all over again.

It was wonderful.

...Except...

Eventually, Lavinia tried to pull herself together again.

Enough was enough.

Only she couldn't.

The more she tried, the harder her shoulders shook. Her hands wouldn't steady. The laughter didn't fade so much as change, catching in her throat and turning ragged around the edges.

More wretched.

...

Oh.

She was crying.

...

The realization didn't stop it.

Even as the sobs quieted, they were ugly to her ears - bitter and raw.

Her hands curled into white-knuckled fists on the counter, and her head stayed bowed as the waves wracked through her.

Even when she stifled them, tremors ran along her shoulders and down her arms.

The tears wouldn't stop, either.

They slid down her face, wetting her cheeks and dripping onto the pages in front of her.

Daniel was a blurred shape at the edge of her vision.

He wasn't looking at her, and she still screwed her eyes shut at the sight of him.

She didn't know why.

She didn't know anything anymore.
...

Everything was wrong.

Everything ruined.
...

Why?

Why. Why. Why?

…

Why?

…

Then she heard it again.

"Hey."

Daniel's voice - only it was different.

Low and so, so sad.

"How about I tell you one last story, if you're up for it?"

Lavinia didn't say anything.

She couldn't even open her eyes.

The numbness was already back.

The seconds ticked on.

Then-

"Once upon a time, there was a kid."
"..."

"A pint-sized little New Yorker like all the rest."

He shuffled a little as he found his rythm.

"Bit of a brat, really, but if you asked his mother-" He slowed on the word. "Well, she'd probably tell you that he was the coolest thing since sliced bread."

A pause.

"It was just them, see, and she loved him very much - and he, her. There was no Dad in the picture, but there didn't need to be. They had each other, and that was enough."

Another beat.

"It didn't last."

His voice dipped.

"Not every story has a happy ending. A few years ago, the kid's mother... he lost her - and it pretty much destroyed him."

"..."

"Recovering from that… moving on… please."

She heard him snort.

"Those things felt like a pipe dream. He was heartbroken, miserable, and cold all over. Like someone had sucked every bit of light and warmth from the world, and left him in the dark."

"..."

"But there was still one thing that could still fire him up - Anger."

Lavinia's breath hitched.

"Not at the universe, or fate… or even the Fates if you want to get technical. No, this was smaller, and pettier, and a lot more personal. The one thing that could always, always get under his skin, come hell or high water."

"…"

"Family, friends, and everyone in between. All the people who tried to reach out to him when he pulled too far away. They meant well, but all it took was the magic words."

"I understand."
"I know what you're feeling."
"It'll get better."

"The words… those kind, gentle little things."

His voice changed again.

Sharper and harder this time.

"He hated them. Damn near more than anything, because they were all lies. Those people that talked to him…"

She heard him shift again.

"They didn't understand. They didn't know what he was feeling, and it wouldn't get better. It didn't matter if they'd lost someone too. It didn't matter if they'd lost everyone - none of them were her. None of them were my-"

The word broke in his throat, and he swallowed roughly.

Lavinia felt her heartbeat press against her ribs.

"...It was a selfish, spiteful way of thinking, but..." He exhaled raggedly, "I did say he was a brat. That's just how it was."

Slowly, her eyes opened.

She didn't look at him - she didn't even look up yet - but she could tell he noticed.

A few more seconds passed.

Then she heard him sigh.

"There's no moral to that story, by the way." He laughed a little humorlessly. "I had to make one up."

Something rustled, and she risked a glance to see him pushing that little notepad away, before bracing his elbows against the counter as he searched for the words.

"Okay, here goes."

Lavinia turned in her seat.

Just a little.

"I think telling people that you 'get it' can be real condescending on a good day. Good intentions matter, and they can help a ton, but comparing suffering..."

He trailed off and took a deep breath.

"It's like multiplying by zero. No matter how big or small a number you start with, it just won't get you anywhere. A losing game through and through."

"..."

"Lavinia."

She went still.

"I may be rambling - it's a bad habit, I know - but the point I'm leading up to is… you've been through a lot. Obviously."

He ran his hand through his hair and sighed.

"And I don't understand what you're feeling. Our situations aren't the same, or even close to it. I don't get it."

For a moment, neither of them moved.

Then, he finally - finally - looked at her, and their eyes met again.

"But I know that you're in pain, and I am sorry."

His smile was warm and soft.

"If there's anything I can do to help, I'll do my best. That's a promise."

…

Trusting a stranger was the height of stupidity.

Lavinia knew that.

Especially after everything she'd survived.

She'd learned.

...

...And still...

...

Faced with that absolute sincerity...

...

She was just lost.

...

When it was all said and done, the only thing she could do was bury her face in her hands, and let the tears come again.

...

...

...

Eventually, the waterworks ran dry.

By then, Lavinia had given up on trying to understand how Daniel Winchester moved the way he did.

Or how they'd ended up like this.

He had his arm around her, loose and easy, and she leaned against his side almost bonelessly.

Any other time, it would have been mortifying.

Right then, she didn't have the energy to care.

Her body felt like a wrung-out dishtowel. Everything ached, all the way down to her soul.

Between that and her tear-streaked face, she must have looked utterly pitiful.

But better that than empty.

She stayed right where she was, and he didn't seem the least bit bothered.

"I don't know what I'm going to do now."

Grauzerberer.

Organisations hunting her.

Pretty much everything else on top.

Daniel made a small, sympathetic sound.

"Sounds like trouble. Still taking any suggestions?"

Lavinia let out a weak, breathless huff that could pass for a laugh by the skin of it's teeth.

"Any and all."

"Awesome."

He gave her that half-smile again - the same one as before - before closing his eyes and straightening slightly.

"Brace yourself."

That was all the warning she got.

Then a flash of silver light washed over the room, and the air changed.

À̶̳b̶͓̀s̷̻͠ò̶͈ḽ̴͒ȕ̴̹t̸̟͒e̵̫͆ ̶̻͘D̶͔̎e̸͇̚m̵͖̓ì̴̟s̶͇̐e̶̟̚ ̷̣̈p̵̢̏ụ̵̃l̶̢͌s̶̰̋e̷̖͝d̵̝̕.̷̫̿

Lavinia stiffened at Daniel's side, instincts blaring at the sight of the woman standing across the room.

Black leather jacket, combat boots, white-blonde hair and striking silver eyes.

Powerful.

Very, very powerful.

'Hey, Aunt A."

Of course.

Elsewhere:

As far as locations for a good old-fashioned emergency parley went, the small, wind-worn isle off the northern Levantine coast wasn't half bad.

Dreary and barren, sure - Nothing but sun-bleached rock and stubborn tufts of scrub clawing at cracks, and with all the personality of a water-logged corpse, but it'd do.

If Azazel, Governor General of the Grigori, wanted something with more of a pulse, he had options.

And people.

Preferably options and people, with fun to be had in between, but today…

Today was not that day.

The only thing standing on the isle was a small, domed citadel, quickly raised and warded for just the occasion.

Like everything else around it, it was nothing special.

Rough stone and blank, empty walls, and a single hollow chamber in the middle.

Even the lighting was harsh and stark, like it had something to prove.

Riveting scenery, truly.

Azazel lounged in a high-backed chair at the table - one of three - and swirling a goblet of wine purely for dramatic effect.

Flair was half the game, after all.

Stone-faced Baraqiel sat to his right, as his second.

And across from them - alone - was Gabriel.

Herald of the Word, Messenger of the Most High, and about twenty different titles just off the top of his head.

None of them did her justice.

His once-sister sat there, beautiful and perfect in every carefully measured angle, with golden hair and eyes an inhuman shade of blue.

Her wings were folded away, but even so her presence pressed against the room - light and holy enough to sting against his being like a persistent, irritating itch.

The cold, dispassionate gaze was just the cherry on top.

Family reunions, eh?

Two Fallen Cadre, and one Great Seraph.

Some people might think that, in the event of a diplomatic kerfuffle, the odds would be tipped in their favor.

Some people were also suicidal idiots, and Azazel wasn't nearly drunk enough - or at all, tragically - to consider that line of stupidity.

Either way, the stare off continued.

The silence stretched.

Gabriel didn't move, or blink, or even pretend to offer him the courtesy of a reaction.

He almost rolled his eyes.

Fine then.

"I feel like I'm being held in contempt."

"I always hold you in contempt, Azazel." She didn't hesitate. "You deserve nothing less."

Ouch.

It wasn't even a joke, or casual banter - just plain fact.

Of course, the words didn't faze him.

"Hostile way to start, don't you think? That hurt, right here." He patted his chest theatrically. "I called for this little get-together in good faith."

She said nothing, but frankly, he wasn't banking on much to begin with.

Messages didn't need words, after all, and most of the mail Gabriel sent the Grigori's way usually came in the form of assorted smitings and violent eviscerations.

Getting her to sit at a table was already half a miracle - and no, that wasn't a pun.

He preferred his low-hanging fruit riper.

"Speak."

"Come on, don't be like that."

Azazel took a swing of his goblet and mentally grimaced at the terrible vintage.

This is what he gets for letting the interns pack his booze.

"You know full well why I'm here. Olympus is acting up again."

Or at least some of their agents were - and one in particular.

Chiron Kentauros had apparently come out of retirement, and that alone was worth ringing all the alarm bells, and then some.

Case in point?

"The old war-horse paid a few of my research facilities a visit."

A 'few' being an even two dozen, and a 'visit' a cataclysm.

Collateral damage was limited to labs, higher-ranked Fallen and any other aspiring morons who tried to get in his way - which Azazel appreciated, he really did.

Those paychecks had to be earned somehow.

The losses, on the other hand...

Ah, hell.

He was down useful manpower, centuries of valuable research, and the world's most dangerous pagan pony had kicked down his doors, wiped the floor with his people, and trotted right back out without so much as a scratch.

And worst of all?

He. Had. Pretext.

Azazel wanted to seethe.

Again.

It would've been bad enough if that Council of arrogant bastards had broken isolation just to poke the Grigori.

But no. They had to show up with a reason.

A good one.

There was no simple eye-for-an-eye here.

Even if he wanted to strike back - and he damn well didn't - it couldn't be done without support,

Support that would lead to escalation, and then everything would spiral straight to kingdom come.

Thanks, but he'll pass.

Call him crazy, but he wasn't feeling that kind of Tuesday.

"Look, sis, I'll keep it short. Rogue Fallen. Some upstart descendant - not one of mine!" He raised a finger. "He attacked one of the big bad centaur's guests, and now the Greeks are up in arms because someone took a dump all over their front porch."

There was more to the story, obviously, because it was suspiciously short on details, but the headlines weren't fake.

He'd checked.

Gabriel was unmoved.

"This is no concern of Heaven," she declared coldly.

"Getting there."

Until a couple of decades ago, Ezren Vale had been... not ordinary, exactly, but not trouble either.

A nosy little punk with pedigree, some real power, and the skill to back it up, but that was about it.

The fact that he'd vanished off the radar and resurfaced alongside this Utausemi Agency was interesting, but on its own it probably wouldn't have even crossed Azazel's desk.

Not until someone realized who the brat was actually subordinate to.

"The Fallen wasn't one of mine." He put the goblet down and settled his expression into something distinctly less easygoing. "He was Satanael's."

...

Gabriel remained perfectly still - icy stare and everything.

"This is no concern of Heaven."

Oh, or the love of-

Besides him, Baraqiel grunted.

Terrible poker face, that one, but at least he didn't speak.

She wouldn't have acknowledged him regardless.

"You sure about that?" Azazel spread his arms. "I think everyone here is well aware of what a rogue Original Watcher can get up to if they put their mind to it."

Especially if they put their mind to it. Especially that one.

The Grigori had gone through enough restructuring over the course of its existence that "stability" was more of a theoretical concept than a lived experience.

Of the survivors of the First Order, some had modernised - slapped on a fresh coat of paint and adapted with the times, at least on the surface.

They were still Fallen, but now they had dental, severance packages, and even an HR department.

Progress.

There were the occasional upstarts unionising and stirring up trouble, along with the solo acts who were more likely to give him - read: Penemue - political migraines, but they were the minority.

And then there was the old guard - Like Sahriel.

Like Kokabiel.

Everyone avoided Kokabiel these days, because he'd made it clear what would happen if they didn't.

With spite.

Azazel still hasn't lived down that Vasco Strada fiasco from the Forties, and he wasn't looking for a repeat performance any time soon.

Unfortunately, Satanael was old guard too.

"He's splintered off from us entirely," he admitted, making a show of scratching behind his ear. "Took his handpicked students, whatever he was working on with Armaros, and vanished off to who knows where."

Azazel hadn't thought much of it at the time - hadn't noticed at all, honestly - but in his defense, he'd been busy.

The hoops an angel had to fly through to lock down a meeting with a Dragon King.

And now this.

"With one of Satanael's idiots picking a fight with the Greeks, and them not exactly being big on 'nuance'-"

"Your inability to manage your fellow rebels and the consequences of their actions is your own failing."

Of which there are many.

She didn't say it, but he could hear it just fine.

"Fair." He'd heard worse from Shemhazai. "But again, he's a solo act now."

"Scum under any other banner is still scum."

Aaaand there's the sanctimonious judgment.

Always a classic.

Baraqiel finally spoke. "We did not come to exchange insults."

To no one's surprise, Gabriel didn't even look at him.

"Satanael is our problem, true," Azazel continued before Barqiel could beat him to it. "But now he's gone and poked the bear. We'd like to ask for... let's call it a favour."

"Denied."

His expression didn't twitch, but it wanted to.

"Hear me out: We're not asking you to fight our battles for us, if it comes down to that. We're not weak… but a show of unity between Heaven and the Grigori would be a powerful deterrent."

And a necessary one, potentially.

People tended to behave better when they thought the "Biblical Factions" would close ranks against outsiders, cold war or no.

It was why he'd be calling up Serafall when he was done here.

Just to be safe.

Then again..

Maybe avoiding any overt devil-support was in everyone's best interests.

Between ancient history and that gloriously stupid Evil Piece blunder a few centuries back, the Greeks loathed them.

They hated all of them, really, but the Devils had gone home with the cup there - and that was just the Olympians.

He wasn't even going to mention Hades.

One nightmare at a time, please.

"We've been talking about peace talks for years now, but we never seem to get anywhere, do we?"

Azazel flashed her his best salesman's smile.

"This could change that. A gesture of goodwill-"

Gabriel's eyes flashed, and the pressure of her light intensified.

"There is no goodwill between us."

Baraqiel stilled warningly, the flux of his power rising like a tempest, but Azazel shot him a look before he did something stupid.

"Heaven stands first in upholding His tenets and His legacy. Above everything," she intoned. "That is the sole reason we consider treating with you further. Do not mistake it for permission to overstep."

This again.

Azazel let that bit of drama simmer.

Then he laughed, leaning back without breaking eye contact.

Seraphs.

Like righteous splinters under his nails, every last one.

"Sorry, sorry." He gave her another smile, and it wasn't all that nice - the irritation was beginning to show "My bad. I've never been good with permission. Did the black wings not give it away?"

Gabriel said nothing.

The contempt was loud enough on its own.

"Besides, I don't think I'm being too unreasonable here," Azazel went on, drumming his fingers against the table. "By your own words, peace lets Heaven do its job. A little agreement now could pave the way, and maybe someday - fingers crossed - we can all agree to stop bleeding each other out in an endless war nobody's ever going to win."

And see, it's not a lie.

At this point, after everything, official peace would be just about perfect - but he also wasn't holding his breath.

He'd settle for warning the Olympians off if they came for a fight.

"We-"

"You're only the Messenger, sister."

He didn't do innocent looks, but he gave her his best shot anyway.

"Unless I've missed something big, you have no business charting the path of the Heavenly Kingdom alone. Or has that-?"

And then he was there.


"̸A̴z̵a̴z̵e̷l̶.̷"̴​

A thousand years ago, Azazel wouldn't have hesitated.

One pulse of power, and he'd have lashed out.

Blasted this island to nothing, vaporised the sea around it, and incinerated everything for miles.

Then he'd have gone from there, assuming he wasn't already dead.

Now, though-

Baraqiel was halfway out of his chair, crackling with ozone, when the tide of Azazel's power caught him.

Sit. Down.

The wave snuffed out the nascent lightning, reinforced his chair, and slammed him back into it before he could reflexively get himself killed.

Then he turned, as casually as he could.

Golden-blond hair, just a hint of curl.

Eyes like searing light, fractals of blue-green and silver-gold spinning inside of them.

A face that mirrored Gabriel, a little, and a body that was a foot taller, armoured in flawless, thrumming silver.

The same glow, but a thousand times more otherworldly, and every bit as deadly.

"Michael."

The Taxiarch looked back impassively, and Azazel smirked with every bit of confidence he didn't feel.

"Azazel."

That voice haunted his nightmares.

"Didn't know you'd be crashing the party." His smile grew enough to show teeth. "Gabriel should have told me - I'd have worn my Sunday best!"

Why was he here?

This wasn't the Dark Ages - The Prince Of The Heavenly Host didn't make a habit of crossing the pearly gates on the regular.

Because Heaven needed him.

Because he didn't need to.

Because everyone and their Chief God would throw a hissy fit if so much as set a toe across any recognised border.

Pick your poison. Any would fit.

"Your proposal has been heard, and it is rejected."

Of course it was.

"Heaven will commit no support to cleaning up your mess."

The words landed like steel, and Azazel felt something inside him shrivel.

His plans.

His poor, poor plans.

"It's in all our best interests to curb a potential Olympian encroachment-"

"If they do, the matter may be reconsidered. But make no mistake: His Kingdom does not intervene for the Fallen."

Damn it.

Still, he tried.

Carefully.

"And Satanael?"

"Should he act to harm humanity, or move against Heaven, I will descend myself."

Baraqiel twitched.

Azazel couldn't even mock him for it.

That was the last thing most gods wanted to hear - the smart ones, at least.

"That's it, then?"

It was - Michael was already turning away, his presence pulling back like a passing eclipse.

Most people would have stopped there.

Unfortunately, something about that unspoken dismissal…

It rankled.

"For someone who never rejects the idea of peace outright, brother, you never seem willing to commit."

The Taxiarch stopped, and Azazel's wariness' kicked back in with a double shot of vindictive satisfaction.

Point landed.

What?

He wasn't perfect.

And, to prove that, he immediately doubled down and rammed his foot down his throat.

"Shame. Suppose we'll deal with the Greeks on our own if push comes to shove."

He sighed and reached for his wine again.

"You'd think dear old Pops would have lived up to his own hype and not left all these unfairly powerful pagans running around, but I suppose Helel's arrogance had to come from-"

...

And then there was a gauntlet around his throat.

...

Okay, this one's on him.

The table was gone - reduced to atoms - and Gabriel was standing right in front of Baraqiel.

Menacingly.

"Move, and you die."
...

Rough, that.

Azazel was still more concerned with Michael's death grip, and the look he was giving him now.

The fractals in those eyes were falling away, splitting into twisting motes of light and fire.

That gaze alone burned at his skin, and deeper beneath it.

"These negotiations permit you liberties I have otherwise ended armies for."

Even his voice changed.

Still calm and level, but now it also echoed and unfolded in ways that would make an Irish Banshee feel inadequate.

"But have you truly become so glutted on your own rot that you would so freely insult Him in my presence?"

Gee, what do you think?

He chuckled as best he could.

"Would you believe me if I said it just slipped out?

He was the Lord of the Watchers - Being eternally irreverent was pretty much in the job description.

Michael gave him nothing back.

His grip didn't waver, and the pressure rose, until Azazel could feel it grinding against his bones.

Scorching and without end.

The tip of the iceberg, if that.

It still couldn't shut him up.

"Careful there, Mikey."

He never lost his smirk against that ancient, endless focus - even though he had to fight for it.

"Your Wrath is showing."

...

As far as jabs went, it was pathetic.

He hadn't been expecting it to get him much.

Certainly not that smile.

"Azazel."

Michael's lips stretched, and whatever smugness he'd managed to hold on to began to evaporate.

Fast.

"Poor, small, foolish Azazel."

It wasn't humour, or joy.

It wasn't even condescension - it's monstrous older cousin, perhaps.

Merciless.

"You who delights in making noise and rebelling against your own failures with spite and denial."

Azazel's expression grew to show teeth again, but Michael didn't stop.

"Tell me, little Seraphim."

He pulled him closer, until the light of his eyes was inescapable.


[The shapes within expanded into supernovas]


"Have you forgotten who I am?"


Q̵͙̣̏ú̷̯̞ǐ̶̟s̵̝͖̈̈́͝ ̸̧̅̾͑ư̷̞̞t̵̛͚̕ ̵̿́͝ͅD̴̲͋̔ẽ̴̘̋u̴͍͙̐́̏͜s̸̞̔̃͜

̵̨̘̎̄̆
̸̭̜̎́͘W̸͇̰͇̒͝͝Ĥ̵̱̕Ō̷͕͇͝ ̷̼̐̀I̴͙̳̓S̵̙̄͌ ̷̠̂̓̀L̷̰̙̋̓̑Ì̵̩͘ͅK̶̢͎͇̔͂E̶͎̚ ̸̢̛͚̌Ğ̸̠̹̈́̐O̷̡̺͗D̶̠̑?̴̤͇̈̀͜​


"Enough."

Twelve wings unfurled with enough power to split the citadel in half and turn the roof into a shower of supersonic projectiles, and Michael let him go.

Azazel had been point-three seconds away from tearing his way free, even if he had to rip his throat and half his face off to do it.

The silver lining ended there.

His feathers bristled.

His body was coasting on so much energy it could have passed for a pressure cooker waiting to blow.

The worst of it was building deep in the layers of his soul and pooling behind his eyes, and he had a not inconsiderable urge to carve them out and cauterize whatever was left.

Wouldn't be the first time.

Meanwhile, Michael hadn't moved.

He just stood there, completely untouchable.

Son of a-!

In the instant it took him to breathe again, Baraqiel blurred to his side.

Gabriel rejoined Michael.

"I will not hear you besmirch Him again."

A warning, a threat, and a promise, all in one.

Azazel wanted to snarl.

He wanted to tear his throat out with his teeth.

He hated that he couldn't.

They were completely outmatched.

Their Father was dead, but Michael had been His greatest enforcer before he ever Mantled the Throne.

Now the bastard was something else entirely.

That was the only thing keeping the rage from spilling over.

Azazel hadn't survived this long by picking unwinnable fights.

He settled for a wry shrug.

"I'd apologize, but there's no point, is there? Can't help my nature."

There.

That should have been it.

Michael had other ideas.

"Another lie."

Not even going to let him have the last word?

Typical.

He was going to get poisonously drunk the second he was back in his lab.

"I was there when you came into being. When He shaped you from Grace and Light and Purpose, just as all the rest our kin."

Michael's gaze locked on him, Gabriel's mirroring it to his right.

His golden brother and sister, forever united in their scorn.

"The greatest tragedy of your existence, Azazel, is that you were not born a pitiful disappointment."

They turned away.

"You simply chose to be one."​

...

And then they were gone, with only light and silence in their wake.

...

...

...

"Baraqiel."

"Your orders?"

"We're rescheduling the meeting with Serafall."

"The devils won't like that."

He waved him off.

"Sent them a fruit basket - and then tell Penemue to work the Chiron situation. Find out what the hell else is going on there."

Because he'd eat a Twice Critical and go for seconds before he ever bought that this hornets nest had been kicked over some unnamed guest.

"Understood."

"Good. Now scram."

Ordinarily, Baraqiel would have had something to say to his tone.

His old friend was also smarter than many gave him credit for, so he knew full well when to push - and when not to.

The sound of a thunderbolt carried him away, and Azazel was left alone.

...

Satanael...

He'd have to deal with that himself.

...

The Olympians too.

Michael might intervene - something could have lured him from Heaven - or he might not.

Either way, Azazel had to plan for the worst.

...

Then the vague promise of Peace.

...

The light in Michael's eyes taunted him.

...

You simply chose to be one.

...

He took a deep breath.

...

He shook out his wings.

...

He counted back from ten in his head.

...

Then he soared into the air, stretched his wings, and razed the isle from the face of the Earth, before rocketing off to find something to tear apart.

Preferably alive.

And screaming.

He had some baggage to work through.

...​

So…

Alright, you got me.

One last interlude chapter, but this one is more of a sidestory because of how far it is from the main show (while still existing because of the massive ripples Dan and Sai have kicked off on the other end of the world, and this is basically just a preview.)

So, important enough to get a threadmark, with some huge developments within it, but don't expect what happens here to hit the main chapters any time soon.

Also, of the two OC's with important roles in this chapter, one of them has sort of a tie-in that was set up way, way back in the story. Curious to see how many of you spot it, since there've been a number of little Easter eggs in the last chapter too that were seemingly missed XD.

joker-the-dark-knight.gif


The Parents:

It was a beautiful morning on Fujimi Street, Kuoh Town, Tokyo.

The sun was out, the birds were singing, and it was a Saturday, which meant the neighbourhood was wonderfully peaceful.

Just a nice, quiet weekend morning.

Gorou Hyoudou sat at the breakfast table, leaning back comfortably in his favourite chair and humming under his breath as he worked his way through the morning paper.


His lovely wife was already hard at work, roving through the kitchen and getting a head start on lunch.

Buta no Kakuni

Thick cubes of pork belly braised until they practically melted apart under a spoon, simmered low and slow alongside daikon radish until the whole thing became perfection incarnate.

The smell alone was enough to make a grown man cry.

Gorou lowered his newspaper and inhaled deeply.

"This is the life."

Miki laughed from the kitchen.

"You're hopeless."

"Only for you, honey."

She waved the wooden spoon at him.

"Don't try that with me, you shameless playboy. Flattery won't get you extra servings!"

Eh, worth a shot.

He shrugged and went back to Kobo-chan in the paper's comic strip.

Their son, on the other hand, had already finished breakfast.

Rice bowl cleared, grilled fish gone, and miso soup vanished off without a trace.

Good - growing boys need their strength.

He hadn't touched his natto, though.

Issei avoided the beans like the plague, and now they sat there in lonely, fermented isolation.

Heresy.

The second his son disappeared upstairs to grab whatever the children needed before leaving the house, Gorou calmly reached across the table and claimed the abandoned portion for himself.

His foolish progeny's loss was his gain.

Half a minute later, Issei came thundering back down the stairs.

"I'm going to the park! My friends are already waiting!"

"Be careful!" Miki called after him from the kitchen.

"I will!"

"Watch the street when you're crossing!"

"I know!"

"And have fun!"

"Heck yeah!"

She laughed and waved him off. "Go!"

He was already halfway across the yard before the front door slammed shut, aaaaannnd his shoelace had been untied.

Gorou snorted and turned another page.

"Think he's figured little Irina out yet?"

He heard Miki sigh, which was answer enough.

Look, Gorou loved his boy, he really did - more than anything.

He was their little miracle, and he had enough heart to outpace a sports car.

Still…

Issei could be about as oblivious as they came.

'Ri-kun' didn't seem to have corrected the misunderstanding at any point since it began - for some unfathomable reason - but how his son still hadn't realized that his friend wasn't a boy...

Ah, well.

He'd get there eventually.

Gorou and Miki were only praying they'd be there when it happened, with a camera to boot.

It would be hilarious.

Moving on...

The skies were bright, lunch was on the way, and everyone was happy.

All in all?

It was quickly shaping up to be a good day in the Hyoudou household.

...

That's when the doorbell rang.

Gorou blinked and lowered his newspaper slightly.

"Are we expecting anyone?"

Miki looked just as surprised as she wiped her hands on a kitchen towel.

"No?"

If Issei had somehow forgotten something and come back already, the entire neighbourhood would know about it - the tyke would have rung the doorbell twenty times in a row and kicked the front door for good measure.

So who?

The doorbell rang again.

Gorou exchanged a look with his wife.

"I'll get it."

She turned off the heat and patted her hands dry as she walked through the hall.

Gorou heard the sound of the door opening fully.

Then voices.

One he didn't recognise.

Curious now, he folded up the newspaper and followed after her.

By the time he reached the genkan, Miki was already standing just inside the doorway - and outside stood a man.

At the genkan stood a tall man in a sharp suit, easily over six feet, with sun-tanned skin and dark, curly hair.

He gave a small, respectful bow of his head as Miki looked him over.

A foreigner?

Beside him was a woman with as just as neat a look to her - blouse, glasses, and hair tied back in a low pony-tail.

Miki glanced back at Gorou, surprised, and the man straightened slightly.

"Mr. Hyoudou, I presume?"

Flawless Japanese

"That's me, yes."

The look in those muted grey-blue eyes wasn't intimidating or even impolite, but it made Gorou mimic him and stand taller as well.

"My name is Hector Lyte."

He gestured lightly to the woman beside him, who nodded as well.

"And this is my associate, Katerina Papadopoulos."

She smiled lightly. "Good morning."

This Hector fellow turned back to them with an easy smile.

"Might we have a moment of your time?"


...

Ten Minutes Later:

"I'm sorry, what?"

Miki sounded floored, jaw-dropping, and Gorou couldn't blame her for it.

Right then, he felt about the same.

Across from them, on the living room couch where they'd just been invited, Hector and Katerina sat.

Katerina looked sympathetic, and Hector lowered his teacup with a soft clink.

"I can see that this is quite a bit to digest, so shall I begin from the start, for expediency's sake?"

Gorou and Miki nodded slowly.

"From the top, then."

Hector leaned back into the cushions like he was settling in for a ride.

"The Silver Crescent Group is a Greek private holding company based in Heraklion. Mostly long-term investments - real estate, shipping, infrastructure, and the like. There are also a few charitable foundations tied to cultural preservation across Europe and the Mediterranean-"

He paused, thinking it over for a moment.

"Well… suffice it to say the company has a fairly expansive portfolio. We can leave it at that for now."

He shifted his gaze between them.

"I sit on the board of the SCG. Katerina here is present in her capacity as legal counsel."

Which... sounded impressive enough, Gorou supposed.

And also completely out of left field.

Where was this going?

Then Hector's eyes locked on Miki specifically.

"Your uncle - Mr. Takahiro Saitō - was one of our major shareholders."

Gorou turned to stare at his wife right away.

She still looked absolutely gobsmacked.

"I don't-"

"As I understand it, he was estranged from your family," Hector said, tone gentle and leading. "A falling out in the past?"

Miki blinked once, then twice, before her eyes clouded in thought - like she was trying to reach for a memory just barely out of reach.

They all waited patiently.

"Ah… yes."

Yes?

"Uncle Taka?"

Hector nodded firmly.

"That's the one."

"I haven't seen him since I was a little girl," his wife whispered quietly. "He didn't get along with my grandparents. They fought over and over again. There was this horrible row..."

She shook her head.

"It was the last one. He sold his house and left the country when I was ten, and no one ever heard from him again."

Hector and Katerina exchanged a quick look.

"That matches what we have, yes."

"He went to Greece?"

The man nodded easily.

"In the early seventies, yes. He made some good investments early on, got involved with what eventually became the Silver Crescent Group, and built up quite a fortune over the years. A sizeable shareholding as well."

Miki stared at him for a moment, still surprised, before breaking into a small, genuine smile.

"Good for him. I'm glad he did so well for himself."

And that, right there, was one of the many reasons Gorou loved his wife.

Completely genuine.

Miki had lost her parents when she was young. Her grandparents had stepped up and raised her after that, but it hadn't exactly been easy.

Money had been tight more than once.

Having some mysterious rich uncle around to lend a hand would have helped plenty.

And yet... here she was, happy that he'd gone out into the world and made something of himself.

That's my girl!

But the internal victory lap didn't last.

Hector and Katerina were both quiet for another moment afterwards, and the air between them all changed.

Something was up.

Gorou's brow furrowed, but the foreign businessman leaned forward and braced his hands against his knees before he could get a word out.

"Regrettably," he said, "I have to inform you that he recently passed away."

Oh.

Oh.

Of all the rotten-

Miki let out a small sound, and Gorou's hand darted out to clasp hers.

To hear about this like this, after all this time...

He shook his head.

"Illness," Hector explained solemnly. "He was looked after properly. It was peaceful in the end."

"That's awful."

"Death takes us all when it will, Mrs. Hyoudou. A good life before the end is all any of us can really hope for."

Wise words.

Weighty and respectful, too, and so was the moment of silence after them.

But...

There was something about the way the man had voiced them that Gorou couldn't quite put his finger on.

Some strange oddity that made them feel just a little heavier.

The thought was derailed before he could do much of anything with it - Katerina adjusted the briefcase on her lap and set it on the table, and they all reflexively followed the motion.

"Please accept our sincere condolences for your loss. With that said, however-"

Hector didn't straighten, but it felt like he did.

"There is still the matter of your uncle's estate."

…

"…What?"

"Katerina, if you would."

"Right."

The woman nodded on cue, and both of the Hyoudous' eyes snapped over to her.

"As he had no direct heirs, Mr. Saitō left everything to his closest living relative."

The briefcase clicked open smoothly.

"That's you, Mrs. Hyoudou."

"..."

...Well then.

That, he hadn't seen coming.

"Excuse me?"

Katerina dutifully repeated the words, and Gorou watched his wife's mouth fall open again.

"But why?"

"I couldn't say." The lawyer shook her head apologetically. "I imagine he wanted it to stay in the family."

"Fam- I hardly knew him!"

She looked from Katerina to Hector and back to Katerina again.

"I forgot he even existed until just now!"

Which, admittedly, sounded… mildly terrible, but the man had apparently up and vanished just as she hit the double digits, entirely by choice.

Not so much as a letter or a phone call in well over thirty years.

Miki could hardly be blamed for that.

Their guests didn't seem to have much in the way of judgment, either.

"Blood is still blood, even a world and a lifetime away. That's the best answer I can give you, Mrs. Hyoudou."

Which was…

Unsatisfying, maybe - Miki still looked so uncertain - but not exactly unpleasant.

And not the point, either.

Katerina drew out a sheaf of papers half as thick as Gorou's wrist before clearing her throat.

"Now, we have a few things to go over here..."

A few things, as it turned out, read like an attempt to get back at the world for the invention of written language.

There were forms.

Then there were forms explaining the other forms.

Then there were forms acknowledging that those forms had, in fact, been properly explained.

And that was just to begin with.

"As for the estate itself…" Katerina said, checking a page, "There's cash, properties, investments, shares in the SCG itself, of course…"

She just kept going.

By the end of it, Gorou was starting to suspect his uncle-in-law had been the sort of man people made documentaries about.

One of those wild, one-in-a-million success stories everyone liked to pretend could be them someday… or the sort of news special that ended with mugshots and a very serious narrator saying 'authorities are still investigating the source of his initial capital.'

Either way…

This should not belong to a single human being.

His wife clearly agreed.

Gorou glanced at her again.

…Or maybe not, actually.

From the looks of it, the light of his life was still a good ten minutes behind and actively losing steam.

They'd probably lost her somewhere around the second set of forms.

She accepted the final stack of documents automatically when they were slid across the table, expression dazed, and Katerina straightened the remaining paperwork.

"Past this, there's one more matter I think it would be best to get ahead of now."

That got Miki to snap back to the present.

"What now?"

The flash of genuine panic in her eyes was entirely fair, all things considered.

Gorou was halfway there himself.

At least Katerina seemed to notice, because her expression softened slightly.

"I understand that this must all be very sudden and overwhelming for you, and I sincerely apologize for that. However-"

She stressed the word just enough to make him immediately suspicious.

"I am also obligated to inform you that this is a conditional bequest."

"Conditional…?"

Katerina nodded, and Gorou's eyes narrowed.

That sounded ominous.

"The inheritance cannot be claimed in full until the stated conditions have been fulfilled."

She glanced over another page, and he took the chance to raise his cup and go for a bracing sip.

"Just the one, really."

More ominous!

Miki perked up hopefully, though.

"The beneficiary must take up primary residence in any one of three designated properties for a minimum period of three consecutive years."

Gorou choked on his tea.

Katerina gamely pretended not to see it, or the way his wife slowly slumped back against the couch seat, suddenly looking more than a little faint.

"On that note… How do you feel about Greece?"

…

Later:

There were more questions after that.

A lot more.

But it didn't take long for them to piece together the gist of it all.

Apparently, Miki's mysterious Uncle Taka had been many things.

Successful.

Rich.

Important, at least wherever it was he'd settled.

He'd also been a bit - or maybe more than a bit - of a control freak.

Not that Gorou would ever say it aloud, mind you.

The man was dead.

But...

The intent behind it all was supposedly very clear, according to Katerina.

'Mr. Saitō' wanted whoever inherited his estate to actually experience the life he'd built.

Walk the same streets, live in the same home, and see the world the way he had.

Follow in his footsteps, at least a little, and see just how much he'd achieved all on his own.

Honestly?

Gorou could respect that.

Absolutely he could - The old man had spent decades building a life overseas and wanted the next generation to understand what it meant.

Fair enough.

Perfectly reasonable, even.

There was something oddly romantic about it, and even Miki had been charmed by the thought once the first bout of panic wore off.

Read: 'First'

The problem was that her Uncle Taka's sentimentality clearly dried up and withered away right about there, because there was also a deadline.

Six months.

Six. Months.

To move countries, or else the inheritance went kaput.

People needed six months to decide on a new refrigerator.

Gorou needed six months to decide on a new refrigerator, and even that wasn't a sure thing.

The one in the garage had been making dangerous noises for almost a year now and he still hadn't gotten around to replacing it.

That kind of time to relocate their entire lives?

"I'm sorry, but this is ridiculous."

Their guests didn't argue the point.

"There is a reason we chose to come in person."

Hector folded his hands together as he made his voice heard again.

"The delay is unfortunate."

Miki frowned.

"Delay?"

"The will should have been processed months ago."

There was an edge of picture-perfect irritation under that polite expression.

"Unfortunately, there were disputes regarding several international holdings, tax assessments, and jurisdictional matters. Matters which required resolution before the estate could proceed properly."

So... Lawyers had discovered other lawyers, and they didn't get along.

What a twist.

"The deadline itself was Mr. Saitō's," Hector continued. "Not ours. Had matters progressed as intended, you would have had considerably more time."

That did sound more reasonable, if entirely unhelpful.

"Regardless," Hector said, "the situation remains what it is. The Silver Crescent Group would prefer the transfer of Mr. Saitō's holdings to occur as smoothly as possible."

Gorou and Miki exchanged a look.

"What does that mean?"

"Mr. Saitō remained one of our largest individual shareholders until his passing. It is in everyone's interests that ownership is properly accounted for."

Ah.

That made... a lot of sense, actually.

If somebody owned enough of a company to make executives fly halfway around the world personally, it was probably worth keeping track of.

Though thinking about it in that sense did nothing to make this conversation less daunting, and it hadn't been a walk in the park to begin with.

"The Board has therefore authorised me to make an offer."

They exchanged another look.

"If you choose to relocate, the Silver Crescent Group will provide any assistance required."

Miki opened her mouth, and closed it again.

"Assistance?"

"Relocation expenses. Shipping. Legal support. Residency applications. Language assistance if desired."

He rattled them off one by one, like he was reading off a list.

"Property management. Educational placement for your son-"

That... had they mentioned Issei-?

"-Temporary accommodation if necessary, and more within reason."

Gorou's mind caught on that 'more.'

"Employment?"

"Should either of you require assistance securing positions after relocation, we would be happy to help facilitate introductions within your relevant fields, if not within the SCG itself."

He gave them a winning - but still restrained - smile.

"We're always looking for new talent, after all. Katerina here can attest to that."

The lawyer shot him a dry look, but her lips twitched anyway.

"He's not wrong. The hours are long, but the vacation days are generous, and the dental plan is to die for."

Miki snorted - more bewildered than anything else - and some of the tension deflated.

The rest of them cracked smiles, but Gorou...

How to put this?

He liked to think he wasn't a cynical guy - a man was never fully dressed without a smile and a good attitude in the morning - but everything about this situation sounded fantastical and perfect.

Too perfect.

"Why?"

Even for a big corporation, there had to be a line somewhere.

Why go through all the trouble?

Hector seemed to understand the question, and he smiled lightly.

"Due to unforeseen circumstances beyond your control, you are being asked to uproot your lives and move across the world."

True.

"The least we can do is ensure the process is not unnecessarily painful."

Which sounded great and all, but-

"And," Hector added airily. "In the effort of full disclosure, the complete distribution of Mr. Saitō's estate helps us even more than it helps the Hyoudou family. A small investment to move things along is nothing in the grand scheme."

This time, Gorou blinked.

When he put it that way....

The conversation wound down shortly after that..

There were final questions - about three dozen of them.

One last round of tea and several business cards for safety's sake.

Eventually, the pair rose from the couch and offered them polite bows.

"We appreciate your time."

"We'll need to discuss this," Miki admitted.

"Of course. We'll be staying in Kuoh for another month, subject to change. Please don't hesitate to call on us with any more questions or concerns."

No pressure.

A few minutes later, the front door closed behind them.

Gorou stood in the hallway for a moment before letting out a long breath.

"Huh."

Miki nodded weakly.

"Huh."

They looked at each other, before simultaneously glancing back towards the mountain of paperwork living it up on their coffee table.

His wife squinted suspiciously.

"I swear it grew three inches when we weren't looking."

"Of course it did."

She raised a brow at him.

"Honey, every man who's ever worked a desk job knows the golden rule."

"Don't yell at your boss?"

"Close," he admitted. "Never turn your back on the paperwork. That's what it wants you to do."

"Eh?"

"You work your way through it. You get close to the bottom of the pile. You think you're nearly done, and it lulls you into a false sense of security."

He looked at her with haunted eyes - a veteran of a thousand sleepless nights.

"When you look away, it multiplies. It breeds. Always and forever."

Cut off one head, and two more would spring out to drag you into overtime.

The horror.

He shuddered.

"Gorou…"

"I'm serious!"

His poor, naive wife shook her head at his invaluable wisdom - but he also saw her swallow a smile, so not all was lost in the end.

That didn't mean her nerves had settled, though.

"What are we going to do?"

"Move, obviously."

He said it so casually it took her brain a solid five seconds to process the words.

Three, two, one, and-

"What?!"

-Jackpot!

She whirled on him so fast she nearly tripped the other way.

"It's your inheritance." He shrugged off her incredulous stare with a grin. "What else are we going to do?"

"We can't just go-"

"Why not?"

The audacity of the question seemed to stun her, but only for a breath.

"Your parents-"

"Will be fine."

Thrilled, even, considering the circumstances.

"We can visit whenever we like - that's what holidays are for."

"Your job-"

"Just because 'not yelling at your boss' isn't the golden rule," he said very, very seriously, "doesn't mean I don't have to resist the urge."

Going out with a screaming match would be the highlight of his career, consequences be damned.

She seemed stumped for a second, but she still rallied for another go.

"The house-"

"Will keep. It's a house, honey, not a wooden shack."

It was only a few years, anyway.

"Worst comes to worst, we could always sell it." He paused, pretending to think about it now. "Or, if you want to go out with a bang, I'm pretty sure we have some lighter fluid and a box of matches somewhere-"

"Gorou!"

"Think of the insurance money, Miki!"

"We don't have that kind of insurance plan!"

"Well, thanks to all this, we don't need one anyway!" He stretched his arms and his grin wide. "Win-win!"

She looked at him like he'd lost his mind.

He looked back and unrepentantly owned the fact.

...

""Pffft-""

And just like that, they were both laughing. Gorou wrapped an arm around her shoulders, pulling her in close against his side.

It took a good little while for her to get it out of her system and slump against him.

"Better?"

She hummed against his chest

"Mhm."

He smiled and rested his cheek against the top of her head.

Perfect.

Now they could actually talk this through.

Jokes aside, he wasn't all that keen to just up and leave everything he'd ever known - even if he'd only been half-joking with that whole "stick it to the boss" routine.

The house... their life here…

Goodness, the memories.

All of the above, and then some.

The Hyoudous had a good thing going in Kuoh.

But - because it bore repeating - this was Miki's inheritance, and Issei's after hers.

Depriving them of that?

Gorou just didn't have it in him.

And hey-

"I've always wanted a Mediterranean vacation," he murmured to her soothingly, pulling her a little closer. "This is just that with a few extra steps."

"…Me too."

See?

They'd be just fine.

…

…Right after they figured out what to tell Issei when they made their choice.

Oh no.

Miki realized it right as he did.

"Not it!"

"Not - damn it!"

…

The Old Hunter:

Two months later - or thereabouts - the man known in this current age as 'Hector Lyte' watched the moving team haul boxes from the house.

He stood alone on the opposite sidewalk, hands in his pockets, completely obscured from ordinary mortal perception by a minor, tightly woven ward.

Across the asphalt, the Hyoudou household was a hive of activity. He could see the couple themselves gesturing animatedly through the window, directing the movers where to haul this and move that, but those specifics mattered little and less to him.

He didn't care about their interior decorating choices - the fact that they were moving at all was enough.

The mission was already halfway complete.

And to think they'd managed it without any heavy-handed tactics…

That was the trick of it.

Takahiro Saito had existed, and he had left Japan decades ago - they'd checked - but the man had died in an entirely mundane backpacking incident in Northern Europe years ago, and he hadn't been half so successful as implied.

Or affiliated with the SCG at all, for that matter, be it in its mundane operations or on the other end of the Masquerade.

Yet he needed to be, and thus he was, and so the Hyoudou's were unknowingly reeled in.

Hector sighed deeply.

As far as plots go, it was elaborate, convoluted and dishonest to the point of ridiculousness, but it was better than outright mental compulsion.

That had its inevitable uses, unfortunately, but considering the power dwelling in the family's child…

He shook his head.

Best not give a Longinus wielder a reason for future spite and vengefulness if they could avoid it.

The carrot served better than the stick here, even if said vegetable was near-entirely counterfeit.

And speaking of which…

Hector tilted his head to the side and stepped back, just in time for little Issei Hyoudou to come sprinting by, hollering at the top of his voice.

A moment later, an orange-haired blur darted after him, and neither of the children perceived him at all.

As expected.

He was aware of the girl, of course - the daughter of one of the locally stationed biblical exorcists.

Clearly untrained, unremarkable, and debatably informed about the wider supernatural world as it is.

A non-issue.

Her father was a bigger concern, but between him, his half-dozen associates, the assortment of stray yōkai and creatures of the night that drifted through the region, and the devil noble overseeing Kuoh's territory, the unassumingly small town was fit to burst with potential security risks.

He had worked around all of them without issue.

If a child barely into her double digits could sense his presence where the rest hadn't, then something had already gone very, very wrong.

"There you are."

He tilted his head back as Katerina jogged up to him in a pair of jeans, a jacket, and sturdy boots in a style reminiscent of a certain goddess they both worshiped.

And wasn't that an odd thing to think about - he still remembered the era where tiered flounced skirts and open-front bodices were the height of womanly fashion

The Bronze Age had been an experience.

"Problem?"

"Nothing I couldn't handle."

She came to a stop beside him and followed his gaze out toward the park.

Hidden from prying eyes, the two watched the children play in the distance.

"I'm going to need more than that for an answer, Katerina."

She rolled her eyes at him.

"It was nothing, Mr. Lyte - and gods that's a silly nickname."

'Hector' was unimpressed, and she surrendered after a look.

"The boy was playing with some friends over at the park. There was an old man there."

Her expression darkened into a scowl.

"Rotten old creep, really. Spewing stuff kids have no business being exposed to. I roughed him up a little and flagged down a policeman to handle the rest. Problem solved - and I did it before he could traumatize Mr. Future Red Dragon Emperor over there." She nodded in Issei's direction. "Aren't I a saint?"

"You're a Huntress."

"You know what I mean!"

He did, and he turned away before she could see him smirk.

Young talent. Always so easy to rile up.

"I will trust your judgement. Your thoughts on your charge?"

"He's a good boy," she answered without hesitation. "Very bright, super outgoing, and damn loud, too."

He nodded, tracking her gaze.

"Also, definitely a bit spoiled," she added.

He raised a brow.

"Nothing terrible," she explained quickly, "but look at the little tyke and tell me he isn't the apple of his parents' eye. They'd let him get away with just about anything short of burning their house down."

Yes, he'd gotten that impression as well.

It was nothing a firmer hand couldn't settle, should circumstances call for it in due time.

That said...

"You would know, wouldn't you?"

She immediately turned her nose up at him. "I have no idea what you're talking about."

"I'm sure."

Her sister, Elena, had left the Hunt some time ago and had since had children of her own. Katerina utterly delighted in playing the 'cool aunt' whenever she wasn't attending to her duties with the rest of the Hunters.

If Elena didn't actively put her foot down, Katerina would happily ply them with presents and indulge their every whim the first chance she got.

She still tried anyway, and Elena's rants on the matter were always inspired.

"Now, what else-?"

An electronic chime cut him off, and he reached into his suit pocket and pulled out a sleek cell phone in the same breath.

Katerina watched him closely, but his expression went entirely impassive as he scanned the text.

The look on her face sharpened in turn, and above them, the afternoon sky was quietly bruising into a heavy, leaden grey.

"Something wrong?"

"Nothing we need to concern ourselves with now." His eyes traced the words carefully. "But it seems Lord Chiron's rampage against the Grigori some time back was the gift that just keeps on giving."

He knew why, of course:

A demigod born on this day and age, and a son of Apollon at that.

How serendipitous.

But whatever circumstances had led to that same young man being attacked under the Wise Centaur's protection …

Well, the results were a thing unto themselves.

The Fallen Angels had been made to bleed for the insult, but it was their own sheer malice and stupidity that made the immediate aftermath so catastrophic for them.

Lord Chiron had retaliated - and emptied their cages on his way out.

And what cages they were.

Prisoners and test subjects and everything in between, belonging to any number of supernatural species high and low.

More than a few of them, were under the aegis of much greater factions - which was political disaster enough - but for the Crows, this latest debacle struck much closer to home.

"It's come to light that certain rogue and fringe elements within the biblical Church have been caught experimenting on their famed Holy Factor."

"The stuff that gives their elite exorcists that extra edge?"

He nodded shortly.

"Their goal was to find a way to harness and synthesize it within chosen candidates, rather than just relying on natural inheritance or base luck to find potential wielders for their holy arms."

Katerina blinked in surprise, but his focus had already drifted back to the phone and the details therein.

From a purely practical standpoint, it was a sensible goal.

A strong Holy Factor ensured a certain degree of promise. It made wielding particular Church-issued weaponry easier, and greatly improved a candidate's chances of eventually attuning to some of the more powerful relics in the Church's possession.

On paper.

Trying to artificially increase the number of prospective warriors under their command made perfect strategic sense.

The problem was how they went about doing it.

"Some of these rogue actors collaborated with the Grigori, outsourcing elements of their 'research'."

The word echoed unpleasantly.

"To hide it from their high command. Their contacts were apparently only too happy to assist in human experimentation - up to and including on children."

Katerina reared back as if struck, a vicious string of curses slipping past her lips.

"Bastards."


Quite.

Granted, the conspiracy seemed to center around one major player - an Archbishop by the name of Valper Galilei - but he certainly hadn't lacked help among his more monstrous peers.

They had wanted plausible deniability, but what was that saying again?

About their Lord working in mysterious ways?

Whatever the irony of it all, Vasco Strada himself had reportedly descended upon the Vatican to drag the man and everyone remotely connected to him to justice.

Fitting.

Even before he'd sworn himself to his goddess, he could never stand the mistreatment of children.

Call it the prerogative of a prince.

The few stray droplets began to fall and speckle the dark asphalt, and he slid the phone back into his pocket.

"As I said. Distasteful in the extreme, but nothing we need-"

The power in the air warped.​

Both of their heads snapped south as the first distant explosion rumbled across the edge of Kuoh.

...​

The Exorcist Who Fell In Love:

By the time everything was nearly said and done, the rain over the outskirts of town had turned the dirt around them into a thick, crimson-tainted mud.

Masaomi Yaegaki staggered heavily against a shattered stone lantern, his breath coming in ragged, wet wheezes.

His ears rang and his vision swam. His skull pounded.

Even breathing was hell.

Across the courtyard were the bodies of half a dozen high-ranking Exorcists - people he'd know and trained with, fought alongside, and now…

He swallowed, and it hurt.

His uniform was shredded to ribbons, and a jagged, deep gash tore across his ribs, leaking enough blood to make him lightheaded, and the rain couldn't wash it away fast enough.

The jagged piece of shrapnel from a sword he could barely remember breaking was worse, rammed deep into his left shoulder from the force of the blast and making his vision go white from pain every time he twitched the arm.

The grip he still had on his sword was pathetic, and the holy light around the steel was flickering dangerously, on the edge of giving out.

Just like he was.

"Masaomi."

God damn it all.

Touji Shidou was still there, standing twenty paces off and hefting that ridiculous family blade of his against one shoulder.

Ridiculous orange hair and mournful eyes and all.

Even through the rain, the solemn sadness and grief was pouring off of him like tide.

As if all regret in the world was supposed to make killing him better.

"Enough, Masaomi."

Son of a-

"They're using you, Sensei," He choked out, spitting a mouthful of thick blood onto the wet stones.

He could say that the brutal agony paled in front of the betrayal - something poetic about how the man who had taught him how to hold a sword was standing between him and the only thing that mattered, trying to end him - but right then, they were about even.

"You betrayed the path of God," Touji said, and his voice was calm and flat.

Like a judge passing sentence.

Masaomi saw red.

"I didn't!" he roared, and his one voice cracked with the sheer… everything. "Are you even listening to yourself right now!?"

He forced himself upright, his legs shaking violently under their own weight, more blood dripping from his fingertips and down into the mud.

I just need a chance.

Touji shook his head.

"You allowed that Devil to seduce you, and you sold out Church secrets-"

"I'm an upstart, first-generation Holy Sword wielder who thinks half the current Cardinals can go pound sand!" His scream was beyond hysterical now, and it was only halfway because of the pain. "What secrets do I know?!"

Facts didn't matter anymore - he knew that - but how could Sensei be so damned stupid?

The higher-ups just needed an excuse to kill him.

To kill Cleria.

And they couldn't even be bothered to come up with something that made sense.

What a pitiful joke.

"You have to believe me."

And the worst part?

He almost got through to him.

Touji's grip on his massive hilt didn't loosen, but Masaomi could see his eyes flicker - just a little - and his stance hesitated.

It was the only invitation he needed.

Now.

Drowning out the agony in his ribs, Masaomi poured the absolute remainder of his energy into his blade, and Touji tensed.

"Don't-!"

With a savage, upward rip, he unleashed a blinding arc of pure light directly at his face. The crescent of gold screamed through the rain, bursting towards the man like a thunderclap.

Touji snapped out of the hesitation instantly, ducking low as it sheared a few strands of his hair and detonated against the shrine gate behind him.

His sword came up then, pulsing and ready to counter the next one-

But Masaomi was already gone.

He tore past Touji's left flank in a streak of mud and filth and blood, hurtling across the courtyard and toward the tree line so fast he could almost feel something inside of him give away.

Many somethings, maybe.

It didn't matter.

Cleria.

They'd ambush her too.

He had to get to her, now.

"Masaomi!"

His sensei could always recover with terrifying speed.

Too fast.

He could hear him thundering behind him, closing the distance with monstrous speed.

No, no, no!

His lungs burned like wildfire, and every step sent white-hot knives from his mangled ribs up to his punctured shoulder.

Masaomi couldn't outrun him.

Not like this.

Spinning on his heel mid-sprint, he used his momentum to throw every last ounce of strength he had left into a desperate, two-handed overhead strike. His Holy Sword flared with a brilliant, dying burst of golden fury-

CRACK!

Touji met the blow with a brutal, single-handed parry. The shockwave rattled every atom in Masaomi's ruined body and nearly tore the sword from his grip. He snarled savagely and tried to slash from the side, but Touji planted a heavy kick straight to his chest, sending him skidding backward through the mud until he crashed into the root of a massive cedar tree.

And there go the rest of the ribs.

The thought was delirious, muted by the second mouthful of blood he spat out as he staggered to his feet. It was an ugly sort of movement - so unstable that he had to use his flickering sword as a crutch just to force his protesting muscles to move.

"I have to... save her..." he whispered hoarsely.

But he could barely lift his head.

"It's over for both of you, Masaomi." Touji shook his head quietly and hefted his sword, looking resolute. "Please, lay down your sword and let it end."

…

That…

…

He…!!!!

…

It was the pity in the words that set him off again, and pure rage howled through his veins and tore out of him with a deafening scream.

"LIKE HELL!"

Masaomi erupted off the tree with enough force to detonate it and the forest floor behind him, hurling himself forward and taking a wild - desperate - slash at Touji's neck.

Have it your way, sensei - to the death!

For a split second, it even looked like it might land.

But his teacher knew his every move - he'd taught him most of them himself.

Forgetting that was his deadliest mistake to date.

Touji ducked beneath the arc of the blade, stepping inside his guard.

The lethal closeness allowed Masaomi to see the genuine tear tracking down his master's face just before the impact.

No-!

The massive blade drove forward, a clean, devastating thrust that punched straight through his stomach in a shower of spraying gore.

…

…

…

Oh.

…

…

…

Thunder burst against the sky.

…

…

…

The rage vanished. The pain dulled.

The desperate adrenaline that had kept him moving crumbled away like so much dust.

…

…

…

The golden glow of his standard Holy Sword shattered like glass, the fragments dissolving into the rain as the hilt slipped from his fingers.

He barely heard it land against the mud.

…

…

…

When Masaomi blinked, he'd joined it on back, staring up at the raging heavens with this… awful confusion.

Slow and heavy and impossible to escape.

It was the only thing he could really feel as his strength faded, and the darkness began to creep over the edges of his vision.

It can't end like this.

…

…

…

It can't.

…

…

…

"Rest, my student."

Touji Sensei was still there - this vague outline of a shape standing over him to the right, head bowed.

His voice was low and pitiful, and maybe, if Masaomi had any life left in him - if he wasn't actively losing what he had to his name right then and there - he could have taken some spiteful satisfaction in that."

But there was nothing.

Confusion and despair and failure he'd never make up for if he had a thousand lifetimes to try.

"May God forgive you - and myself - for all our sin- Hurk!"

He choked.


At first, Masaomo didn't understand what he was looking at. His eyes were swimming, and the world was sickening blue of grey rain and creep in black

But then a neuron or three fired, and he registered the second outline.

A bigger, fainter shape standing directly behind his sensei.

The same one that had reached out and clamped a hand around the other swordman's throat, and hoisted him completely off the ground by his neck with effortless power.

…

What?

…

Touji's legs kicked out wildly as Masaomi stared, but he might as well have been a fly raging against a mountain for all the good it did.

"When you've walked this Earth as long as I have, you tend to develop patience and a level head by sheer necessity,"

The stranger's voice was as flat as a sheet of paper… and somehow still full of cold, cold anger.

"But if there's one thing that still drives me to a youthful rage… it is betrayal."

Thunder snapped across the clouds again.

The flash lit up the woods for half a heartbeat and twisted the shadows into something monstrous, but the sound of it wasn't nearly loud enough to drown out Sensei's strangled scream.

Schrriiiip!

The wet, jagged crunch of something violently tearing and breaking cut it short. Something heavy landed in the mud a second later, too far away for Masaomi's fading vision to make out.


…

Silence.

…

He blinked, and now the stranger was staring down at him.

"Now... what to do with you?"

Masaomi didn't understand what was happening. He didn't understand anything anymore.

Death was right around the corner, and it was swallowing everything he had to give.

But even as the lights were going out, he still knew what was important.

The only thing that mattered.

"Cleria…"

It was so low and so weak, it was barely a vibration against his lips.

"Cleria Belial?" The words were truly empty now, impossible to read. "The Devil overseer of this region?"

Masaomi managed to nod.

Once.

A newborn could have done it better, but it was just about all he had left in him.

"If you're not with them… if you're not here to kill… save her," he wheezed, and even his own voice sounded a million miles away. "Please."

"You would have me save a Devil?"

It came out calm and level, but Masaomi could imagine the disbelief behind the question.

He'd felt it himself, once upon a time.

"She's… she's not like them," he tried desperately.

He wasn't even sure how much of it the stranger could actually understand - everything was mangled and slurred, his throat thick, and the taste of blood and blood and more blood kept welling up in his mouth, threatening to choke him.

But he couldn't stop.

He had to make whoever this was understand.

It was the only chance left.

"No peerage," he gasped, babbling, throwing out anything and everything he could scramble for. "She loves the human world. She… she cried at every movie we watched where a dog dies. Thinks pineapple on pizza is the worst crime in history."

Nothing in Heaven or Earth could have stopped the tears then.

"She made this place safe… for any supernatural who wanted a quiet home. Never asked anything in return. She's good."

Lovelier than all the stars in the night sky.

"Kind."

He could almost see her now - that smile that drove him out of his mind and back - and the memory of it made his failing eyes burn that much more.

"Please."

The rain felt cold on his face, but the inside of his chest was growing numb.

"I beg you."

One more time, with the last of his heart.

"Save her."

…

…

…

And the darkness won.

…

…

…

"Very well."

The Old Hunter:

Instinct.

It was a valuable thing - a blade with an edge forever capable of being honed.

It was what had him ordering Katerina to transport the Hyoudou family away the instant this violent spectacle began, consequences be damned.

They could deal with the fallout later.

Instinct was also what had him observe the battle between the two exorcists - just long enough to get an idea of what was happening.

(Old, old wounds were what had him punishing Touji Shidou so violently, but that was a story for another time.)

In the end, it was also instinct that had him saving Masaomi Yaegaki's life, listening to the desperate man's pleading before sending him away into Katerina's care. A devil and an exorcist bound by love, destined to be struck down on the same day in what could only be a betrayal instigated by their own.

How positively Shakespearean.

There was something of value here; if nothing else, he would not be a hunter worth the name if he couldn't follow such a trail.

Stepping forward from the blood-soaked clearing, he vanished, teleporting directly to the other end of Kuoh.

The thick, cloying magical barrier that had sprung up in sync with the first explosion loomed over an area roughly the size of a dozen city blocks.

Impossible to perceive for mortals, and evidently powerful enough that cracking it open from the outside would have been an impossible feat for someone of Katerina's caliber.

But he was a far different beast.

He didn't bother breaking it down - instead, in a flash of sharp, pointed silver light that wrapped around his body like an old friend, he simply stepped forward and burned a hole right through it.

A sound followed - faint and crisp and not unlike shattering glass - but it wasn't worth noting.

Inside, the sky was a heavy blanket of choking black smoke. The surroundings were fiery, crumbling ruins, and he could immediately tell that every human in the vicinity was dead.

They likely had been from the very first strike.

The needless slaughter made his already foul mood significantly worse.

That was why, when he followed the trail of dead and mangled Abrahamic devils leading into a particular power-blasted neighborhood reduced to a crater, he only spent a split-second observing the scene.

Cleria Belial he recognized, though she was now an unconscious, bloody mess.

One of her bat-like wings had been completely torn off, the flesh flayed raw on her other side, limbs broken unevenly, and her silver hair was matted with so much blood it clung to the cracked earth like a gruesome, morbid halo.

Still alive, if only just.

The other untouched, unruffled figure standing over her he also recognized.

What in Her name-?

The man was a pristine, meticulously tailored portrait of modern Underworld nobility, sporting the kind of immaculate blonde hair, blue eyes, and high-class aristocratic tailoring that practically begged to be dragged through the mud.

A palpable storm of demonic power rolled off him, and he was quite evidently enjoying his victim's suffering.

Hector spared another second to wonder why a high-ranking Devil Rating Game Champion would be involved in a convoluted affair like this - whatever it actually was - and in that brief window of silence, Bedeze Abaddon turned toward him.

The blonde devil raised an eyebrow, and his gaze gleamed with malice.

"And who are-?"

He never finished the sentence, because Hector's fist drove squarely into his face.

The impact was cataclysmic.

Boom!

Rubble was instantly blown backward in a violent shockwave. The displaced air snuffed out the fires. The very earth heaved up and ruptured as the devil was propelled away like a fallen meteor, tearing through the debris and carving anew crater of his very own.

Cleria Belial was safely enclosed by a protective dome of silver light that hardly cost him a thought to summon.

A necessary precaution - she looked as though a gentle tap would be the absolute end of her.

With a flick of his wrist, he teleported her away to safety alongside Yaegaki.

But he stayed behind.

With how closely this catastrophe had struck to the Hyoudou home, there might be relevant information that needed extracting from this high-ranking devil.

Vital, even.

At least a reason for this sudden carnage, because a mere dalliance between two members of two opposing factions wouldn't warrant this - not alone.

Something else was at play.

And…

He could admit, deep down, that he had some sudden aggression to work through.

Summoning his ancient armor over his frame and calling his spear to his hand was the work of a single, fluid thought.

The gleaming bronze and silver reformed around him, heavy with the weight of innumerable lifetimes of battle.

Then, Hector -

No

He stopped, mentally refusing the false name.

He did not feel like a Hector at this moment.

A bloodied roar tore out of the fresh crater ahead of him, and a localized hurricane of demonic energy flattened the world as the enraged Abaddon came screaming back into the battle.

He didn't wait for him to finish the dramatic entrance.

Instead, Hippolytus - son of Theseus, Prince of Troezen, He Who Was Risen, and eternal devotee of Artemis Agrotera - leveled his spear and launched himself forward into the teeth of the storm.


…
