For the first - and last - time, we shall have a double-update!

Over 22k words in total, I'm crying rn

Kuoh Town, Japan.
Months later:

The day had been grey from the moment Irina Shidou woke up.

Not raining, and not sunny, either.

Just a low blanket of cloud hanging over Kuoh, turning the park into a collection of muted greens and browns.

If she were the more poetic-minded, she'd probably say that it was the sort of day that made everything feel quieter than it really was.

As it was, she was a ten-year-old at the tail end of the worst months of her life.

Her thoughts on the weather started and ended with: "Dull, and I hate it."

But that wasn't really a surprise, was it?

There wasn't much that wasn't muted and halfway soulless in her life these days.

Whenever she tried to trace everything back to the beginning, her mind always returned to the same night.

The night she'd learned what an emergency ward really smelled like.

Antiseptic and bleach.

Plastic and panic.

Total, cold horror.

That, she could never forget - had been everywhere that night, and thick enough to choke on.

The lights overhead had been painfully bright, and the floor had seemed to stretch forever beneath her little shoes as she followed her mother through the corridors of the intensive care unit.

They had looked enormous to her.

Her father had been lying in a bed surrounded by machines, and he hadn't looked like he was supposed to.

He hadn't looked like her Papa.

Touji Shidou was a big, strong man. And he was loud, and his laugh was big and rumbly, and he was supposed to cackle too loudly at his own jokes and scoop her up without warning, like she weighed nothing at all.

And, and, and…

None of that helped.

That Papa was gone, and what was left behind that night had been pale and still, buried beneath blankets, tubes and bandages.

His left arm was gone.

She remembered staring at the thick layers of gauze around his shoulder and not understanding how something so important could simply... not be there anymore.

It didn't make sense - where did it even go?

Mama and the doctors had talked, and the words meant nothing to Irina.

Bad, scary things about his spine, and his hurts, and she only understood enough to know that Papa would never be the same again.

He couldn't speak, or raise his other hand, or even move at all.

He would never move again.

All he could do was look at her.

That was the part she remembered most.

His eyes.

They followed her whenever she entered the room.

And Irina couldn't stand it.

Not because she didn't love him - she adored her Papa.

But… seeing him like that…

She just couldn't.

She was a terrible daughter.

For months afterward, their house became something straight out of a nightmare.

Even when Papa was brought home, everything was always so cold.

Irina would sometimes stand outside his bedroom door with her hand on the handle and just... freeze.

She'd known it was important.

She knew Papa needed her too, just like Irina had always needed him.

She desperately, desperately wanted to - so much that she'd cry herself to sleep more often than not.

There wasn't any reason to be afraid, right?

And then she'd remember those eyes, and that would do it.

Sometimes she'd manage to enter - she'd fix his pillows, or bring him water, or help her mother with whatever little things needed doing.

Other times, she wouldn't even make it past the door.

Her mother didn't do much better.

The woman Irina had once known became thinner and quieter as the weeks passed. She spent more and more time speaking with the men who came to their home in dark suits.

There were meetings, and boring adult conversations, and doors that slammed shut the moment she saw Irina trying to peek through.

Later was always the answer.

Until, eventually, her mother sat her down and told her the truth.

Not all of it - Irina was too young for that.

But enough.

The supernatural was real.

Monsters were real, and devils too, and fallen angels before them and so, so much more.

So many things that belonged in stories and nightmares were walking around in the real world, right that very second.

And one of them had done this to her father.

Knowing that changed everything.

The nightmares - and there were plenty before - didn't stop after she learned the truth.

If anything, they got worse.

The shadows in her bedroom seemed different now, and every strange noise outside her window became something to be afraid of.

She'd wake up gasping in the middle of the night, soaked through with sweat, and stare at the ceiling until morning because she was too scared to close her eyes and see it all again.

It only worked half the time.

Most of the time, she wished Issei was still there.

The Hyoudou family had lived nearby for longer than the Shidous had, and he was her friend.

The most important one of them all, even if he didn't know about… her.

Issei was loud and obnoxious and impossible to ignore - everyone always said he was too loud by half - but he was also brave.

The bravest person Irina had ever met, except maybe Papa.

Even then, it was different with Issei.

A good different - one that Irina had liked.

Then the Hyoudous just... vanished.

They moved away without warning, and one day Irina realized that Issei simply wasn't there anymore.

Poof.

It must have happened right when Papa first got hurt, and she never got to tell him how bad things had gotten, or how scared she was, or how desperately she wished she were half as brave as him when everything came crashing down like a house of cards.

On fire.

Worst of all, she never even got to say goodbye.

If she ever needed proof that the world hated her, that would have been it.

Was this a punishment from God?

Why?

Irina had never - None of them had ever-?​

Eventually, she got used to hurting.

Or at least, she thought she had.

Because just when Irina was starting to believe that this was what her life was going to be now - her and Mama both - something changed.

It started with a man named Ewald Cristaldi.

She remembered him standing at their front door, looking like the sort of grown-up even Issei would have been leery of standing too close to.

He was stern and straight-backed, with a way of speaking that made everyone listen very carefully, or at least try very hard to pretend to.

He was also a Cardinal of the Catholic Church.

Naturally, Irina still didn't understand most of what he said, but this time, that didn't stop her from hiding nearby and listening anyway.

Especially when Mama started crying - and not the sounds that Irina had gotten used to by now, filtering in through her bedroom wall when her mother thought she was still asleep.

No, this was different, and full of relief.

There was a girl who couldn't have been any older than Irina - a young holy woman in the Vatican.

Unlike her, though, she had a gift.

Something special - incomparable - bestowed upon her by God himself.

Sacred Gear - Twilight Healing.

"Cardinal… please…"

"It's true, Madame. The Lord smiles on the faithful."

Cardinal Cristaldi knew Papa.

Not well, but he'd fought alongside him once, and he respected him, and that was enough to 'pull strings' that normally wouldn't have been pulled, and get Papa taken to Italy.

To someone who might actually be able to fix everything.

Whoever she was, Asia Argento's name alone had flipped her entire world upside down.

Again.

Irina remembered how she'd felt when she heard that.

It was almost terrifying.

No, actually - it was.

Like fire burning inside an icy pit inside of her she'd never even known was there.

After that, everything moved very, very quickly.

The transport was large and unmarked, and there were people from the Church there to make sure everything went smoothly.

Mama went with him.

Irina couldn't go yet, no matter how much she begged and pleaded and screamed.

There were too many things to be done, people to talk to, and problems that even the Church needed a stupid amount of time to sort out.

Vasco Strada, Adopted Children, Rogue Actors, Holy Sword project….

Irina doubted any of them were aware of just how much she'd overheard - no matter how little of it she actually understood - and she didn't care either, because she wasn't going.

No matter what she tried, the answer was always the same, and eventually, she was left behind.

For a little while, Mama promised just before the black car pulled away, but as far as Irina was concerned, it didn't make any difference at all.

Why does everyone keep leaving me behind?​

So there she was, sitting and reminiscing and generally wallowing in her own misery, when that little routine was throughly interrupted.

"It is a heavy thing, isn't it? The fear of the unknown."

Irina flinched and looked up.

A man was standing a few paces away.

She hadn't heard him approach, and that immediately made a little alarm bell in her head start screaming - and it wasn't even the one she'd grown used to after the revelation of the supernatural.

Stranger danger!

He was dressed in a dark, impeccably tailored coat, with a polished silver cross pinned neatly to the lapel. His hair was white, almost unnaturally so, and there was something about the way he carried himself that reminded her of the Church men who had been coming to their house.

Was he part of the security team Mama mentioned?

Irina tightened her grip on the bench beneath her, and the man seemed to notice, because he stopped where he was.

"Forgive me. I didn't mean to startle you, Miss Shidou. I'm an associate of the gentlemen you've seen at your home. A… coworker of Father Cristaldi."

He seemed sincere, and it made her shoulders relax just a little.

So, not a random creepy man from the bushes.

Probably.

She still kept her eyes narrowed, though.

"You're from the Church?"

"I am."

She studied him for another moment, and he waited her out patiently.

"You know my papa?"

"I do." Something about his expression softened. "I've been overseeing some of the arrangements concerning his… present condition. Your father was - is - a remarkable man, young Irina. A warrior of the faith, and a good one."

That was…

Irina looked down at her shoes.

She didn't know anything about that.

What she did know were things she didn't want to remember.

…

Papa laughing.

Papa carrying her.

Papa lying in that bed.

…

Those eyes.

Always, always watching her.
…

So sad.

…

She swallowed.

"Is he going to be okay?"

The question was out before she could stop it, and the stranger was quiet for another long moment.

"I hope so."

There was plenty of sincerity there too, and even though the answer made her want to cry a little, she only sniffled and finally slumped down entirely.

She heard him take a few steps closer as she wiped at her eyes.

"Sorry."

"There is nothing to apologize for." He answered kindly. "A little wariness is good for the soul, I think, and fear is no greater sin-"

Irina shook her head so hard the words caught in his throat.

"I don't want to be scared anymore," she whispered.

All she'd been these last few months was scared, and she despised it, more than anything.

The man watched her carefully.

"Of what, child?"

"Everything."

The monsters.

What happened to Papa.

Going into his room and seeing him like that.

Every one of them was a nightmare that kept her up most nights, and every one was valid, but when she looked up at the expectant stranger, the first thing out of her mouth was:

"I don't want to be afraid of Papa anymore, and I don't want to get hurt like he did."

…

Irina really was a terrible daughter.

The man, however, had nothing to say to that at first, and that somehow made it easier to keep talking.

"I don't want Mama to cry anymore either."

If she had to hear her crying through the night even one more time, Irina might lose her mind.
She just knew.

There was another stretch of silence, and the man kept staring at her with those solemn, eerie metal-grey eyes.

Then he cleared his throat and asked, "And what would you do if you didn't have to be afraid?"

If she didn't have to be-?

Irina didn't need long to think about it.

Maybe months before, it would have been a strange, philosophical question.

Tricky and not at all in a child's wheelhouse, but after everything that had happened?

"I'd be brave and strong."

The answer still surprised even her with how quickly it came, but the man nodded slowly, like her words were exactly what he'd been expecting.

Or waiting for.

"Strong enough to protect yourself?"

Irina hesitated.

"Mama and Papa too."

And the man laughed, freely and in a smooth, smooth voice.

"Of course."

Irina knew that he wasn't laughing at her - call it a gut feeling - but a part of her still bristled anyway, because of the feeling curdling deep in her belly.

That same storm she'd been carrying ever since the night everything changed.

Fear and horror and anger and helplessness and anger again.

The desperate need to force things to make sense again.

She didn't want to be scared anymore.

"Then perhaps you should consider becoming an exorcist."

Irina blinked.

It might have been a flinch, too.

"Like Papa?"

"Like your father."

Her heart gave a little jump.

Exorcists… She knew the term.

The people that fought the things that went bump in the night.

Exorcists were like her father had been, before something had gotten the better of him.

…

Exorcists were strong.

"How?"

This time, she knew she wasn't imagining it.

Those eyes were definitely glinting.

"With the right teacher, anything is possible - and I, personally, would be honored to set you on that route."

"You can teach me?"

Anticipation - that's what Irina failed to recognize in that gaze.

Anticipation, and hunger.

"If your parents agree, yes."

He extended a gloved hand toward her.

"I can teach you how to fight. How to use your faith and your Light as something more than just a fleeting comfort. How to stand against the things that frighten you instead of hiding from them, and rise even higher than you ever dreamed."
Irina stared at his hand.

He could teach her.

She hesitated, before abruptly remembering Papa, and his laughter, and missing arm.

Those sad eyes.

She thought of Mama next, and how badly she wanted her family to be happy again.

The man gave her another genial smile when she looked up at him again.

"Let's make your father proud, young lady."

And he had her, just like that.

Slowly, she reached out and took his hand, and his smile went oh so very wide indeed.

"Marvelous. Shall we have a proper introduction, then?"

He didn't wait for her answer.

"My name is Valerio Sellzen, Director of the Sigurd Institute, and I hereby formally welcome you into the fold, Irina Shidou."

The satisfaction in his voice was unmistakable.

"Let's make a good showing of it, shall we?"

And with a simple shake, her fate was sealed.

…
​
Elsewhere:

The mud was cold, but the rain was colder, falling from the heavens as a relentless downpour that bled the remaining warmth from the earth and turned the ancient mountains of Nagano into a labyrinth of slick, treacherous slopes.

For seven long, terrible months, ten-year-old Akeno Himejima had been running.

Her shoes had rotted away weeks ago; her small feet were now wrapped in tatters that barely passed muster and were useless regardless - her physiology was more help there than that pathetic patch job, and even then only barely.

Tonight, the heavy, suffocating scent of the Himejima clan's purification incense seemed determined to drown out the traces of grass and dirt in the air, and Akeno knew they were closing in.

She could feel it, like a sudden, sharp prickle at the base of her neck.

Magic, or a barrier, or something of the sort - she didn't know, and it didn't matter.

So she ran, and ran and ran until she couldn't anymore - then the exhaustion hit her all at once, deep and merciless, and she collapsed into the shadow of a decaying torii gate at the edge of an abandoned mountain village that would offer about as much protection as a sheet of paper would against the rain.

Hot tears mixed with the downpour on her cheeks, and her lungs burned as she shivered violently.

She didn't want to die.

More than that, though, she didn't want them to take her.

Every time she closed her eyes, the rain vanished, replaced by the smell of burning tatami and copper.

She could still hear the sickening, wet tear of steel cutting through flesh.

She could still see her mother, Shuri, collapsed on the floor, a fountain of brilliant, terrible crimson staining her white shrine maiden robes as her own kin slaughtered her right in front of her daughter.

"Run, Akeno!"​

That final, choked scream echoed constantly in her head, over and over again, mixed in with the harsh, cold voices of the hunters calling her a monster, an abomination that needed to be purged from the honor of the clan.

It wasn't enough that they had killed her mother.

It wasn't enough that they had butchered her for the crime of loving a Fallen Angel, and Akeno was the filth left behind.

No, they were determined to finish the job.

All because she had wings.

What did it matter that Akeno hated them herself?

What did it matter that she loathed the black feathers that occasionally sprouted from her back, or the cursed blood in her veins that had cost her mother her own?

If she could have ripped the disgusting, foul things out herself, she would have!

She'd even tried!

Just three weeks ago, cornered in an old barn, she had grabbed the base of her own left wing and pulled with every bit of power she had to her name, but it was no use.

The scream of white-hot fire at the base of her wing was somehow even louder than the wail that had left her throat hoarse and ragged for days afterwards

She had blacked out from the sheer shock of it, and by the time she finally woke up again shivering and surrounded by a pool of her own blood and loose black feathers, the hunters were nearly on her.

Akeno could barely even fly with it as it was, for all the good that'd do.

"Please," she whimpered, curling into a tight, trembling ball against the rotten wood, her fingers clawing at her dirt-caked hair. "Someone... anyone..."

Save her.

Please.

"Well, now. This, I didn't expect."

She froze.

The voice didn't come from the shadows, and it wasn't a frothing, murderous screech fit for the people desperate to kill her.

In fact, it sounded nonchalant and downright conversational, and Akeno snapped her eyes open and looked up through the blinding sheets of rain.

And there he was.

Descending from the sky as if stepping down a flight of grand, invisible stairs was a tall man clad in a dark, sweeping trench coat, fluttering against his descent.

That sight alone would have been ridiculous enough, but her breath seized completely as she spotted the set of massive, midnight-black wings unfurled from his back.

Five pairs, all in all.

Enough that when they spread out at just the right distance and angle, they seemed vast enough to blot out the entire horizon.

Father?

Something like desperate, desperate hope ignited in her chest.

He was actually here - he would save her!

Akeno had run away from him, cursed him, and blamed him for her mother's death, but this hell on earth had swallowed the childish pride right out of her.

She was too small, too cold, and too afraid to do anything but hope that she wouldn't have to die in the mud.

Then, she realized the truth.

That's not him.

The wings were too large, the presence too vast, and the cold, terrifying weight of the sky itself seemed to bend around him.

Hope twisted into fear all over again.

"W-Who are you?" she choked out, and it was so close to a sob even she barely understood herself.

The man descended and loomed over her, and she shrank back into the rotting wood that much more.

"Are you... are you one of his...?"

She couldn't even say it.

The stranger said nothing, at first.

He only tilted his head down at her, inspecting her from head to toe, before suddenly looking up toward the stormy heavens and muttering under his breath.

"When the goddess asked me for a favor, I certainly wasn't expecting this."

…What?

He blinked slowly, before turning his golden eyes back down to her, mud-caked form and all.

"They call me Kokabiel," he introduced himself easily, without any fanfare at all. "And no, I am entirely my own master - it was greatly overdue."

Akeno blinked.

"I was tracking the faint, stray signature of a handful of Fallen Angels, but I certainly wasn't looking for this particular one. Nor a scene quite like this."

His eyes swept over her yet again, before he clicked his tongue.

"You are Baraqiel's spawn, are you not?"

The name made her flinch.

"I-"

"You are." He didn't wait for her to confirm it. "And as far as I know, you have no business being here. Who are you, child, and why on earth do you look so… pitiful."

And Akeno…

Well, there was no dignified way to put it.

Between the biting cold, the trauma, and the suffocating pressure of her hunters, and everything else…

She burst into hysterical tears and shattered entirely.

…​

At some point during her rather alarming - from a purely objective standpoint - breakdown, the girl began to babble.

Evidently, she couldn't hold it in any longer.

In a choked, frantic rush of weeping gasps, a rather morbid tale poured out of her - brutal murder, a short and harrowing life on the run, and even an attempt or two at self-mutilation while being hunted down like a rabid dog for the heinous crime of existing.

Very tragic, truly.

Kokabiel listened politely, letting the rain wash over his sharp features.

When the girl's voice finally dissolved into raw, hitching sobs, he sighed heavily, tipped his head back toward the stormy sky, and pinched the bridge of his nose with two gloved fingers.

"Incompetence," he muttered to himself, already and utterly done with this newfangled fiasco. "Absolute, Father-damned moronic fools, every last one of them."

The worst part was that not an ounce of it was truly surprising, let alone original.

Baraqiel once again cannot keep his domestic affairs in order, the Shinto purists are having a collective aneurysm over a child, and I am standing in the mud playing therapist.

Unbelievable.

And they have the gall to question why he would leave that festering cesspit of a- oh, but never mind that.

He adjusted the collar of his coat, all too aware of the way the little spawn was eyeing him like live ordnance.

Not surprising, that, given her recent experiences.

"I mean you no harm, child."

If he did, they wouldn't be having this conversation to begin with.

"Furthermore, your situational awareness is severely lacking. You are being tracked by more than just your mother's disappointingly dim-witted relatives. There are at least two distinct groups of Fallen Angels trailing your scent through these mountains as we speak."

He'd already surveyed one as it is, and neither of them were of Satanael's get, which made this little interruption in his hunt that much more irritating.

…Though perhaps he shouldn't have mentioned that aloud, on second thought, because the child looked like she'd stopped breathing entirely and that wouldn't do, now would it?

"Be at peace, little-"

"Fallen Filth!"

…

Of course.

Kokabiel wearily closed his eyes, before slowly turning to observe the opposite tree line.

In but a moment, the shadows at the edge of the clearing twisted, and seven figures clad in traditional Shinto robes materialized from the gloom, their hands already forming intricate spiritual seals.

"Fallen filth!" the lead Himejima exorcist roared again, as if Kokabiel hadn't heard him the first time. "Step away from the abomination! She belongs to the Himejima!"

The Fallen Angel arced a single, unimpressed brow.

"Does she really? I was under the impression that she was my ignoramus brother's progeny."

The lead exorcist hissed a rather rotten curse at him.

Certainly nothing suitable in the company of children.

"She is a black taint on the bloodline of our noble clan, and she - it - will be purified on this very night!"

"As will you!" The gibbering buffoon to his right chimed in. "You trespass and interfere with divine mandate, heretical beast!"

"Surrender." A third and last one hefted a blade at them and snarled, deep and from the soul. "There is no escape!"

…

Stars above, they were actually serious, weren't they?

Kokabiel was almost impressed.

The lack of properly developed survival instincts on the lot of them might as well have been a genuine medical marvel, given that even the minuscule faction of the presence he allowed himself to radiate collectively dwarfed them all by far.

Then again, they were zealots.

Never the brightest bulbs, those, regardless of religion or creed.

As for their 'threat'…

There was a time where he would have killed them all slowly for the insult - and other times where he would have shrugged it and the girl trembling behind him off, and left them to do as they will.

It was, after all, none of his concern.

Now, however….

He glanced back at the child for a fleeting beat.

Pale-faced. Shallow breathing. Face the very picture of ceaseless despair.

Clearly already convinced that he would surrender her to her fate, or that he would die first and the result would be the same.

Likely both.

…

Well, then.

Slowly, the faintest hint of a smile pulled at his lips.

Kokabiel had only come here on this night and stumbled onto this scene because he was due to repay a favor to Artemis Argrotera, and that particular moon goddess would not be pleased to learn that he had left an innocent child to face certain death, regardless of her origins.

If nothing else, he saw no need to end this transaction on a sour note that could so easily be avoided.

"I think not."

The girl's eyes went impossibly wide as he continued, much to the exorcists' frothing rage.

"I do believe this child will be staying with me. If any of you would prefer to leave before this becomes unnecessarily unpleasant, I would suggest doing so now."

Naturally, they refused.

Pity.

"Fallen!" The lead exorcist was still working his lungs to their most deafening capacity, surpassing even the rain and the occasional burst of thunder in the distance. "You will-!"

That was as far as he got before Kokabiel's finger twitched, and all seven annoyances vanished within a fraction of a second, obliterated utterly by a swirling vortex of collapsing space and heat and sheer, unforgiving energy.

Baraqiel's daughter gasped and toppled back further behind him, but that was due to the wave of displaced air that buffeted her more than anything else.

Their deaths had been far too quick for her to perceive, though the shockwave continued on and blew the rotten torii gate to splinters, forcing him to flare his wings to shield her from the flying debris.

*Good. *

That was one task done - and now for the other.

Kokabiel's eyes narrowed as he turned to yet another point past the tree line, and he raised his voice by another modicum.

"Do come out now. You are hardly as discreet as you seem to think you are, and my patience is wearing thin as it is."

…

For a moment, nothing happened.

And then, with a faint burst of collapsing magic - no, demonic power - the air on the opposite side of the clearing shimmered, and a reincarnated devil clad in an elegant, foreign suit stepped into the light, flanked by two armored, lower-class Devils.

And not just any reincarnated devil at that.

Despite the unassuming features, he had some power to his name, and the staff he bore carried the distinct, crimson crest of the House of Gremory.

Interesting.

"Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa." He murmured the name levelly, and the lower-class devils stiffened at the sound of his voice. "Bishop to Lord Zeoticus Gremory, Father to Sirzechs."
That last note alone was the only reason he bothered to learn of the man and the rest of the members of that little Peerage, no matter how asinine their roles may have been.

"Lord Kokabiel. An honor."

The Bishop feared him - Kokabiel could all but taste it - but he had the grit not to show it in front of his subordinates at least.

"An annoyance." The Fallen Angel retorted. "What business do you have here, and what does it have to do with this child?"

Because he was many things, but an imbecile was not one of them.

The devil further demonstrated his good sense by not dawdling with his answer.

"An agreement was made, Lord Kokabiel."

An agreement-

Ah.

It only took a moment to connect the dots.

The girl.

The second group of Fallen tracking her every move from the shadows, yet making no move to interfere.

A group entirely distinct from the first set, who had clearly been the work of Baraqiel himself, in some ham-fisted, feckless attempt to watch over his daughter from a distance.

And now a group of Devils - this group of Devils, with their connections and implications - who, had Kokabiel not involved himself in this mess, would have covertly arrived 'just in time' to intercept the Himejima exorcists in his stead.

An agreement, was it?

"Azazel is up to his old tricks again, isn't he?"

The Bishop said not a word, but that on its own was answer enough.

Kokabiel stared at him impassively for another moment, before tipping his head in a rather unmistakable gesture.

"Go on. There will be no agreements carried out tonight."

For the third and final time, Agrippa demonstrated his position as the second most intelligent individual in that clearing by far.

He offered the Fallen Angel one last nod of respect, before a quick magic circle and flare of power carried him - and the shattered fragments of Azazel's plans - away.

…

Only then did Kokabiel sigh again.

"He never learns."

Then again, one should never expect anything of the sort from Azazel to begin with - and now Baraqiel's reaction to this debacle would no doubt be entirely too loud for his liking.

…

*Ever and always disappointing, but that was only par for the course. *

In the end, those two - and the Grigori entire - would reap what they sow, as they did time and time again.

And they would reap them alone.

Kokabiel had better things to do.

With that, he turned his full attention back to the shivering girl.

Akeno had barely moved since Agrippa's departure.

She stood exactly where Kokabiel had left her, shoulders hunched against the cold, her small hands clenched tightly at her sides as though she still expected another attack to come from somewhere in the darkness.

Half petrified with heart-stopping horror that had slowly simmered into something more dazed, and tinged through with just the right amount of insidious hope.

The Fallen Angel had saved her, after all.

That meant something.

She wasn't going to die.

The realizations struck all at once, making her knees tremble, and Kokabiel saw it all.

Her eyes followed him warily when he approached, but she made no attempt to retreat.

She didn't have the strength for that, and he shoved his hands into his coat pockets and looked down at her, letting out a brief, quiet breath.

"…"

"…"

…

…So this was how it was going to be?

"Well, it could be worse, I suppose," Kokabiel said dryly. "You could have been born a nephilim."

Akeno blinked at him again through damp lashes, visibly struggling to process that off-handed statement.

"I don't understand."

That word, or him, or anything that had happened at all.

It might as well have been a fever dream to her.

"Of course you don't."

She frowned faintly, lips wobbling, before wiping at one cheek with the back of her hand and glancing nervously toward the place where the exorcists had vanished.

"Are… you going to hurt me?"

A stupid question, perhaps, but entirely instinctive in the end.

He would allow it.

"No." Was the blunt reply. "Now come along, child."

Akeno hesitated.

Her gaze dropped to the mud beneath her bare, battered feet, then lifted cautiously back to him.

After a moment, she gave the smallest, uncertain nod.

Kokabiel went as far as to hold out his hand for her, and it wasn't long before she took it most delicately.

Her fingers were freezing, but they quickly warmed in his.

"Let us get out of the rain before anyone else decides to interrupt my evening."

And with a flash of brilliant light, they were gone.

…
​
Thessaloniki, Greece:

"Woah woah woah - hold on a second."

Hippolytus didn't look up.

The old prince was too busy sitting in the old high-backed chair beside the fire, one hand resting on the arm while the other leafed through a report from the stack set beside him.

Artemis, on the other hand, was almost sprawled across the couch at the other other end of the room, with one arm draped over her eyes and the other idly flipping a polished coin over and over again.

Katerina had no complaints there.

She'd been having the time of her life leaning over the back of the couch, working her fingers carefully through Artemis' white-blonde hair, the silvery strands slipping easily between them.

Some people might have considered the sight undignified - the great Olympian goddess of the hunt, lounging around in a sanctum while one of her followers played with her hair?

Yeah, those people could go pound sand.

Katerina and her sister had grown up with Artemis washing and braiding their hair when they were little, always patient no matter how long it took to untangle the knots.

Their goddess had been just as happy to let the two girls clumsily return the favour, even when their efforts had been considerably less impressive.

There was no way in Hades Katerina was giving up her privileges now.

Besides, Artemis was no one's fool.

She could lounge however she damn well pleased.

That wasn't the problem that had her sitting up and squinting at them both.

"Can someone run that last one by me again?"

Hippolytus turned another page and still refused to look up from the stack.

"You heard me the first time, Katerina."

"But seriously?"

Look, she'd known from the start that things were going to get complicated once the Grigori had fessed up about this Satanael guy and his little split from the rest after Lord Chiron had finished tearing them a new one.

It sounded very convenient.

Oh no, we didn't attack you and yours, why would we do that? It was actually this one jerk who doesn't even work with us anymore. Take it up with him!

Yeah. Sure.

Except the facts had checked out.

A Twelve-Winged Fallen Angel was out and about and probably committing war crimes out the wazoo.

The Hunters stationed in Japan were already sweeping across the country, looking for this Utsusemi Agency up and down and all over the place, and throwing someone of that weight class into the mix made everything a heck of a lot more dangerous.

And Artemis couldn't exactly start deploying the big guns - cough, the olderhunters, cough - to speed things up, either.

Not without running the risk of Takamagahara and its kami taking notice, and then they'd have a whole new pile of problems to deal with.

No, they had to be careful.

Ugh.

Even Hippolytus' role on the last mission had been strictly recon, and that had nearly exploded spectacularly.

Metaphorically, obviously.

The actual explosions had been pretty damn impressive all on their own, and the windfall after that had been completely worth it too.

Still, the point stood.

So what Katerina wanted to know was how exactly things had gone so funky that another Grigori Cadre was helping them find this rogue one?

"What does Kokabiel Of The Stars even get out of doing us a solid?"

This time, it was Artemis that answered her, though she didn't bother opening her eyes.

"The repayment of a debt. He owes me a small handful."

Eh?

"Is it something I'm allowed to ask about?"

"The long and short of it is that - before their Fall - He and Sahariel of the Moon held, in some aspects, duties equivalent to my own."

Katerina's mouth snapped shut.

"Moon stuff?"

Artemis nodded, once, and that was all the motivation she needed to nod back and take a big mental step back.

Not touching that one with a ten foot pole.

"So he owes you a few favors?"

"He made certain mistakes a long, long time ago that can be lethal at best for the ignorant and the foolish meddling in that domain, and I found myself in a position to interfere. He was smart enough to acknowledge his debts, and that is all there is to it."

"Cool."

Hippolytus snorted and flipped another page.

"What? As far as Fallen Angels go, he sounds way less stupid than I would've thought."

Someone else might have tried to shortchange Artemis, and Katerina would've had a grand old time cackling when it was time to pay the piper.

"He is still a Cadre of the Grigori. Or was, at least."

"Was?"

Artemis finally moved her arm and glanced up at Katerina with those glinting silver eyes.

"What do you know of Kokabiel's battle with Vasco Strada in the first half of the twentieth century?"

The Catholic Church's Violence of Heaven?

Whoo boy - who didn't know this story?

"They tangoed in World War Two when the Grigori started getting up to their extra-nasty business, and he beat the brakes off him, right?"

Just imagining it was enough to put an excited grin on her face.

Katerina was a proper Grecian through and through, and had faction loyalty for days, but even she could take pride in an overwhelming PR victory for Team Human-

"Kokabiel threw the fight."

"…"

"…"

"…"

"…What in the what now?"

"I've told you that his role mirrors my own amongst the Abrahamic Pantheons."

Katerina nodded slowly.

Very slowly.

"Because of this, Kokabiel has always been… more objectively aware of his own relative insignificance in the grand scheme of things than most would expect."

Artemis sighed and finally sat up from her sprawl, running a hand through her hair.

"This does not mean his deeds and lows through the millennia are not as black as his wings, mind you. But he is a less egregious offender than a great many of his former brethren."
Hippolytus set the report in his hands down as their goddess continued.

"By the time the debacle of the Second World War came to pass, he was thoroughly disillusioned with the greater Grigori as a whole. Then, in 1943, several contingents of rather moronic Fallen Angels landed in Italy and launched a campaign of terror across the country, cutting a swathe through it on their way to the Vatican while taking advantage of the Church's forces being stretched thin across the world."

"Vasco Strada was deployed with one of the exorcist squads sent to intercept them," Hippolytus added. "They had little chance of surviving that encounter."

"As it turned out, however, many of these Fallen had connections of their own. Some were children or descendants of important figures within the Grigori's then-current leadership."

Katerina raised a hand.

"I thought the Grigori didn't do the whole 'nobility' thing the Devils like to mainline."

"They don't, as a general rule."

It was Hippolytus who answered this time.

"But nepotism still has its uses, and plenty of them would not have been pleased to have their family trees abruptly pruned by the wielder of the Holy Sword Durandal."

"And so it was that Azazel himself pressured Kokabiel into taking to the field," Artemis finished. "The loss of those little wretches would have shattered his faction's momentum in the war."

She paused.

"What he didn't account for was just how far Kokabiel's patience had worn thin."

"Meaning?"

Artemis smiled.

"Meaning Kokabiel arrived at the battlefield, exchanged a few blows with Vasco Strada, and immediately realized just how absurdly powerful a mere human barely out of childhood - and still far from his prime - had become."

Katerina's grin had already returned.

"He then had to choose between exerting the effort needed to cull such a warrior for the sake of a group of egotistical, spoiled infants who had led themselves to the noose and now needed him to cut them free…"

Artemis' smile grew sharper, and more than a little amused.

"…continuing to serve an organization he could no longer even pretend to stand behind... or making another choice entirely."

Katerina's eyes widened, and Hippolytus chuckled.

"In the end, he chose to do what he should have done long ago."

Artemis' gaze gleamed.

"He cut himself free of Azazel's machinations. He killed the Fallen he'd been sent to retrieve himself, turned the battlefield into a wasteland, praised Vasco Strada for his immense potential, and advised him to realize it before they fought again."

She leaned back against the couch, and went back to flipping her dagger into the air.

"Then he simply walked off the battlefield, and out of the Grigori entirely."

…

…

…

Katerina stared at Artemis.

Then at Hippolytus.

Then back at Artemis again.

Her brain meats were screaming, and she pressed two fingers to her temples and screwed her eyes shut.

"Okay, we can move on, but I have so many questions!"

So, so many.

"You always do," Hippolytus muttered wryly, and she immediately snapped a finger at the beginnings of his crooked smirk.

"Don't start with me, princeling! Not all of us are older than indoor plumbing, and I just learned that a Fallen Angel Cadre-"

"Former Cadre," Artemis corrected mildly.

"-might actually be pretty cool! It's a lot to process!"

Her goddess's soft laugh broke out into the room at that, and Hippolytus - because the buzzkill was physically incapable of letting Katerina have her fun for more than five seconds, - dropped his gaze back to that stupid report.

"He is still an Original Watcher. Being 'pretty cool' in one instance doesn't erase that."

Katerina waved the warning off.

"You know what I mean."

She knew perfectly well that the guy probably had enough history of being a gnarly bastard behind him to fill a few dozen libraries, and then some.

She wasn't an idiot.

That didn't mean she'd pretend that the story hadn't been awesome.

"You can ask all the questions you please another time, Katerina." Artemis chided, and she ducked her head - that voice was lethal. "For now, there are other matters to attend to."

Fair.

She probably wanted an update on the Hyoudou's situation again, which was going…

Well, it was going.

Sometimes well and sometimes not - but hey, it could be worst!

At least it's not the Belial fiasco.

Katerina winced just thinking about that mess.

Hippolytus was free to deal with that whole thing - and those two poor schmucks at the heart of it - all on his own.

Before she could start explaining things on her end, though, the prince beat her to the punch.

"On that note, my lady…"

When the two of them turned back to him, he was frowning down gravely at the latest set of pages in front of him, and something about the expression made the last of laughter drain right out of the air.

"What is it?"

"A development from Laodice." He was already handing the report over, and Artemis took it with a look that matched his tit for tat. "One I believe warrants your immediate attention."

…​

Another novel twist.

With how events had proceeded this year, one could almost be forgiven for thinking the Moirai were pulling at the strings of fate and playing their despicable games again.

Fortunately, that was impossible.

Fate had such little hold on them after Apollon's machinations and ceaseless rage had finished casting the Three from the heavens and burning every last trace of them out of existence.

What a war that had been - one even most of the divine had been unaware was occurring right beneath the cloak of their endless ignorance.

And what a mad, mad day of revelry had crowned that victory.

Yet even still…

Despite knowing what she did, some small part of Artemis's immortal self couldn't help but wonder at the sheer numberof developments stacking one atop another, even as she continued reading through the report her Huntress had provided.

An encounter.

A meeting with a dangerous local swordswoman who had 'caught her scent' in the region.

A photograph attached to a name.

Chikage Miyamato.

Interesting, truly.

But the second set of details was infinitely more so, and far more alarming besides.

A picture of a young girl, perhaps a little younger than Katerina had been when she'd first entered the Hunt, with dark hair and a quiet, almost severe expression that seemed entirely at odds with her age.

It was accompanied by another name.

Zekka Miyamato.

And beneath it, one final set of lines in neat, handwritten script:


Suspected Unstable Sub-Species Sacred Gear.

False Longinus - Eden's Dual.​

…
​
Nowhere In Particular:

A moment.

A century.

All of time and eternity and back again.

Bedeze Abaddon could not comprehend how long ago his torment had begun, and he'd long since begun to wish for an end.

He had screamed at first.

He had screamed until there was nothing left in his throat to give, and then screamed anyway, because the pain had somehow shattered his pride right from the onset and went from there.

Eventually, even that had stopped, though his perception of when meant nothing in this Hell.

The only constant was the light.

The tide of it surrounded him from every direction, filling his vision even when his eyes were closed - until the lids had melted off - pouring into his flesh and blood through his flayed-open skin and rent bones until they boiled right out in the open for anything capable of surviving this to see.

And yet he did not die.

The light… it healed him even as it burned, regenerating everything that was destroyed just so it could eat it all away again and stretch his suffering that much more.

His power was no help here - his demonic power couldn't manifest as even a trick against the sheer holiness of this torment, and the scraps of sanity he had left to his name wouldn't have been able to direct it regardless.

When he somehow found the strength to struggle and writhe, the chain suspending him in the heart of this nightmare - this cruel and unforgiving sun - pulled taut, stretched so tightly even a tug more would rip his limbs clean off his body.

Right to the edge, and not a step more, over and over again.

A true fate worse than death.

Until now.

A faint sound reached him through the light.

Something like footsteps, loud and echoing, and then a voice.

Clear and polished.

Vast and terrible.

"Hello again, little devil."

It was the god who had put him here.

Bedeze didn't have it in him to rage at it anymore.

To roar or beg or plead - not like he had at first.

The best he could do was burn, and cower.

"I see that arrogance had finally failed you. Pity. It was some of the best entertainment I've had in centuries."

Another footstep, closer this time.

"You see, I'm quite pleased to have you here with me today. I've just gotten back from seeing my son - you are not worthy to even hear his name, of course - and by now, he'll be heading back to see his friend. A noble-born Abrahamic Devil, just like you."

The voice remained perfectly calm, but the almost polite disdain in that last word made the light imprisoning him flare, and Bedeze's silent scream was violent enough to pulverize his own vocal cords.

"I've long been aware that my son has… not quite internalized how much I despise your misbegotten race, or just how much patience I must exercise simply to tolerate that companion he so closely keeps to his side. To be perfectly honest, despite acknowledging his worth, every now and then I'll look at him, old wounds will flare, and all I'll feel…"

Another footstep, and then the shape of him was standing right before Bedeze's melting eyes.




"Is H̴̨̳̣͈̭̲͇͍̹͙̒͗͒̀̌͋̆̏͗͑̆͌̚̚͝Ą̵̧̡̯̥̰̹̙͉̇́̈́͠T̶̰̭̥̼̭͒̋͛̉̿͌̎́̔Ë̸͖͇͓͎͛͆͂͊̄͗͛̇͛̽́̕͝͠!̷̬̍̾̽̃̂"​



Somehow, the apocalyptic word was almost a reprieve.

The sheer force of it shattered something fundamental in him, and though he came to moments later, there was an instant of blissful, agonizing darkness.

If he could, he would have wept.

"There you are again."

The god's amused voice floated back in just a moment, along with the resurging fire.

"I have quite a few unpleasant memories to work through now, and it wouldn't do for my outlet to break too soon."

Outlet?

…

"Indeed. You should rejoice, worm. Your unsightly existence finally had some measure of true value."

Whether he'd plucked the thought from Bedeze's mind or simply seen it in the face of his newfound despair was irrelevant.

Everything was, even the impossible pain, in the face of what came next.

"Now then…"

The god's voice softened.

"…let's begin with whatever it is you have melded to your soul."

NO!

Then the god reached into the light.

His hand passed through the searing radiance, through flesh and blood and bone, and deeper still, into the very root of Bedeze's terrified existence.

To the Ruin Lord's gift.

And tore.

It.

Free.​


"What is this?"

Almost immediately, the god's presence seemed to recoil in shock.

Bedeze didn't notice it.

"This... No. It's not possible."

The Rating Games Champion didn't notice anything anymore.

"They - he - couldn't possibly be so stupid."

He was quite thoroughly shattered, in every sense of the word.

"And yet…"

But perhaps that was for the best.

The pain was gone, and in the end, he was spared the final surge of light that followed as Phoebus Apollon tipped his head back, the crimson King Piece held aloft in his hand, and laughed for all the world to hear.

And tremble.

"Oh, look what they've done!"

…​
