Me, to the hectic summer schedule and ceaseless interruptions that have tried to kill my writing vibes since July:

aegon-targaryen.gif

Onwards!

Days Later:

What is a soul?

It was the sort of question that seemed painfully obvious, right up until you actually stopped to think about it.

What is a soul?

A sentient energy field? The body's magical blueprint?

The 'real' you underneath the customisable meat suit?

Short answer: it's complicated

Long answer: it's really, really complicated.

The least poetic answer, though, goes something like this:

A soul is a manifest phenomenon encompassing the totality of an individual's existence.

Remember - least poetic.

Basically, once you boil away all the magical jargon and strip out the parts I can't even begin to understand yet... the soul is everything that you are, and everything that lets you keep being what you are.

Like the ability to change.

Souls change all the time.

In small, reversible ways, or in big, fundamental ones, and everything in between.

And, if you knew what you were doing, you could actually keep track of bits and pieces of that yourself.

"Dan."

"I know."

A week after the mess with Ezren Vale and his Utsusemi lackeys - and all the noise that came after it - Sairaorg and I started the day bright and early.

Well, more early than bright.

The sky above was grey and eerie, with a low curtain of pale light pressing through somewhere beyond the clouds.

Everything around us was broken up into drifting pockets of cold mist.

They moved slowly around us, swallowing distance and depth until there was nothing left but layers of shifting white and grey.

There was nothing but deceptively calm water below.

No waves or current or wind - just zen stillness.

Sairaorg and I floated across from one another, cross-legged against the surface, decked out in nothing but swim shorts.

We had our eyes closed, hands on our knees, and even our breathing matched beat for beat.

Slow and even.

It would have looked almost peaceful - and maybe a little weird - if you ignored the fact that we were sitting on water like it was solid ground.

I know what you're thinking.

Compared to the rest of the magic you've seen me use, this didn't even qualify as a party trick.

Except, using any more power right then and there had a non-zero chance of getting us eaten.

"It's getting closer."

"Of course it is."

Let me explain.

When we woke up this morning and got ready for training, expecting the usual grind, Chiron announced that we were going for a quick field trip instead.

Obviously, that had our blood pressure spiking, because anything that broke our 'work-until-you-drop-and/or-get-pummeled-into-the-dirt' routine was always going to be bad news.

Fool me once and all that, right?

Anyway, Teach never pulled the same trick twice, so you never knew what fresh flavour of pain was coming your way until it was already biting you in the face.

Cue this lake.

I didn't know where we were, or how far the water stretched, but between the eerie lighting, the warped sense of space, and the blatantly supernatural chill in the air, I had a pretty good feeling we were nowhere near Kansas anymore.

As for what we were doing…

Technically, it was meditation.

The cold here had nothing on Cocytus or Absolute Demise's balance breaker, but it was heavy, constant, and the temperature kept dropping every other minute like it had something to prove.

The way Chiron explained it, pushing back against it was all about specific intent, because flaring raw power out wouldn't get us anywhere here no matter how much of it we had to spare.

We had to mean it.

Meditation, then - that was the drill.

The twist?

There was something in the water with us.

It was big and vast and desperately ravenous, lurking in the deep right beneath our dangling feet.

We couldn't see it, but we could feel it - like having phantom teeth scraping against the back of our necks.

And it was absolutely, one hundred percent aware of us, too.

"This is its territory, and you are intruders," Chiron had explained happily before leaving us to our fate. "Too much power too quickly will be seen as an act of aggression, and answered in kind. If you flare your energy, it attacks. If your focus slips and you sink, it attacks you. And if you use too little-"

"We freeze and it gets popsicles for dinner anyway?"

The sadist centaur only laughed.

"Have fun, boys."

Whatever it was, Sai and I combined had zero chance against it, and Chiron had told us as much himself.

So, to recap:

I was half-naked, half-frozen, unable to thaw myself out properly or use any of my weapons or spells, and right within striking distance of some effectively invisible, depth-dwelling nightmare whose mere presence had my demigod lizard brain screaming, 'Move, ya moron!' in twelve different dialects of Ancient Greek and at least three more it must have come up with on the spot.

And you thought your Mondays were bad.

"Dan."

Even with my eyes closed, a vein on my forehead twitched.

"Sairaorg, I. Am. Trying."

"Well, try harder."

"Oh, easy for you to say!"

The point of all of this was fine control.

Being in tune with your power and where it comes from, so you could eventually learn to do more with less.

Sairaorg had me beat there because he started off a lot closer to zero than I did, what with his crippling deficiency ofdemonic power.

It was that absence, mixed with drive and pure, back-breaking effort that had him unconsciously feeling out the edges of his soul and learning to draw pure life force from deep within.

Because he had to force it out in the first place, he also had an easier time throttling the engine down when he needed to.

I was different.

Between the fact that my reserves were comparatively bigger - Senjutsu enhancement didn't count - and fundamentally different, plus the inbuilt instinct to just throw everything at a problem until it stopped moving, I didn't really have a dial.

I had a switch.

On and off, with barely anything in between - trying to delicately skim the surface of my power without letting it all surge out explosively was like trying to work a keyboard with a wrecking ball.

It - I - was too volatile for that, right down to the source of it all.

Which brings us all the way back full circle.

What is a soul?

What is my soul?

I couldn't sense it the way Sairaorg could his, but I think I was finally starting to.

Scratching at the surface meant something else entirely when there was no surface to make sense of, but I was beginning to get…

Let's call them impressions.

Vague outlines, really.

…

Light.

No surprise there.

Warmth.

Pull the other one.

Raging fire-

Hello, Incinerate Anthem. Move along, please.

…

Nothing else

I frowned and pushed deeper, forcing my sixth sense inwards, trying to focus-

Something new.

I almost gasped and lost it entirely.

A different, foreign heat.

…

That's…

I didn't know what it was, specifically, but I recognized the feeling.

It had been like a faint, distant itch at the back of my head for days now, ever since that meeting with Hestia.

A strong, beating ember.

Not harmful - I could tell that much easily - but the second I consciously brushed against it, my control slipped.

Crap.

The light surged, spiking upward with a sudden, violent pulse of pressure.

Below us, the thing in the dark moved, and Sai hissed.

"Too much!"

"For the love of - I know!"

But I'd already lost it.

The awareness winked out, and I was back to square zero.

Damn it.

"Sure looks like you don't! So much for Chiron's better student!"

"Are you still on about that letter?" I gave up and cracked an eye open to glare at him. "What are you, Regulus? Let it go, dude."

"Really?" He met the look with a stink eye to match. "You want to talk about letting things go and you bring up Regulus?"

"Don't bring the kill-stealer into this!"

"You just did!"

"Well, you made me think of him! Invoking evil makes you responsible for it!"

"Of all the stupid, backwards-!"

We could have gone like that for hours, and in our defense, we'd been at this for just as long.

Between the constant hypothermic temperatures and the lowkey psychological torture, we were both all sorts of cranky.

Naturally, we let loose just a little too much then - a spark over the line, I swear - and that did it.

Sairaorg was going for another scathing insult that would be embarrassing for both of us tomorrow when the water beneath us gave a massive, unnatural shudder.

Our eyes widened.

""Oh-""

The phantom teeth at the back of my neck didn't just scrape this time.

They bit down.

""-crap!""

Scatter!

We exploded off the surface of the lake a split second before it dropped out underneath us, plummeting thirty feet in a blink like an elevator at terminal velocity.

I looked down, eyes flaring gold against the rising mist, bracing for the worst.

Cat was out of the bag now.

I was expecting some building-sized monstrosity - probably a dragon, because let's face it, it was always dragons - but instead of that…

It was something much smaller.

It crawled out onto the receding surface of the water on all fours, all sleek and wiry, with a dark, wet pelt that rippled like it was painted on liquid muscle. It had claws that dug right against the water and gripped against it with all the traction anyone could ask for, and a heavy, powerful tail swayed behind it, cutting through the fog this way and that.

It tilted a long, razor-jawed skull upward, locking onto us with , sulfurous eyes.

…

I'm not going to lie:

From up here, it almost looked like an otter.

Wait, no, it was an otter - if otters stood fifteen feet tall, packed hundreds of pounds and came with muck green fur and slit-eyed, bloodthirsty murder-glares.

It stared up at us.

We stared back down.

It was a whole, confusing thing.

"What-?"

Then it whistled.

A piercing, metallic screech tore through the air, lighting up the insides of my eardrums like the Fourth of July.

"▅▅▅▂▅▂▄▅▃▃▄!"

"Gah!"

Which sounds worse than it was - son of Apollon and survivor of the Nemean Lion here - but it was still bad enough to have me flinching and screwing my eyes shut.

Sairaorg too, and only for a blink.

Our new friend didn't waste it.

One second, it was crouching against the lake and projecting just how badly it wanted to disembowel us, and the next, it was launching up in a wild, ballistic arc.

"Grrrrr!"

I blasted it, because of course I did - a concentrated beam of sizzling light right out of my palm, aiming for its center mass.

It would have been a direct hit against ninety-nine percent of the things I've fought, but the growly otter of doom violently contorted to one side. The blast sheared past it, close enough to singe fur, but instead of losing its momentum and falling, the thing let out another sharp, pressurized whistle.

It literally trod the air.

With a stupid burst of speed, it kicked off the empty fog, changing tracks mid-jump.

Sairaorg didn't have the time to dodge, but his Touki surrounded him in a flare of brilliant white right as it came at him.

Crack.

The impact was like a thunder strike, and the mist around us was blown far and away even as the blur of teeth and fur went berserk against Sai's guard.

I tried to lunge in from the side, aiming for its flank, but a long, dark shadow suddenly whipped into the corner of my vision.

The tail-!

It cleaved through the air and nailed me right across the ribs and back, quicker than I could think to teleport.

Ever been whipped by a fire hose wrapped in steel wool?

Because that's what it felt like, and the force was almost as nasty as the feeling of my unarmored skin being flayed open by the strike.

I didn't just get sent down into the grey, rocky shoreline - I skipped.

Boom, boom, boom.

For the record, bouncing off jagged, wet stone at way-too-many miles an hour is exactly as fun as it sounds.

By the time I was done - about three seconds later - I was covered in dust, flat on my back, a little mangled, and everything from my ribcage down to my spine was suing for damages.

But I'd had worse.

I scrambled to my feet, ready to blast right back into the fight, but Sairaorg and Growly beat me to the punch.

The two of them slammed down a hundred feet to my right, carving a fresh furrow into the rock.

From the looks of it, Growly had already carved a set of raw, bloody claw marks across his chest, and his wings weren't doing much better - one of them was twisted back at the wrong angle, and the other was scored through with painful, oozing gashes that leaked blood across his back and into the dirt.

Naturally, that only made Sai angrier.

The Touki around his fist seemed to warp air and gravity as he cocked it back, and the uppercut he drove into the underside of its snarling jaw should have pulverised it, and probably taken off its head for good measure.

Except-

His fist met its hide, and its momentum stopped dead.

If Growly wasn't screeching so loud, you could've almost heard the dull, anticlimactic thud.

Then, right beneath the wet fur where the blow had landed, the flesh bulged.

I mean that - its throat suddenly swelled, expanding outward like a giant, ticked-off pufferfish.

Sairaorg's expression went from flat to panicked as Growly's slitted eyes gleamed, and two of us had just enough time to realize what was happening before the thing reared back and spat.

Fwoom!

A cone of gale-force wind and concentrated pressure erupted out of its maw, catching Sairaorg square in the everything.

Force absorption? Really?

It was strong enough to snap his head back and send him careening head over heels across the rocky shore, cursing up a storm.

Growly would have leapt after him to press the attack, but my second light blast seared into it mid-jump and nixed that plan right from the top.

But the pained snarl and the immediate scent of burning fur - like wet dog crossed with barbecued car tire - was a good sign.

I'd underpowered it on the off chance that it could reflect that too, but there were limits.

Unfortunately, Growly recovered as fast as it moved.

"Grrrrr!"

I got a flash of those sulfurous red eyes blitzing to my left - there there was a face full of dripping, yellow fangs snapping shut right where my head had just been.

I ducked, feeling the wind of its jaws part my hair, and instantly flash-stepped the hell out of there, reappearing twenty feet back with my heart hammering against my ribs.

Too close.

Growly spun on a dime, coiling its legs and trying to come after me again, but the rock beneath its paws rumbled before it could pounce.

"Hey ugly!"

A writhing forest of sharp, jagged roots and gnarled branches erupted from the earth, courtesy of Sairaorg, and immediately hurtled up to skewer it.

Growly bared its teeth, completely abandoning its attack on me to dance backward. It twisted and dodged mid-air, dodging the wooden spikes by the skin of its very sharp teeth.

And its paws.

Anything it couldn't avoid was batted away or shattered with rapid-fire swings, and that active war crime tail swept out and turned bark to splinters with every lash.

I tried to time my openings, firing off occasional potshots at its blind spots wherever I could, but it worked its way around those too, vaulting off the fastest roots to dodge and let the beams sizzle harmlessly into the lake.

Tricky bastard.

On the bright side, so was I.

I risked a glance at Sai and nodded.

He didn't miss it, and another rumble coursed through the ground at our feet before a greater tide of roots began tearing through the rock, twice as many and thrice as frenzied.

The giant rodent didn't even try to fight this time - it kicked off the footing it had left and cleared the coming wave in one jump, and that was exactly what I was waiting for.

The moment it reached the apex of its rise, I took a page fresh out of its playbook and whistled.

"▅▅▅▂▅▂▄▅▃▃▄!"

The concentrated spike of horrific, off-key noise ripped out of my throat and hit Growly like a truck.

Its sulfurous eyes went wide, its ears flattened against its skull, and it flailed, dropping out of the sky like a sack of wet potatoes.

The writhing kicked up again as it fell, flesh and fur swelling out in ugly, uneven pockets as it tried to force its absorption trick to work on the fly - but good luck with that.

It wasn't a spell, but it wasn't pressure and frequency the way ordinary sounds were, either.

I wanted it to hurt, so it just did.

"Got ya!"

And so did Sairaorg's wooden spears, rocketing up towards it before it was even halfway down.

SHRIIIIK!

The sound of the spears ripping into it was wet and brutal, and its pained yowl was almost loud enough to wake the dead.

Credit where credit was due, though, because that still didn't put it down.

Somehow, it managed to bend enough that the worst of the damage came from grazes and fragments broken and lodged against its belly instead of punching all the way through.

The fall drove them in deeper, and you could just about feel it swallow another scream, but when my whistle cut off, Growly was up on its paws in no time flat, and practically frothing at the mouth with homicidal rage.

"Oh, come on." I almost threw my hands up in disgust. "What even are you!?"

And were those cuts regenerating-!?

It roared a proper battle cry and tensed, readying another blitz-

"Aarf!"

-only for the shadows under it to abruptly warp, swallowing both of its forelimbs up to the knee.

I grinned.

The otter panicked and scrambled back from the sudden drop, almost hurling itself out, and accidentally dragged up the hellhound who had his jaw clamped around one long, bristly leg.

Atta boy, Courage!

Growly tried to claw at him with its free paw, but my dog melted back into the darkness and darted away, popping up dead ahead and letting rip his own rumbling challenge.

Even three months ago, that wouldn't have been worth squat.

Now, it was more than intimidating enough to head off another attack, buying Sairaorg and me just enough time to box Growly in from the sides.

"!"

And just like that, we had ourselves a good old-fashioned three-on-one standoff.

Growly paused, glowering at us with a fresh dose of unadulterated bloodlust, and we glared right back.

Its muck-green fur bristled in jagged spikes, while my eyes narrowed, Sairaorg's fingers twitched against his sides, and Courage belted out a low, dangerous sound that had his breath steaming visibly against the cold mist.

For just one second, Growly's muscles coiled, and it almost seemed like it would spring at us again…

Then something changed.

"Grrr…"

It must have run the math and decided we weren't worth the trouble after all, because the battle stance flickered.

The sharp aura it gave off dimmed into something cold and resentful as it took a slow, glacial step back.

A retreat.

Those slitted eyes panned over us, fixing the three of us with one last look that seemed to scream 'next time, meat,' before it bolted.

It launched itself clear over our heads in a final jump, ducked another couple of blasts I hurled its way, and wove around one last surge of spiteful shrubbery from Sai as he tried to cut off its escape.

No dice.

Growly hit the bedrock running and dove headfirst back into the lake, slipping into the dark with barely a ripple to show for it.

By the time the surface settled, it was long gone, and that was that.

…

We didn't break formation yet, but the three of us all exchanged the same look.

Is it over-?

"Enough for now, I think."

We jerked a little, but that was all the reaction we had as Chiron trotted up through a cloud of mist like he was on the tail end of a jaunty little stroll and not... whatever this place was instead.

"Enough for now, I think."

"You mean we're not going to have to go after it for round two?"

I tried not to sound too hopeful, and smiled.

"Given that your opponent has rather conclusively thrown in the towel, the victory is already yours. Well done."

I punched the air and Sai groaned in relief… and something a good bit pained, too.

"Awesome." He held out a hand to me. "Fleece, please."

I glanced back at his wings again and winced.

That was some nasty tearing.

"Coming right up."

…

Ten minutes later, Chiron had lit us a fire, Courage was back in my shadow, and the two of us were dressed and patched up, good as new.

We sat around the flames knocking back sandwiches and fruit smoothies while we went over the fight again.

"The counter-whistle was a good touch."

I shrugged over a bite of PBJ.

"If you can't beat 'em, plagiarize 'em"

It worked for Theseus, after all.

Say what you will about the way his story ended, but between the Club-Bearer, the Line-Bender, the Cliff-Kicker and the Wrestler, that guy was legendary for defeating his enemies by turning their own tricks and traps against them.

Chiron nodded approvingly.

"Question - what was that thing?" Sai asked, draining his cup and going for seconds. "Because getting halfway shredded by an overgrown river weasel is going to sound a lot more embarrassing than it actually was if it doesn't have a cool name to go with all the claws."

And see, he wasn't wrong.

"Primarily? A Dobhar-chú," Chiron answered easily enough. "I encountered a small nest a few centuries ago in the Welsh countryside while visiting an old friend."

Dobhar-

I blinked.

"An Irish Otter-King?"

The library back at the estate had books on just about every magical beast and monster under the sun, and I'd burned through plenty of them during my downtime.

Most of them were interesting enough, and even the worst of'em doubled as awesome campfire stories for Katie and Alex.

Still...

I frowned.

"Hang on."

Sairaorg beat me to it.

"What would an Irish lake monster be doing in Wales?"

"Yeah," I nodded. "What he said."

It wasn't that the two were all that far apart - not even by mortal standards - but magical creatures tended to stay in their own backyards even without local powers like the Celtic equivalent of Aunt Artemis's Hunters laying down the law and wiping out any especially vicious stragglers.

Especially over there.

Back in their heyday, the British Isles -the old Isles of Men - had been a total madhouse, and this is coming from a Greek.

Your average peasant couldn't have swung a cat without hitting at least three different kinds of supernatural horror, and the horrors always swung back.

"The credit there belongs to a group of particularly enterprising flesh crafters we came upon at the time," he explained patiently. "They captured a handful of pure breeds through illicit means, and acquired other magical creatures from across the world - some through purchase and some through considerably less 'legal' means - before experimenting with them and their various traits in the hopes of creating a chimaera greater and more dangerous than the sum of its parts."

He paused.

"And, of course, more valuable."

"Valuable?"

Chiron shrugged.

"There is always a market for raw power, and the demand for living weapons is never lacking."

Which… sounded depressingly accurate, yeah.

Sai's face twisted, just like mine.

"So how'd this one end up here?"

I raised a hand too.

"And - again - where is here?"

He chuckled and snapped his fingers to refill all of our cups.

"This is an expanded spatial realm I helped craft for just that occasion - a self-sustaining artificial habitat to house the modified Dobhar-chú after their creators were… dealt with."

Both of us stopped mid-chew on our sandwiches, staring at him.

"And, as a pleasant benefit, it makes for a wonderful environment for some practical experience."

What'd I tell you?

Sadist centaur!

"How big exactly-?"

"Enough. The Dobhar-Chu need space to roam and hunt, and though they are far and away the apex predator of this particular patch water, they aren't the only inhabitants of the region."

That made Sai startle.

"Wait, there are other things around here?"

"Not anywhere close at the moment, but yes, of course." He took another slow drink. "A self-sustaining ecosystem requires a food chain, Sairaorg. The Dobhar-chú must eat something when overeager young heroes aren't trespassing on their territory."

"I'm pretty sure we were dragged here against our will, Teach. Practically kidnapping."

"Would you like to go back in the lake, Daniel?"

"And since kidnapping builds character, I wouldn't have it any other way!"

"I thought so."

Sai snorted, but he was still nodding along to the words.

"So it's sort of like a Familiar Forest?"

"The enclosures the children of your pillar nobility visit to contract creature-companions?" Chiron stroked his beard thoughtfully. "I suppose there are some similarities, yes"

Ooh, I knew this one too!

A few millennia ago and change, the original Barbatos - the Devil, not just the clan name - decided to take up competitive zookeeping as a hobby.

He was obsessed with collecting magical beasts and monsters from all over the world, especially from the territories the Devil armies raided during the old wars.

The critters - things that did a lot more than just go bump in the night - would end up imprisoned, trained into weapons of war, or scattered across the Barbatos clan territories and forgotten about until they were useful again.

Fast forward a few generations, and his descendants were famous across the Underworld for their demonic beast menageries and backyards stuffed to the brim with teeth and claws.

Eventually, they realized they were sitting on a goldmine, slapped some safety wards around the best territories, and started charging the rest of the Seventy-Two Pillars and the occasional outsider an arm and a leg for custom orders and the right to go monster-hunting for pets.

Presto: The Familiar Forests.

Great business model. Very profitable.

Or it was, right up until the devil civil war kicked off and the then Lord of the house, his heir, and just about every member of every branch family bar one or two all collectively caught a terrible case of 'Sirzechs Lucifer wants you to not exist anymore.'

Tragically, none of them made it.

After that, the survivors switched sides real quick and quiet, and gifted the New Satan regime a good chunk of their choicest lands as a gesture of goodwill, and the rest was history.

…Including the part where one of the strongest dragons to ever exist suddenly moved smack dab into the heart of those lands with no warning at all, but that was a whole other sort of circus.

Ask me again later.

"And your friend? The one you went out there to visit?

We both glanced at Sai.

"What? I can be curious too." He focused Chiron again. "You called him an old friend, so is he someone important? A spirit or god or something?"

"Far from it," Chiron chuckled, and for a fraction of a second, he flashed us that 'I know something you don't' look.

"He was a splendidly talented mage, and a few more things besides. I would be surprised if you hadn't heard of him before." His voice shifted to something a little considering then. "In truth, both of you would both be quite interested in meeting him for differing reasons beyond the obvious... but that is a proposition for another time."

Wait, what?

"Nevertheless."

He clapped his hands together and startled the thought out of us both.

"We'll leave off here today. Take the rest of the day off to recover and reflect."

"…"

"…"

That silence you're hearing?

Pure suspicion.

It was never that easy-

"You'll want to be well rested for tomorrow."

-And there it is!

"What happens tomorrow?"

He smiled, and Sai and I didn't.

"Chiron, what happens tomorrow!?"

Normally he'd have let us stew in our panic a little while longer, but for once, he let us off the hook early.

"I think it's about time we pay Esgaroth and the Lonely Mountain another visit, don't you think?"

"Esga-?"

I had to stop and do a full double-take in sync with Sai before either of us could speak again.

"Seriously?"

Chiron nodded firmly, and we both leaned back, stumped.

Huh.

I know we'd planned to go back and see how things were panning out after Smaug's death eventually, but between everything that had happened since and all the training in between, I'd pushed it to the back of my mind and forgotten all about it.

"It's been more than enough time for the situation to develop as it will, and though your role there began and ended with the dragon, it never hurts to double back and check one's work."

Sai and I agreed, and he seemed satisfied with that.

"Good. We'll have a look around, and perhaps make an attempt or two to better understand the mechanics of that remarkable ability of yours, Daniel. I have some theories as it is."

"Theories?"

He waved the question off on the first word.

"Later. I have some business to attend to, and you have an appointment of your own to keep."

I sat up a little straighter

Right.

"In a couple of hours, yeah."

It wasn't life or death, but it was important.

"Then you'll have plenty of time to freshen up, just as soon as you get back home."

Sai squinted warily.

"You're making it sound like we're not popping back with you."

"You aren't." Chiron agreed brightly, which was always a terrible sign. "Daniel needs to work on his spatial arrays."

I deflated and groaned.

"No."

"Yes." He almost sing-songed it back at me. "You need the practice."

And the thing is, I did.

Teleporting point-to-point in the mortal world was 'easy' enough, whether I was using divine thaumaturgy or spell circles, but the further apart you were, the more complicated the technical details got.

Math.

It was always math, and even though that wasn't a dealbreaker on its own - I loved magic and I refused to let calculus and algebra ruin it for me - traveling between spatial dimensions could get weird and twist the usual equations and formulas into pretzels the second you blinked.

Total migraine fuel, every time - and knowing Chiron, this place would be even harder to make measurements for because that's just how he would have built it.

What a drag.

"No cheating." He warned us pointedly, wagging a finger our way. "Or it'll be remedial lessons again, and none so gentle as this."

We paled - only an idiot wouldn't - and he chuckled, deep and from the chest.

"Oh, and do watch out for the company, please."

And just like that, the other shoe dropped, and things started happening way too quickly.

RUMBLE.

Sai jumped up at the exact same instant I did.

"I knew it! You said more than one! There's more of those things coming, damn it!"

I didn't even bother saying anything out loud.

I'd clocked that too, but I'd been hoping against hope that we'd somehow get a pass for once in our lives.

Demigod plans, and fate busts a gut.

"Hardly," Chiron derailed my train of thought completely, taking a leisurely sip from his mug. He looked entirely too entertained by our panic. "While its peers are certainly agitated now, your first opponent was among the fiercest of them - a leader of the herd, so to speak. With him scared off, none of the other adolescents will attack."

"Adolescents?!" Sai squawked.

RUUUMBLE.

The ground vibrated harder this time, sending tiny ripples across the surface of the lake.

Chiron didn't even spill a drop of his tea, and a little glint sparkled in his eyes as he stirred another sugar cube in for sweetness.

"Their mother, on the other hand…"

Mother-!?

An absolutely enormous, matted-furred limb tipped with curved, black claws breached the water with a deafening splash.

When it slammed down onto the shore - at least the size of a semi truck on its own - it hit it hard enough that the surrounding rock spiderwebbed with ridiculous fractures.

…Thaaaat's what we were sensing before.

I stared blankly.

Fair enough.

"Two hours, students of mine. Make them count."

Behind us, Chiron vanished into the mist like he was never there at all, and it was on.

"Seriously!" Sai yelled.

A second furry limb tore out of the lake, pulverizing the exact patch of dirt we'd been standing on as we bolted.

Then came the colossal, wet head with glowing, slit-pupiled eyes-

Nope, nope, nope.

I didn't stick around long enough to process what that alien death glare looked like.

"Scram!"

"Scramming!"

The two of us took off like bats out of hell, sprinting for dear life as Mama Growly bellowed a furious, earth-shaking roar and came right for us.

…​

It took an hour and a half, six near-death experiences, and the two of us nearly losing an arm and a leg respectively before we were finally home free.

All in all?

Still not as bad as The Chicken.

Then it was time to meet up with a new friend.

The National Archaeological Museum of Athens was only a couple of miles across town from Chiron's estate, which meant that I could've flipped a nickel into the air and been there and back again before it ever hit the ground.

I took the scenic route instead, parkouring across a couple stretches of rooftops and leaping through a few of leafy tree lines before hitting the pavement at a dead sprint and heading up from there.

Soon enough, the trees parted and the museum came into view - this massive, pastel yellow and pink building with a big stone plaza out front and a grand staircase leading up to the stone columns along the front wall.

All regal and fancy, minus the front steps crammed with pigeons, tourists ducking into the shade, and tour guides trying to keep'em all together.

"Shoot."

By the time I got a ticket - twenty minutes later - Lavinia had already been waiting for me for a little while.

I followed the familiar feeling of her presence - cool and muted, like shade on a hot day - and found her tucked away in a quiet side corridor branching off the main Mycenaean hall.

She was standing in front of a wall-mounted glass display case, staring at a pair of ancient bronze daggers inlaid with faded gold, but she looked up right as I turned the corner, and a wide, brilliant smile split across her face.

It suited her.

"Daniel!"

"Hi." I grinned and waved a little as I jogged up to her. "Sorry I'm late. There was a… pest control thing I had to deal with, and-"

"No, no. Don't worry," The smile didn't dim, and neither did its warmth. "You're right on time."

I glanced back toward the mounted clock near the entrance.

Fifteen minutes late.

"Thank Dad for that, then."

That made her snort, and my grin grew a little before smoothing out again.

"So," I said, keeping my voice low, and her expression evened out too.

"So?"

"For starters, how're you holding up?"

She didn't look bad, decked out in jeans, white trainers, and a light summer shirt - and with none of that desperate, exhausted energy from a week ago, either.

It made all the difference in the world.

"I am…" She hesitated, thinking. "… adapting."

"Fair."

If you haven't caught on yet, I'll just come out and say it.
Aunt Artemis had taken Lavinia under her protection, and it hadn't taken much - or any - convincing to pull that one off.

Between the Longinus, her innocence in the Oz fiasco, and the genuinely gods-awful hand Fate had dealt her, Aunt A had barely blinked when I asked her for a favor.

Odds are she hadn't even finished hearing us out before agreeing.

Now, Lavinia wasn't technically a Huntress, but she could train with them, study under them, and she had the run of Greece and the surrounding territories our pantheon ruled… within reason, obviously.

She wouldn't be walking into Olympus or anything anytime soon, but she had plenty of legroom outside of that.

She could also go back to Grauzauberer whenever she wanted with my aunt as her sponsor - good luck trying to stress test that, ya weasels - but for now…

Well, everything was huge and needed some getting used to, no matter how kindly she was being eased into it.

It's why I checked in on her every couple of days.

"It's all a bit overwhelming," she admitted, her eyes trailing over a glass case of bronze arrowheads.

"A good overwhelming, at least?"

Her brow quirked. "There's a 'good' kind of overwhelming?"

I nodded very seriously.

"Absolutely. Take it from a guy who constantly lives his life somewhere between 'too much' and 'seriously, why?' - there's always a sliding scale to this stuff."

That got me another smile.

"Good overwhelming it is, then."

"Awesome."

And I meant it, too.

"I do like my new home." She added, tucking a strand of hair behind her ear. "The apartment has a lovely view of the sea."

"Scenic?"

"Very."

"Sounds about right." I threw her a thumbs-up. "We Greeks are crazy about dramatic effect, you know. If a place doesn't look postcard-worthy, it might as well be a dump."

She giggled, and I almost missed a step.

Couldn't tell you why, but man was it embarrassing.

Get it together, Winchester.

"Anything you need help with?" I asked, clearing my throat. "I'm only ever a call away-"

"No," she said gently. "The Hunters have been… very kind. Really."

"Good. I'm glad."

And for a while, that was it.

I could talk all the live long day if I wanted to, but for some reason, finding stuff to say around Lavinia was harder than with anyone else.

My tongue kept getting completely clumsy for no good reason.

At least she seemed to be in the same boat.

We walked along the museum exhibits in silence for a minute, our sneakers squeaking against the polished floor, before she tried to open the conversation back up again.

"I guess being here must feel like an inside joke to you," she said, glancing around. "Or a bit awkward, maybe?"

I blinked at her. "Come again?"

"The museum," she explained, gesturing up toward a display set on the wall - a giant Mycenaean mural of Poseidon, crowned as King of the Gods. "The inaccuracies. Standing in a crowd of people who see it all as myth and fiction."

"Oh." I looked up at the wall, then back at her, rubbing the back of my neck. "Not really? I don't think I've ever given it that much thought."

She blinked, looking a little surprised. "Truly?"

"Yeah. I mean, the myth-and-fiction part is just everyday life at this point," I said, looking back up at the faded plaster artwork. There was no mistaking the guy sitting on the main throne in the center - golden crown, trident in hand, surrounded by a crowd of kneeling worshipers. "And as for the inaccuracies... well, it's not like it's all off-base."

Lavinia blinked.

"Pardon?"

I tilted my head at the mural.

"That one's pretty light on the details, but Poseidon was on the throne for a hot minute."

Or not quite, but he sure gave it his best shot, and then some.

"…"

She was looking at me funny.

"What?"

Then I remembered that what I knew wasn't exactly common knowledge, not all of it.

Not everyone had Chiron for a teacher.

"The Earth-Shaker was…" Her face twisted when I nodded. "But that doesn't make sense. I thought the Titanomachy and the crowning of Zeus Olympios as first and supreme king of the gods was fact."

"And it is." I agreed. "My grandfather freed his siblings and overthrew the Titans, replacing them as rulers of the universe with him as top dog."

"Then how-?"

"Because the mortals don't have all the facts."

There were stories about Poseidon having a stint ruling the heavens, and no matter what anyone tells you, they were right.

They just got the timing wrong.

"Zeus was crowned. Ruled for a bit. Then things got messy."

"… In what way?"

Just about all of'em, I almost said, but that wasn't the answer she wanted.

Why not?

There was a light in her eyes I usually only saw in the mirror, and this was the kind of trivia I lived for anyway.

"It's a long story, but if we're going to get into it, I should ask you a question first."

She practically jumped to agree, and it nearly made me grin again.

"Have you ever wondered why, with so many big pantheons in the world - Greek, Norse, Hindu, Abrahamic-" I waved a little. "-And all the rest, you never hear about them running into each other in the old myths?"

Her nod melted into a curious frown, but she didn't interrupt.

"Because I can tell you right now, it wasn't because of politics or because the pantheons are that good at cleaning up or rewriting their own histories."

Sure, if you looked deep and long enough, you could trip over some story of a plucky hero or bored god or anything in between 'switching lanes' and kicking a hornet's nest or two, but that was small potatoes in the long run.

…

The real reason was a lot bigger than that.

A lot.

"It's because, even though those stories were happening on the same planet?" I trailed off, and she leaned in like she was itching for the punchline. "They were also happening in their own Worlds."

She froze.

"What?"

"You heard me."

I couldn't blame her for the double-take.

It took me a while to wrap my head around it too, after Dad finally opened up on that whole 'the world used to be bigger' thing.

Turns out, that was very literal.

"Once upon a time, the realms and aspects of creation ruled over by every great pantheon you can think of - and probably a few you can't - existed in their own little 'bubble' of reality, completely separated from the rest.'

"As in different dimensions?"

"Nope." I shook my head. "But it's a good place to start from."

I wasn't sure even I understood much past that, but Chiron said - and I'm quoting here, word for word - 'They were akin to individual universes in miniature, supported by unique Foundations and the powers that governed them.'

Everything back then was more, in a way. The rules were different and changed completely depending on what 'World' you were in.

Time. Space.

Life and Death.

Time again, because there's a reason the gods who ruled over it are almost always the scariest of them all.

Lavinia's eyes went wide, staring at the floor as her mouth opened and closed silently, trying to catch up.

"That explains so much," she whispered in awe, before the flood gates cracked open entirely. "There were theories... a thousand different arguments for things that couldn't possibly be true... but... this can't be true anymore, either."

"Yeah."

"The entire world doesn't work that way in the modern day."

"Yep."

"Then what changed?"

"They were bubbles, right?"

She nodded, and I shrugged helplessly.

"They popped."

Which sounds like a joke, except it totally wasn't.

All I know is that the Great Flood - the Biblical one - had something to do with it, but Chiron, Dad, and Aunt Artemis wouldn't tell me what actually went down there no matter how many times I tried to bring it up.

"But how?" she pressed.

"No clue."

Her face fell, and I couldn't help but wince.

"Super annoying, right? I'm sorry."

"No, this is fascinating." She shook her head vehemently. "I just have so many questions - goodness, I wish I could take notes."

That was familiar too.

"If it's notes you want, we should probably be sitting down for this," I said, tossing a thumb over my shoulder. "Pretty sure I saw a café with a garden out that way. Iced tea, my treat?"

She blinked in surprise, then gave me this happy little look that made the skin on the back of my neck feel weirdly warm.
Weird, that.

"I'd like that," she said.

"Great."

We started heading toward the exit.

"Don't stress the bubble-world details too much, by the way," I told her as we walked. "I only brought it up because it's the only way to explain why the story I'm about to tell you sounds totally wrong compared to the usual myths."

Poseidon's ancient grab for the crown?

That whole nightmare started way back, and believe it or not, it had almost nothing to do with the guy to begin with.

Or Zeus, while we're on that, or any of the other big-name Olympians, except Demeter in act two.

No, this whole fiasco started with another goddess entirely.

The Underworld's very own Dread Queen.

Persephone

…​

Let's take this from the top:

In the era that dawned right after the Titanomachy and the beginning of Olympian rule, Persephone was one of the first goddesses born to the new age, and she was...

Look, I have no idea where some of the modern stories of her being an innocent flower girl whose kidnapping nearly destroyed everything came from, because they got a lot more wrong than they ever did right.

If anyone was going to wreck the world, it'd have been her, all by herself.

Back in the day, people usually just called her Kore.

Which doesn't make a lot of sense at first glance, because that epithet just translates to 'Daughter' or 'Maiden', and plenty of other goddesses and daimones fit the bill, but they were maidens, plural.

As far as the folks around her were concerned, Persephone was THE Maiden.

As in, the most dangerous one of them all.

A wild, untamed adventurer and fierce warrior in the making, she heeded nothing and no one, rampaging through the world however and whenever she pleased - and even that doesn't do her justice.

Persephone could be your best friend before breakfast and your worst enemy by lunch, and only her mother, Demeter, was spared the worst of the whiplash.

Or maybe she got the worst of it, and everyone else was just too scared to say anything about it.

Either way, that whole attitude was definitely more of a nature-versus-nurture thing, given that Zeus, her father, had absolutely nothing to do with raising her.

See, the way she'd been conceived was... well, it was an ugly thing. And even though Zeus and Demeter made peace eventually, it was built on the mutual agreement of staying way, way clear of one another.

Demeter especially wanted him nowhere near their kid, and Zeus was only too happy to agree. So Persephone got all the gold and glory of being a child of the Thunderer, with none of the actual oversight.

Surprise, surprise - that caused problems.

To be fair, Demeter did try to rein her in, but again, Persephone started wild and only took off from there.

So, predictably, a tale as old as time goes down.

Protective mother grounds rebellious teenage daughter.

Rebellious teenage daughter cusses her out, marches up the stairs and slams her bedroom door shut.

Then she sneaks out.

Which is where the story takes a twist.

Most girls would sneak out to the movies, or to that one boyfriend's house who they think is 'deep' and 'soulful' but justcomes off as an insufferable douchebag to everybody else.

Persephone, though?

She decided to go to the Underworld.

Now, reminder: This was right after the Titanomachy, when the rule of the gods was almost as young as she was.

The Underworld of that era wasn't the orderly kingdom it would become later down the line.

Matter of fact, Hades had only just descended and started whipping the place into shape, and a good chunk of it was still a festering cesspit of chthonic weirdness, ancient monstrosities, and all kinds of bad juju.

Persephone descended, saw all of that, and her reaction was something along the lines of 'Great stuff, but why not more?'

So she cut a bloody swathe through the place, drenched herself in the blood of her new and newly deceased enemies, and leapt off the edge of the Underworld and into Tartarus itself.

…

What can I even say here?

To this day, no one even has a straight answer on why.

It was pure, unhinged lunacy through and through, so of course it was right up Persephone's alley - but enough about that for now.

After she took a swan dive into the Pit Of Creation, Hades himself got wind of what had happened.

Maybe a servant sent word to him, or maybe he'd seen it himself but been unable to stop it.

Whatever it was, he didn't just sit around twiddling his thumbs - no, he marched straight out of his new crib and up to Mount Olympus.

When the Lord of the Dead materialized smack in the middle of the throne room, unannounced and practically radiating bad vibes, you knew things were about to go down.

He marched right up to Zeus, who was leaning back and soaking in all the hype, and went:

"Dude. Your kid. My basement. What in the literal super hell gives?"

After a spit-take, Zeus probably threw his hands up and went:

"I dunno, man. It's Persephone."

Which was a horribly valid answer, but Hades still had to resist the urge to strangle him right then and there.

They went back and forth for a little while, before Hades finally took a deep breath and got serious.

"I would set my realm to order. After that, give me leave to pursue your daughter."

Now, the wording here isn't exact - duh - but the meaning is important.

Somehow, people down the line got the idea that this was Hades asking for Persephone's hand in marriage with Zeus agreeing eventually, and not him going "Let me track down your lunatic kid before she gets herself killed, or gets herself killed and stirs up some primeval abomination from the depths of the pit."

Probably a gossiping wind spirit getting the story wrong or something.

The only part of this mess the historians did get right was the brothers agreeing not to tell Demeter what was going on.

Stupid, that - but you could also kinda see where they were coming from.

"Hey, Sis! I know we don't talk anymore for very good reasons, but I just wanted to let you know that your missing child just took a header into the evilest place in all of creation. Toodles!"

That would have gone over real well.

The only thing guaranteed to make the situation worse was another Olympian leaping into the Pit to find the rogue goddess regardless of the danger, so mum was the word there.

Meanwhile, back in the mortal world, Demeter had been running herself ragged trying to find her daughter.

And when I say running herself ragged, I don't mean she was just knocking on doors and putting up MISSING posters on phone poles.

She poured her essence into every corner of the known world, bleeding her power through the dirt, the roots, the forests, and the fields - basically infusing all of Greece with the stuff, trying to light up a connection to Persephone.

Nothing. Not a blip.

Because, you know, Persephone was busy doing parkour in the literal abyss.

It was useless, and spending all that power burned Demeter down to the quick.

Even gods can get tired, and spent, drained, and completely out of options, she finally collapsed out of the sky and crashed into the mortal realm.

Specifically, she landed as an exhausted, weeping mess on a lonely, quiet beach.

A pale ghost of herself, with the waves lapping at her feet.

That was where Poseidon found her.

…

What came next…

I almost wish I didn't know this part.

This was the Lord of the Sea at the height of his power, having just finished conquering his kingdom.

He beat back the monstrous gods Phorcys and Keto and hurled them into the Pit, routed out the last of the sea daimones and beasts, and had proven himself an all-around mighty King.

And kings back then weren't in the habit of taking no for an answer.

Poseidon had always considered Demeter beautiful, and she wanted nothing to do with him, and with her so vulnerable…

You see where this is going, and you might have even heard the story before.

She turned into a mare to try and escape, and he followed as a horse, and…

In the end, it was the Persephone situation all over again, and every bit as terrible.

When the deed was done, Poseidon slunk back off to his domain, leaving Demeter alone in the dirt. It took everything she had, but she eventually mustered the strength to crawl to a secluded cave and trap herself inside, hiding from the world.

She even ended up having a couple of kids in that cave, but we'll circle back to them later.

The important thing is what happened afterward. Trapped in the pitch-black cave, suffocating under a mountain of anger, disgust, loathing, and utter helplessness - made so much worse by the fact that she still hadn't found her daughter - she snapped.

Remember all that divine power she'd spent pouring into the earth earlier?

It was still out there, infused into everything. And now, the second she really lost it, it twisted in on itself.
Demeter was the goddess of the harvest, and a harvest is all about life, growth, and prosperity.

Her grief completely turned those concepts inside out, and the world began to starve, rot, and decay as her pain poisoned it all at the very roots.

Even the gods felt it.

The main Olympians were strong enough to tough it out, but the lesser divine spirits - dryads, satyrs, river nymphs, and everything in between - were having a really sucky time.

They were hit with ravenous, poisonous hunger and a soul-deep emptiness that ruined everything they touched.

At least the humans got the mercy of dying from starvation relatively quickly.

The immortals had no such luck - they were forced to just sit there and endure the unending misery.

It got so bad, so fast, that Zeus finally had to step in.

He descended to Demeter's cave, backed by a small army of desperate Olympic daimones and cloud spirits, and immediately started trying to calm her down for the sake of the world.

Which was… let's say brave, considering their history, but the craziest thing of all?

He actually nearly pulled it off.

The daimones and spirits begging her, I can understand, but I don't even know what Zeus had to promise to work that miracle.

An apology from Poseidon was not happening - and that arrogance was going to lead to disaster, just watch - but maybe Zeus agreed to kick his teeth in for her when he had the chance?

Dedicate all of Olympus to finding Persephone?

Something else?

Whatever it was, he almost cracked it.

He was right near the finish line, in fact, when everything went wrong.

Because down in the Underworld, Persephone had finally risen from the depths of Tartarus.

Time didn't work the same way down there, so even though it had been a while since she jumped in, it felt even longer for her.

She rose from the Pit - older and stronger, changed, and greater and more terrible than ever before.

Her powers had grown and warped, and at her feet knelt the Erinyes - the Three Furies themselves - pledging eternal loyalty to their newly ascended Dread Queen.

The Underworld itself trembled at her footsteps, and Hades was the first of the gods to lay eyes on her.

And boy, did he.

The Rich One took one look at this terrifying goddess steeped in unholy power, and did the most Greek thing he possibly could.

He fell in love.

Head over heels. Instantly. No take-backs - but more on that later.

In the middle of all this, Persephone found out what had happened while she was gone.

She learned that her mother - who she loved above all others, arguments or no - had been attacked.

Hurt.

Demeaned.

Defiled.

And all because Demeter had been left weakened searching for Persephone herself.


And all. Hell. Broke. L̵̫͎̪̜̼͔̮̹̲̘̃͛͗̀͆̐̂͘͜ȏ̴̡̬̗͚̮̠̏̒͑̒̅́͝͝͠͝ͅo̷͓̥̤͛̓̊͗́́̄̄͘ŝ̴̟̘͔̦̘̻͎̭̲̉̌͒ẹ̶͓̩̩͈̣̩̖̲͓̹̙̫̾̈̽͗́͑͐̅̚͜͜!̸̞̪̙̦̦̋̔̀̌̔̈́̈́̂̅̕͝ͅ



…​

The voice that eventually interrupted my story came out of nowhere.

Lavinia and I had been sitting at a quiet table at the back of the cafe, sipping our drinks through multi-colored straws and going over it piece by piece—the look of stunned wonder she was giving me was a whole experience, I tell you—when a stranger cut me off.

"Lavinia?"

She startled, snapping out of her undivided attention, and I nearly summoned Serpent's Downfall right then and there.

The woman who stepped into my line of sight wasn't anything special, at first glance.

Tall and slender, with rich bronze skin and bright eyes. Her hair was pulled back in a low ponytail, dark and curly, and she was wearing a light coat over a purple turtleneck and jeans.

She blended in with the tourists just fine, and I hadn't sensed her until she was almost right on top of us.

My eyes narrowed.

Huntress.

She had that same feeling Aunt A's people gave off, but there was something else to it too.

Something more.

If she was put off by my look, she didn't show it.

In fact, her smile was all bright and polite, and it looked like she was about to introduce herself before Lavinia beat her to it.

"Hyperoache?"

The woman turned her attention to Lavinia, and I blinked.

"Is this your escort?"

I knew she never went anywhere without one, on the off-chance that the Utsusemi losers or the Fallen tried to pull a fast one, but by the time I glanced back at her, she'd already given me a small nod, almost a bow.

It was subtle, but there was no mistaking the respect behind it.

"'Hyperoache?'"

I… recognised that name.

"Yes, young lord. An honor to make your acquaintance."

…

Okay.

That kind of confirmed it - The formality, I mean, but I asked anyway.

"You wouldn't happen to have a sister called Laodice?"

Her smile brightened.

"I do indeed."

Called it.

"Nice to meet you too." I tried to return her little half-bow. "And thank you for your service?"

She was a Hyperborean - and not just any old one, either.

Hyperoache and her sister Laoadice were both devotees of Dad and Aunt A - Aunt A especially - who were so dedicated to the bit that they got the Heracles treatment after death and were rewarded with immortality for their troubles.

She inclined her head again.

"Your thanks are appreciated, young lord."

Something about the way she said it made me think she actually meant it.

Then she turned back to Lavinia.

"I hope I'm not interrupting?"

Lavinia blinked, then glanced toward the café clock on the far wall, and her cheeks went a rosy pink.

"No. I'm sorry, we just lost track of time."

She looked back at me, and I waited patiently.

"Somewhere you need to be?"

"Grauzauberer."

"...What?"

Why would she ever-?

"My old home, not the organization itself," she explained quickly. "Hyperoache was accompanying me to get some things and close it off."

"Oh."

That made sense.

"My bad, then." I gave Hyperoache another polite smile. "I was the one who kept talking."

"And I wish you hadn't stopped."

…

There was a split second of silence -just long enough for Lavinia to realize she'd muttered that just a little too loud - and then she went from red to crimson.

"I mean-!" The words basically sprinted out of her mouth. "It was just... incredibly interesting! I didn't realize how much I didn't know-how much I couldn't even imagine."

"I... totally get that."

Poker face, poker face, poker face!

Somewhere up on Olympus, Dad was probably looking down here and howling with laughter, and it was entirely because I was praying my face wasn't turning the same shade as hers.

"So." I coughed into my fist and tried to play it cool. "Raincheck?"

"Raincheck." She agreed just as fast.

Hyperoache might've snorted off to the side, but there was no chance I was catching her in the act, so why even try?

I take it back.

Please let Dad not be looking.

Lavinia was still staring down at the table when the flush in her cheeks finally started to fade.

But it wasn't because she'd recovered.

I felt the shift almost immediately.

"Lavinia?"

She didn't answer right away.

Instead, her eyes drifted past me toward the Hyperborean in the room, and I followed the motion.

She'd been standing a few feet away this whole time, watching us talk, but that faded into something a little too solemn when Lavinia looked at her.

She felt it too.

"Is something wrong?"

Lavinia hesitated.

Then, quietly:

"I'll be right along. I only need a minute?"

"Of course."

Hyperoache gave her a gentle nod, then offered me a slightly deeper one.

"Until we meet again, young lord."

And just like that, she turned and walked away.

I watched her disappear into the crowd, slipping between tourists and tables without ever breaking stride until she was simply... gone.

One of Aunt A's heavy hitters and all.

I'd have liked to have talked to her some more, but I already had someone else to focus on.

When I looked back, Lavinia was slowly getting to her feet.

She straightened her shirt, smoothed down her hair, then looked at me.

And then, out of nowhere, she also tipped her head in something like a bow.

"I'm sorry."

"Come again?"

The heck was this about?

"I never thanked you."

"For what?"

"For saving me."

"Oh." I almost laughed. "You didn't have to-"

"I did."

She said it so firmly that I stopped.

"After I woke up, I was so dazed, and then everything that happened..." Her fingers tightened slightly against the edge of the table. "It only really came to me last night, and I wanted to make that right."

"You didn't have to," I tried again, but she wasn't having it.

"No." She took a deep breath. "I also wanted to apologize to you for something else."

I frowned.

Now what?

"Glenda."

...

"Okay." I pushed my chair back and put my hands on my knees. "That, you're going to have to explain."

"She said some cruel things to you, down in Cocytus. It was unsightly and undeserved, and even though I know you're not one for empty platitudes, it didn't feel right not to apologize."

She finally looked up, and eyes met mine again.

"Not on her behalf. But from meanyway, for whatever that's worth."

Plenty.

It was worth plenty, but at the same time...

"You, with all your gifted potential... you are of them, not us. Whatever achievements you have... whatever glory you may hoard... all of it will always exist solely on the merits of your inherited divinity, and nothing more."

I'd almost forgotten about that total garbage.

"Thank you, really, but there's nothing to apologize for." I tried to play the heaviness off with a joke. "It's like every bad guy and wanna-be I've ever fought reads off the same script, honestly. Zero originality."

It fell flat.

I could tell, because it was right there on her face, clear as day.

"I should go catch up with Hyperoache." She hesitated, one last time. "Same time next week?"

"Make it two weeks, because I might be out of town for a little while." I offered. "But yeah, for sure. We have a story to finish."

That seemed to cheer her up a little, and she turned to follow Hyperoache.

Just like that, I was alone at the little table.

Then I slumped into my seat.

"Really closed off on a high note there."

I couldn't blame her for not wanting to talk about it - that would have been all kinds of rich, coming from me.

Still, I meant it.

"You are not human."

You don't say, you evil old hag.

Glenda Silverbrook's spite was worth all of jack to met… just maybe not for the reasons she or anyone like her would have expected.

I'd have said as much to Lavinia, but the words had stuck on the tip of my tongue.

This time, anyway.

I shook my head and got up.

There was always next time.

For now, I had to start packing for another little side quest instead.


...​

"Oh. It's you."

I didn't need it, but teleporting home gave me conclusive proof that my time with Lavinia was going to be the highlight of my day, hands down.

Why?

Because Regulus was back.

I reappeared in the garden, and there was Sairaorg, munching his way through a bag of candy and leaning back against the tree.

The big, lousy cat was sprawled in the shade along its other side, though he did crack open an eye when I appeared.

"Sun Brat."

"Kill-stealer. Back already?"

"You blind as well as stupid now?"

"More wondering why you didn't stay away, actually. Did slaughtering all the defenseless demonic wildlife get boring?"

He snorted, his maw shifting into a glinting glare of fangs. "The strongest of them died first. The rest were wimps. They reminded me of you."

"That right?"

"Mowing them down was good for the meat, if nothing else, but there's only so much time you can waste on trash before culling it is more effort than it's worth."

"Interesting."

My smile was half poison.

"Well, on your next sabbatical, you should go further out. Maybe swing by the Dimensional Gap? I hear there's a big red dragon there who'd love to meet you."

He bared his teeth at me some more

Maybe then your greatest contribution to Greek history and civilization wouldn't have been an over glorified fur coat."

Toothbrush, change of clothes, enough gold and jewels to buy a small town or two, alchemical potions, random loot, and a handful of spare weapons from Chiron's armoury on the off-chance I ended up needing them.

Nothing on the level of my usual stuff, but better safe than sorry anyway.

A long, narrow bundle wrapped in dark oilcloth, tucked away behind the rest of my clothes.

Regulus was there too.

Because apparently I couldn't have nice things, and he was coming with us.

Sairaorg had laughed like a hyena when he'd heard.

A little of his attention.

Chiron's sighed, Sai palmed his face, and Regulus looked like he already regretted coming.

Heh.

"We'd like to remind you never to unfasten your seatbelts - don't let go of one another, ever - and that there will be no refreshments aboard this flight."

I pointed at Regulus.

"Kill-Stealer, if you want to let go, by all means."

"One day, brat. One day."

I grinned and flared my power.

Focusing on the memory of Esgaroth was easy.

All I had to do was think about that merry goose chase we led the town guard on last time, and the image crystallized in my head.

Bingo.

"And away we go!"

With that, space parted, and I tipped us headfirst into the chaos between worlds.

…

Light. Shapes. Infinity and Eternity hand in hand.

…​

Something's wrong.

The moment we landed, it was unmistakable.

There was some light, but it was swallowed almost immediately by an ocean of mist and fog stretching out in every direction.

Cold mist, too.

A normal person would have barely been able to make out anything more than a few dozen feet ahead of them, and what I could see wasn't exactly reassuring.

Esgaroth was a lakeside town, but this was different.

The closest wooden houses were dark and silent, their doors cracked or left wide open. Some looked like they'd been forgotten in the middle of whatever their owners had been doing.

The streets were abandoned too, and the rickety bridges linking up the bigger buildings weren't any better.

Eerily quiet and empty.

It was early, sure, but not that early.

And then I caught the scent.

Heavy and metallic, almost rust-like.

My stomach tightened.

Blood.

Lots and lots of it.

"What the...?"

Sairaorg got there first.

"What happened here?"

"Nothing good, I imagine." Chiron's voice was impassive as his eyes panned across the fog. "There has been a great deal of death in this place, and quite recently at that."

Sai and I paled.

The people…

Suddenly, Regulus's easy stance melted into something sharper, and his head tilted to one side.

"Incoming."

He didn't have to explain more - Chiron already knew, and Sairaorg and I picked up on them at the same time.

A group of unknowns heading towards at speed - a little over the mortal kind, but nothing impressive - and just about radiating a thick, obvious miasma of wrongness.

Sick and full of bloodlust.

We didn't have to wait long before the shapes began to push through the mist.

They had broad shoulders, hunched backs, and weapons jutting at odd angles.

Humanoid, then, but that didn't mean anything.

They were squat and built on the heavy side, with long arms and ugly, gnarled faces complete with jutting brows, flattened noses, and mouths full of yellowed, uneven teeth. Their skin ran through a spectrum from bland gray to muddy brown, stretched tight over muscles and what should have been a lethal amount of scars.

Their amour was mismatched and battered, mostly in iron and leather, with the occasional rusted plate, thick belts, and scraps of chain that clattered as they headed towards us.

Some of them had jagged, badly made swords. A few had axes, spears, and even some bows that looked like they'd been an insult to the entire domain of archery a hundred years ago, and were now an insult period.

Over a dozen all in all, and leading them was something even nastier.

A massive, shaggy wolf padded through the fog beneath a rider, with mottled grey and shoulders two heads higher than mine. Its jaws hung open as it breathed, strings of glistening drool dangling between its rows of teeth.

The rider looked down at us, and even through the gnarly looking helmet, I could tell he was no prettier than his buddies

Up close, the feeling they all gave off was even worse, somehow.

Everything about them was hideous, and I don't just mean their faces.

"Greetings," Chiron said before anyone else could speak.

Probably because Regulus looked like he'd smelled something that crawled out of the world's nastiest sewage plant while Sai and I were both still trying to figure out exactly what the hell we were staring at.

"Might I trouble you-"

"Hah!" The rider's laugh was like a cheese grater to the eardrums. "A good hunt today!"

My translation spell did its job, which means I understood ever word.

Unfortunately, the voice it gave me still sounded like a chainsaw grinding against a rusty car engine.

"More meat for the pits."

The others laughed like he'd just delivered the greatest joke ever told.

The rider - the leader - bared his teeth at us in a grin, then his eyes shifted toward Regulus.

His smile widened.

"Bring them. And bring the beast. I'll have its pelt for a rug."

The wolf-thing growled.

Apparently, that was supposed to be intimidating.

Regulus wasn't impressed, and neither were we.

Then one of the bastards - apparently the overachiever of the bunch - raised his bow.

Twang.

The arrow might as well have been moving at slow motion. I plucked it out of the air before it could shatter against Sai's forehead, and the entire group froze.

The leader's eyes narrowed.

Even the beast seemed to hesitate.

I looked down at the arrow in my hand.

It gave me a bad feeling, and something about the way the arrow head caught what little light there was spelled bad news.

Poison, then?

"That was a bit rude, don't ya think?"

The leader's gaze widened, and most of them startled some more.

"You speak-?"

"Yeah, I do."

I rolled my neck, and gave him that one smile I always used when I was starting to get really mad.

Beside me, Sai clenched his fists and stepped up next to me..

"And I'm still talking," I continued when no one else said anything. "So can it and listen."

A few more shifted uneasily, and the leader's expression started turning red beneath all that ugly skin.

"My teacher is right here."

I pointed at Chiron - calm and unbothered - and then I held up the arrow and gave it a little wave.

"So I'm going to be extra nice and give you one chance to surrender, and tell me what the hell happened to this town and everyone who lived here.

I tightened my grip, and the shaft creaked.

"After that?"

My smile disappeared.

"We do this the hard way, and we still get our answers anyway."

Silence.

"What do you say?"

Nothing, as it turned out.

The goons shifted uneasily.

The leader's expression kept darkening, the fury clearly building by the second, and the wolf beneath him shuffled its paws, more drool dripping from its jaws as the twisted hunger rolled off the thing in waves.

And then the moment snapped, and he cursed at us so hard it had spittle flying everywhere.

Disgusting.

"Kill them all- Hurk!"

That's as far as he got before the command ended in a wet choke, courtesy of the arrow shaft buried through his eye, the force hurling him sideways out of the saddle.

He toppled from the beast and hit the ground.

For one beautiful second, everyone just stared.

Sai just threw me a quick high five.

"Nice."

"Thanks, man."

Then the wolf finally seemed to catch up, and let rip an enraged howl before charging straight at me.

The shadows at my feet answered that one, erupting upward in a black blur, and Courage came tearing out of them with a roar that made the thing's battle cry look like a whimper in comparison.

Its eyes had time to widen in panic, and then my hellhound crashed into it and dragged it into the fog.

There was a snarl, a few yelps, and then a whole bunch of wet, painful sounds as Courage went to work.

Gods am I proud of him.

The goons were still locked in absolute horror - one of them looked close to hysterical tears - and the two of us?

"So."

We started cracking our knuckles, and they all jerked back like they'd been struck.

"Who's next?"

Then the carnage began.

…​

Forty minutes later, two elves walked the perimeter of the ruins of Dale.

Ruins was, unfortunately, the right word.

The now-dead dragon's Desolation had done a number on the old city. What had once been streets and towers and grand halls was now little more than broken stone, blackened foundations, and heaps of rubble poking through the lingering mist.

But for the people of Esgaroth, huddled behind barely existent walls and whatever shelter could be thrown together in the time they'd had, it would have to do.

So would the army that had come down from the Woodland Realm in Mirkwood.

Hundreds of elves now stood watch around the makeshift settlement, bows at the ready and blades close at hand, having descended from the forest to support the survivors against the Uruk invasion from the north.

And there were other reasons for their presence besides, but it was not for mere soldiers of their rank to guess at them.

The first elf stopped atop a broken stretch of wall and looked out across the ruined city.
His companion joined him, and for several seconds, neither spoke.

There was too much to see.

Smoke still curled from somewhere beyond the eastern quarter. Fires burned in scattered pockets between the ruins, their orange glow barely visible through the haze. Farther off, beyond the remains of Dale, the dark shape of the mountain loomed over everything.

The first elf's hand tightened around his bow.

The Lake-Men of this region - longstanding trading partners of the Woodland Realm - were in a pitiful state indeed.

Even now, they huddled together beneath patched canvas and hastily erected shelters. Elvish healers moved between them. Guards stood watch. The children who were not orphaned clung to parents who spent every waking moment fearing for their lives.

And all the while, the Dwarves of Erebor remained sealed in their reclaimed Mountain, uncaring of the ruin the call of their fabled treasure had brought upon those lesser than them.

Truly, the greed of the Naugrim was their most defining trait-

"Hi there!"

The voice came from behind where there had been nothing a moment before.

Both elves let loose sounds most undignified and whirled around with drawn blades, only to see...

Children?

Their eyes were not deceiving them.

Two children of the Secondborn stood there, dressed in the oddest clothes either elf had ever seen.

And yet...

Something about them raised the hair at the back of the first elf's neck.

Judging by the swallow from his companion, the same was true for him.

Before either could say a word - to ask how, or why, they had somehow slipped through the perimeter - the first child raised a hand in greeting.

He was blonde, golden-haired, and was that a glint of gold in his eyes as well?

"Hi. I'm Daniel Winchester."

The other raised his hand too.

"Sairaorg Bael."

Both elves choked.

They...

They knew those names.

Everyone knew those names.

But it could not be.

It simply could not be.

And yet...

Daniel beamed.

"You don't seem like a raving murderous lunatic, so we've got some questions to ask you. First things first, though."

He threw a thumb over his shoulder.

"Can you get any of these people some help?"

The elf looked over his shoulder.

And nearly choked again.

It was the closest he'd come to death in nearly three centuries.

A crowd was coming toward them - dozens of people in various states of disarray, dressed in rags, torn clothing, and whatever else they had managed to find.

Some were weeping. Others simply looked exhausted beyond words.

There were even one or two elves among them, to their horror, already moving to help the frailer humans.

And though every one of them was in a pitiful state, not a single person appeared to be seriously injured.

The elf stared.

Then slowly looked back at Daniel.

"We found them with a few people with terrible attitudes."

The boy gave him another perfectly polite smile.

"Care to lend a hand?"

Both guards looked at him.

Then looked some more.

And then, for one final stretch of several seconds, they simply glanced at one another and nodded with eerie, half-stupefied calm.

"We need to inform the King."

A beat.

"Now."

…​

And so word reached Thranduil Orophilion - Sovereign of the Woodland Realm - first.

He received it in his tent alongside a very peculiar Wanderer in Grey.

It spread from there to the temporary leaders of Dale, and through them to the Raven envoys of the Kingdom of Erebor, until at last it reached the ears of the King who ruled Beneath It.

A proud Dwarf who had only just reclaimed the throne held by his father, and his father before him.

The moment it did, his fists clenched, his jaw tightened, and a light of sheer fury erupted in his eyes.

"Thieves."

…

And thus it began.
